#1 — Highly Innovative (87)

CTTE: An Open Dual-Protocol RISC-V Trace Encoder for N-Trace and E-Trace

A Weiss, A Schulz · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CTTE, an open synthesizable SystemVerilog RISC-V trace encoder with a shared protocol-agnostic front end and selectable N-Trace/Nexus or E-Trace back ends, together with decoder extensions, verification infrastructure, and multi-hart integration artifacts. - Why it's important: Reliable instruction tracing is needed for debugging, coverage, timing analysis, and runtime assurance, but existing results provide limited open hardware and rarely evaluate the bandwidth, process migration, and loss conditions of real multi-hart operating systems. - How it does it: CTTE separates filtering, synchronization, stateful compression, and event generation from the final protocol formatter, and explicitly announces output loss before clearing compression state and re-anchoring the decoder. - The good: The artifact is evaluated across six cores, Linux on 64-bit multi-hart hardware, formal and dynamic verification, and controlled protocol comparisons; it shows 0.21–4.90 bits per retired instruction across workloads and doubles target-process observation depth through source-side filtering. - The missing: The N-Trace/E-Trace comparison is performed on RV32 rather than the 64-bit Linux regime, and the loss-threshold study covers only the N-Trace back end, two simulated benches, and limited backpressure patterns. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate RISC-V trace infrastructure, especially open hardware, decoder verification, or operating-system-scale tracing; skip it if you need a fully timing-closed production IP comparison or broad application benchmarks rather than a deeply documented reference implementation.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (82) are strong because CTTE unifies protocol-neutral tracing, dual back ends, explicit loss re-convergence, multi-hart integration, and process-aware filtering in an open hardware artifact. Rigor (91) is exceptional for a systems paper, with formal properties, layered dynamic verification, adversarial tests, coverage reporting, FPGA campaigns, decoder checks, and a comprehensive released RTL/software package. Completeness (86) and Resilience (85) are supported by detailed disclosures about RV32/RV64 comparability, E-Trace loss evidence, harness exclusions, ingress width, process-filter limitations, and synthesis-tool sensitivity. Impact (92) reflects synthesizable open RTL, decoder support, integration flows, and a working Linux-capable board demonstrator, although power, ASIC closure, wide-retirement, and sustained transport remain untested. Weighted composite: 0.15*82 + 0.15*91 + 0.10*82 + 0.15*86 + 0.15*85 + 0.30*92 = 87.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses trustworthy, bandwidth-limited instruction tracing for RISC-V systems used in debugging, bring-up, coverage, hybrid WCET analysis, and runtime monitoring. The target users are hardware designers and tool developers integrating trace into multi-hart systems running virtual-memory operating systems. Prior implementation evidence is fragmented across protocols, mostly closed or unavailable as synthesizable RTL, and commonly evaluates bare-metal or single-hart workloads. The paper identifies a specific methodological gap: N-Trace and E-Trace share the instruction-trace ingress but differ in compression, message representation, and framing, so cross-paper bandwidth and area comparisons confound protocol effects with front-end design, synchronization policy, workload, and accounting conventions. It also targets the under-evaluated regime of 64-bit sparse address spaces, SMP Linux, process migration, source-side filtering, and output backpressure. Key Idea: The central insight is to make the trace front end protocol-neutral and treat decoder synchronization as an explicit correctness contract rather than an implementation detail. A shared event and compression pipeline feeds separate N-Trace/Nexus or E-Trace formatters, allowing controlled comparisons on the same retirement stream and configuration. The second important design insight is that every discontinuity that can invalidate stateful compression—including loss, pause/resume, flush, and mode changes—must announce the event and force both encoder and decoder models to a known re-convergence state. The process-filtering contribution is less a new protocol mechanism than an integration insight: use a stable architectural process key, such as the page-table-root PPN when ASIDs are unavailable, and discard nonmatching events before they consume trace bandwidth. Methodology: CTTE is a five-clock-domain ready/valid pipeline. A preprocessor accepts the RISC-V Trace Control Interface or adapted ingress, performs clock-domain crossing, delay, privilege/context and address filtering, watchpoints, synchronization/quota generation, counters, timestamps, and instrumentation composition. A protocol-neutral message generator tracks instruction counts, branch histories, synchronization, resource-full events, trace-off correlations, and compression state. The selected formatter then emits either TCODE-based Nexus messages serialized with MDO/MSEO framing or E-Trace te_inst packets; an optional packet-aware funnel merges up to four sources without switching mid-message. N-Trace supports history and branch modes, while eight configurable compression features include implicit returns, repeated history, wide instruction counts, repeated branches, synchronized indirect-history messages, repeat instructions, a jump-target cache, and branch prediction; the latter three are vendor extensions outside strict N-Trace 1.0. The loss protocol injects an error message identifying affected classes and emits a synchronization message with an overrun reason; state-clearing invariants require zero instruction count and cleared mirrors at recovery. The decoder was extended for 64-bit addresses, multiple sources, vendor features, data trace, in-band capability discovery, and scheduler switches. Critical design decisions—separating front end and back ends, making configuration self-describing in-band, and clearing state at re-anchoring—are well motivated by integration failures and decoder requirements. However, some choices remain only partially justified quantitatively: the one-retirement-per-cycle ingress is evaluated as a scope boundary, and the E-Trace implementation's synchronization behavior differs from the configured policy in important cases. Key Results: CTTE integrates with six RISC-V cores from five suppliers, including CVA6 RV32/RV64, TGC5B, EMSA5, Rocket, and MicroBlaze V; three integrations run Linux and two exercise 64-bit Linux. On an AMD Kria KV260, full profiles use approximately 24,354–29,148 LUTs for a single back end at 97–111 MHz out of context, while a minimal slim N-Trace profile uses 2,106 LUTs at approximately 255 MHz. A same-revision synthesis comparison reports E-Trace at +1,610 LUTs, -1,866 flip-flops, and 14.1 MHz lower closure than N-Trace under Vivado 2026.1; under Vivado 2022.1.2 the LUT premium is +3,986 and the frequency difference is -26.7 MHz, demonstrating strong tool-version sensitivity. Placed KV260 designs achieve 74.5 MHz for an application-class RV64 core plus encoder, 83.3 MHz for a second RV64 core plus full encoder, and 94.4 MHz for two RV64 cores, two slim encoders, and a funnel. In matched open-PDK cell-area estimates, slim CTTE is 14–15% of an application-class RV64 core, 34–36% of an RV64 tile including L1 caches, and 102% of an RV64 core without L1; full CTTE is 66–75% of the application-class core. Workload bandwidth spans 0.206–4.900 wire bits per retired instruction on one encoder and configuration, a 23.8x range: loop 0.206, CoreMark 0.726, SQLite 1.784, and pointer chasing 4.900 with the full feature set. Branch density remains 12–16% while bandwidth varies substantially; indirect-transfer frequency, call/return density, predictability, and history novelty are more informative. Branch prediction halves bandwidth for a 97.5%-predictable loop but increases it by 19% for the least predictable pointer workload. Source-side process filtering on hardware increases target-process observation depth from 96,384 to 192,768 instructions in a fixed 1 MiB ring, a factor of 2.00, while excluding the other process's instructions; 30 of 61,120 remaining address fields point into the other process's text, all due to documented trap-source behavior, so the mechanism is not an isolation boundary. A two-hart funnel reconstructs 4,206/4,206 and 5,311/5,311 instructions in a directed test and preserves separation over 3,141,532 instructions. A Linux decoder fix increases reconstruction from 34,537 to 818,663 instructions after scheduler switches. The N-Trace/E-Trace comparison on a common RV32 front end shows E-Trace wire ratios from 0.242 of N-Trace on a loop workload to parity on pointer chasing; payload-wise E-Trace is 12–13% wider for pointer chasing. The comparison is not a pure protocol result because synchronization cadence and beat packing differ. Announced-loss recovery is one message, four bytes, and zero instructions across 3,305 simulated N-Trace loss episodes, but this result is not established for E-Trace or board streams. In backpressure sweeps, loss begins around 1.11–1.16 times average demand, and bursty stalls can cause 6.94% loss versus 0.19% for uniform throttling at nearly identical normalized capacity. These results are specific to the reported configurations, workloads, and measurement infrastructure; the paper explicitly warns against ranking them directly against prior bpi or area figures without normalization. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and limited NEW FORMULATION. The main novel deliverable is an open, synthesizable dual-protocol encoder with a shared front end, self-describing configuration, decoder support, and verification assets; the strongest empirical contributions are the workload-dependent N-Trace/E-Trace comparison, multi-hart Linux/process-scoped evaluation, and measured loss/re-convergence behavior. The underlying compression mechanisms, trace standards, multi-hart operation, and most individual optimizations are established techniques, while the loss-and-state re-convergence contract is a useful explicit formulation rather than a wholly new compression algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The verification plan is unusually explicit and layered. It combines instruction-exact round trips against execution answer keys, independent working-group decoder checks for standard messages, byte-identity and disabled-state-neutrality tests for vendor features, 16 adversarial gates, eight standing RTL assertions, formal proofs over the emission core, 94.7% line and 82.0% branch coverage, and machine-judged FPGA campaigns. Reported campaigns include 95/95 directed passes and 411/411 valid randomized-soak passes, with nine runs excluded because a 1 MiB capture window wrapped before drain; the authors disclose this exclusion and identify it as a harness limit. Formal properties include unbounded or bounded proofs for overflow injection, synchronization arbitration, message generation, MDO/MSEO output, and quota paths, with pre-fix or mutation-based red counter-proofs. The artifact is released at https://github.com/accemic/TraceEncoder under CERN-OHL-S-2.0 or a commercial license, with SystemRDL sources, RTL, testbenches, formal properties, CI scripts, and build flows; the decoder is released at https://github.com/accemic/CTTD. Reproduction is strongest for CVA6 and Rocket configurations; supplier-licensed cores cannot be rebuilt from the artifact. The key independence limitation is that vendor-feature decoder support was written by the authors, so those round trips are not fully independent; the paper compensates with byte-identity and negative-control tests. Quantitative comparisons are also sensitive to synthesis version, workload phase, synchronization cadence, capture-window saturation, and whether framing is counted. One pointer-chasing/full-feature measurement was rejected because of an unresolved instruction-count issue, and the paper correctly excludes it from robustness evidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — the paper delivers synthesizable RTL, a decoder, integration shims, a funnel, and a board demonstrator, and evaluates both implementation and behavior. Practical: The design runs on commercially available AMD Kria KV260 hardware and open RISC-V cores, although full deployment still requires a compatible core ingress, capture sink, transport, decoder, and integration-specific context-key handling. Efficient: Resource cost ranges from 2,106 LUTs for a minimal slim profile to roughly 24,000–36,000 LUTs for full or dual-back-end FPGA configurations; E-Trace has a measured area premium and timing penalty in the same-revision comparison, while data trace and acquisition add 2,859 and 8,965 LUTs respectively in the reported small-profile measurements. Effective: The evidence shows instruction-exact reconstruction, multi-hart separation, process filtering, Linux bring-up utility, and explicit loss detection/recovery, but it does not evaluate a complete runtime monitor, safety certification workflow, or sustained production transport. Scalable: The work demonstrates six integrations, two harts, and 3.14 million merged instructions, but does not test 10x–100x more harts, wider superscalar retirement, long-duration external streaming, or large-scale deployment; the current evaluated ingress accepts only one control-flow retirement per cycle. The work delivers a reusable open hardware and software artifact rather than stopping at paper form, but licensed-core integrations and some integration infrastructure remain unavailable for independent rebuilds. Strengths: - The shared front end and selectable back ends create a controlled experimental instrument that is substantially more informative than comparing unrelated encoder papers. - The paper treats decoder correctness, loss announcement, and state re-convergence as first-class system contracts, and backs them with assertions, formal proofs, negative controls, and hardware-discovered bug regressions. - The Linux/SMP evaluation exposes concrete system-level issues—context-key availability, scheduler-switch decoder failure, address-regime effects, and source-filter boundary behavior—that bare-metal benchmark evaluations would miss. - The artifact scope is unusually broad: synthesizable RTL, register sources, decoder extensions, formal properties, testbenches, CI, build scripts, six integration experiences, and a working on-device demonstrator are released. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that CTTE accepts one control-flow retirement per cycle in the evaluated integration, so it does not claim support for wide superscalar ingest; multi-retirement remains an unmeasured optional mode. Process filtering is an observation filter rather than a security or isolation boundary because trap-source addresses can remain visible, and its process key is unavailable until the first page-table-root write. The controlled N-Trace/E-Trace comparison uses RV32, whereas the Linux 64-bit evaluation exercises only N-Trace, so the protocol comparison does not cover the address regime where long virtual addresses matter most. Virtual-address MSB elision is not implemented, despite modeled benefits of 21.2–23.2% on canonical Sv39 streams and costs on physical-address streams. ASIC figures are unconstrained cell-area estimates, not timing-closed or sign-off silicon results, and all area ratios depend heavily on the selected core denominator. Byte identity is not guaranteed under overflow because clock-domain phase affects drop positions; post-pause positional ambiguity can remain in homogeneous code. The authors also note that the vendor-feature decoder is not independent, the process-scoping experiment requires recovering the target context from an unfiltered capture, and the loss-threshold study does not cover E-Trace or long blockage patterns. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest evaluation gap is the absence of a matched N-Trace/E-Trace comparison on the 64-bit Sv39 Linux workloads that motivate the paper; the reported RV32 comparison may materially understate address-width and synchronization effects. The paper does not compare CTTE against the strongest available open E-Trace RTL and N-Trace implementations under the same synthesis flow, target constraints, feature set, and ingress width, so the area/timing claims remain mostly within-design rather than competitive. It reports no power measurements for CTTE, no timing-constrained ASIC result, and no external-link throughput or sustained capture experiment beyond on-chip resources. The robustness evidence is strong but concentrated on N-Trace and controlled simulation; the E-Trace back end lacks equivalent loss/re-convergence evidence, and randomized hardware runs exclude nine overflowed captures due to the harness window. The source-filter benefit is measured with two processes and a known recovered page-table-root key, not as an end-to-end workflow from an operating-system process identifier. The paper presents live in-fabric consumption and runtime verification interfaces but evaluates no actual checker, coverage monitor, security monitor, or latency/throughput bound for those consumers. Finally, the claims about practical bring-up value rely on a single internal experience and qualitative time reporting, not a controlled comparison against conventional debug workflows. Bottom Line: This is a valuable, unusually auditable systems paper and reusable open artifact for RISC-V trace researchers and integrators, with its strongest contributions in methodology, verification, and realistic workload evaluation rather than in fundamentally new compression algorithms; read it, but do not treat its protocol or area comparisons as final until 64-bit matched back-end experiments and broader transport-scale evaluations are available.

#2 — Highly Innovative (84)

Making Unsafe Sequences Unexecutable: Formal Protocol Enforcement For Cyber-Physical Systems

A Amorim · stars.library.ucf.edu · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This dissertation introduces SPECTRE, a formal protocol-enforcement framework that derives mechanized RMPST metatheory, application-safety verification, and runtime monitors—including allocation-free C monitors—from a shared Refined Communicating Finite State Machine (RCFSM). - Why it's important: CPS attacks can use individually valid messages in an unsafe order, so message-level validation, anomaly detection, and cryptographic protection may fail before physical damage occurs; legacy UAV systems also cannot readily replace endpoint firmware or host managed runtimes. - How it does it: FACET reifies F⋆-embedded Refined Multiparty Session Types into checked RCFSMs, F⋆ACT verifies a user-supplied safety simulation by nuXmv or kernel-checked guard implications, and PLATUM synthesizes a centralized fat-C proxy from the same RCFSM. - The good: The work combines machine-checked structural results with a concrete MAVLink/ArduPilot enforcement artifact, reporting 0.12–3.88 microseconds of monitor cost, 4.22 microseconds of incremental logic overhead, and a 4x total-latency reduction versus DATUM. - The missing: The central deployment guarantee remains conditional because the supplied proofs do not establish operational trace refinement for the generated C monitor or extracted endpoint, and the evaluation does not run on actual ARM flight-controller hardware. - Read it or not: Formal-methods and CPS-security researchers should read it for the shared-RCFSM architecture and explicit assurance boundaries, while practitioners seeking a deployment-ready safety guarantee should treat it as a promising prototype rather than a complete end-to-end certification.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. Novelty (88) and Non-Obviousness (88) are excellent because SPECTRE makes a shared RCFSM the semantic pivot for session-type metatheory, application-safety verification, and allocation-free legacy enforcement. Rigor (84) is supported by machine-checked formal components, explicit assurance tiers, model checking, certificate proofs, runtime trials, ablations, and a realistic MAVLink/SITL case study, while the unproved C trace-refinement link prevents a higher score. Completeness (84) and Resilience (80) benefit from candid treatment of unsupported guards, fixed participants, model assumptions, external solvers, and missing physical-hardware validation. Impact (82) reflects a concrete low-latency C-monitor artifact and a credible path to embedded deployment, despite the absence of ARM measurements and a complete end-to-end certification argument. Weighted composite: 0.15*88 + 0.15*84 + 0.10*88 + 0.15*84 + 0.15*80 + 0.30*82 = 84.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses stealthy sequence-level attacks in cyber-physical systems, especially UAV and industrial-control communication protocols. Such attacks use syntactically valid, authorized messages whose ordering or cross-message values violate an operational safety invariant; the motivating MAVLink example allows a ground-control station to declare one mission item but transmit more, causing stale or unauthorized waypoints to be consumed later by ArduPilot. Existing signature-based, statistical, physics-based, and transport-security defenses inspect the wrong abstraction level or detect the consequence only after the unsafe sequence has been accepted. The stated gap is threefold: RMPST tools lack mechanized metatheory, protocol conformance is not connected to application-level safety, and existing monitors do not provide a formally grounded, lightweight deployment path for legacy hardware. Key Idea The central insight is to make a single RCFSM—with explicit executable guards, loop state, variable histories, and transitions—the shared semantic pivot for specification, proof, model checking, and deployment. Rather than separately encoding an RMPST in a theorem prover, model checker, and monitor generator, SPECTRE reifies the user’s F⋆ specification once and reuses that representation. A safety theorem over RCFSM-conforming traces can then transfer to an artifact by trace inclusion. This is a substantive architectural unification, although the final transfer to C execution remains an assumption rather than a fully mechanized compiler-correctness result. Methodology The pipeline begins with a shallow F⋆ DSL for global RMPSTs containing point-to-point choices, payload refinements, recursive binders, loop invariants, and update expressions. FACET uses Meta-F⋆ normalization and reflection to translate the shallow term into a deep RCFSM whose guards are explicit ASTs over Boolean connectives, comparisons, variables, literals, tuples, and arithmetic terms; unsupported predicates become `GUnknown` and abort extraction. It validates graph progress, target preservation, recursive back-edges, variable scope, history-sensitive projection, projectability, and local/global agreement, then projects local RCFSMs and checks endpoint processes using finite session subtyping. Three critical decisions are well motivated: using a shallow/deep embedding to combine specification ergonomics with inspectability; storing guards as Boolean-valued computational terms so type erasure does not remove runtime checks; and enforcing a conservative merge rule based on identical or guard-disjoint branches, trading expressiveness for decentralized-monitor soundness. F⋆ACT accepts a simulation function over an application state with an absorbing `Wrong` state. It jointly reifies the RCFSM and simulation function and checks that each protocol-permitted step preserves the simulation invariant. The nuXmv path renders bounded RCFSM state and guard information into an SMV model and checks `AG(sim_n != 0)`. The certificate path checks protocol-guard-to-simulation-guard implication for each transition using a finite guard decision procedure and F⋆/Z3-backed lemmas. The execution-witness path instead encodes safe executions as an inductive dependent type, making unsafe paths untypeable but requiring protocol-specific witness construction. PLATUM consumes the global RCFSM, maps protocol schemas through generated F⋆ types and a five-function `naming_convention`, and emits a fixed-size, allocation-free C state machine deployed as a transparent centralized proxy. The Composition Theorem states that RCFSM safety transfers to an artifact whose admitted traces are shown to refine the RCFSM; this theorem is mechanized, but the artifact-to-RCFSM premises are not. Key Results FACET accepts all five protocols in its evaluation corpus—Authentication, Two Buyer, Fibonacci, Calculator, and Online Wallet—including protocols with recursion, refinements, and cross-scope dependencies. Compile-time measurements over three invocations report approximately 33.28–35.46 seconds for extraction-only and 34.15–37.69 seconds for the full pipeline; the reported incremental full-minus-extraction costs range from -200 to 2,230 milliseconds, with the negative value attributed to measurement noise. Across 20 runtime trials, the maximum median local validation time is 0.170–0.335 milliseconds, representing 0.80%–1.52% of a 21.267–22.338 millisecond loopback TCP process lifecycle. F⋆ACT is evaluated on Authentication, Calc, and the MAVLink mission-upload protocol. The reported proof developments contain 170–198 nonblank core lines, 148–163 infrastructure lines, and 64–220 automatically generated SMV lines. All three verifications terminate in under one second. For mission upload, the dissertation reports an approximately 10^60-state generated space—described as roughly 54 orders of magnitude larger than the authentication case—and successful nuXmv verification in under one second. The certificate path also succeeds by using active constraints such as `curr <= N` and `N < Nmax` to imply the simulation bound. Three non-vacuity witnesses cover a one-item upload, a maximum-capacity upload, and an early abort. PLATUM is evaluated using ArduPilot SITL, ArduCopter V4.7.0-dev, QGroundControl 5.0.8, a Python proxy, and a C monitor called through `ctypes`; the workload uses 100 repeated waypoint transactions. The reported monitor latency is 0.12 microseconds in the idle state and 3.88 microseconds during active monitoring, with 13.33 microseconds total system latency and 4.22 microseconds incremental logic overhead. DATUM is reported at 56.74 microseconds total latency, yielding an approximately 4x reduction. PLATUM adds no measurable RSS beyond the 8.39 MB Python-proxy baseline, whereas DATUM is reported at approximately 13.72 MB RSS. The monitor rejects the documented overrun/premature-acknowledgment trace when `curr != mc_count`. These measurements use a Mac mini with an Apple M4 and SITL rather than actual ARM microcontroller deployment; claims of native ARM suitability are therefore not directly measured. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution claimed is the combination of a mechanized RMPST metatheory, shared-RCFSM application-safety verification, and direct fat-C legacy enforcement in one pipeline, together with the conditional Composition Theorem. Computational reflection, session types, model checking, SMT solving, and C synthesis are established techniques; the novelty lies in their RMPST-specific integration and in applying it to sequence-level CPS enforcement. The “first” claims are dissertation claims supported by the described related-work survey, but the document is a 2026 university dissertation/repository artifact rather than a top-tier peer-reviewed conference paper. Rigor & Reproducibility The dissertation presents an appendix with F⋆ proof modules and identifies eight FACET theorems plus F⋆ACT lemmas as Tier A when checked by the F⋆ kernel without admitted steps. It explicitly distinguishes these from Tier B claims involving nuXmv semantics, C synthesis, extraction, compiler behavior, MAVLink decoding, integer arithmetic, and deployment completeness. It reports standard deviations for three compile-time runs and 20 runtime trials, retains observed outliers, and tests multiple protocol examples. However, the document does not state a public code, dataset, model-weight, or artifact repository URL; it also does not report multiple hardware platforms, significance tests, independent replication, or a controlled comparison across equivalent native implementations. The model-checking conclusion depends on the generated transition system and nuXmv soundness, while the C-monitor conclusion depends on an unproved operational trace-refinement argument. A notable technical concern is that the SMV renderer maps `GUnknown` to `TRUE`, although extraction is said to abort on unsupported guards; the safety of that fallback relies on the abort discipline being enforced in every relevant path. The evaluation is largely on the authors’ own framework and a small literature-derived protocol corpus, with the main deployment case limited to one MAVLink subprotocol. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS with substantial EMPIRICAL and formal-methods content. Practical: The generated monitor uses fixed-size state, no heap allocation, no garbage collector, no operating-system calls, and ordinary C interfaces, so it should run on commercially available ARM-class embedded hardware; this was not demonstrated on physical hardware. Efficient: PLATUM reports 3.88 microseconds active monitor latency, 4.22 microseconds incremental logic overhead, and no measurable RSS increase over the Python baseline, versus DATUM’s 56.74 microseconds total latency and approximately 13.72 MB RSS, but the comparison includes different language/runtime and proxy configurations. Effective: The RMPST monitor rejects the documented MAVLink overrun/premature-acknowledgment trace, and F⋆ACT verifies the modeled invariant over the RCFSM; evidence covers a protocol-level proxy and simulation rather than physical flight safety or all MAVLink behavior. Scalable: The framework reports transition-count-linear certificate checking and handles a generated mission-upload state space of about 10^60 symbolically, but it does not test 10x–100x larger protocol graphs, participant populations, broadcast traffic, dynamic participants, floating-point predicates, or actual high-rate embedded workloads. The work delivers F⋆ source and described artifacts—FACET OCaml endpoints/monitors, F⋆ACT verification infrastructure, and PLATUM-generated C monitors—but no public distribution URL is stated; it stops short of a machine-verified C compiler/backend and complete deployment proof. Strengths - The RCFSM-as-single-source-of-truth design gives the dissertation a coherent technical center rather than presenting three unrelated tools. - FACET addresses a difficult mechanization problem—cross-scope refinements and history-sensitive projection—and explicitly checks which participants have observed each variable. - F⋆ACT cleanly separates bounded exhaustive model checking, scalable kernel-checked guard certificates, and stronger but more manual execution witnesses, exposing the trade-off between counterexamples, scalability, and assurance. - PLATUM targets a real deployment constraint and achieves a meaningful runtime reduction while preserving legacy endpoints and protocol schemas; the dissertation also clearly labels its C path as Tier B instead of overstating formal coverage. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the guard algebra is restricted to a decidable fragment such as quantifier-free arithmetic and Boolean combinations; unsupported predicates cause extraction failure. The framework assumes a fixed participant set and point-to-point communication, and it does not currently handle dynamic participants, native broadcast semantics, general floating-point or nonlinear predicates, or kernel-checked liveness certificates. The formal progress result is graph-level only and does not prove asynchronous deadlock freedom, scheduler properties, or buffered-queue correctness. The authors also acknowledge that the simulation function may fail to faithfully encode the physical invariant, that nuXmv is external to the F⋆ kernel, that OCaml extraction is trusted, and that PLATUM’s C compiler semantics, MAVLink decoder equivalence, C integer behavior, and deployment completeness remain assumptions. They confront these limitations directly and classify assurance tiers accordingly. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The core end-to-end security claim is conditional on the most deployment-relevant link: no supplied theorem proves that the generated C monitor or extracted endpoint admits exactly—or only—RCFSM-conforming traces. - PLATUM is evaluated through Python, `ctypes`, macOS, and SITL; the claimed ARM microcontroller deployment, worst-case execution time, memory footprint on target hardware, interrupt behavior, and real-time scheduling impact are not measured. - The evaluation covers five small benchmark protocols and one MAVLink subprotocol, with no comparison against strong general runtime-verification, formally verified C, or embedded-monitoring baselines beyond DATUM and no large-scale stress test. - The safety model is user supplied and intentionally does not model the physical plant, actuator behavior, packet loss, replay, concurrency, buffering, malformed serialization, cryptographic identity, or compromise of the proxy itself; consequently the measured result establishes a protocol invariant, not comprehensive CPS safety or security. - The conservative projectability rule is acknowledged as incomplete relative to standard MPST merging, but the practical cost of rejected specifications and the frequency of required re-encoding are not quantified. - The dissertation’s proof sketches and reported source-level summaries are not accompanied in the provided text by a reproducibility package, independent proof audit, or artifact validation by a third party. Bottom Line This is a technically ambitious and unusually candid formal-systems dissertation whose shared-RCFSM architecture and lightweight C-monitor prototype offer real value to researchers in session types, formal verification, and CPS security, but its strongest practical claim remains a conditional, SITL-backed construction argument rather than a complete end-to-end verified deployment guarantee.

ProxyGuard: Direct Reliability Inference for Randomized Data Release Mechanisms with Shared Targets

DT Mahato, P Dhungana · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ProxyGuard, a finite-sample framework for certifying either particular proxy releases or the probability that a randomized proxy-generation mechanism produces a valid release, even when all releases are evaluated on one shared target set. - Why it's important: Proxy selection after searching many generators, privacy settings, transformations, or random seeds can inflate false validation, while success of one release does not establish that the underlying randomized mechanism will succeed repeatedly. - How it does it: Named-release mode combines bounded-risk tests, intersection–union testing, and Holm correction, whereas direct shared-target mode lower-bounds the favorable-score rate across independent releases and subtracts a high-probability bound on favorable scores generated by invalid releases. - The good: In the main shared-target simulation, direct mode increased validation power from 5.6% to 64.2% at reliability 0.95 with 1,000 releases and 1,000 target records, while the corrected procedure produced no false validations in 500 boundary repetitions. - The missing: The direct method’s strongest empirical advantage appears mainly in simulated moderate-signal regimes; none of the real audits produced a direct-only decision, and the smooth-score extension was demonstrated only in a one-requirement, high-reliability stress test. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on statistically valid auditing of randomized synthetic-data or data-release mechanisms; skip it if you need broad utility or privacy guarantees beyond prespecified losses on one target distribution.

Problem & Motivation The paper addresses the problem of deciding whether a proxy dataset supports a prespecified downstream decision on a target population, and whether a randomized mechanism producing such proxies succeeds with probability above a reliability target. The setting includes synthetic data, transformed data, older cohorts, other sites, and other stand-ins used when the source table cannot be shared. Existing downstream utility evaluations can be invalidated by searching over many candidate generators, privacy configurations, transformations, or seeds and then applying an uncorrected threshold. Conversely, validating one favorable release does not estimate the fraction of future randomized releases that will satisfy the same requirements. ProxyGuard targets this distinction while allowing multiple bounded loss requirements, including relative proxy-versus-source regret and absolute proxy risk. Its guarantees are deliberately narrower than distributional similarity, causal transport, subgroup performance, inferential validity, or general privacy: they apply only to registered losses, limits, target distributions, and mechanism randomness. Key Idea The central insight is to separate release validity from favorable performance on a finite shared target. For named releases, the paper identifies particular valid releases using simultaneous risk tests and Holm correction. For direct mechanism inference, it avoids identifying releases: conditional on a fixed target sample, independent mechanism draws yield independent favorable-score indicators, so their favorable-score frequency can be bounded with a binomial confidence bound. Because an invalid release may nevertheless score favorably on a finite target, the method subtracts a target-side contamination allowance. This allowance is derived from a bounded-loss Chernoff/KL ceiling on an invalid release’s expected favorable-score probability and Markov’s inequality. The paper proves that the resulting mean-only correction, proportional to κ/αZ, cannot be uniformly improved using only the expectation constraint. A secondary smooth ramp score uses bounded target sensitivity and McDiarmid concentration to replace the Markov correction with an additive concentration radius when the registered score has useful structure. Methodology The workflow registers requirements, tolerances, slacks, reliability targets, candidate mechanisms, error allocations, and all design choices before opening a sealed target audit. A learning procedure independently fits source and proxy models, including model selection, calibration, and threshold selection, using development data. For each requirement, the per-record quantity is either relative regret, D_i = proxy loss minus source loss, or absolute proxy loss; all quantities must have known bounds. A release is valid when every requirement has population mean below its registered limit. In named-release mode, the method constructs empirical-Bernstein or Hoeffding upper bounds for each requirement, inverts them into super-uniform p-values, combines requirements with an intersection–union p-value equal to their maximum, and applies Holm correction across releases. Recognized releases are then counted within each mechanism, and an outer binomial tail test assesses whether the mechanism reliability η exceeds η0, with another Holm correction across mechanisms. For evidence of unreliability, the procedure reverses the confidence bounds and applies analogous corrections to detected violations. In direct mode, R independent mechanism draws are evaluated on the same n target records. Release r receives a hard favorable score of one when every empirical requirement satisfies X̄_r,j <= τ_j − s_j. Conditional on the target, these scores are independent Bernoulli observations across mechanism draws. An exact one-sided binomial lower confidence bound π_CP is computed for their conditional favorable-score probability. For invalid releases, the probability of crossing all empirical cutoffs is bounded by κθ, the maximum over requirements of an exponential Bernoulli-KL term based on the target size, loss range, tolerance, and slack. Markov’s inequality gives a target-side contamination allowance κθ/αZ,θ, yielding L_dir = [π_CP − κθ/αZ,θ]_+. The error allocation separates mechanism-draw uncertainty αQ from target-contamination uncertainty αZ. The smooth extension replaces hard indicators with products of ramp functions, estimates a conditional score mean, and subtracts min{1, κh + ρh sqrt(log(1/αZ)/2n)}. The paper also gives stratified-target extensions, a block-witness certificate, independent-batch partial-conjunction alternatives, planning inequalities, alpha spending for sequential candidate streams, and a preregistered hybrid taking the maximum of named and direct bounds under a union-bound error budget. The major design decisions—pre-target registration, conditioning on the shared target, and explicit contamination subtraction—are theoretically justified; the choices of slacks, ramp widths, error splits, and planning grids are treated as policy/design parameters and are not optimized universally. Key Results The controlled search experiment used 5,000 trials with 20 invalid candidates and three requirements. Point thresholds validated an invalid candidate in 100% of trials; separate uncorrected tests had 44.0% familywise false validation, while Holm correction reduced this to 1.94%. Selecting the smallest p-value and reusing the same target produced 43.46% false validation, compared with 3.08% when the selected candidate was evaluated on a sealed target. In a five-mechanism calibration with 50 releases per mechanism and 500 target records, the plug-in passing fraction falsely validated 99.70% of boundary mechanisms, point-rule-plus-binomial testing falsely validated 5.9%, and corrected per-release IUT plus binomial testing falsely validated 0.56% while attaining 99.57% power at reliability 0.98. The proposed two-level and collective procedures had 0.6% false validation and 99.6% power in that setting. The primary shared-target comparison used R = n = 1,000 and 500 confirmation repetitions. In the moderate-evidence regime, named-release validation power was 0.2%, 4.2%, and 5.6% at true reliabilities 0.80, 0.90, and 0.95, while direct mode achieved 0.0%, 56.4%, and 64.2%; the preregistered hybrid achieved 0.0%, 2.4%, and 57.2%. In a separate one-requirement confirmation with R = n = 1,000, direct power was 69.0% at reliability 0.90 and 89.2% at 0.95, compared with 79.9% and 80.1% for named mode. This ranking reversed under high-signal evidence: across the reported grid, direct mode was weaker in 36 of 45 cells and tied in 9. At n = 500 the direct contamination allowance became vacuous in the moderate-evidence design. Omitting contamination correction caused 8.05% false validation in a 2,000-trial boundary diagnostic; the corrected direct procedure had 0/2,000 false validations but abstained in all trials because the registered bound was vacuous. The smooth certificate validated 86.45% of mechanisms at reliability 0.99 in a high-margin, one-requirement, n = 200 stress test, while both Markov-based certificates validated 0%; at reliability 0.95 all feasible-data certificates remained unresolved. The independent-batch collective partial-conjunction experiment used 2,000 repetitions per grid cell and found a selected moderate-evidence result of 12.66% power for named Holm, 65.01% for tail-Simes, and 90.35% for post hoc tail-Fisher at reliability 0.95, with boundary false-validation rates of 0.00%, 0.05%, and 0.05%, respectively. Tail-Fisher was added after inspecting the registered tail-Simes results, so the comparison is not confirmatory. Prospective real-data audits showed successful corrected validation for several configurations but did not produce a direct-only decision. The MAGIC bootstrap mechanism obtained a simultaneous reliability lower bound of 0.884; Spambase-AIM produced a prospective negative result with a reliability upper bound of 0.116, mean proxy AUC 0.535 versus source AUC 0.899, and mean Cost5x risk 0.100 versus source risk 0.041. Lightweight neural mechanisms validated on CDC and Covertype in high- and moderate-fidelity settings, but Online Shoppers remained unresolved in non-degraded settings. Rice–TVAE validated at high fidelity with named/direct lower bounds 0.852/0.864, remained unresolved at moderate fidelity with 0.405/0.428, and had a degraded-mechanism violation upper bound of 0.375. A categorical, post-processing-only Secondary Mushroom mechanism produced direct and named lower bounds of 0.941216 and 0.963783. The 20 Newsgroups unigram mechanism validated at high and moderate settings with named/direct bounds 0.9810/0.9743 and 0.9905/0.9869, while its degraded setting remained unresolved. These applications use small or standard generators, not modern large language models or broad privacy evaluations. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the direct shared-target finite-sample formulation that lower-bounds randomized-mechanism reliability by conditioning on the shared target and explicitly controlling invalid-release favorable-score contamination, together with the sharpness result for the expectation-only correction. Named-release testing, Holm correction, empirical-Bernstein bounds, binomial reliability inference, partial-conjunction testing, and McDiarmid concentration are established tools; the novelty lies in their particular two-axis composition for shared-target mechanism reliability and in the empirical characterization of when direct inference outperforms release identification. The implementation, registration, hashing, stratification, and audit tooling are useful execution contributions but are not individually algorithmically novel. Rigor & Reproducibility The formal development states assumptions explicitly, provides theorem and proposition statements with proofs in the appendix, distinguishes target randomness from mechanism-draw randomness, and correctly limits claims to registered specifications. The main simulations were registered with fixed seeds and new-seed confirmations; the paper reports Monte Carlo uncertainty in several tables and gives exact one-sided Monte Carlo upper bounds when no errors occurred. It includes ablations and diagnostics for the contamination term, direct versus named mode, smooth versus Markov corrections, target size, release count, error-budget allocation, rare-group stratification, and independent-batch collective testing. Code and experiment scripts are available at https://github.com/dipeshbabu/ProxyGuard, with registry files, package versions, repository commits, SHA-256 data and registry digests, commands, and record-lineage mappings. However, several real-data analyses are explicitly retrospective, pilot-informed, or record-overlapping and therefore do not inherit the theorem-backed prospective guarantee. Tail-Fisher was added post hoc, some analyses amended computational configurations before target access, and the primary empirical comparisons rely heavily on simulated loss structures. The baselines are mostly statistically relevant procedures rather than competing modern auditing systems; comparisons against richer hierarchical reliability models, adaptive risk-control methods, conformal or selective-inference alternatives, and stronger contemporary synthetic-data generators are limited or absent. The paper does not report conventional confidence intervals for every empirical rate, nor does it establish robustness to violations of bounded-loss, independent-draw, target-independence, or correctly specified mechanism-law assumptions. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a substantial theoretical component and an accompanying software artifact. Practical: The experiments run on ordinary commercially available hardware; reported generation times range from 14 seconds for 500 lightweight-neural draws to 2,103 seconds for 40 Rice–TVAE draws, and the implementation is publicly available. Efficient: Direct mode can be cheaper in target observations than identifying every release but still requires many independent mechanism draws, and the contamination correction can become vacuous; costs depend strongly on target size, release count, mechanism retraining, and the registered error split. Effective: The evidence supports calibrated error control and large power gains in selected moderate-signal simulations, while prospective audits establish useful positive and negative decisions for some configurations; it does not show that direct mode generally dominates named testing, and no real audit yields a direct-only decision. Scalable: The method was tested with up to 1,000 releases and 6,000 target records in the reported studies, but 10×–100× scaling behavior, especially for expensive full-pipeline generators and large modern models, was not evaluated; the theory gives planning constraints rather than empirical evidence at those scales. The work delivers an open-source risk-control/audit implementation, registry and provenance tooling, and experiment scripts, but not a new generator, released synthetic dataset, or trained production model. Strengths - The paper isolates a practically important estimand—reliability of a randomized release mechanism—rather than conflating it with validation of one realized proxy table. - The shared-target construction is technically nontrivial: conditioning restores independence across independent mechanism draws while a separate target-side event controls the dependence-induced false-pass contamination without requiring release-level p-value independence or PRDS assumptions. - Proposition 7 gives a meaningful optimality result: under only an expectation bound on invalid favorable-score mass, the Markov correction cannot be uniformly reduced, clarifying when conservatism is fundamental rather than an artifact of loose analysis. - The experimental design takes statistical validity seriously through sealed targets, preregistration, explicit amendment logs, target-lineage audits, negative results, and clear separation of theorem-backed prospective evidence from retrospective or descriptive analyses. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that guarantees cover only registered losses, limits, target distributions, and mechanism randomness, not unregistered subgroups, distributional similarity, causal transport, arbitrary downstream analyses, or general inferential validity. They acknowledge that relative transfer does not establish absolute adequacy, balanced-target claims may differ from natural-prevalence risk, and decisions depend materially on registered tolerances, slacks, reliability targets, and error allocations. They report that the mean-only direct correction can be vacuous, that direct mode trades target labels for mechanism draws, that smooth concentration is not uniformly tighter, and that ramp selection and sharper sensitivity bounds remain open. They also acknowledge that the text mechanism is a simple unigram, the neural studies are corrective rather than demonstrations of direct-mode superiority, and no real audit produced a direct-only decision. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, including the invalidation of earlier analyses caused by treating balanced reserves as i.i.d. and the explicit labeling of record-overlapping reruns as lacking theorem-backed guarantees. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The empirical case for direct mode is strongest in deliberately constructed simulations with a shared target fluctuation and moderate per-release evidence; the paper does not demonstrate comparable gains on a realistic, independently designed real-world audit where named testing is genuinely multiplicity-limited. - The key invalid-release contamination ceiling uses bounded losses and Hoeffding/Chernoff inequalities, which may be too conservative for realistic correlated multi-requirement losses; the paper provides extensions but does not compare against sharper distributionally robust or dependence-aware alternatives. - The real-data evaluation uses mostly small public benchmarks, lightweight neural generators, a simple unigram text generator, and a narrow set of downstream classifiers. It does not test modern diffusion, large language-model, or high-dimensional private synthesis pipelines at operational scale. - The planning procedure uses pilot estimates and can choose the wrong mode; the reported worst-case regret is about 0.165 in the tested perturbation grid, but the paper does not provide a principled finite-sample guarantee for pilot-based mode selection beyond requiring the final choice to be preregistered. - Some analyses use policy-set tolerances that are selected by the authors, and several absolute ceilings are explicitly loose safeguards rather than externally justified deployment standards. This limits the practical interpretation of a validation decision even when statistical validity holds. - The paper does not substantially compare ProxyGuard with adaptive learn-then-test, selective-inference, conformal, hierarchical random-effects, or modern partial-conjunction procedures under matched estimands and computational budgets. The novelty claim would be easier to assess with such comparisons. Bottom Line This is a technically serious preprint that contributes a useful and unusually explicit framework for mechanism-level reliability inference under shared-target reuse; practitioners auditing randomized synthetic-data or proxy-release pipelines should read it, but its practical superiority over named-release or other collective methods remains regime-dependent and is not yet established on realistic large-scale deployments.

Daedalus-150M: A Convolution-Attention Hybrid Designed for CPU Inference (6 ▲ )

Christos Koutsiaris · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Daedalus-150M, a 160.49M-parameter language model that replaces 12 of 18 attention blocks with gated depthwise short-convolution blocks for batch-size-one CPU decoding. - Why it's important: Single-user CPU inference is constrained by weight traffic and growing attention KV-cache reads, especially for long contexts and memory-limited edge deployments. - How it does it: It retains six distributed GQA attention layers for long-range retrieval while giving the other 12 layers a two-timestep recurrent convolutional state, reducing cache growth from 24 attention layers to six. - The good: At 2048-token context, the hybrid decodes at 739.3 ± 35.5 tokens/s versus 420.3 ± 5.5 for a parameter-matched dense twin, a 1.76× ratio, while achieving slightly better validation bits-per-byte. - The missing: The central 0.81% quality advantage is based on a single seed and a 5B-token ablation, with no multi-seed confidence interval, depth-ratio ablation, or retrieval-sensitive evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on small language models, CPU/edge inference, or hybrid sequence architectures; skip it if you need evidence for multilingual, long-context extrapolation, or broad task quality beyond the tested 2048-token English setting.
Why this rank

The paper offers strong novelty (78) and non-obviousness (82) by designing layer composition around CPU cache traffic and showing a context-dependent advantage over a parameter-matched dense twin. Rigor (72) is credible because of the controlled twin, preregistered quality margin, repeated timing measurements, and candid reporting of negative results, though the single-seed quality comparison and unequal kernel optimization limit confidence. Completeness (84) and resilience (78) are especially strong because the authors directly acknowledge missing ratio ablations, retrieval evaluation, training interruptions, quantization degradation, and limited context scope. Problem & Motivation: The work addresses low-latency, single-user autoregressive language-model inference on ordinary CPUs, where batch size one prevents amortization of weight loads, memory bandwidth limits throughput before arithmetic capacity, and attention repeatedly rereads a KV cache whose size grows linearly with context. Existing small models generally retain large-model transformer designs and optimize them after the fact for CPU execution. Recurrent and state-space alternatives remove growing state but can lose precise associative retrieval, while attention variants such as GQA reduce cache constants without removing context-length growth. The specific gap is a controlled small-model architecture designed around CPU memory traffic that preserves some full attention for retrieval while making most layers constant-state. Key Idea: The core insight is that, for batch-size-one CPU decoding, the fraction of layers that maintain a growing attention cache is a more consequential deployment variable than simply reducing parameter count. Twelve gated depthwise convolutions use a kernel length of three and retain only two timesteps of state, while six interleaved attention layers provide periodic global retrieval. The paper argues that this arrangement should produce a context-dependent speed advantage rather than the context-independent speedup expected from a uniformly smaller model. Methodology: Daedalus-150M contains 18 blocks, model width 768, feed-forward width 2048, a 49,152-token vocabulary, context length 2048, tied input/output embeddings, and 160.49M parameters. The six attention blocks use 12 query heads and four KV heads with head dimension 64, RoPE, scaled dot-product attention, and GQA; the 12 convolution blocks apply RMSNorm, a 768-to-2304 input projection split into B, C, and x, elementwise gating B⊙x, depthwise convolution with kernel length 3, a second gate C⊙y, an output projection, and a residual connection. The model is trained autoregressively from scratch for 59.9B tokens using a 16.93B-token, ten-source English mixture, with Muon for matrix parameters and AdamW for embeddings, norms, and biases; the warmup-stable-decay schedule linearly decays learning rates to zero over the final 45%. The primary architectural test trains a 161.25M-parameter, 24-layer all-attention twin with width 640 and feed-forward width 2304 on the same data and schedule for 5B tokens. The pre-registered comparison uses validation bits-per-byte over 645M held-out tokens with a 0.5% margin floor, while downstream evaluation uses a five-task lm-evaluation-harness mean. CPU decoding is measured with 4-bit weights, eight threads, 128 generated tokens after context priming, alternating model arms within a pass. The main design decisions—six attention layers, short depthwise convolutions, and GQA—are motivated by cache traffic and CPU kernels, but the exact six-to-twelve ratio is not isolated from other architectural differences; the paper explicitly leaves a depth/width-controlled ratio ablation unrun. The training objective is next-token language modeling, but no explicit mathematical loss equation is provided. Key Results: The 5B-token parameter-matched ablation gives the hybrid validation bits-per-byte of 0.910398 versus 0.917774 for the dense twin, reported as a 0.81% advantage and above the pre-registered 0.5% margin. On the five-task mean, however, the dense twin scores 44.82 versus 44.68 for the hybrid, a nominal 0.14-point advantage that the authors characterize as noise; individual task rankings switch in both directions, and WinoGrande is effectively at chance. The fully trained Daedalus model reaches 47.31 on PIQA, ARC-Easy, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, and OpenBookQA, versus a pre-set 42.20 bar; its per-task scores are 65.78, 50.42, 50.04, 37.93, and 32.40, respectively. It exceeds the listed Pythia-160M score of 41.0, GPT-Neo-125M at 41.9, OPT-125M at 42.1, GPT-2 124M at 42.2, and MobileLLM-125M's published 46.3, but remains below the 2T-token external 135M peer at 51.2; the peer evaluations are not all methodologically symmetric because MobileLLM is reported from its publication while the four primary comparison peers were rescored locally. Validation bits-per-byte is 0.8685 on the 645M-token holdout. At depths 0, 512, and 2048, hybrid versus dense-twin throughput is 1111.9 ± 25.7 versus 922.8 ± 14.2, 960.3 ± 10.7 versus 664.4 ± 6.5, and 739.3 ± 35.5 versus 420.3 ± 5.5 tokens/s, yielding 1.20×, 1.45×, and 1.76×. Against an external 135M peer, the ratios are 1.06×, 1.49×, and 2.08×, although the hybrid has 19% more parameters. A first-order cache-byte model predicts only 1.17× at depth 2048, while measurement gives 1.76×; the paper attributes the residual to attention latency and the dense model's 24 versus 18 layer fixed costs, but does not directly measure those components. The hybrid's 4-bit file is 95.56 MiB versus 101.62 MiB for the twin, 6.3% smaller, and its 2048-token KV cache adds approximately 12.6MB. Approximately 47.99% of convolution channels are inert, corresponding to an estimated 13.6M parameters, but runtime shape checks prevent structural pruning without modifying the stock runtime. Post-training Q4_0 quantization raises perplexity from 9.18 at half precision to 9.75 on held-out encyclopedic text, approximately a 6% penalty at the final scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the convolution operator, GQA, tied embeddings, and recurrent/hybrid modeling precede this work, but the paper contributes a CPU-specific layer-composition design, a released 150M model, and evidence that the hybrid's context-dependent decode advantage exceeds a simple cache-byte prediction; the exact layer ratio is an engineering choice rather than a demonstrated universal optimum. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study has a useful parameter-matched dense twin, identical data and training schedule for the central ablation, a decision rule timestamped before scoring, locally rerun benchmark results, context-depth measurements, alternating-pass timing, and an explicit negative pruning control. Decode measurements report means and standard deviations, but the paper does not state the number of repetitions underlying the reported deviations, and no confidence intervals or statistical tests are supplied for quality. The key 0.81% validation advantage comes from a single seed, while downstream-task differences are acknowledged to be below reliable resolution. The evaluation is narrow: five English knowledge/commonsense tasks, a 645M-token holdout, and contexts no longer than the 2048-token training limit. The dense twin receives a better-optimized attention graph than the hybrid convolution path, which makes the speed result conservative but also leaves implementation optimization unequal. The paper states that a public repository contains the results, scripts, half-precision weights, and 4-bit weights, and that the corpus uses public datasets, but it does not provide a repository URL in the supplied text. Reproduction is therefore plausible, but exact hardware model, CPU model, runtime commit, operating-system configuration, timing repetitions, and thread-affinity details are not fully specified. The training run also experienced optimizer-state restart, data-cursor reset, a 0.42B-token corpus snapshot reduction, mixture drift beyond its pre-set limit, and failed quantization-aware training. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial empirical model-quality and performance evaluation. - Practical: The released Q4_0 model is intended to run in an unmodified stock CPU inference binary on commercially available hardware, occupies 95.56 MiB, and requires approximately 12.6MB of KV cache at 2048 tokens. - Efficient: Against the matched dense twin, it is 1.20× faster at empty context and 1.76× faster at 2048 tokens, with a 6.3% smaller 4-bit file; absolute throughput depends on the unspecified measurement CPU and background load, and the convolution kernels were less optimized than the attention path. - Effective: The evidence shows near-equal language-model validation quality and a five-task mean of 47.31 while delivering the intended CPU decode benefit, but it does not establish better retrieval, generation quality, multilingual capability, or end-to-end latency including prompt processing. - Scalable: The measured advantage grows from 1.20× at zero context to 1.76× at 2048 tokens and is consistent with the cache model, but the paper does not test 10×–100× scale, contexts beyond 2048, larger models, larger batches, or multi-user serving. The work delivers a reusable model artifact, half-precision and 4-bit weights, evaluation/pruning scripts, and a deployment configuration rather than only a paper-form proposal. Strengths: - It tests the architectural thesis with a parameter-matched all-attention twin trained on identical data and schedule, rather than relying only on comparisons to unrelated published models. - The context-dependent throughput curve is diagnostic: the hybrid's ratio increases from 1.20× at empty context to 1.76× at 2048 tokens, supporting the proposed cache mechanism more strongly than a single aggregate speed number would. - The paper pre-registers the quality decision rule and reports outcomes that do not favor the proposed model on downstream tasks, including the dense twin's 44.82 versus 44.68 five-task score. - It documents consequential negative results and deployment failures, including the approximately 48% inert convolution channels, failed structural pruning under stock-runtime constraints, quantization-aware-training failure, and training-mixture drift. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly report single-seed results, English-only training, evaluation only at the 2048-token trained context, no retrieval-sensitive assessment, no depth-ratio ablation, failed quantization-aware training, approximately 6% final-scale perplexity degradation from Q4_0 quantization, an oversized vocabulary, a 10.42 percentage-point L1 mixture drift against a 10.0 limit, and an interrupted final 8% of training with optimizer and data-cursor resets. They also acknowledge that the 5-task ablation is near a noise floor, that WinoGrande is at chance, that the external 2T-token peer remains better on quality, and that the absolute CPU throughputs are depressed by background load. These limitations are confronted directly rather than hidden, although some proposed explanations—such as the latency source of the residual speedup—remain unmeasured. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central quality-margin claim lacks multi-seed replication; a 0.81% bits-per-byte difference may be smaller than training variance, and the paper does not report variance for validation bpb across seeds or checkpoints. - The comparison does not isolate the convolution/attention ratio from depth and width: the hybrid has 18 layers at width 768, whereas the dense twin has 24 layers at width 640, so the result combines layer count, width, attention count, feed-forward shape, and kernel implementation effects. - The speed explanation is plausible but not fully causal: the paper does not separately measure memory bandwidth, cache misses, softmax latency, kernel launch or dispatch overhead, or performance after equivalent optimization of the convolution runtime. - The external-peer comparison is not fully controlled because the peer has a different parameter count and architecture, and at least MobileLLM's quality number is published rather than rerun under the stated harness. - The evaluation does not test the principal capability tradeoff of replacing attention: long-range retrieval, needle-in-a-haystack behavior, document QA, or degradation as the attention fraction decreases. - The model's English-only corpus, inherited 49,152-token vocabulary, training interruptions, and 4-bit post-training quantization limit conclusions about general small-model quality and deployment robustness. Bottom Line: This is a credible and unusually candid systems paper showing that a cache-aware hybrid can materially improve long-context, batch-size-one CPU decoding at roughly unchanged measured quality, but its strongest architectural conclusions should be treated as promising evidence rather than a fully isolated or statistically replicated result.

#5 — Highly Innovative (81)

On-Policy Self-Distillation in Diffusion Models (48 ▲ )

Wei Zhou, Xiongwei Zhu, Lingdong Kong, Bo Chen, Lei Zhang, Yongyuan Liang, Xiaoxia Hou, Ye Tian, Xian Sun, Yingshuo Wang, Linfeng Li, Shengqiong Wu, Leigang Qu, Feng Li, Wei Liu, Julian McAuley, Tat-Seng Chua · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces DiffusionOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method that converts image-level reward gradients into bounded positive and negative clean-output targets at intermediate diffusion queries and fits them with detached supervision. - Why it's important: It addresses the mismatch between endpoint-only reward signals and the intermediate denoising predictions that actually determine a diffusion model's final image, while reducing post-training cost for the evaluated models. - How it does it: A frozen EMA behavior policy supplies rollout states and anchors, reward ascent/descent constructs trust-region targets around each anchor, and a trainable policy fits the targets before the behavior policy is refreshed. - The good: Across two backbones and ten evaluators, it obtains the best held-out score in 19 of 20 reward-matched settings, including all ten settings on native 9-step Z-Image-Turbo, while using 40% and 63% fewer GPU-hours than DiffusionNFT on the two backbones. - The missing: The paper does not establish broad scalability or robustness beyond two backbones, LoRA fine-tuning, Pick-a-Pic/DrawBench prompts, fixed low-noise queries, and mostly model-based evaluators; it also does not isolate the end-to-end contribution of the EMA behavior update or fully explain the finite-fitting gap. - Read it or not: Diffusion post-training researchers should read it for the explicit reward-to-intermediate-target interface and the construction-versus-realization analysis, while practitioners should wait for released code and evaluations on larger, more diverse models and human preference data.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (84) are the main drivers: the explicit reward-to-intermediate-target interface and the construction-versus-realization diagnosis provide a technically distinctive contribution beyond routine diffusion alignment. Rigor (80) is supported by two backbones, ten evaluators, extensive ablations, held-out prompts, cost accounting, bootstrap analyses, and a human comparison, although the preprint status, incomplete independent-seed reporting, protocol differences among baselines, and absent public artifact URLs prevent a higher score. Completeness (84) is unusually strong because the authors directly acknowledge local-theory assumptions, finite-fitting gaps, evaluator limitations, CFG dependence, and small human-study scope. Resilience (78) remains high but is reduced by uncertain component attribution, dependence on model-based evaluators, limited scale and distribution shift testing, and incomplete protocol matching; Impact (74) reflects strong reported efficiency and quality gains but no clearly documented public software or model-weight release.
