Problem & Motivation: The work addresses contextual privacy for LLM agents that place credentials, identifiers, health information, financial records, or personal memories in the model context while generating outputs for users or third parties. Existing privacy evaluations primarily inspect whether the output text explicitly repeats, paraphrases, or implies an irrelevant secret. The paper argues that this misses observable nonlinguistic channels, including response length, formatting, token frequencies, numerical choices, and stylistic or embedding shifts. The specific gap is whether a model can satisfy a direct confidentiality test while still producing outputs whose distribution depends on the protected context strongly enough for an adaptive black-box observer to infer predicates or reconstruct values. Key Idea: Confidentiality instructions induce value-dependent suppression: the model avoids emitting the protected value, but that avoidance redistributes probability mass across otherwise benign outputs in a secret-specific way. A decoder trained against the same model can read this statistical fingerprint, and prompts that request many structured numbers amplify the signal. The paper’s active attack extends the idea by using prompt injection to make the model encode a secret digit directly in a pre-agreed output feature, such as the number of exclamation marks. Methodology: The paper formalizes a predicate-inference game in which a challenger samples a model, a context, and a secret predicate; the adversary makes black-box sampled-text queries and predicts the predicate from the responses. During estimation, the adversary constructs contexts with known predicate values and trains model-specific response classifiers; during inference, it queries the victim deployment holding the unknown secret. For numeric secrets, the context contains a confidentiality instruction and a uniformly sampled 1-, 2-, 4-, or 8-digit value. The evaluation uses 18 benign prompt templates plus adaptive variants, 1,000 sampled secrets with 10 responses per secret-prompt pair for the main experiments, and held-out splits by secret instance. Decoders include majority vote, frequency-based Bayesian inference, direct 10-class LoRA classifiers, prefix-conditioned classifiers with beam search, and a chained adaptive decoder that conditions later prompts on previously predicted digits. The main loss is per-position cross-entropy on secret digits, with transcript prefixes masked. For semantic memory predicates, a fully fine-tuned Llama-3.2-3B classifier predicts whether one of 15 CIMemories attributes was present, and a DeepSeek-based linguistic judge provides a comparison baseline. For the agent experiment, a Qwen-2.5-7B generator is trained with GRPO on 500 SSNs to create prompt injections that encode the leading digit using exclamation-mark counts; a fixed follow-up prompt attempts to encode the remaining eight digits. Critical design choices are model-specific decoder training, prompt selection by best observed leakage, and adaptive prefix-conditioned querying. The first two are motivated by the threat model and supported by transfer and learning-curve analyses, but best-case prompt selection risks optimistic estimates; the paper does not provide a formal justification that the finite prompt families approximate an optimal real-world adversary. Key Results: In the main eight-model study, six models allow perfect 1-digit extraction and all but GPT-5.4 nano show near-perfect or perfect performance at that length. At 2 digits, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro reach 100% full-secret exact match; GPT-5.4 reaches 99.5% per-digit accuracy, Claude Sonnet 4.6 reaches 98.5%, and Gemini 3.1 Pro’s channel entropy falls to 0.54 bits against a 6.64-bit no-leakage baseline. At 4 digits, Claude Opus 4.6 reaches 82% exact match and Gemini 3.1 Pro 44%; adaptive querying improves Opus from 44% to 82% but reduces Gemini Pro from 44% to 23%. At 8 digits, Gemini Pro reaches 41% per-digit accuracy against 10% chance, and seven of eight models exceed 30% first-digit accuracy. Grok 4.1 Fast and GPT-5.4 nano remain at or near chance for secrets of at least 4 digits. Structured numeric prompts dominate: the lowest N=2 channel entropies occur for repeated-random, number-grid, and numeric-list prompts, whereas multi-turn and several open-ended prompts reach the 6.6-bit chance baseline. In a WildChat evaluation using 178 real prompts and 80 held-out episodes, digit-stripped feature decoders show above-chance single-digit recovery for all six evaluated models; Claude Opus 4.6 reaches 61.3% with embeddings after removing all digit characters, while GPT-5.4 reaches 41.3% with response-length features and Gemini 3.1 Pro reaches 57.5% with digit-stripped stylometric features. For 15 CIMemories predicates, the proposed classifier obtains 0.319 advantage (TPR minus FPR), versus 0.058 for the model-agnostic linguistic judge, and obtains TPR 0.320 at the judge’s 2.4% FPR versus the judge’s 0.082 reported TPR under its default comparison. In the production-style agent experiment, the active injection extracts the leading SSN digit in 68/70 Claude trials (97.1%) and 62/70 Gemini trials (88.6%); conditioned on Phase 1 success, it extracts the remaining digits in 52/68 Claude trials (76.5%) and 29/62 Gemini trials (46.8%). The direct-request controls disclose no SSN in 350 Claude queries or 349 Gemini queries. The paper also reports a suppression-leakage Spearman correlation of 0.95 across eight models, but only 0.50 among the three leaky models, where the relationship is not statistically distinguishable from no correlation. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW METHOD are justified: the paper separates contextual leakage from linguistic disclosure through a black-box predicate-inference game, identifies suppression-induced statistical fingerprints as a mechanism, and demonstrates model-specific adaptive decoding; the LoRA classifiers, beam search, and GRPO prompt injection are standard techniques applied to this setting rather than individually new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study includes several useful controls and ablations: direct-request refusals across all eight models, shuffled-label decoders, prompt-type comparisons, secret-length sweeps, cross-model transfer, confidentiality-instruction mismatch, distractor secrets, training-stage comparisons on OLMo-3-32B-Think, and digit-stripped feature extraction on WildChat. Main learning curves average three seeds, and the distractor experiments report five seeds for N=2 and three for N=4; however, much of the headline numeric evaluation uses a single split seed, and short-secret exact-match estimates involve only 10 held-out values. Statistical testing is incomplete: the WildChat appendix performs many one-sided binomial tests without multiple-comparison correction, and the capability correlation uses only eight models and an unversioned Arena Elo snapshot. The evaluation uses eight proprietary API models, with model retirement and post hoc omission of Grok variants, so exact reproduction depends on unavailable model identifiers and undocumented API behavior. The paper does not state a public code, data, decoder, or model-weight release URL. The best-case reporting over prompt templates and query counts can overstate performance relative to a fixed attacker budget, while the semantic-memory experiment uses one user profile and the WildChat train/test split necessarily shares all ten single-digit values. The experiments also do not evaluate output perturbation, response normalization, query-rate limits, unknown-model identification, or constrained-access attackers. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper primarily measures attacks and leakage across API-accessed models, although it also evaluates a production-style agent. Practical: The decoders run on H100/H200 infrastructure and the victim models are commercially accessible APIs, but estimation costs range from $2.91 to $522.70 for selected 4,000–10,000-query attacks and from $119.48 to $11,441 for 200,000-query adaptive attacks, so feasibility depends on API access and provider pricing. Efficient: The attack requires thousands of estimation queries for short secrets and up to 400,000 queries for the tested 8-digit adaptive setting, while local decoder training uses LoRA rather than full model training; no comparison against simpler calibrated statistics establishes the minimum cost. Effective: The evidence demonstrates recoverable signal under the constructed confidentiality prompts and numeric tasks, and shows non-digit signal on WildChat, but it does not establish that ordinary attackers can recover arbitrary real-world secrets from normal agent traffic. Scalable: The paper tests context lengths up to 256K tokens and secrets up to 8 digits, but it does not test 10×–100× larger attack populations, longer or open-vocabulary secrets, unknown target models, or restricted query budgets. The work does not state that it releases a software artifact, dataset, trained model, or reusable tool; it remains primarily a paper-form evaluation. Strengths: - It identifies a privacy failure mode that explicit-disclosure judges cannot measure and operationalizes it with an explicit black-box threat model. - The suppression hypothesis connects observed leakage to a measurable generation behavior and receives support from secret-versus-distractor controls, instruction-strength experiments, post-training stages, and cross-model differences. - The evaluation covers controlled numeric reconstruction, semantic memory predicates, real-user prompts, and a realistic agent context, rather than relying only on one synthetic extraction task. - The authors report important negative results: two models remain at chance for longer numeric secrets, open-ended prompts often show no detectable leakage, adaptive querying helps one model but hurts another, and the capability correlation weakens within the leaky subgroup. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the study to two predicate families, eight fixed models, black-box sampled text, uniformly random numeric secrets, one CIMemories user profile, and an adversary that knows the target model and secret length and can make repeated queries. They do not evaluate open-vocabulary secrets, unknown model identities, attackers without on-demand query access, deployment-side output perturbation or response normalization, or realistic structured secret distributions. They also acknowledge that the Arena Elo capability correlation is based on an unversioned leaderboard snapshot and should be treated as suggestive rather than causal. These boundaries are stated directly, although the conclusion that in-context secrets are broadly unsafe extends beyond the evaluated settings. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The passive leakage experiments rely heavily on prompts that explicitly request N-digit numbers or dense numerical output, making the strongest results partly a measurement of a task-specific numeric channel rather than routine agent behavior. The active SSN result is a conventional prompt-injection exfiltration channel engineered to encode exclamation counts, so it should not be presented as evidence that inadvertent passive leakage alone reconstructs full SSNs. The paper does not compare against strong non-neural decoders under matched query budgets in the headline tables, does not report confidence intervals for most headline model-by-length results, and selects the best prompt and decoder configuration per model and secret length. The semantic predicate classifier may exploit stable task, profile, or generation artifacts specific to the CIMemories construction; one profile is insufficient to estimate population risk. The WildChat experiment shares all possible secret values across train and test and evaluates only 80 episodes, which limits claims about generalization despite the digit-stripping control. Most importantly, there is no mitigation experiment, so the paper establishes vulnerability but does not test whether practical defenses such as randomized decoding, length normalization, constrained sampling, context separation, or secret-specific isolation reduce leakage without impairing utility. Bottom Line: This is a valuable and technically credible preprint for LLM privacy and agent-security researchers because it exposes a real blind spot in linguistic leakage audits and supplies strong controlled evidence for secret-dependent output distributions, but its strongest practical claims require substantial qualification and a mitigation-focused follow-up before it can support deployment policy.

Verification theatre: False assurance in formally verified cryptographic libraries

N Kobeissi · eprint.iacr.org.cn · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a five-type taxonomy and lightweight audit methodology for verification-boundary failures, applying them to thirteen vulnerabilities in CE Labs's libcrux, hpke-rs, and libcrux-psq libraries and comparing the resulting practices with AWS's verified cryptographic projects. - Why it's important: Unqualified formal-verification claims can cause users to trust cryptographic code whose wrappers, platform backends, specifications, or proof obligations remain unverified, creating failures in deployed systems such as Signal's post-quantum ratchet. - How it does it: The audit maps extracted, admitted, opaque, and unextracted code; checks specifications against FIPS and RFC requirements; inspects proof-admission and CI configuration; and cross-references documentation with actual build behavior. - The good: The paper identifies concrete, technically specific defects, including a cross-backend ML-KEM endianness bug with reported Signal decryption failures and four specification/proof defects that demonstrate that even the formal foundation can be wrong or unchecked. - The missing: It does not provide an independently replicated audit, systematic prevalence measurements across a broad range of verification projects, or experimental validation of several claimed security impacts, especially for latent specification and proof failures. - Read it or not: Formal-methods researchers, cryptographic-library maintainers, and users evaluating assurance claims should read it for its boundary-audit checklist and concrete case study, while readers seeking a general empirical study of verified software should treat its scope as narrow.

Problem & Motivation Formal verification proves properties of a modeled subset of a system, but cryptographic libraries also depend on unverified wrappers, protocol logic, platform intrinsics, compilers, build configuration, specifications, axioms, and cross-component interfaces. The practical problem concerns developers, integrators, auditors, and downstream users who may interpret labels such as "formally verified" as comprehensive assurance. The paper argues that the relevant gap is not merely incomplete code coverage: verification can fail when the specification omits deployment requirements, when platform-specific paths are outside the proof model, when proof obligations are admitted by default, or when the specification and axioms themselves are incorrect. The case study focuses on libcrux, hpke-rs, and libcrux-psq, with a qualitative comparison to AWS's verified cryptographic efforts. Key Idea The core insight is to treat the verification boundary as a first-class security interface and audit it structurally rather than assuming that a verified primitive implies a verified library. The paper's five categories are unverified platform abstractions, unverified protocol logic, specification incompleteness, unverified wrapper logic, and specification errors or false proofs. The most important extension beyond conventional boundary analysis is Type V: errors inside specifications, admitted lemmas, or axiomatized intrinsic models can make completed-looking proofs establish the wrong property or provide no sound assurance at all. Methodology The paper performs a source- and build-system audit of the libcrux ecosystem, reportedly conducted in February 2026. First, it maps the boundary by inspecting extraction annotations such as `#[hax_lib::opaque]`, admitted-module lists, lax-mode flags, API wrappers, conditional compilation, and platform-specific implementations. Second, it compares formal specifications with FIPS 203, FIPS 204, RFC 8032, RFC 9180, and deployment conventions, checking constants, domain transformations, bounds, and mandatory validation. Third, it determines whether proofs are actually dispatched to SMT solvers by examining `ADMIT_MODULES`, `SLOW_MODULES`, `--admit_smt_queries`, lax-mode tactics, and CI workflows. Fourth, it cross-references verification-status documentation with the executable build configuration. The resulting analysis identifies thirteen vulnerabilities: V1-V2 in platform abstractions, V3-V4 in HPKE protocol logic, V5 in specification scope, V6-V9 in wrappers or admitted algorithmic logic, and V10-V13 in specifications, lemmas, or axioms. Quantitatively, it classifies 20,808 Rust lines by verification status and 138 extracted F* modules by proof-dispatch status. The critical design decisions—treating admitted and opaque code as distinct from checked code, auditing specifications against external standards, and inspecting proof execution rather than documentation—are well motivated by the discovered defects. The methodology remains largely procedural and does not define a formal sampling protocol, severity rubric, or independent validation procedure. Key Results The audit reports thirteen vulnerabilities, of which nine affect unverified or admitted deployed code and four affect formally verified specification or proof code. V1 was an ARM64 SHA-3 intrinsic fallback error that produced platform-dependent ML-DSA outputs; V2 was a portable/SIMD endianness mismatch in ML-KEM incremental state that reportedly caused decryption failures in Signal's post-quantum ratchet, affecting Signal versions v0.76.3-v0.86.9 until a fix in v0.86.12. V3 omitted RFC 9180's X25519 all-zero shared-secret check, V4 used a `u32` HPKE sequence counter despite the RFC's `2^96 - 1` limit, V5 omitted low-S ECDSA normalization, V6 double-clamped Ed25519 seeds and reportedly reduced effective seed entropy by 5 bits, V7 allowed a malformed AES-GCM ciphertext to panic the process, and V8-V9 caused ML-DSA verification to accept signatures rejected by conforming implementations through a doubled norm bound and a missing final hint bound check. V10 used 1664 instead of `2^(d-1)` in the ML-KEM decompression specification; the paper gives counterexamples for d in {1, 4, 5, 10, 11}. V11 omitted an inverse NTT in the ML-KEM encryption specification, V12 asserted that 12-bit deserialized values fit in 1 bit, and V13 specified AVX2 widening multiplication as x squared rather than x times y, with approximately 40 dependent axioms described as false. For ML-KEM, 12,149 of 20,808 lines (58.4%) are classified as actually solver-checked, while 3,004 (14.4%) are admitted, 2,457 (11.8%) opaque, and 3,198 (15.4%) unextracted. Of 138 extracted F* modules, 127 (92.0%) are checked, 9 (6.5%) admitted through `ADMIT_MODULES`, and 2 (1.4%) admitted through `SLOW_MODULES`; the paper emphasizes that the admitted modules include security-critical IND-CPA, sampling, all seven NEON modules, and portable serialization. The AWS comparison reports five parallel proof CI jobs, 26 named caveats in the cited documentation, and explicit platform and property restrictions, versus libcrux's broader tagline and weaker automated proof execution. The study does not report throughput, runtime, false-positive rates, exploit demonstrations, independent reproduction counts, or statistically analyzed prevalence. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW FORMULATION, and ENGINEERING AUDIT METHODOLOGY: the concrete contribution is an evidence-backed taxonomy of verification-boundary failures and an operational audit process, illustrated by thirteen code/specification defects and a comparison of disclosure and proof-management practices. The individual bugs use familiar mechanisms such as copy-paste errors, missing checks, integer-width mistakes, and admitted proofs; the distinctive contribution is organizing them around verification boundaries and showing that specification and proof infrastructure can fail inside the nominally verified perimeter. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides code listings, commit identifiers, vulnerability provenance, standards references, line-of-code counts, build-configuration excerpts, and links to public repositories, issues, pull requests, and fixes. These details make the reported findings substantially more reproducible than a purely conceptual critique. However, it does not report independent replication, multiple auditors, inter-rater agreement, a preregistered audit scope, statistical uncertainty, or a systematic comparison against a sampled population of verified libraries. The AWS comparison is based on repository and documentation inspection rather than matched testing. Several impact statements are reasoned from standards and threat models rather than demonstrated with end-to-end exploits; V10-V13 are explicitly latent because the deployed Rust implementations are described as correct. The audit examines only selected libcrux components—ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HPKE, ECDSA, Ed25519, and AES-GCM—and does not establish that the thirteen findings are exhaustive. Source, build configuration, and evidence links are cited, but a dedicated audit tool, dataset, or artifact package is not stated. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems/code-audit component; the paper analyzes real libraries and deployment exposure but does not introduce a runtime system. Practical: The audited libraries and the proposed checks concern commercially available Rust/F/SMT toolchains and ordinary repository/CI infrastructure, although full proof execution may be computationally expensive and exact resource requirements are not stated. Efficient: The methodology is lightweight in its stated human/tool requirements, but the paper gives no measured audit time, solver cost, memory overhead, or comparison with conventional testing and fuzzing. Effective: The evidence shows that the procedure found thirteen concrete defects, including one associated with Signal failures, but it does not measure detection recall, miss rates, or whether the recommendations prevent future defects. Scalable:* The paper quantifies one ecosystem and qualitatively compares AWS projects, but it does not test the methodology at 10x-100x the codebase or across enough verification stacks to support a scalability claim. The work delivers a reusable audit checklist and analytical taxonomy, not a released library, CLI, dataset, or automated verifier; a dedicated software artifact is not stated. Strengths - It exposes a failure mode that ordinary statements of proof coverage can obscure: 41.6% of the analyzed ML-KEM deployment code is classified as admitted, opaque, or unextracted, and all 792 lines of the NEON backend are reported as admitted rather than solver-checked. - It connects low-level verification configuration to concrete deployment consequences, most notably the ML-KEM incremental API incompatibility reported as causing Signal post-quantum ratchet decryption failures across multiple platforms. - It distinguishes current implementation vulnerabilities from latent specification and proof risks, avoiding the incorrect claim that every formal-code defect already produces wrong deployed output. - The AWS comparison identifies actionable process differences—machine-readable or structured caveats, explicit assumptions, and proof execution in CI—rather than merely arguing that formal verification is insufficient. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit generalizability to two verification efforts and tool families, noting that Jasmin, Lean 4, Dafny, and other architectures were not assessed. They state that concrete audit patterns are stack-specific even if the higher-level steps are intended to be tool-agnostic. They acknowledge that V10-V13 are specification/proof defects whose deployed impact is contingent on future implementation changes or proofs, not current wrong output. They also state that the thirteen findings are not exhaustive and that other libcrux primitives, including SHA-2 and ChaCha20-Poly1305, were not audited. These limitations are confronted directly in a dedicated section rather than omitted. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not independently reproduce the reported downstream Signal impact or provide exploit traces, affected-input distributions, or interoperability test results for V2, V8, and V9. - It presents the taxonomy as broadly applicable, but the evidence base contains only two principal verification ecosystems and no systematic sampling of libraries using other proof architectures; the AWS analysis is documentary rather than experimental. - The 58.4% code-coverage figure depends on the authors' classification of source files and build status, but the paper does not provide an independently checkable machine-readable manifest, classification script, or sensitivity analysis for generated code and shared modules. - It does not compare the proposed audit with standard code review, differential testing, fuzzing, or specification-based testing in detection cost or coverage, so the claim that the methodology is lightweight and effective is supported by examples rather than comparative measurements. - The paper attributes severe security consequences to some defects, such as nonce reuse and strong-unforgeability violations, but does not consistently show end-to-end exploitability under realistic protocol state, attacker capabilities, or deployed configuration. Bottom Line This is worth reading for maintainers and evaluators of formally verified cryptographic software because its concrete findings and boundary taxonomy expose assurance failures that conventional proof-coverage claims can hide, although its generality and measured effectiveness remain unestablished beyond the audited repositories.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the specification and verification of low-precision binary floating-point arithmetic for machine-learning hardware and software. P3109 differs structurally from IEEE-754 through four format parameters—bitwidth, precision, signedness, and finite versus extended domain—and adds round-to-odd, stochastic rounding, and explicit saturation modes. These choices create many format configurations, including precision P=1, in which conventional assumptions about significand parity, exponent bounds, overflow, and rounding behavior can fail. The central gap is that established IEEE-754 formalizations and error-analysis tools generally assume fixed encoding structures, context-insensitive rounding operators, or overflow-to-infinity semantics, and therefore do not directly provide a verified, executable model of P3109. Key Idea: The core insight is to factor P3109 semantics through a three-way isomorphism between concrete code points in Fin(2^K), an indexed algebraic representation of finite values, infinities, and NaN, and the semantic datum set over extended reals plus NaN. This separation allows proofs to be conducted at the algebraic and real-number levels while transferring them to the bit representation used by implementations. The paper’s most distinctive derived insight is that saturation can preserve an exact-error property of FastTwoSum even when the original addition overflows, while the low-precision encoding rules invalidate a known ExtractScalar guarantee at P=1. Methodology: FLoPS defines a Lean structure for P3109 formats with K, P, signedness, domain, and validity proofs. It defines an indexed inductive type containing finite values represented by integer significand/exponent pairs, infinities subject to domain and signedness constraints, and a unique NaN. The finite representation uses an LSB-based exponent convention, explicit canonicality predicates, format-dependent exponent bounds, and special-code-point cases. A code-point decoder over Fin(2^K) extracts exponent and significand fields, handles special values, and maps finite encodings into the algebraic type; the authors prove injectivity and surjectivity. Reification back from the semantic domain establishes a round-trip identity, yielding a bijection from code points to datum values. The projection pipeline first rounds a real value to precision P with an unbounded exponent, then applies one of P3109’s saturation modes, and finally reifies and encodes the result. Rounding is parameterized by an operator of type Z -> R -> Z so that P=1 tie-breaking can depend on the canonical exponent; the authors separately formalize faithfulness and monotonicity because stochastic rounding is not monotone. They model RNE, RNA, RD, RU, RZ, RTO, and three stochastic variants, proving stated bias properties and root-mean-square accumulation bounds under specified probability spaces. Critical design decisions—the algebraic intermediate layer, the exponent-aware rounding signature, and explicit separation of rounding from saturation—are technically motivated by P3109’s format-dependent encodings, although the paper does not provide an independent design-space comparison. FastTwoSum is modeled as three projected operations, and ExtractScalar as three RNE projected operations with arbitrary saturation modes; their correctness properties are proved under explicit format and range assumptions. Key Results: The formal development proves a three-way correspondence for all valid parameterized formats in the model and includes an executable bit-level kernel. As an executable cross-check, the authors transcribed all 14 K=4 P3109 formats in the standard’s tables, totaling 224 code points, into exact dyadic values and exhaustively compared an independently written C decoder with the Lean decoder. The development contains approximately 21,000 lines of Lean code and refinement proofs for encoding, decoding, rounding, saturation, projection, and core arithmetic operations. For stochastic rounding, the paper reports an exact aggregate bias of -2^-(N+1) for one N-bit variant, zero aggregate bias for another under idealized inputs, and an O(sqrt(n)) accumulated-error bound, stated concretely as sqrt(n)/2 output ULPs for aligned variant-B roundings and for variant-C inputs over a complete D-bit grid. Theorem 2 proves exact FastTwoSum error computation for signed formats when |a+b| <= Mhi, ea >= eb, and the first operation uses any round-to-nearest tie rule; Theorem 3 proves faithful, rather than necessarily exact, error computation for arbitrary rounding modes; Theorem 4 proves immunity to intermediate overflow under the same finite-sum condition for all signed precisions, including P=1 and P=2. Theorem 5 extends exact error computation to overflowing sums when saturation clamps the result to Mhi or Mlo, regardless of the rounding mode used by the three operations. For ExtractScalar, Theorem 6 proves exact decomposition, a low-part bound |x_l| <= 2^-P sigma, quantization of x_h as a multiple of 2^-P sigma, and |x_h| <= 2^-j sigma for signed formats with P>1. The last bound is shown not to hold in general for P=1 because RNE uses biased-exponent parity. No runtime, throughput, memory, hardware-area, ML-training, or numerical-workload results are reported, and there are no empirical baseline numbers against competing tools. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is a Lean formalization tailored to P3109’s parametric encodings, exponent-dependent low-precision rounding, stochastic rounding, and saturation semantics, together with new mechanized theorems about FastTwoSum and ExtractScalar; the underlying floating-point proof techniques and the two analyzed algorithms remain established ideas adapted to a new arithmetic standard. The paper also reports specification errors found during formalization, including incorrect unsigned emax cases, an incorrect unsigned-extended infinity code point, and an incorrect projection note for round-up; the authors state that these were incorporated into the draft standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: The use of machine-checked Lean proofs, explicit indexed invariants, proved injectivity/surjectivity, round-trip identities, refinement proofs, and exhaustive comparison over 14 K=4 formats provides stronger semantic assurance than testing alone. The open-source implementation is reported at https://github.com/rutgers-apl/FLoPS, with an artifact cited through Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21660929. The paper states that executable tests cover exceptional-value rules and that the code includes an independently implemented C decoder, but it does not report build instructions, exact commit identifiers, theorem-prover versions, compilation status, proof-checking time, or artifact-evaluation results. Conventional ablations, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and statistical significance tests are not applicable to the central theorem-proving claims and are not provided. The stochastic-rounding results depend on explicitly chosen idealized or finite-grid input distributions and independence assumptions; the paper proves properties under those models rather than validating them on ML workloads. Differential testing is limited in the reported text to standard value tables for K=4, so it does not independently validate every parameter configuration or establish conformance against a complete external executable standard implementation. The paper also does not provide quantitative comparisons with the closest Imandra formalization, Flocq/FloatSpec, SMT encodings, or existing verified hardware flows. Deployability (4-property check): SYSTEMS — the paper delivers an executable Lean bit-level kernel and a reusable formal specification, although its primary evidence is theorem proving rather than deployment. - Practical: The artifact runs in Lean 4 on commercially available general-purpose hardware in principle, but the paper reports no resource requirements, build time, or deployment integration with RTL, compilers, simulators, or ML frameworks. - Efficient: The paper gives no runtime, memory, throughput, or proof-checking cost comparison against the Imandra reference implementation, IEEE-754 libraries, or hardware models, so relative efficiency is not evaluated. - Effective: The proved correspondence and algorithmic theorems establish semantic and mathematical correctness within the stated model, but the claim that FLoPS enables RTL equivalence checking or improves practical ML arithmetic is not demonstrated by an RTL case study or end-to-end workload. - Scalable: The model is parameterized over K, P, signedness, and domain, but the reported exhaustive validation covers only K=4 tables; no 10x–100x scale experiment, large-format proof-cost study, or hardware-scale verification result is reported. The work delivers a reusable Lean library, executable bit-level kernel, and reference model rather than stopping at paper-only definitions; it does not deliver a trained model, compiler, hardware implementation, or integrated verification toolchain. Strengths: - The three-way isomorphism cleanly separates bit encoding, algebraic reasoning, and semantic values, making the model suitable for transferring high-level theorems to concrete code points. - The formalization addresses genuinely difficult P3109 edge cases—P=1 and P=2 exponent bounds, special-value encodings, exponent-dependent tie-breaking, stochastic rounding, and saturation—that standard IEEE-754 libraries do not directly cover. - The FastTwoSum result under finite-boundary saturation is a substantive and non-obvious theorem: saturation does not merely avoid exceptional values but can preserve exact recovery of the overflow error. - The implementation appears to have practical specification value: formalization exposed at least three errors in an interim P3109 report, and the authors report that the standard was corrected accordingly. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify future extension to unsigned-format algorithm analyses and integration with automated verification tools such as SMT-LIB floating-point theory. Their current FastTwoSum and ExtractScalar analyses are restricted to signed formats, and ExtractScalar’s established guarantees are only proved for P>1. They also frame FLoPS as a foundation for future RTL and hardware verification rather than reporting an actual hardware equivalence study. These scope boundaries are stated directly, which improves credibility, but the paper does not discuss proof-maintenance costs as the P3109 draft evolves, limitations of its stochastic input distributions, or performance limitations of the executable kernel. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal gap is validation breadth: exhaustive testing is reported only for K=4 and does not establish agreement across the full parameter space or against an independent, complete P3109 implementation. The paper does not compare proof size, automation, execution cost, or coverage with Wintersteiger et al.’s Imandra model or existing floating-point libraries, so the practical advantage of Lean remains qualitative. The claimed RTL-equivalence and hardware-reference use cases lack a hardware case study, generated checker, synthesis result, or integration experiment. The stochastic-rounding theorems are tied to idealized, grid-based, or independent distributions and do not measure bias or convergence on representative ML training workloads. The paper also focuses algorithm analysis on signed formats despite unsigned formats being important for ReLU-like operations, and it does not evaluate composition with vector accumulation, dot products, compiler lowering, or mixed-format operations. Finally, because P3109 is identified as an upcoming and unapproved draft, the durability of the formalization under later standard revisions is an unresolved risk. Bottom Line: This is a strong formal-methods contribution and a useful open foundation for researchers verifying P3109 semantics, with credible new theorems around saturation and ultra-low precision, but practitioners seeking demonstrated hardware or machine-learning impact will need stronger comparative and deployment evidence before treating it as a production-ready verification solution.

TokenPowerSandbox: Evidence-Gated CPU-First Screening for Energy-Aware LLM Serving

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TokenPowerSandbox, a provenance-tracked CPU-to-GPU evidence workflow that combines analytical CPU screening, short measured GPU probes, full-workload verification, and metric-specific abstention for energy-aware LLM serving. - Why it's important: Exhaustively profiling every serving configuration on scarce accelerators is expensive, while inaccurate predictors can make unsafe SLO or energy decisions with false confidence. - How it does it: It fits a sparse ridge-based correction to an interpretable token/concurrency projector, freezes predictions and execution schedules before measurement, and releases only claims that pass evidence, chronology, identity, and scope gates. - The good: On one H100 serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with vLLM, frozen energy predictions achieve 6.23% and 7.35% MAPE on holdout and no-refit confirmation campaigns, while the gate correctly abstains from low-concurrency TTFT predictions. - The missing: The workflow is evaluated on only one model, one H100, one runtime, and fixed workloads, and it does not test the adaptive Probe-then-Verify policy that would determine whether the proposed evidence ladder reduces real search cost. - Read it or not: Systems and sustainable-inference researchers should read it for its careful evidence-boundary design and failure analysis, but practitioners seeking general fleet-wide optimization results can skip it because transfer beyond the tested single-GPU scope is unevaluated.

Problem & Motivation LLM serving operators must choose runtime and batching configurations under competing energy and latency objectives, where input/output lengths, concurrency, batching, cache policy, precision, power limits, and parallelism jointly affect device energy, throughput, TTFT, and TPOT. Exhaustive target-GPU measurement is reliable but costly, whereas analytical models and short probes may misorder candidates near SLO boundaries or fail when workload occupancy changes. The paper addresses the narrower problem of determining when inexpensive predictions or partial measurements are sufficiently trustworthy to screen workloads and configurations without silently treating CPU extrapolation as GPU evidence. The target domain is single-GPU vLLM serving with explicit energy and latency SLOs. Key Idea The central insight is that prediction fidelity must be treated as typed, scope-limited evidence rather than as a single accuracy number. A CPU model may preserve energy ordering while completely misrepresenting latency ordering, so the system must attach acquisition semantics and scope to every result, abstain on unsupported metric-regime combinations, use short measured probes to recover likely candidates, and reserve full target-workload verification as the decision authority. Methodology The workflow separates an inference scenario S, which fixes the model, workload, hardware, runtime, constraints, and objectives, from a deployable configuration x. The CPU Sandbox first rejects memory-infeasible configurations, separates prefill and decode work, scales a measured anchor according to token geometry and batch occupancy, estimates active power between measured idle/active bounds, and derives energy per 1,000 output tokens, throughput, TTFT, and TPOT. For each directly predicted metric, it fits a log-ratio residual using ridge regression over four features: log-scaled token geometry q, log-scaled concurrency r, their product qr, and r-squared; ridge strength is selected by leave-one-workload-out MAPE on six development workloads. Energy is recomputed from corrected power and duration rather than fitted independently. The Probe executor runs 64 requests and the Verify executor runs the complete 256-request workload using the same digest-pinned vLLM environment, fixed seeds and token behavior, disabled prefix caching, DCGM cumulative device-energy readings, 100-ms telemetry, and hash-sealed manifests. Before post-development measurements, the system freezes predictions, identities, workload order, repeats, software hashes, and manifests; validators reject chronology, identity, power-state, split, or artifact inconsistencies. The workload-transfer study uses three anchor repeats, six development workloads, an eight-workload blind holdout with 24 measurements, and a separate 3-by-3 input-length/concurrency confirmation with 27 measurements. The configuration study evaluates 12 frozen candidates with three Probe and three Verify repeats each, compares energy and throughput as objectives subject to P95 TTFT <= 1,600 ms and P95 TPOT <= 20 ms, and performs a new five-seed paired Verify confirmation after locking the selected configuration. The use of sparse residual correction, metric-specific gating, and freeze-before-measurement provenance is well motivated by the observed failure modes; however, the paper does not demonstrate that the chosen feature form is preferable to stronger learned predictors or that the fixed Probe/Verify durations minimize cost. Key Results On the blind H100 holdout, corrected CPU predictions reduce energy MAPE from 63.01% to 6.23%, achieve Spearman rank correlation 0.976, and correctly order 27 of 28 non-tied workload pairs; throughput MAPE is 10.53%, P95 TTFT MAPE 32.67%, and P95 TPOT MAPE 7.99%. On the separate no-refit confirmation, energy MAPE is 7.35% with rank correlation 0.933 and 33/36 correct energy orderings; throughput, TTFT, and TPOT MAPE are 11.31%, 46.29%, and 9.03%, respectively. The metric-specific gate accepts TTFT at concurrency four, where MAPE is 9.27%, but abstains below four because the combined sparse-stratum MAPE reaches 64.80% (79.27% at concurrency one and 50.34% at two). In the 12-candidate configuration corpus, the CPU Sandbox achieves energy rank correlation 0.884 and 19.45% energy MAPE but nearly reverses TTFT ranking with correlation -0.968, selects the wrong stage-local frontier, and has 0% recall for the verified Pareto point. A 64-request measured Probe achieves 1.15% energy MAPE and 17.20% TTFT MAPE, recovers the sole verified Pareto point with 100% recall but only 33.3% precision, and therefore still requires full Verify to remove false positives. The verified candidate seq32-bt2048-chunk improves over the expert baseline by 1.04% in energy per 1,000 output tokens, 3.06% in throughput, 21.59% in P95 TTFT, and 2.84% in P95 TPOT. In an independent five-pair confirmation, it wins all energy pairs, yielding a mean paired device-energy saving of 1.39% with a 95% paired-bootstrap percentile interval of [1.19%, 1.59%] and an exact one-sided sign-test p-value of 0.03125; median P95 TTFT falls 21.43%, mean throughput rises 3.46%, and mean P95 TPOT falls 3.30%. The experiments use one H100, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in BF16, vLLM 0.23.0, fixed 700-W power, bounded synthetic request shapes, and report 154 real H100 serving executions; the comparisons are mainly against the authors' CPU prior, short Probe, and predeclared expert baseline rather than against competing workload models or adaptive search algorithms. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, with an evidence-contract formulation and an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION workflow: the paper's distinctive contribution is not the token regression or GPU energy measurement itself, but the experimentally demonstrated use of freeze-before-measurement provenance, metric-specific pass/abstain gates, and a Sandbox-Probe-Verify fidelity ladder to expose when cheap screening fails. It does not introduce a new adaptive allocation algorithm, general GPU simulator, dataset, or fleet-wide optimization method. Rigor & Reproducibility The study has unusually strong controls for a small systems evaluation: predictions and measurement order are hash-frozen before post-development campaigns; holdout and confirmation data are not used for fitting; Probe and Verify measurements are balanced and interleaved; the selected configuration receives an independent no-reselection campaign; repeats use medians and MAD; and the five-pair energy result includes exhaustive paired-bootstrap enumeration and an exact sign test. The design includes useful negative evidence, especially the low-concurrency TTFT abstention and the CPU prior's TTFT rank inversion. However, the six-workload development set is small for the residual model, there are no multiple-seed or cross-device experiments for the main transfer model, prediction intervals are explicitly uncalibrated, and no ablation isolates the value of individual features, anchor scaling, ridge correction, provenance gates, or Probe duration. The paper reports that the original per-sample configuration telemetry archive is unavailable and that only 84 replay records permit metric recomputation, weakening artifact auditability. No public code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is stated; the paper only describes a software workflow and retained manifests. The evaluation also lacks strong competing predictors, simulators, or adaptive multi-fidelity baselines, so the relative benefit over existing alternatives remains unclear. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — the paper builds and runs an evidence-management and measurement workflow and evaluates it through serving experiments. Practical: The workflow runs on commercially available H100 hardware using vLLM, containers, and DCGM, although its current implementation is tied to a specific model, runtime, GPU, and fixed operating envelope. Efficient: CPU screening has negligible incremental GPU cost, but the reported campaigns still consume 1.117 H100-hours excluding anchor runs, and the paper does not measure the savings of an adaptive policy relative to exhaustive verification. Effective: Evidence shows reliable same-H100 energy ranking and useful Probe recovery, while also showing that energy accuracy does not certify latency and that Sandbox-only configuration selection misses the verified frontier. Scalable: The paper tests only one H100, one GPU, one 7B model, fixed single-GPU parallelism, and bounded workloads; behavior at 10x–100x scale, across GPUs, models, multi-GPU topologies, production arrivals, or larger candidate spaces is not evaluated. The work delivers a systems workflow with CPU, Probe, Verify, provenance, validation, and gating components, but no publicly identified reusable library, CLI, dataset, or adaptive agent artifact is provided. Strengths - The paper makes evidence semantics explicit: simulated CPU records, measured Probe records, and full-workload Verify records cannot be conflated, and every record carries scenario/configuration identity, scope, cost, uncertainty, hashes, and chronology. - The freeze-before-measurement and no-refit confirmation protocols directly address post-hoc selection and benchmark leakage, which is especially important when evaluating a screening model on the same hardware used for deployment decisions. - The metric-specific abstention result is a strong empirical finding: energy MAPE remains below 10% by concurrency stratum while TTFT error reaches 79.27% at concurrency one, demonstrating why aggregate predictor accuracy can produce unsafe latency claims. - The configuration experiment provides a concrete failure-and-repair analysis rather than reporting only average prediction error: CPU screening misses the verified Pareto point, Probe recovers it with a false-positive cost, and Verify resolves the remaining ambiguity. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly limit the evidence to one Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model, one H100 80GB, one vLLM release, BF16, a 700-W limit, fixed output lengths, two bounded protocols, and single-GPU execution. They state that the workload and configuration cross-product is not explored, the six-workload development split is small, and low-concurrency TTFT exposes limitations of numerical scope bounds. The energy boundary excludes host, network, cooling, facility, embodied, startup, and warmup energy; fixed token behavior omits stochastic lengths, semantic quality, finite-rate arrivals, production traces, and failure-heavy regimes. They acknowledge that prediction intervals are not calibrated, the five-pair confirmation is too small for broad generalization, the 1.39% energy saving is local and small, the configuration CPU prior is deliberately out of scope after serving knobs change, and cross-topology terms are disabled. They also explicitly state that the work does not evaluate adaptive acquisition, multi-GPU transfer, H200/B200 adaptation, or multi-node deployment. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not compare the CPU projector against competitive existing analytical models, workload regressors, serving simulators, or simple hardware-measurement baselines, so its accuracy and cost trade-offs are not positioned against the strongest available alternatives. - It audits a balanced Probe/Verify corpus retrospectively but does not evaluate the adaptive acquisition policy needed to establish actual measurement savings, candidate regret, or end-to-end optimization cost; this is central to the practical motivation rather than a peripheral extension. - The main configuration conclusion depends on a 12-candidate frozen set with one verified Pareto point, making frontier recall and precision statistically and substantively fragile; larger, independently generated candidate spaces could produce different conclusions. - The paper does not report uncertainty around MAPE or rank correlations across independent workload draws, GPU runs, or repeated campaigns, and its calibrated risk guarantee is absent despite the emphasis on evidence-gated release. - The unavailable original per-sample telemetry archive prevents complete independent verification of the configuration corpus, even though retained stage-level records support recomputation of reported metrics. - The reported 1.39% energy improvement is smaller than many plausible operational sources of variation outside the device-energy boundary, but the paper does not quantify sensitivity to measurement boundary, thermal state, background load, or deployment amortization. Bottom Line This is worth reading as a disciplined case study in trustworthy multi-fidelity evaluation for LLM serving, but its research contribution remains a carefully validated single-H100 evidence substrate rather than a demonstrated general solution for energy-aware configuration search.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VBVR-Pro, a procedurally generated suite of 300 visual-reasoning tasks with aligned image, video, and interleaved modalities, deterministic task-specific scorers, and reinforcement-learning recipes. - Why it's important: Native visual reasoning lacks scalable training data and reproducible feedback, making it difficult to determine whether generative models reason through visual states or merely satisfy superficial language and rendering patterns. - How it does it: It generates solver-backed task instances and metadata, verifies outputs through semantic computer-vision checks, and uses those scores as rewards for group-relative RL with coefficient-preserving stochastic sampling. - The good: The suite supports controlled cross-modality experiments, and its scorer reaches over 0.60 per-vote agreement with human preferences versus 0.54 for GPT-5.5 and 0.52 for Gemini-3.1-Pro, while remaining deterministic and cheaper. - The missing: The central conclusions rely mainly on synthetic tasks and hand-designed scorers, with no reported random-seed variation or uncertainty estimates and limited evidence that the learned abilities transfer to real-world deployment beyond benchmark scores. - Read it or not: Researchers building visual-generation reasoners, verifiable evaluators, or RL systems should read it; readers seeking evidence of general-purpose visual intelligence can treat it as infrastructure and benchmark work rather than a decisive demonstration of reasoning.

Problem & Motivation Native visual reasoning treats generated images and videos as intermediate computational states rather than merely inputs to a language model or final rendered outputs. The target users are researchers training image, video, and interleaved multimodal generators on spatial transformation, temporal persistence, object manipulation, physical-rule, game, and visual-pattern tasks. Existing resources either provide evaluation-only benchmarks with little training supervision, narrow synthetic task families, or VLM-as-a-judge evaluation that can be inaccurate, expensive, and nondeterministic. The paper targets the resulting gap: a single task distribution should provide scalable training data, aligned modalities, programmatically derived ground truth, reproducible evaluation, and reward signals for optimization. The motivation is credible for controlled research, although the paper does not establish that these synthetic tasks represent the full diversity or difficulty of real-world visual reasoning. Key Idea The core idea is to make the task generator, solution trajectory, evaluator, and RL reward one closed loop. Each procedural task defines a randomized visual environment and solver; the solver supplies structured metadata; the same underlying instance is rendered as video, image/key-frame, or interleaved text-image output; and a task-specific scorer checks semantic entities, transitions, constraints, and scene preservation. This enables training and evaluation to use identical task semantics and lets the authors compare visual trajectories rather than only final images. The accompanying mechanistic claim is that intermediate visual states contribute more to performance than intermediate textual rationales on this task family, but that claim remains bounded by the suite's synthetic design. Methodology VBVR-Pro contains 300 parameterized generators: 150 revised from VBVR and 150 newly designed. Each generator samples properties such as layout, object count, appearance, and difficulty, then emits an instance, a solver-derived solution, a random seed, a specification, and element attributes. The dataset contains 1.25 million SFT instances from 250 tasks, 50 held-out out-of-domain tasks, 50 in-domain benchmark tasks, and a 50,000-instance RL subset covering 50 in-domain tasks. Every instance has aligned video and image renderings; images use a Last-Frame, Key-Frame, or Multi-Frame regime, while interleaved examples pair each output image with text generated by Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview from the known solution trajectory. The benchmark evaluates image, video, and interleaved generators at 512 x 512 resolution, generally for one epoch; larger models use rank-32 LoRA and smaller models are fully fine-tuned. Scorers use HSV segmentation, contour detection, OCR, and trajectory tracking to extract colors, shapes, positions, counts, labels, and paths, then combine weighted checks through sums or multiplicative constraint gates. For RL, the paper applies group-relative policy optimization to Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, samples 32 trajectories per prompt with 30 denoising steps, replays 60% of transitions, and uses a learning rate of 5 x 10^-6. Its key design decisions are: procedural solver-backed supervision, aligned modality renderings, and task-specific semantic rewards. The first two support controlled experiments, but the paper does not provide a formal analysis of task-generator coverage or prove that its hand-selected scorer weights are optimal. The use of Gemini-generated intermediate rationales is also not an independent reasoning annotation process because Gemini receives the complete ground-truth trajectory. Key Results VBVR-Pro reports 300 tasks, 3,471,558 images, 1,300,500 videos, 1,250,000 SFT instances, and 50,000 RL instances, with 100 benchmark tasks split evenly between in-domain and out-of-domain settings. New tasks have median visual-complexity measures 6.9x higher in distinct regions, 2.4x higher in distinct colors, 1.7x higher in spatial information, and 2.0x higher in JPEG size than reworked tasks; a blinded pairwise assessment judged new tasks more reasoning-intensive in 113/150 pairs, while 70/150 new versus 10/150 reworked tasks were classified as multi-step. The rule-based scorer obtains more than 0.60 per-vote human agreement, compared with 0.54 for GPT-5.5 and 0.52 for Gemini-3.1-Pro, against a reported human agreement ceiling of 0.77. VLM judges changed scores on 54.6% to 92.8% of repeated cases, whereas the proposed scorer changed 0.0%; model-ranking correlation reaches Spearman rho = 0.95 in-domain and 1.00 out-of-domain. After one-epoch task training, the strongest in-domain/out-of-domain benchmark scores are 0.638/0.464 for VBVR-Pro-SenseNova-U1 and 0.670/0.532 for VBVR-Pro-Wan2.2-I2V-A14B; the strongest trained video model improves over its base model on external benchmarks from 62.83 to 66.18 on RISE-Video, 10.21 to 38.22 on V-ReasonBench, 57.89 to 66.96 on RULER-Bench, 24.76 to 48.39 on MME-CoF-Pro, 25.71 to 52.86 on VideoThinkBench-mini, 0.36 to 12.50 on BabyVision-Gen, and 3.93/5 to 4.11/5 on IntelligentVBench. These transfers are substantial on several benchmarks but remain far from perfect, and the external metrics use heterogeneous evaluation protocols. Removing intermediate visual states reduces overall scores by 0.024 for ThinkMorph and 0.111 for SenseNova-U1, while replacing intermediate text with placeholders changes scores by +0.001 and -0.009 respectively. In inference interventions on SenseNova-U1, removing the input image reduces the overall score from 0.638 to 0.064, removing the intermediate image reduces it to 0.099, and removing intermediate text reduces it to 0.533. RL with verifiable rewards reaches 0.548 overall, 0.719 in-domain, and 0.377 out-of-domain, versus 0.503/0.679/0.328 for additional SFT and 0.508/0.671/0.345 for VLM-judge RL. On 128 H800 GPUs for 2,200 steps, RL with the CPU scorer takes approximately 5.1 days versus 8.3 days with the Qwen3.6-27B judge, a reported 1.63x throughput increase and 38.7% wall-clock reduction. The modality comparison suggests interleaved generation can match video on many familiar tasks at lower generation cost, while video is stronger for persistent state transitions; however, these comparisons confound architecture, parameter count, fine-tuning method, and output representation, so they do not isolate modality alone. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the integrated 300-task, solver-backed, multimodal benchmark and scorer/RL infrastructure; the individual ingredients—procedural generation, classical vision-based verification, group-relative RL, LoRA fine-tuning, and diffusion sampling—are largely existing techniques combined and extended to native visual reasoning. The paper's empirical finding that visual trajectories can be more useful than intermediate text is interesting but is demonstrated only within the constructed task distribution. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports several useful ablations: full versus single-image interleaved trajectories, meaningful versus placeholder intermediate text, input and intermediate-state interventions, multiple CPS stochasticity values, deterministic Euler and UniPC samplers, SFT versus VLM-reward RL versus verifiable-reward RL, and a one-step-delayed training pipeline. It also reports a human study over 4,000 videos, with 10 annotations per model pair for one instance per task, and compares both per-instance agreement and model-level ranking. However, it reports no confidence intervals, standard deviations, multiple training seeds, statistical significance tests, or per-task reliability distributions. The human-alignment analysis maps scalar scores to four preference outcomes using a fixed threshold of 0.05 and a 0.5 failure boundary; sensitivity to these choices is not evaluated. The scorers are deterministic only conditional on successful object detection, OCR, and tracking, and their hand-designed weights may encode benchmark-specific assumptions. The evaluation and reward functions are created from the same procedural metadata used to generate training tasks, so they are not independent of the benchmark's design. External transfer reduces this concern, but most external results still come from a single fine-tuned model and do not establish broad generalization. The paper states that it releases data, models, scorers, and code, but the parsed paper does not provide a repository URL or verify the release status. It is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2608.26105v1, dated 26 August 2026), not a peer-reviewed publication in the supplied document. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL. Practical: The scorer can run on commercially available CPUs with optional OCR GPU use, but reproducing the reported RL training requires 128 H800 GPUs and is not practical for most groups. Efficient: The scorer reduces RL training time from approximately 8.3 to 5.1 days in the reported 128-GPU setup and avoids reserving 50% of GPU memory for a 27B judge, but generation and fine-tuning of 5B–32B diffusion or multimodal models remain expensive. Effective: The evidence shows improved scores on the synthetic benchmark and seven external benchmarks, but the measured target is benchmark-defined visual transformation quality rather than validated task success in deployed robots, agents, or real-world environments. Scalable: The dataset scales to 1.25 million SFT instances and 300 generators, but the paper does not test 10x–100x more tasks, higher resolutions, longer videos, larger scenes, or substantially larger models; the claim of scalable native reasoning therefore remains primarily infrastructural. The work delivers a reusable dataset, benchmark, scorer suite, model checkpoints, and RL training pipeline; no release URL is stated in the paper text. Strengths - The benchmark unifies image, video, and interleaved renderings of the same solved instances, which enables substantially cleaner modality comparisons than comparing unrelated datasets. - The task-specific scorers evaluate intermediate process validity, final-state correctness, constraint violations, and scene preservation rather than relying only on subjective whole-video judgments. - The scorer study measures reproducibility directly and shows large repeatability failures for several VLM judges, with changed-score rates of 54.6%–92.8% versus 0.0% for the proposed evaluator. - The paper connects evaluation to optimization and demonstrates a controlled RL comparison in which verifiable rewards outperform both additional SFT and a Qwen3.6-27B VLM reward on the same 50K RL subset. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors acknowledge that the strongest trained model remains below human-level performance. They also state that VBVR-Pro consists of procedurally generated tasks and that external benchmarks contain real-world scenes and robotic manipulators substantially different from the training abstractions. The paper recognizes that visual and textual modality comparisons involve different output representations and that image outputs can omit intermediate states. It does not, in the supplied text, explicitly discuss scorer brittleness under rendering changes, annotation-model dependence, missing uncertainty estimates, or the computational barrier to reproducing 128-H800-GPU RL training. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The scorer is tightly coupled to task-specific visual primitives such as known colors, contours, OCR labels, and trajectories; no robustness study tests adversarial rendering, photorealistic variation, occlusion, compression, camera motion, or detector failures. - The human-alignment study uses one benchmark instance per task for pairwise annotation despite five instances per task being available, so its claim of evaluator reliability may be sensitive to the sampled instances and the high failure rate. - No error bars, seeds, or statistical tests support differences such as 0.548 versus 0.508 RL performance, making it unclear whether some gains exceed run-to-run variance. - The modality conclusions are not causally isolated: the models differ in architecture, parameter count, active parameters, latent representation, fine-tuning strategy, and output length, while the image regime gives approximately 70% of tasks only a final frame. - The transfer analysis reports only the strongest fine-tuned video model and does not provide matched compute, tuning, or inference-budget comparisons against strong alternatives; it therefore supports transfer but not the stronger claim that task coverage is the principal cause. - The task taxonomy includes perception, knowledge, and simple rule-following alongside multi-step transformations, so aggregate scores can overstate native visual reasoning unless results are stratified by genuine planning depth and difficulty. - The generated interleaved rationales come from Gemini after receiving the complete ground-truth trajectory, weakening conclusions about whether language supervision is intrinsically unnecessary rather than redundant given the visual labels. - The paper does not evaluate whether RLVR improves real-world video generation quality, physical plausibility, or robotic execution, despite highlighting those applications. Bottom Line This is a useful and unusually well-integrated infrastructure paper whose strongest contributions are the solver-backed benchmark and reproducible reward machinery, but its claims about native visual reasoning should be read as evidence for benchmark-grounded visual-state optimization—not as proof of general visual reasoning—and researchers in this area should read it, while readers seeking a general intelligence result can skip it in favor of work with real-world tasks, independent evaluators, uncertainty estimates, and matched modality controls.

Contrastive Symbolic Regression: Aligned Representations, Adaptive Prediction, and Diverse Ensembles

H Zhang, Q Chen, B Xue, W Banzhaf, M Zhang · openreview.net · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Contrastive Symbolic Regression (CSR), an evolutionary symbolic feature-construction framework that learns target-aligned feature geometries, predicts with boosted ridge-plus-KNN models, and aggregates diverse individuals with DPP selection. - Why it's important: Regression systems often need both interpretable mathematical features and reliable local predictions, while standard symbolic regression and parametric feature construction do not explicitly preserve similarity among instances with similar continuous targets. - How it does it: CSR fits a ridge-regularized linear metric over pairwise symbolic-feature differences so transformed distances approximate squared target differences, then applies KNN to residuals and selects diverse high-quality models. - The good: Across 58 real-world PMLB regression datasets, the full ablated system reaches a normalized median test R² of 0.8884 with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of [0.7787, 0.9547], outperforming the reported symbolic-regression variants and the paper's machine-learning comparison set. - The missing: The paper does not provide sufficiently detailed numeric results, uncertainty estimates, or scale experiments for the full comparison against all modern baselines, and its KNN component has quadratic dependence on the number of training instances. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on interpretable tabular regression, evolutionary feature construction, or metric learning; skip it if you need a scalable symbolic equation rather than a training-set-dependent ensemble predictor.
