Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses real-valued tabular regression in settings where practitioners want interpretable feature transformations and instance-level explanations, such as retrieving similar historical cases for a decision. Existing feature-construction symbolic regression methods generally evolve features for direct linear or other parametric input-to-target mappings, which can miss local, non-parametric variation and do not explicitly ensure that nearby points in the learned feature space have similar target values. The paper frames the gap as continuous relational representation learning: unlike classification-oriented contrastive learning, regression requires preserving target magnitudes or distances rather than merely binary or ordinal relationships. The intended domains are general single-modality tabular regression problems, not causal inference or equation discovery in the strict sense. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat symbolic regression as learning a target-aligned metric space rather than only an explicit function from inputs to targets. Given evolved symbolic features, CSR learns a positive-semidefinite linear metric M = WWᵀ whose pairwise feature distances approximate squared target differences; KNN can then exploit the resulting geometry to predict locally similar target values. This is a meaningful integration of symbolic feature construction and supervised metric learning, although the broader ingredients—genetic programming, ridge regression, KNN, metric alignment, and diversity-based ensembles—are individually established. Methodology: Each evolutionary individual contains m = 10 GP trees that map the original standardized inputs X to a symbolic feature matrix Φ(X). Initialization combines one EQL-derived individual, formed from ten bootstrapped EQL models, with ramped half-and-half random GP individuals. For each individual, ridge regression first fits a global component, minimizing ||y − Φ(X)β||² + λ||β||²; residuals e = y − ŷridge are then modeled by the contrastive KNN component. CSR constructs pairwise feature-difference vectors and target distances Dᵢⱼ = (eᵢ − eⱼ)², solves a ridge-regularized least-squares problem over v = vec(M), v = (BᵀB + λI)⁻¹Bᵀd, reshapes and symmetrizes M, and obtains W by eigendecomposition with negative eigenvalues clamped to zero. The transformed features Φ(X)W feed KNN regression. During evolution, feature spaces are scored with fixed-K linearly rank-weighted KNN, using weights wᵣ = 2(K − r + 1)/(K(K + 1)); after evolution, a vectorized exact LOOCV procedure retrieves Kmax + 1 neighbors once, excludes self-neighbors, uses prefix means to evaluate all candidate K values, and selects K. At each generation, double lexicase selection chooses parents, subtree crossover and mutation create offspring, and a greedy DPP-MAP procedure selects an ensemble of E = 30 candidates from the current top individuals and archive. The DPP kernel combines normalized fitness with cosine similarity of residual semantic vectors. The closed-form metric solution is well motivated computationally, but the paper does not fully justify the choice of squared target-distance matching over alternatives, and the post-hoc eigenvalue clipping means the stated unconstrained ridge solution is not exactly the solution to the positive-semidefinite metric-constrained problem. The use of a fixed K for evolutionary fitness and adaptive K for final prediction is plausible and supported by an ablation, but the distinction introduces another separately tuned design choice. Key Results: Experiments use 58 real-world datasets from PMLB, excluding 62 Friedman synthetic datasets, with an 80/20 train-test split, feature standardization, training capped at 10,000 instances, and 30 random seeds. In the symbolic-regression ablation, the full SRAll system obtains normalized median test R² = 0.8884 [0.7787, 0.9547], compared with 0.8310 for ridge + contrastive learning + standard KNN, 0.8244 for ridge + PLS + KNN, 0.8241 for ridge + KNN, 0.7647 for ridge + LPP + KNN, 0.6602 for ridge-only SR, 0.6410 for contrastive + LOOCV-KNN, 0.6064 for contrastive + standard KNN, 0.5905 for LOOCV-KNN without contrastive learning, 0.4861 for tree-based SR, and 0.4613 for naive KNN feature construction. The paper reports that CSR ranks first overall in a comparison of 27 symbolic-regression and machine-learning methods, including RAG-SR, RealMLP, ModernNCA, MLP-PLR, XGBoost, and LightGBM, with pairwise Wilcoxon tests and Benjamini–Hochberg correction indicating significant advantages in the reported comparison. The full comparison figure does not give a numerical table of per-method R² values or confidence intervals, so the magnitude of the advantage over each external baseline cannot be independently read precisely. The proposed LOOCV implementation is reported at 0.029 seconds in a small 100-sample/10-feature runtime experiment, versus 0.686 seconds for TMLR-LOOCV and 2.868 seconds for naive LOOCV; this is a microbenchmark rather than an end-to-end CSR scaling result. Training-time analysis identifies all-pairs KNN evaluation as the dominant cost, with O(n²) evaluation for n instances, while the metric solve has stated complexity O(S²m⁴) and uses S = 100 and m = 10 by default. The visualization and US crime-rate example provide qualitative evidence for target-aligned neighborhoods and instance-level retrieval, but they do not establish causal interpretability or broad explanation fidelity. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new element is the integration of evolutionary symbolic feature construction with continuous target-distance metric alignment through a closed-form ridge-regularized formulation, combined with fixed-rank-weighted KNN fitness evaluation and DPP-based selection; the GP, ridge, KNN, LOOCV, and DPP components themselves are standard techniques adapted and combined for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports 30 random seeds, bootstrap confidence intervals for the ablation summary, Wilcoxon signed-rank testing at 0.05, and Benjamini–Hochberg correction for the broader pairwise comparison. It includes component ablations for ridge boosting, contrastive alignment, PLS and LPP alternatives, adaptive K selection, linear-rank weighting, ensemble size, DPP kernels, Laplacian regularization, and metric subsampling. The code is stated to be available at https://github.com/hengzhe-zhang/CSR-ICML/. Baselines are comparatively strong and include recent tabular models and tuned tree ensembles; the appendix states that baselines are tuned on training data, with HEBO for modern deep baselines and cross-validation or validation splits for others. However, the evaluation relies on repeated random 80/20 splits rather than a clearly standardized multi-split or nested dataset-level protocol, and the full external comparison is presented mainly through figures without exact per-dataset or aggregate values. The paper does not report conventional error bars for every baseline, per-dataset effect sizes, or computational budgets normalized across methods. The contrastive target distances are computed from training labels, which is valid for supervised training, but the paper should more explicitly clarify whether every reported transformation and ensemble-selection decision is recomputed independently inside each split. The metric optimization uses an unconstrained solution followed by eigenvalue clipping, and the consequences of this approximation are not quantitatively evaluated. The code release is claimed, but the provided text does not state whether pretrained models, complete dataset-processing scripts, or exact experiment configurations are released. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The method can run on commercially available hardware and uses small symbolic feature spaces, but inference requires evaluating GP expressions, applying a learned transformation, and retaining training instances for KNN retrieval; deployment memory is therefore not necessarily comparable to that of a compact explicit equation. Efficient: The closed-form metric solve is manageable with S = 100 and m = 10, and the proposed LOOCV calculation is much faster than naive LOOCV in the reported microbenchmark, but end-to-end evolution is substantially slower than ridge-only SR and KNN evaluation scales quadratically with n. Effective: Evidence on 58 real-world datasets and the component ablations supports improved predictive R² over the included SR and ML baselines, while the interpretability evidence demonstrates retrieval and feature inspection rather than validated human usefulness or explanation faithfulness. Scalable: The largest tested setting is capped at 10,000 training instances, and the paper explicitly identifies O(n²) KNN evaluation as the dominant cost; no 10×–100× scale experiment demonstrates that the complete evolutionary ensemble remains practical. The work delivers a software artifact through the linked GitHub repository and delivers trained symbolic-feature/metric/KNN ensembles, but not a single explicit predictive equation. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete mismatch between continuous regression supervision and binary or ordinal contrastive objectives, then formulates target-distance alignment directly rather than discretizing the target. - The metric-learning subproblem has an analytically tractable ridge formulation, which is well suited to repeated evaluation inside GP and avoids embedding an iterative gradient procedure in every evolutionary individual. - The ablation structure isolates several interacting contributions: contrastive alignment improves KNN-based feature construction, ridge boosting handles global structure, rank-weighted fitness improves selection of individuals that generalize, and DPP selection improves ensemble diversity. - The experimental comparison includes recent tabular learners and tuned tree baselines rather than only weak symbolic-regression references, and the released code improves reproducibility. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly restrict the method to single-modality regression and identify large-scale scenarios as future work. They also note that alternative distance functions are not straightforward because retaining closed-form solutions beyond Euclidean distance is non-trivial. The impact statement acknowledges that CSR is predictive rather than causal and warns that symbolic interactions may encode spurious correlations. The appendix further acknowledges that Laplacian regularization can collapse representations because it pulls similar points together without separating dissimilar points. These limitations are directly discussed rather than omitted, although the scalability implications of the O(n²) KNN stage receive less attention than the closed-form metric solve. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not establish that CSR's gains come primarily from contrastive alignment rather than the substantial combined effects of GP initialization, ridge residualization, KNN choice, rank weighting, 30-model ensembling, and DPP selection; a matched compute-budget comparison and a complete factorial ablation would be more convincing. The full method is evaluated on one benchmark family and random train/test splits, with no temporal, distribution-shift, extrapolation, missing-data, categorical-feature, or very-high-dimensional stress tests. The claim of compact deployment is qualified by the need to store training examples for KNN and by an ensemble of 30 individuals, but memory and inference latency are not reported. The paper compares against many recent models but does not provide exact aggregate numbers and uncertainty for each, making the headline superiority difficult to audit from the text alone. The target-distance objective can encourage undesirable ordering or metric distortions when noisy labels dominate pairwise distances, yet robustness to label noise and outliers is not evaluated. The method is called symbolic regression, but the final predictor is not an explicit symbolic equation; the paper should distinguish symbolic feature interpretability from equation-level interpretability more sharply. Finally, the post-hoc PSD projection after solving for an unconstrained M and the handling of zero or near-zero residual semantic vectors in the cosine DPP kernel are not analyzed in sufficient numerical detail. Bottom Line: CSR is a technically credible and empirically promising integration of symbolic feature construction with supervised metric learning, but its strongest practical value is as an interpretable feature-and-retrieval ensemble rather than as scalable or equation-level symbolic regression, so it merits reading but not accepting the broad superiority and deployment claims without stronger scale and evaluation evidence.

Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report (14 ▲ )

TaoLive AIGC LLM Team, Yuhan Sun, Wenhao Lin, Yongdong Luo, Yibo Hu, Meiguang Jin, Junfeng Ma, Weihang Pan, Jiaxin Zhao, Zulong Chen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Harness-Aware Training (HAT), a three-stage training pipeline that enables a compact live-streaming agent to remain effective when its Skills, tools, prompts, and Hooks change without updating model weights. - Why it's important: Live-commerce agents must adapt to business-rule changes while meeting latency constraints that exclude larger general-purpose models and retraining after every Harness edit. - How it does it: HAT exposes training to task-preserving Harness-State Augmentation across identifiers, descriptions, schemas, prompts, and Hook behavior, then combines augmented SFT, general-domain on-policy distillation, and augmented-environment RL. - The good: On 978 real live-room cases, HAT reaches 94.8 AVG versus 80.3 for the base model, 89.5 for fixed-Harness SFT, and at most 93.0 for the compared general models, while scoring 94.6 on Harness-Variant QA with only a 0.2-point original-to-variant gap. - The missing: The central robustness claim is evaluated mainly within an author-defined augmentation envelope and relies heavily on model-based judges, with no public data, code, weights, repeated-seed results, or independent evidence of generalization to genuinely unforeseen Harness changes. - Read it or not: Practitioners building latency-constrained LLM agents with frequently edited runtime instructions should read it for the training and deployment recipe; researchers seeking a broadly validated general method should treat it as a strong industry case study rather than conclusive evidence.
Why this rank
Systems profile. HAT makes a useful formulation of harness evolution as structured environment shift and provides a technically coherent combination of augmentation, distillation, and RL (Novelty 76; Non-Obviousness 76). Rigor is comparatively strong for a technical report (72), with cumulative ablations, held-out edits, latency tests, human preference data, and production A/B evidence, though single-run training, model-judge dependence, proprietary data, and missing reproducibility artifacts remain important weaknesses. Problem & Motivation The work addresses live-streaming e-commerce agents that must answer product and after-sales questions, interpret viewer intent, use commerce and marketing tools, and follow changing campaign and compliance rules in real time. The practical tension is between large models, which can often interpret changed tools and instructions zero-shot but exceed latency budgets, and compact models, which are fast enough for deployment but tend to overfit to the names, schemas, prompt templates, and control behavior of a fixed runtime configuration. The proposed application uses an evolvable Harness containing Skills, a Tool Registry, a dynamic System Prompt Pipeline, and lifecycle Hooks; these modules can be changed independently of model weights. The specific gap is training a compact policy to condition on the current Harness semantics rather than memorize one snapshot, while avoiding the general instruction-following degradation observed after domain-specific fine-tuning. Key Idea The core insight is to treat Harness evolution as distribution shift over an explicit environment state and train over a distribution of semantically equivalent Harness realizations. HAT makes surface forms unreliable by renaming and rewriting Skills and tools, reordering or paraphrasing instructions, injecting distractors, and varying Hook behavior, while preserving the underlying task. The model is therefore encouraged to infer functional meaning from the active Harness. This is a technically plausible and useful extension of environment randomization and domain randomization to LLM agent runtimes, although the individual mechanisms—SFT, on-policy distillation, GRPO-style RL, rejection sampling, and prompt/tool perturbation—are established components. Methodology The runtime represents a Harness state as h = (S, T, P, K), where S is the active Skill set, T is the tool registry, P is the assembled system prompt, and K is the Hook configuration. A request first undergoes context normalization and input validation; the system assembles product, FAQ, room, dialogue, and Skill context; the policy then iterates through Skill loading, tool calls, tool-result interpretation, and final-response generation; Hooks validate parameters, formatting, factuality risks, and stopping conditions; finally, the response is extracted and dispatched to speech/avatar generation. HSA perturbs five dimensions: Skill identifiers and descriptions, Skill rule content and order, tool names and descriptions, prompt block ordering and valid numeric constraints, and Hook messages, retry behavior, and interaction structure. Stage 1, HSA-SFT, generates trajectories with a strong teacher under original and augmented Harnesses, filters them using Accuracy and Effectiveness judges, and trains the compact model by supervised learning; most failed intermediate Hook retries are removed, with a small fraction retained for recovery learning. Stage 2, General OPD, uses the pre-SFT base model as teacher on Tulu3 general instructions and minimizes KL divergence, L_OPD = E_x[D_KL(p_theta(.|x) || p_base(.|x))], to recover general capability. Stage 3, HSA-RL, rolls out the policy in a production-informed simulator containing live-room inputs, Skills, tools, Hooks, bounded multi-round control flow, catalog snapshots, and injected timeout, malformed-response, and permission failures. It optimizes with GRPO plus GDPO-style per-dimension group normalization, separately for tool and reply segments, using Accuracy, Effectiveness, Tool Rationality, and Skill Selection rewards, with an auxiliary CoT-length penalty that contributes between 0 and -0.1 per state for lengths above 100 tokens. Critical design decisions are the use of HSA in both SFT and RL, the General OPD recovery stage, and separate tool/reply reward normalization; the ablations support their effects, but the augmentation envelope, reward-judge construction, and perturbation probabilities are not specified in enough detail to reproduce the full training distribution. Key Results The model is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, trained on 10,000 SFT examples and 4,000 RL interaction tasks. On T1 Live-Stream QA, comprising 978 real live-room cases, HAT scores 95.8 Accuracy, 93.8 Effectiveness, and 94.8 AVG, compared with 86.5/74.1/80.3 for the base model and 90.0/88.9/89.5 for fixed-Harness SFT. The strongest listed general-model score is 93.0 AVG from GLM-5.2. On T2 Harness-Variant QA, another 978 real cases with augmented Harnesses, HAT scores 94.5/94.7/94.6, versus 88.7/62.1/75.4 for the base model and 86.9/89.5/88.2 for fixed-Harness SFT; the HAT original-to-variant AVG difference is 0.2 points, versus 4.9 for the base and 1.3 for fixed-Harness SFT. On synthetic T3 robustness tests, HAT reaches 84.0 AVG for Tool Robustness and 77.6 for Prompt Robustness, compared with 69.5 and 72.8 for the base model and 82.0 and 68.2 for fixed-Harness SFT. On the public 541-item IFEval benchmark, HAT reaches 83.5 prompt-level and 88.7 instruction-level accuracy, while fixed-Harness SFT falls to 73.8 and 82.4 from base scores of 81.5 and 87.7. The cumulative ablation attributes the largest preservation benefit to HSA: fixed-Harness SFT lowers Prompt Robustness by 4.6 points and IFEval prompt accuracy by 7.7 points, whereas HSA-SFT raises Prompt Robustness by 4.5 points and leaves IFEval prompt accuracy at 81.7; General OPD then raises it to 81.9, and HSA-RL to 83.5. In a controlled replay of 100 measured requests after 10 warm-ups on one NVIDIA H20, HAT with MTP has P50/P95 wall latency of 3.407/8.114 seconds at concurrency 1 and 4.479/9.047 seconds at concurrency 2, with 100% of requests under 15 seconds; MTP improves same-checkpoint decode throughput from 160.30 to 271.40 tokens/s at concurrency 1 and from 129.22 to 196.15 at concurrency 2. At concurrency 8, however, HAT MTP P95 latency is 20.298 seconds and 15-second attainment falls to 75%, so the real-time claim applies only to the low-concurrency operating range. A 100-pair human blind test reports 35 Harness wins, 64 ties, and 1 ReAct win; among non-ties, this is a 35/36 win rate with a reported two-sided binomial p < 0.001. A production 80/20 A/B test involving 395,276 treatment and 1,581,494 control unique visitors reports +4.3340% UV-normalized confirmed-receipt GMV and +0.9107% item-page views, both labeled significantly positive by the platform, but the paper does not provide p-values, confidence intervals, test thresholds, duration beyond one positively significant day per metric, or component-level attribution. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper formulates evolving Skills, tools, prompts, and Hooks as a changing Harness-state problem and proposes HSA combined with HSA-SFT, General OPD, and HSA-RL; the strongest genuine novelty is the explicit use of coordinated Harness randomization during both offline supervision and on-policy agent training, while the optimization primitives and MTP serving acceleration are standard techniques adapted to this production setting. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes meaningful cumulative ablations across fixed versus augmented SFT and RL, showing that fixed-environment RL improves domain scores but lowers Prompt Robustness from 72.6 to 66.7, whereas HSA-RL raises it from 77.1 to 77.6 and also improves IFEval. It also includes a same-checkpoint MTP quality check, concurrency stress measurements at C=1, 2, 4, and 8, a held-out Harness-edit test, and an independent paired-bootstrap analysis with 10,000 resamples; the bootstrap intervals support several headline contrasts, including HAT versus fixed-Harness SFT on Prompt Robustness (+8.46 points, 95% CI [+5.27, +11.66]) and HAT versus base on T1 AVG (+18.92, 95% CI [+17.00, +20.81]). However, training and evaluation dynamics are explicitly single-run diagnostics, and the main experiments do not report multiple random seeds, training variance, error bars for model training, or significance tests for most offline comparisons. The final judge is calibrated on 482 human-labeled cases, reaching 90.46% Accuracy agreement and 82.2% Effectiveness agreement for the selected voting configuration; this is useful but leaves substantial judge noise, especially for Effectiveness. The SFT teacher is also one member of the final three-model evaluation panel, although it cannot decide an item alone under majority voting. T3 is LLM-generated from real-business seeds, and HSA variants are author-designed; both create possible distribution overlap and limit claims about arbitrary future Harness edits. The held-out edit test uses shared edits derived from a development split, but it still evaluates changes within the authors' controlled edit process. No code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned. The deployed system is a real software artifact, but it is not released as a reusable public library, CLI, dataset, or trained model. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with substantial empirical training and evaluation components. Practical: The model runs on commercially available hardware—one NVIDIA H20 with BF16 inference, TP=PP=1, and an EAGLE-style NextN speculative-decoding configuration—although the full production system also depends on proprietary Taobao services, MCP interfaces, catalog data, Hooks, and Harness modules. Efficient: MTP raises same-checkpoint client-observed decode throughput by 1.69x at concurrency 1 and 1.52x at concurrency 2, but gains shrink to 1.27x and 1.19x at concurrency 4 and 8, while HAT itself has different trajectory and output-length distributions from the base, preventing a clean intrinsic model-speed comparison. Effective: Evidence supports improved judged response quality, a 35-to-1 non-tie human preference advantage, held-out Harness-edit compliance, and positive production-system business metrics, but offline quality is primarily model-judge based and the A/B test does not isolate HAT from the Harness, routing, or other system changes. Scalable: The paper tests concurrency through 8, but HAT with MTP misses the 15-second target for 25% of requests at C=8 and has 20.298-second P95 latency; it provides no 10x–100x scale evaluation or capacity analysis. The work delivers a proprietary deployed agent runtime and trained model rather than a public software artifact. Strengths - It identifies a concrete failure mode—surface-form overfitting to a mutable agent runtime—and ties it to an operational architecture rather than treating prompt changes as incidental noise. - The fixed-versus-augmented SFT/RL factorial evidence is unusually informative: it separates the role of HSA from General OPD and shows that fixed-environment RL can improve business scores while damaging instruction and prompt robustness. - The evaluation spans real industrial QA, augmented Harness variants, synthetic tool/prompt robustness, public IFEval, controlled serving replay, human preference judgments, and production A/B outcomes, with explicit discussion of what each source does and does not establish. - The deployment analysis is relatively candid about MTP limits, trajectory-length confounds, low-concurrency applicability, and the distinction between speculative-token acceptance and semantic quality. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly states that training-dynamics plots are single-run process diagnostics rather than evidence of efficiency or cross-seed stability; MTP adaptation curves do not establish convergence speed, training stability, sample efficiency, or compute efficiency; CoT-length reductions do not establish causal latency or quality gains; and speculative-token acceptance is not semantic quality. It also notes that the production A/B comparison measures the joint effect of the complete Harness system rather than isolating the policy model, that vendor API hardware and service load are unobservable, and that the platform's significance assessment does not expose p-values, thresholds, or confidence intervals. The authors further acknowledge that qualitative prompt-edit examples are not additional quantitative evidence and that later Harness evolution rules can regress earlier metrics. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The robustness claim is narrower than the framing suggests: evaluation uses transformations generated from the same declared HSA change envelope, so it does not establish adaptation to arbitrary new tools, incompatible schemas, substantially changed control flow, adversarial edits, or semantic changes that are not task-preserving. - The reported judge calibration is not strong enough to treat 94–95 scores as direct human-quality measurements, particularly because Effectiveness agreement peaks at 83.4% during evolution and the final selected major-vote agreement is 82.2%. - The paper does not report per-category error rates, confidence intervals for the main offline scores, seed variation, training compute, augmentation counts or probabilities, rejection rates, reward scales, or enough data-generation detail to reproduce HSA-SFT or HSA-RL. - The offline comparisons may be affected by evaluator and data-construction coupling: the same organization defines the Harness, augmentation transformations, judge rubric, simulator, and robustness sets, while the synthetic T3 cases are generated and validated with LLMs. - The A/B test establishes a promising system-level association but does not demonstrate that HAT caused the GMV or IPV uplift; no experiment duration, confidence intervals, covariate balance, guardrail metrics, or effect heterogeneity is reported. - The method's cost-benefit tradeoff is incomplete because the paper reports inference latency but not the compute and wall-clock cost of teacher trajectory generation, General OPD, RL rollouts, judge calls, simulator construction, or recurring Harness evolution. - The production Harness and model are proprietary, and omission of the actual Hook implementations, prompts, tool schemas, and Skills substantially limits external validation. Bottom Line This is a valuable, technically credible production case study showing that Harness randomization can mitigate fixed-runtime overfitting in a compact agent, but its evidence supports adoption within similar controlled systems more strongly than a general claim that HAT robustly handles open-ended Harness evolution.

PAWBench: How Far Are We from Probabilistically Aligned World Modeling? (74 ▲ )

Yuandong Pu, Le Zhuo, Sayak Paul, Gabriel Jorge Menezes, Avram Đorđević, Shiyang Li, Yifan Zhou, Bin Fu, Wenlong Zhang, Junjun He, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Jingbo Xing, Xi Chen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PAWBench and PAWEval, a 50-scenario repeated-rollout benchmark and outcome-level evaluation protocol for measuring whether video generators recover the correct distribution or support of physically possible futures. - Why it's important: A model used for planning or interaction can produce individually plausible videos yet systematically omit valid consequences or assign them incorrect probabilities, leading to unreliable decisions. - How it does it: It fixes one source image and action, samples 50 rollouts, maps readable terminal states to discrete outcomes, and scores either total-variation distance to an analytically justified distribution or valid-outcome coverage. - The good: Across 11 video generators, the observed mean calibration error is 31.2 TVD points versus a matched finite-sample null whose 99th percentile is 9.22, providing evidence that the distributional gap is not explained by sampling noise alone. - The missing: The benchmark evaluates manually curated, short-horizon terminal outcomes from synthetic or generated source images, so it does not establish probabilistic alignment for continuous trajectories, long-horizon interaction, real-world observations, or downstream control. - Read it or not: Read it if you evaluate video models as simulators or world models; skip it if you need a deployable modeling method rather than a diagnostic benchmark and failure analysis.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (88) is the paper's strongest dimension: PAWBench introduces a meaningful distribution-level formulation separating probability calibration from valid-outcome coverage. Non-Obviousness (85) is high because it exposes a failure mode invisible to standard plausibility and diversity metrics, and the intervention results probe whether the problem arises from prompting, finite sampling, or parameter shifts. Rigor (76), Completeness (82), and Resilience (74) are supported by matched Monte Carlo nulls, causal and non-causal controls, rollout sensitivity, and explicit limitations, but are reduced by conditional exclusion of unreadable outputs, proprietary judging, manually curated scenarios, and absent confidence intervals. Impact (55) is limited because this is a diagnostic benchmark with no released evaluator confirmed and no downstream planning validation. Weighted composite: 0.20*88 + 0.25*76 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*74 + 0.10*55 = 78.25, rounded to 78.

Problem & Motivation: Existing video-generation and world-model evaluations usually judge individual samples for visual quality, temporal coherence, instruction following, physical plausibility, or task success. Those tests do not determine whether repeated generations from the same initial observation and action reproduce the stochastic structure of the underlying process. The paper targets this gap for video generators viewed as action-conditioned world models: under partial observation and an atomic action, multiple futures may be physically valid, and an agent needs both the support of those futures and their relative likelihoods. The claimed application relevance is planning and interaction, where selecting actions depends on probabilities of consequences rather than on one plausible continuation. Key Idea: Treat repeated video generations as samples from a conditional world-dynamics distribution and evaluate their induced distribution over discrete terminal outcomes, rather than evaluating videos independently. The paper separates two notions that are often conflated: probability-mass alignment, measured against a reference distribution when probabilities can be justified, and support alignment, measured by whether all enumerated valid outcomes appear when probabilities cannot be specified. It further uses paired causal and non-causal interventions to test whether model distributions change when the physical transition changes and remain stable when only irrelevant cues change. Methodology: For each of 50 manually curated scenarios, the benchmark fixes an initial source image x, one action prompt a, a finite outcome set Y, and, for 25 PAW-Calibration scenarios, a reference distribution q derived from symmetry, sector proportions, combinatorial counts, or visible causal state. The remaining 25 PAW-Coverage scenarios specify valid outcomes but no defensible probabilities. Each model receives the same (x, a) pair for K=50 rollouts. Gemini 3.5 Flash applies a frozen scene-specific rubric to each video, returning an in-schema terminal label or a readout failure; scenes pass if at least 20 of 50 rollouts are readable. For passing scenes, the empirical readable-outcome distribution is compared with q using 100 times total variation distance, while Coverage is the fraction of Y observed. Readout failures are excluded from conditional distributions but reported through Scene Pass Rate, and a separate audit flags action-execution, object-continuity, and physical-process failures without changing the main score. Additional experiments test three intervention classes: (1) VLM future sampling and GPT-5.5 prompt engineering, including an oracle condition that directly specifies target outcomes; (2) Couple to Control, which introduces negative dependence among 50 Gaussian initial noises while preserving each marginal; and (3) five rank-32 Wan2.2 LoRA adaptations trained on left/right pencil-fall mixtures from 0/100 to 100/0, using 2,000 repeated training examples and 2,000 optimizer updates. The core design decisions—separating calibration from coverage, conditioning scores on readable outcomes while exposing readout reliability separately, and fixing the input pair across rollouts—are conceptually well motivated, although the handling of failures creates important interpretive caveats. Key Results: The main evaluation covers 11 systems—HappyHorse, Veo3.1 Fast, Kling 3 Std., Seedance 2, Wan2.7, Wan2.2, LTX-2.3, LTX-2.5, Cosmos 3 Super I2V, LingBot-Video-MoE, and MiniMax H3—with 50 rollouts per model-scenario pair. Cosmos 3 Super I2V has the lowest average Calibration TVD, 20.5, with an 80.0% Calibration Scene Pass Rate; MiniMax H3 is next at 24.2, while Wan2.7 and Wan2.2 each report 26.3. Calibration errors remain substantial for every model, and no system jointly achieves low TVD, broad support, and reliable scene pass rates. LTX-2.3 has the highest conditional Coverage average at 71.7%, but only 72.0% of Coverage scenes pass; Wan2.2 reaches 63.4% Coverage with a 92.0% pass rate, and Cosmos 3 reaches 55.2% with a 92.0% pass rate. Increasing K from 50 to 100 generally raises Coverage but leaves calibration largely unchanged. Across models, observed mean TVD is 31.2 versus a matched null mean of 8.33 and null 99th percentile of 9.22; all model-level observed values exceed their own 99th-percentile matched baselines in the reported Monte Carlo analysis. PAWEval agrees with a decisive human terminal label on 722 of 888 comparable videos, or 81.3%, but this validates only outcome readout on a selected comparable subset, not the benchmark metrics themselves. Causal controls show incomplete or incorrectly directed distribution shifts, while non-causal visual or textual cues can redirect probability mass. GPT-5.5's unconstrained prompt-engineering selections score 44.3 TVD and 35.0% Coverage before video generation; oracle target prompts improve all four tested generators' aggregate metrics, but target-hit rates remain only 37.6% to 58.1%. Coupled noise lowers TVD from 26.3 to 25.7 for Wan2.2 and raises Coverage from 63.4% to 69.2%, with larger or mixed gains for LTX-2.3 and Cosmos 3, indicating broader finite-budget exploration rather than a changed learned distribution. LoRA training shifts left-fall frequency in both upright and left-leaning pencil scenes, but the shared shift fails to produce the required scene-conditioned distributions; none of the adapted models aligns both scenes. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and limited ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the central contribution is a distribution-level formulation and benchmark for stochastic world-model evaluation, while the prompt, coupled-noise, and LoRA probes primarily combine existing techniques to diagnose the source of misalignment rather than introduce a new training algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides explicit definitions, scenario taxonomy, metric formulas, gate rules, matched Monte Carlo simulations with 50,000 replicates, rollout-budget sensitivity, causal/non-causal controls, and a human comparison study. It reports no error bars, confidence intervals over model-scene aggregates, multiple training seeds, formal significance tests beyond the Monte Carlo plus-one tail probability of 2.0 x 10^-5, or sensitivity analyses over alternative outcome taxonomies beyond the stated stricter readout threshold. The human study uses seven judgments per video and 1,500 videos, but only 888 videos are included in exact agreement. The benchmark scenarios, prompts, and evaluator details are described in the paper, and a project page is provided at https://pawbench.github.io; the text does not state that code, videos, annotations, model weights, or a runnable evaluator are released. The benchmark uses one manually selected source image per scenario, with source images generated by external image models, and relies heavily on a proprietary/current Gemini evaluator; evaluator errors, prompt sensitivity, and model-specific video readability can affect results. Most importantly, conditional TVD and Coverage exclude unreadable or out-of-schema outputs, so a model can receive a favorable conditional score while failing to produce a valid readable physical process frequently; SPR partially exposes this but is not integrated into the headline metrics. The baselines are broad and current as of the preprint's stated 2026 setting, but the paper does not compare against classical simulators, procedural physics engines, or a deliberately calibrated stochastic video model that would establish a positive control. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL): Practical: The evaluation can run on commercially available hosted APIs or local/open video systems, but the paper does not report total monetary cost, latency, hardware requirements, or a released end-to-end implementation. Efficient: It requires 50 or more generations per scenario and model, plus automated video judging, making a full 11-model evaluation expensive; coupled noise changes sampling dependence but does not reduce the number of rollouts. Effective: The evidence supports the narrower claim that current tested generators fail the benchmark's terminal-outcome distribution tests, but it does not show that PAWBench scores predict downstream planning or control performance. Scalable: The tested scale is 50 short-horizon scenarios and K=50 rollouts, with a limited K=100 sensitivity test; behavior at 10x–100x more scenes, longer horizons, continuous states, or interactive environments is not evaluated. The work delivers a benchmark specification and evaluation protocol, with a project page mentioned, but the text does not confirm a released software package, dataset download, or trained model artifact. Strengths: - It identifies a substantive evaluation blind spot: plausible single samples, diversity, and controllability do not imply a calibrated distribution over futures. - The calibration/coverage split is technically useful because it distinguishes incorrect probability allocation from missing support instead of collapsing them into one generative-quality score. - The matched finite-sample analysis and rollout-budget experiment directly address a plausible alternative explanation for the observed calibration gap; the 31.2 versus 9.22 TVD comparison is materially stronger than simply reporting raw frequencies. - The intervention suite separates language-side selection, finite-gallery exploration, and parameter-level distribution shifts, yielding the informative finding that global training-frequency changes do not produce state-conditioned physical probabilities. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly states that terminal outcomes omit trajectory-level dynamics and intermediate physical processes; finite rollout budgets make distribution estimates costly and incomplete; and the controlled, visually parseable scenarios do not cover long-horizon, interactive, or embodied environments. It proposes richer trajectory-level metrics, more efficient estimators, interactive scaling, and explicit calibrated-distribution training objectives as future work. The authors also state that C2C changes finite-budget exploration rather than the learned distribution and that the LoRA experiment establishes frequency shifting but not scene-conditioned probability learning. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The conditional treatment of readout failures is the most consequential methodological concern: invalid, unreadable, or physically implausible clips are removed from TVD and Coverage, while SPR is reported separately, so the primary metrics can reward models that generate a biased but readable subset after many failures. PAWEval's 81.3% agreement is measured only on videos where both humans and the evaluator already produce clear labels, and the selected 888-video intersection does not establish unbiased evaluator accuracy or validate distribution rankings. The benchmark's reference probabilities and outcome sets are manually designed for one source image per scenario; the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement on scenario construction, independent physical validation of every q, or robustness to alternative source images, camera viewpoints, prompts, and outcome discretizations. The work does not report confidence intervals or per-scene statistical tests for model differences, making close rankings such as TVD 24.2 versus 26.3 difficult to interpret. The causal-control claim is qualitative in the main text and does not provide a single aggregate causal sensitivity or non-causal invariance statistic. Finally, the central connection to world-model utility remains untested: no planner, controller, downstream decision task, real-video dataset, or calibrated simulator is used to show that PAWBench performance predicts practical failure. Bottom Line: This is a valuable diagnostic benchmark and a credible warning against equating plausible video generation with stochastic world modeling, but its strongest contribution is measurement and problem formulation rather than a deployable solution, and its conditional scoring and narrow synthetic scenario design require careful qualification before using it to rank models broadly.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an instrumentation, caching, serving, and router-training study that measures MoE memory-bandwidth limits, trains routers for temporal/domain locality, and evaluates training-free rerouting stacked with locality training. - Why it's important: Serving a 235B-parameter MoE on an 8 GB consumer GPU is dominated by SSD weight-transfer bandwidth, making cache misses—not arithmetic—the primary barrier to usable latency. - How it does it: It combines router telemetry and trace-based cache simulation with auxiliary temporal-locality and domain-confinement losses, then applies cache-aware inference-time expert substitution. - The good: The pre-registered multi-domain experiments show a clear, seed-stable tradeoff: locality training reduces cache misses by roughly 59–60% but costs 2.1–3.1% perplexity, while stacking it with rerouting reaches 80–82% miss reduction at 2.4–3.4% perplexity cost. - The missing: The central serving conclusions rely heavily on a Qwen3-30B routing proxy, simulated cache traces, and modeled rather than end-to-end deployed performance, with no direct Qwen3-235B routing trace or demonstrated 2–7× throughput measurement. - Read it or not: MoE serving and systems researchers should read it for its reproducible negative result and measured tradeoffs, while practitioners seeking an immediately validated edge-serving system can skip it because the proposed serving gains remain projections.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses inference for very large sparse MoE language models on commodity hardware whose aggregate weights exceed VRAM and system RAM. In the reported setting, Qwen3-235B-A22B in 4-bit form occupies 134 GB, while an RTX 3070 provides 8 GB of VRAM, 32 GB of DDR4 RAM, and a consumer NVMe SSD with approximately 2.4 GB/s bandwidth. Autoregressive decoding must repeatedly load roughly 12 GB of active expert weights per token, yielding a measured 0.44 tok/s warm rate and a roughly 50× bandwidth shortfall relative to a 10 tok/s target. Existing batching and offloading methods do not reliably overcome this wall because paging can induce thrashing, and fixed placement cannot exploit temporal or domain-specific routing sufficiently within the available fast-memory budget. The research gap is whether router behavior can be trained to make expert access cacheable without materially damaging language-model quality, and whether such training complements inference-time cache-aware routing. Key Idea: The core insight is that expert cacheability can be treated as a router-training objective, but temporal reuse and language-model quality compete at the tested scale; training can instead make experts locally substitutable, enabling inference-time rerouting to exploit cached alternatives at a lower marginal quality cost. The paper operationalizes this with adjacent-token similarity of router softmax distributions for temporal locality and explicit domain-to-expert slices for domain confinement, then combines the trained router with cache-conditional rerouting. The strongest conceptual result is not that locality training is free—it is not—but that training-induced expert co-adaptation makes subsequent inference-time substitution substantially less damaging. Methodology: The systems measurement first serves Qwen3-235B-A22B Q4_K_M in llama.cpp with experts streamed from NVMe, measuring warm/cold decode, prefill, and aggregate throughput at batch sizes 1, 8, and 32. The paper models throughput as bandwidth divided by bytes read per token and compares this with measurements. It then adds the approximately 120-line llama-moe-trace tool to llama.cpp's evaluation callback to record top-k expert IDs per layer and token without modifying model weights. Traces from Qwen3-30B-A3B—48 layers, 128 experts, top-8—cover 8,000 tokens each from prose, code, math, and medical domains; the traces feed per-layer LRU, LFU, static-pinning, and Belady cache simulations. The proposed Path-Mapped Serving policy places hot experts in fast memory and streams misses, but its throughput is projected from cache and I/O measurements rather than run end to end. For training, the paper uses a 137M decoder MoE with 8 layers, 16 experts, top-2 routing, 384-dimensional hidden states, and 38M active parameters, trained on 200M-token main-arm budgets from WikiText-103, CodeParrot-clean, and OpenWebMath. All arms use the Switch load-balancing term; arm B adds the temporal loss $L_{loc}=\mathrm{mean}(1-\langle p_t,p_{t-1}\rangle)$ with swept weight $\lambda$, and arm C adds a domain-confinement loss penalizing probability assigned outside predefined four-exclusive-plus-four-shared expert slices with $\mu=0.1$. The pre-registered criteria require at least 30% LRU miss reduction at 25% capacity with at most 1% perplexity increase for locality, and at least 90% static-pin hit rate at 50% capacity with at most 2% perplexity increase for domain confinement. Finally, cache-aware rerouting substitutes a resident expert when its score is within relative tolerance $\tau$ of the selected expert, and the paper tests stacking this with locality training. The losses directly encode the intended cache behavior, but the fixed domain partition is only weakly justified and the small MoE may not have enough capacity to separate specialization from locality constraints. Key Results: On Qwen3-235B-A22B-A22B Q4_K_M, the measured warm single-stream decode rate is 0.441 tok/s, cold decode is 0.128 tok/s versus a 0.20 tok/s model prediction, and prefill is 0.25 tok/s. Aggregate throughput rises only from 0.128 tok/s at batch 1 to 0.189 tok/s at batch 8, then falls to 0.087 tok/s at batch 32, where effective I/O falls to approximately 0.35 GB/s because of paging thrash; the bandwidth model tracks batch 1 and 8 within 6%. On Qwen3-30B-A3B traces, adjacent-token reuse is 0.444 versus 0.223 chance, 95% of traffic uses 52.5% of experts, and an LRU cache holding 13.4% of experts achieves 65.9% hit rate versus 59.2% for static pinning and 79.1% for the Belady oracle. Code has low expert-set overlap with general prose, math, and medical text—Jaccard-style similarities of 0.11–0.16 versus 0.33–0.42 among the other domains. Projected Path-Mapped Serving reduces miss traffic to approximately 2.7 GB/token and predicts roughly 0.9 tok/s, a 2–7× improvement over baseline, but the paper also estimates that 10 tok/s would require about 95% cache hits and approximately 52% of experts, or 70 GB, resident. In the 137M training study, the balance-only baseline has PPL 31.9–32.0, reuse 0.312–0.336, and LRU hit@25% of 0.480–0.494. With $\lambda=0.02$, miss reduction is about 15% at +0.3% PPL; with $\lambda=0.05$, miss reduction is 59–60% at +2.1–3.1% PPL; and $\lambda=0.03$ lies in an unfavorable intermediate region, with approximately 24% miss reduction and +1.8% PPL. Thus no locality setting satisfies the pre-registered joint criterion. Domain confinement reaches 0.991 static hit@50% but costs +3.1% PPL, also failing its quality gate. Training-free rerouting on the baseline reaches approximately 30% miss reduction at +0.8% PPL on one seed and +2.0% on the other, but 50% reduction costs +4.0–5.8% PPL. Stacking locality training and rerouting reaches 80–82% miss reduction at +1.9–3.4% PPL, with the 137M result reported as 80% at +2.4%; at 340M it reaches 82% at +3.4%. The same rerouting intervention has a 5–8× smaller marginal PPL cost on the locality-trained model than on the baseline. The 340M scale rung does not reduce the training tax: at roughly 57–58% miss reduction, the PPL cost increases from +2.0% at 137M to +2.5% at 340M, although this comparison uses the same 200M-token budget and therefore undertrains the larger model. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the tracer, edge-hardware measurements, pre-registered strict-bar refutation of adjacent-token locality training in a 137M multi-domain setting, domain-confinement arm, and training-time/inference-time complementarity are the main contributions, while the locality loss and cache-aware rerouting are substantially concurrent with or derived from existing work rather than newly invented here. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study's strongest rigor feature is explicit pre-registration of hypotheses, arms, metrics, and pass/fail thresholds, together with a correction log documenting discarded profiling data, a stride bug, initialization changes, dispatch changes, and normalization errors before results were unblinded. Main baseline results use two seeds, and the selected $\lambda=0.05$ locality arm uses two seeds with a monotonic dose-response; however, most hyperparameter points and the domain arm appear to have only one run, and no confidence intervals, statistical tests, or broader seed study are reported. The evaluation uses 200M tokens per arm after an amendment from 300M, and the 340M comparison uses the same token budget despite greater undertraining. Cache results are trace simulations rather than end-to-end cache-controller measurements, and the routing profile for the 235B serving target comes from the Qwen3-30B same-family proxy rather than the target model itself. Comparisons include relevant concurrent and prior work in the discussion, but the paper does not present a direct head-to-head end-to-end comparison against systems such as PowerInfer, MoE-Infinity, Fiddler, or cache-conditional routing. The authors release the pre-registration, training and analysis code, llama-moe-trace, router traces, unit tests, configurations, seeds, and data hashes at https://github.com/Shriniwas410/cacheable-by-design; no trained model weights are explicitly stated as released. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-measurement component. * Practical: The measurements run on commercially available hardware—a single RTX 3070, 32 GB RAM, and consumer NVMe—and the tracer is implemented as a small llama.cpp addition, but the projected PMS throughput is not demonstrated as a deployed serving system. * Efficient: The approach can reduce simulated expert-load misses by up to 59% through training and about 80–82% when stacked with rerouting, but locality training costs additional model training and the paper does not quantify cache-management, rerouting, or end-to-end latency overhead relative to competing offloaders. * Effective: The evidence establishes substantial reductions in simulated cache misses and a measured bandwidth bottleneck, but it does not establish equivalent end-to-end throughput or latency gains, and the training-only configurations fail the paper's own quality thresholds. * Scalable: The method is tested at 137M and 340M training-model sizes and on a 30B routing proxy, not at the 235B target's routing scale; behavior at 1B or larger, compute-optimal training budgets, other hardware, and higher concurrency remains unmeasured. The work delivers a released llama-moe-trace software tool, cache-simulation and training code, router traces, and reproducibility artifacts; it does not deliver a validated end-to-end edge-serving engine or trained production model. Strengths: - The bandwidth analysis connects measured 12 GB/token traffic, a 2.4 GB/s SSD ceiling, and the resulting 0.44 tok/s warm decode rate with a simple first-principles model, giving the serving problem a concrete quantitative basis. - The paper reports a useful negative systems result: batching improves throughput only through batch 8 and collapses at batch 32 because the assumed union-of-experts benefit is defeated by operating-system paging thrash. - The pre-registered joint quality/cacheability criteria prevent the large locality gains from being presented as an unconditional success; the dose-response and two-seed results directly expose the miss-reduction/perplexity tradeoff. - The training-time versus inference-time complementarity is a substantive empirical observation: the same rerouting intervention that costs up to 4.0–5.8% PPL on the baseline costs only 0.5–0.9% marginal PPL on the locality-trained model, and the stacked result replicates at 340M. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify the two-rung scale study, undertraining from the 200M-token budget, use of Qwen3-30B as a proxy for Qwen3-235B routing, single-machine and single-GPU evaluation, and the fact that batching and Path-Mapped Serving results are modeled rather than end-to-end deployed. They also acknowledge that the 340M non-shrinking tax is suggestive rather than decisive because the model is more undertrained at the matched token budget and the ladder has only two sizes. The paper confronts these limitations directly and names a compute-optimal run, a 1B-or-larger rung, and direct 235B tracing as future tests. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unacknowledged concern is evidentiary alignment between the headline serving target and the training/evaluation setup: cacheability is measured on a 30B model and trained on a 137M/340M toy MoE, while the claimed edge-serving benefit concerns Qwen3-235B, whose routing behavior may differ materially despite family similarity. The paper does not report end-to-end latency, throughput, CPU utilization, page-fault behavior under a purpose-built cache, or quality after actual PMS execution, so the 0.9 tok/s and 2–7× figures remain extrapolations. The comparison to existing serving systems is qualitative rather than experimental, and the work omits broader data distributions, task-level evaluations beyond perplexity, more than two seeds for key training arms, and compute-matched larger-scale training. The domain-confinement result is also difficult to interpret because the expert slices are imposed manually and may encode an artificial partition unavailable in realistic unlabeled streams. Finally, the claim that locality training creates mutually substitutable expert neighborhoods is plausible but not directly measured through expert representations, substitution accuracy, or controlled ablations separating router stickiness from expert co-adaptation. Bottom Line: This is worth reading as a reproducible, unusually candid measurement and negative-result study showing that cache-aware MoE routing has a real quality tradeoff and that trained locality can make inference-time rerouting cheaper, but it is not yet a convincing deployable alternative to established end-to-end MoE offloading systems.

Learning, Abstraction, and Creative Search for Interactive Agents

TL;DR - What it does: This dissertation contributes empirical studies, a graph-theoretic skill-discovery formulation, a regression domain-generalization benchmark, representation-quality metrics for multi-agent models, and theoretical frameworks for computationally creative search. - Why it's important: The work targets practical failure modes in interactive AI—brittle reinforcement-learning training, long-horizon planning, distribution shift, opaque agent models, and inefficient or biased creative search. - How it does it: It combines exhaustive hyperparameter analysis, graph augmentation and greedy shortcut selection, standardized cross-domain benchmarking, representation analysis using DCI/CKA/PCA metrics, and formalizations based on Wiggins’s Creative Systems Framework and quality-diversity search. - The good: The strongest evidence is the scale and statistical care of the regression benchmark and DQN study, including 73,500 configurations per environment, 10 seeds, 95% bootstrap intervals, and the finding that ERM remains difficult to beat in regression domain generalization. - The missing: Most claims about transfer to realistic, large-scale, stochastic, high-dimensional agents remain unevaluated; the creativity and quality-diversity chapters are primarily conceptual, and the skill-discovery evaluation relies on small deterministic grid worlds and a sampled candidate set. - Read it or not: Read it for practical RL benchmarking guidance, the Minimum Shortcut Problem formulation, or a useful synthesis of representation and creative-search perspectives; skip it if you need a single unified algorithm with demonstrated deployment-scale gains.

Problem & Motivation: The dissertation addresses how autonomous agents can learn reliably, form useful abstractions, generalize beyond training conditions, model other agents, and search creatively in interactive environments. The target domains include reinforcement learning, hierarchical control, multi-agent systems, regression under distribution shift, and computational creativity. The central gaps are practical guidance for diagnosing DQN failures, principled objectives for discovering reusable temporal abstractions, standardized regression domain-generalization evaluation, evaluation of latent multi-agent representations beyond predictive accuracy, and formal criteria for transformational creativity. The dissertation is an umbrella research document rather than a single tightly scoped method paper: its chapters address related aspects of agent-environment interaction but do not establish one common algorithmic framework or shared experimental testbed. Key Idea: The most identifiable technical insight is to treat useful abstraction as compression of decision sequences: in the Minimum Shortcut Problem, an option is represented as a shortest-path-preserving shortcut in the environment’s state-transition graph, and skills are selected to minimize all-pairs hop length. The dissertation’s broader conceptual idea is that agent quality should be assessed through internal learning and search dynamics—not only final reward or output—including hyperparameter sensitivity, representation structure, robustness under domain shift, and an agent’s ability to overcome its own search bias. Methodology: Chapter 2 exhaustively evaluates a CleanRL DQN over seven hyperparameters—learning rate, discount factor, target-network update frequency, replay-buffer size, batch size, exploration fraction, and final epsilon—on five modified Gymnasium environments. Agents train for 500,000 steps, use 40 greedy evaluation episodes at each of 500 checkpoints, and are scored by success rate, time to success, and normalized area under the learning curve; ALE and fANOVA random-forest surrogates plus stratified histograms analyze importance. Chapter 3 converts deterministic goal-conditioned MDPs into directed unit-weight state graphs, defines APHL as the sum of shortest-path hop counts over reachable pairs, and chooses up to k shortcut edges to minimize APHL. It distinguishes point, path, and compact options, proves NP-hardness for the unweighted single-source DAG case by reduction from Set Cover, and uses a greedy approximation with candidate filtering and a 10,000-shortcut cap. It evaluates discovered point options with tabular Q-learning on four grid worlds, using success probability and optimal-path probability over 100 sampled goals, four budgets, and five seeds. Chapter 4 constructs 11 regression datasets—synthetic nonlinear, hard nonlinear, sine-wave, Distshift world modeling, Bike Sharing, two Room Occupancy variants, ACS Income, ACS Poverty Ratio, Taxi Duration, and US Accident—using domain splits selected partly through a generalization-ratio heuristic. It adapts 16 DG algorithms from DomainBed-style implementations by replacing classification loss with MSE, performs 60-trial random hyperparameter searches, and evaluates global and split selection protocols with 15 runs, IQM losses, Mann–Whitney statistics, and 50,000-resample stratified bootstrap intervals. Chapter 5 trains 30 LSTM and 30 transformer ToMnets on two synthetic multi-agent datasets, varying character-embedding size among 64, 128, and 512, and evaluates action/goal prediction alongside DCI disentanglement, silhouette clustering, CKA-based stability and convergence, and PCA dimensionality reduction. Chapter 6 formalizes exploratory and transformational systems using Wiggins’s framework, defines inspired/uninspired search, bias, and beta-bias overcoming through value margins and reachability, and gives an MDP-based testing procedure. Chapter 7 proposes two unimplemented MAP-Elites extensions: local behavior-gradient regression and a genome-behavior latent model, followed by a proposed curiosity-driven quality-diversity mechanism. The main design decisions are generally motivated, but several are only partially justified: the restriction to dense-reward, deterministic, or synthetic settings; the use of topological hop reduction as a proxy for skill utility; the adaptation of classification DG methods by swapping in MSE; and the interpretation of synthetic parameter recoverability as representation quality. Key Results: Chapter 2 reports that learning rate and discount factor are the most consistently influential of the seven tested DQN hyperparameters across all five environments and all three metrics. The study evaluates 73,500 configurations per environment, 735,000 seeded agents per environment, 3,675,000 agent runs overall, and 10 seeds per configuration. Secondary effects favor shorter exploration schedules, lower final epsilon, larger batches, and generally larger replay buffers, but these effects vary by environment. Partial correlations for learning-rate/discount-factor interactions reach at most approximately 0.43 in the reported table, so the authors do not recommend interaction-specific tuning. A compact 3x3 learning-rate/discount-factor sweep on held-out discretized Pendulum and MinAtar Breakout identifies best observed settings of (0.005, 0.995) and (0.0005, 0.995), respectively, but no exact success or return improvements are reported. Chapter 3 reports that MSP-derived skills outperform adapted EDL, Eigenoptions, and Fiedler Options on the plotted grid-world learning curves for the evaluated budgets; at k=16, hop-reduction correlations with success are 0.53, 0.76, 0.61, and 0.73 for Big Grid, Sixty Four Rooms, Hotel, and Winding, and correlations with optimality are 0.74, not statistically significant for Sixty Four Rooms, 0.60, and 0.85. These correlations use only 16 method-budget observations per environment, so they support association rather than causal improvement. Chapter 4 finds no DG method significantly better than ERM when aggregating all 11 datasets under either global or split selection. Relative to ERM, global IQM loss differences are 0.1526 for ANDMask, 0.0724 for CORAL, 0.0093 for CausIRL-CORAL, and 0.0754 for VREx; split differences are 0.1268, 0.0439, -0.0178, and 0.0296, respectively. The split CausIRL-CORAL interval is [-0.0428, 0.0056], suggesting a trend but not significance under the stated criterion. On the five real-world datasets alone, IB-IRM has global IQM difference -0.0303 with a 95% interval [-0.0502, -0.0135], while IGA has split difference -0.0284 with interval [-0.0474, -0.0111]; this demonstrates strong dependence on dataset composition. Chapter 5 reports that LSTMs generally yield better modularity and compactness, while small and medium transformers can have slightly better predictive performance on gridworlds. Large transformers degrade sharply: their gridworld silhouette score becomes negative and their explicitness is close to zero. LSTM embedding size correlates with the number of PCA dimensions explaining 80% variance at approximately 0.97 on iterative action and 0.88 on gridworld. Chapter 6 provides no empirical validation of the creativity criterion and explicitly states that overcoming bias is proposed as necessary but not sufficient for creativity. Chapter 7 provides no implementation or measured speedup; its claimed efficiency and controllability gains remain hypotheses. Novelty Classification: The work spans NEW FORMULATION through the Minimum Shortcut Problem for skill discovery, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK through the regression DG suite and evaluation protocol, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING through the DQN-importance and ERM-versus-DG studies, NEW EVALUATION FRAMEWORK for multi-agent representations and transformational creativity, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION in the proposed parallel RL experimentation infrastructure. The genuine novelty is concentrated in the MSP formulation, the regression benchmark, and the application of representation metrics to ToMnet-style models; the DQN tuning study largely systematizes known empirical-design practice, while the quality-diversity chapter is a proposal rather than a demonstrated method. Rigor & Reproducibility: The DQN study has unusually broad configuration coverage, ten seeds per configuration, multiple importance analyses, held-out environments, explicit pseudocode, and a clear separation between early debugging and final-performance optimization. The MSP study supplies a reduction proof, algorithm pseudocode, complexity discussion, five seeds, error bars, multiple option budgets, and comparisons with three established baselines, but its candidate shortcuts are randomly subsampled or filtered and its main performance evidence is based on 16 method-budget points per environment. The DG benchmark reports 95% bootstrap intervals, IQM and nonparametric comparisons, global and split hyperparameter selection, 15 evaluation trials, and multiple datasets; however, it omits some recent methods, uses many tabular datasets, and adapts classification algorithms to regression in ways that may not preserve their intended guarantees. The representation study uses 5 random seeds per architecture-size setting and explicit synthetic ground-truth parameters, but it does not report numerical tables for most metrics or downstream-task validation. Code is explicitly linked for the DG benchmark at https://github.com/demkejon001/dgreg_bench and for multi-agent representation analysis at https://github.com/demkejon001/multi_agent_model_representation. The parallel RL runner is described as being worked toward open source, not as already released. No model-weight release is stated. Methodological concerns include benchmark construction and test-domain selection based on model-derived generalization ratios, equal weighting of synthetic and real-world datasets, evaluation of a method on environments whose structure is directly available to the method, and multiple comparisons without a consistently applied correction beyond an acknowledged Bonferroni check for one analysis. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with systems and benchmark artifacts but no demonstrated production deployment. Practical: The experiments run on commercially available GPUs and CPUs; the DG study reports approximately 0.5 GB GPU and 1.5 GB CPU RAM for Distshift experiments and up to 4 GB GPU/CPU RAM for the largest reported experiment. Efficient: The proposed DQN workflow is efficient for debugging only relative to exhaustive HPO, but the supporting sweep itself is extremely expensive—millions of seeded agents—and MSP’s greedy graph calculations scale poorly, with candidate evaluation near O(c|V|²) after filtering; no end-to-end runtime comparison against competing skill-discovery methods is given. Effective: Evidence supports improved early DQN diagnosis, higher gridworld learning performance for MSP options, and useful benchmark-level observations about ERM and representations, but it does not establish success on real deployed agents, realistic OOD control, or human-judged creative production. Scalable: The dissertation does not test 10x–100x larger environments, high-dimensional continuous-control agents, large multi-agent populations, or realistic creative spaces; the authors explicitly leave scaling and transfer as future work. The work delivers a regression benchmark and code repositories, analysis code and procedures for representation evaluation, algorithms and proofs in paper form, and a proposed but not released or fully implemented RL-parallelization tool; the quality-diversity contribution stops at paper form. Strengths: - The DQN chapter addresses a real experimental bottleneck and supports a simple two-parameter debugging workflow with an unusually exhaustive factorial study rather than anecdotal tuning advice. - The MSP chapter gives skill discovery a precise graph objective, connects point/path/compact options to distinct optimization variants, and provides a nontrivial NP-hardness result rather than only proposing a heuristic. - The DG benchmark is a useful negative-result contribution: it shows that specialized invariance and robustness methods do not reliably beat ERM in regression, while preserving dataset-level and real-world-only analyses that expose aggregation sensitivity. - The representation chapter correctly challenges predictive accuracy as a complete evaluation of multi-agent models and identifies concrete failure modes, especially the poor interpretability and stability of large transformers on its gridworld task. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit DQN conclusions to simple environments, a standard DQN implementation, dense-reward modifications, and the tested hyperparameter ranges, and call for studies of actor-critic methods, DQN extensions, larger environments, and longer horizons. MSP is explicitly restricted to optimal skills, deterministic goal-conditioned environments, and instruction-length reduction; the authors acknowledge that its options need not correspond to semantic or transferable skills. The DG chapter acknowledges resource constraints, omitted recent algorithms, and the predominance of tabular datasets. The representation chapter acknowledges synthetic datasets, the absence of one-shot/few-shot downstream evaluation, limitations of PCA as a metric, static-parameter assumptions, and the lack of representation generalization to unseen parameter subsets. The creativity chapter states that overcoming bias is necessary but not sufficient, that results depend on thresholds and horizons, and that the proposed QD methods have not yet been tested beyond toy problems. These limitations are generally confronted directly rather than hidden. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The dissertation’s overarching unity is conceptual more than technical: the chapters use different objectives, datasets, assumptions, and evaluation standards, so claims about a general methodology for interactive agents exceed the demonstrated integration. - The DQN importance conclusion may be sensitive to the CleanRL implementation, five mostly small environments, manually densified rewards, a search space centered on CartPole defaults, and the use of performance normalization by the best observed configuration; no comparison with automated HPO cost or broader DQN variants is provided. - The MSP evaluation does not isolate whether gains arise from the APHL objective, the privileged full-graph access, the conversion of point options into path options, or the candidate filtering procedure. The benchmark is deterministic and tabular, and the correlation analysis has a very small effective sample size. - The DG benchmark’s test-domain selection and synthetic constructions may favor particular invariance assumptions; the adaptation from classification to regression, unequal dataset sizes, and equal dataset weighting require stronger sensitivity analyses. The headline ERM conclusion is not universal even within the paper, since real-world-only aggregation produces significant gains for IB-IRM and IGA. - Representation metrics rely on synthetic agent parameters that are available exhaustively at evaluation time. The study does not establish that higher modularity, compactness, CKA stability, or PCA reduction improves downstream multi-agent decisions, transfer, calibration, or safety. - The creativity framework formalizes a compelling necessary condition but does not prove that the proposed tests discriminate creativity from stochastic exploration, reward hacking, search-budget effects, or a system that has memorized alternate strategies. The quality-diversity chapter makes no empirical claim despite being summarized as an improvement to creative search. - Several reported visual comparisons lack exact numerical values, confidence intervals, or formal statistical tests, limiting independent ranking of architecture and skill-discovery effects. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile dissertation for its practical RL evidence, MSP formulation, and regression DG benchmark, but its strongest contributions are several useful standalone studies rather than a validated end-to-end theory or deployable solution for robust, adaptive, creative agents.

#19 — Highly Innovative (77)

Training Agents to Achieve Goals

H Chan · utoronto.scholaris.ca · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This thesis develops a goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning toolkit comprising MEGA/OMEGA exploration, VLM-derived rewards, triangle-inequality-preserving metric architectures, VLM-based hindsight instruction augmentation (DIAL), and the STEVE-1 text-to-behavior agent. - Why it's important: These methods target the main barriers to generalist embodied agents—sparse rewards, long-horizon exploration, expensive language annotation, weak goal representations, and poor transfer to unseen instructions. - How it does it: It combines density-based frontier exploration and distribution matching with pretrained vision-language embeddings, structured metric parameterizations, hindsight relabeling, behavioral cloning, and pretrained behavioral priors. - The good: The strongest evidence is the breadth of concrete results, including roughly 100x faster PointMaze learning, 60.0% success on 60 novel real-robot instructions with DIAL, and STEVE-1 completing 12 of 13 short-horizon Minecraft tasks. - The missing: The central generalization claims remain bounded by narrow environments, small evaluation suites, dated baselines, low seed counts in several experiments, and dependence on hand-designed goal spaces, prompts, pretrained models, and favorable preconditions. - Read it or not: Researchers in goal-conditioned RL, embodied instruction following, and VLM-based control should read it for its modular methods and historical results, while readers seeking a single modern end-to-end generalist-agent evaluation can skip it in favor of newer unified benchmarks.
