Problem & Motivation: Security operations centers must triage alert outputs from IDS/IPS, WAF, firewalls, EDR/NDR systems, vulnerability scanners, and SIEM rules under high-volume, heterogeneous, and changing conditions. Periodic operational activity creates large false-positive populations, while genuine threats can also be periodic, low-and-slow, or context-dependent. Static device severity labels and alert-by-alert classifiers do not adequately incorporate asset criticality, vulnerability exposure, threat-intelligence evidence, attack stage, environmental posture, or analyst capacity. The paper targets the operational gap between isolated alert classification or correlation methods and a closed-loop triage system that reduces workload without deleting high-risk alerts. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat periodicity as a conservative routing signal rather than a deletion criterion: FFT detects candidate periodic groups and Pearson correlation validates them, but a risk gate protects alerts carrying IOC, exploitable-vulnerability, critical-asset, or kill-chain evidence. This fast branch is combined with a deeper evidence-fusion branch for aperiodic or uncertain alerts, followed by graph-contextual risk scoring. The multi-agent component is not a collection of autonomous generative models; it is a deterministic controller coordinating retrieval, plugin queries, and a BERT classifier. Methodology: The pipeline ingests alert records, traffic logs, asset inventories, vulnerability scans, and threat intelligence, then represents each alert as timestamp, structured fields, and raw message. Alerts sharing source, destination, and alert type are aggregated into hourly triplet-level time series. FFT identifies a dominant nonzero frequency when the peak-dominance ratio is at least 3.0 and the inferred period lies between 2 and 72 hours; Pearson correlation accepts a period only when the mean adjacent-period correlation exceeds 0.85. Groups failing these tests, or groups containing risk evidence, enter the multi-agent branch. A deterministic Master Agent parses alert context and invokes a local Knowledge Retrieval Agent, an Association Query Agent using IOC, IP-reputation, NetFlow, Whois, asset, and vulnerability plugins, and a BERT Reasoning Agent that predicts true-alert versus false-positive probability. Their outputs are fused using weighted confidence scores and a risk-gate term: alerts with a fused true-alert score at least 0.60 are retained, scores at most 0.30 are filtered, and intermediate cases go to manual review; confirmed high-risk evidence overrides the BERT prediction. Separately, the system constructs a cybersecurity graph from ATT&CK, CVE/CWE, CAPEC, D3FEND, APT, and IOC sources and links it to an asset-vulnerability graph. A semantic-integrity layer canonicalizes entities, checks schema and relation constraints, verifies timestamps and provenance, detects conflicts, quarantines invalid or stale facts, and publishes versioned snapshots. Dynamic risk is computed using six criteria and 17 sub-indicators, normalized to [0,1], weighted with expert-derived AHP weights, and scaled to [0,100], with external and internal environmental multipliers. The six criterion weights are 0.16 for target criticality, 0.31 for attack-stage hazard, 0.18 for intelligence match, 0.22 for attack feasibility, 0.07 for attack persistence, and 0.06 for environmental factor. Critical design decisions are the conservative risk gate, hierarchical workload routing, and explicit graph validation; the paper reports validation-based threshold selection and expert agreement, but gives limited justification for the specific fusion weights, hand-coded normalization rules, and choice of AHP over learned ranking objectives. Key Results: The false-positive classification benchmark contains 100,000 alerts collected over six months from four SOC environments, with 30,000 labeled false positives and 70,000 retained true alerts across scanning/probing, brute force, web attacks, malware communication, and policy-violation categories. Tenfold cross-validation reports accuracy 0.9467, precision 0.9220, recall 0.8971, F1 0.9102, and AUC 0.9730 with a 95% AUC interval of [0.969, 0.977]; the reported confusion matrix contains 67,757 correctly retained true alerts, 2,243 true alerts incorrectly filtered, 3,090 false positives retained, and 26,910 false positives filtered. The full noise-reduction configuration processes 780 alerts/s, versus 920 for FFT-PCC alone, 410 for multi-agent orchestration alone, and 486 for orchestration without BERT. Its F1 of 0.910 exceeds the strongest plotted baseline, XGBoost at 0.852, by 0.058 absolute, described as a 7.1% relative improvement; the compared methods also include alert correlation at 0.791, hybrid IDS at 0.816, semi-supervised filtering at 0.833, and active-learning NIDS at 0.846. The risk gate reduces high-risk erroneous filtering from 3.1% without the gate to 0.4%, while candidate-group reduction changes from 74.6% to 72.0%. On a separate 100,000-alert unlabeled production stream, manual samples of 1,000 filtered and 1,000 retained alerts yield a 72.0% alert-level noise-reduction rate, 89.2% filtering accuracy, and 95.4% retention accuracy. The vulnerability NER subsystem reaches 89.64% F1 at 34.6 ms mean inference latency, compared with 87.77% for BERT-BiLSTM-CRF and 63.20% for CRF. AHP ranking obtains Kendall tau 0.85 with a 95% interval of [0.81, 0.89], versus reported lower values for equal, entropy, and random weighting, and maintains precision above 0.92 at 90% high-risk recall in the plotted comparison. Under 10% removed IOC/CVE edges, 20%, and 30%, Kendall tau falls to 0.82, 0.78, and 0.74; with perturbed asset and vulnerability records, high-risk recall falls from 0.94 to 0.90 and precision from 0.93 to 0.89; on an unseen fourth SOC environment, false-positive F1 falls from 0.910 to 0.882 and ranking tau from 0.85 to 0.79. In a 30-day replay with ten analysts, the framework reports 6.5 minutes mean response time, 240 alerts/hour, NASA-TLX 43.1, and high-risk recall 0.94, compared with Splunk ES at 12.0 minutes, 118 alerts/hour, NASA-TLX 68.4, and recall 0.86. These results are promising but rely heavily on author-collected data, sampled production audits, and a controlled replay rather than live prospective deployment. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING are the best classifications: the paper contributes a production-oriented hierarchical routing and risk-gating architecture with graph integrity checks and contextual AHP scoring, while FFT, Pearson correlation, BERT classification, plugin orchestration, knowledge graphs, semantic validation, and AHP are individually established techniques combined for SOC alert triage rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm or ranking theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study includes component ablations, comparisons with XGBoost, alert correlation, hybrid IDS, semi-supervised filtering, and active-learning NIDS, robustness tests for missing graph edges and noisy asset data, an unseen-environment test, tenfold cross-validation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and expert annotation agreement. It reports Krippendorff's alpha of 0.82 for false-positive labels and 0.79 for risk levels, AHP consistency ratio 0.041, and expert-weight agreement statistics. The data/code statement gives an OSF repository at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/4KB5D containing processed data, anonymized alert records, scripts, configurations, and evaluation outputs, while the full sensitive alert dataset is available only from the corresponding author. Reproducibility remains incomplete because the full production data, plugin services, rule repository, graph-construction sources and transformations, BERT training details, branch weights, and end-to-end platform integration are not fully specified in the text. The evaluation description mixes chronological, triplet-isolated, cross-environment, and tenfold cross-validation settings without clearly stating which split produced each headline number. Thresholds and several indicators were tuned on validation data, but the paper does not fully document whether all graph-derived features, expert labels, or temporal aggregates were isolated from test periods. Baselines are reproduced on the authors' dataset, but their implementation details and operational tuning may not be equivalent to mature commercial systems. The reported statistical tests do not clearly account for clustered alerts, repeated measurements, analyst assignment, or platform-level dependence. The AHP evaluation also partly compares expert-derived weights against expert assessments, which limits independence of the validation target. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper implements and evaluates an integrated SOC triage system in replayed operational environments, although the evidence is primarily empirical rather than a prospective live deployment. Practical: The CPU FFT branch and V100 GPU BERT/evidence branch ran on commercially available Xeon and NVIDIA hardware, but deployment requires substantial integration with Syslog, Kafka, SIEM APIs, EDR/NDR, CMDB, vulnerability scanners, SOAR systems, graph synchronization, queues, and fallback services. Efficient: The full noise-reduction pipeline reaches 780 alerts/s and uses less than 8 GB memory for 100,000 alert groups in the reported configuration, but its comparison omits complete cost, latency, plugin-query overhead, and GPU utilization data relative to alternatives; the end-to-end throughput is only 240 alerts/hour because analyst handling remains the bottleneck. Effective: The benchmark and replay evidence shows improved false-positive discrimination, high-risk recall, response time, throughput, and NASA-TLX workload under the tested high-noise scenario, but it does not establish reduced incident loss, improved attack containment, or causal superiority in a live SOC. Scalable: The system claims asynchronous queuing, caching, distributed inference, and threshold-based runtime adaptation, but it is tested on one V100, four SOC environments, 100,000-alert datasets/streams, and a stated 10,000-alert-per-second load without a corresponding demonstrated end-to-end capacity analysis; behavior at 10×–100× scale is not evaluated. The paper delivers scripts, configurations, processed/anonymized data, and evaluation artifacts through the OSF repository, but it does not clearly establish that a complete deployable SOC software stack or all external plugins are publicly released. Strengths: - The risk-gated hierarchy addresses a real safety trade-off: it exploits periodicity for workload reduction while explicitly preventing periodicity alone from deleting alerts with threat, asset, vulnerability, or attack-stage evidence. - The paper evaluates on 100,000 alerts collected from four production SOC environments rather than relying only on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, or other network-traffic benchmarks that do not represent device-generated SOC alerts. - The evaluation separates complete-label classification from sampled production-stream auditing and reports the distinction between 94.67% benchmark accuracy and 89.2% sampled filtering accuracy, avoiding one common metric conflation. - The graph snapshot validation, provenance tracking, freshness checks, quarantine behavior, and robustness tests make the system's operational failure model more explicit than many alert-prioritization studies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the full real-environment dataset cannot be released; evaluation covers only four SOC environments; IoT/OT, cloud-native, and encrypted-traffic settings require adaptation; external queries introduce overhead and service-dependency risks; BERT can misclassify; the knowledge graph requires continuous updates and semantic validation; and the deterministic runtime controller has not been compared with multi-objective reconfiguration algorithms. They also acknowledge the need for conservative filtering, manual review of uncertain cases, validated graph snapshots, and broader standardized benchmarks. These limitations are addressed directly, although the paper still presents the end-to-end platform results more strongly than the experimental controls warrant. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unacknowledged concern is causal attribution in the platform comparison: the proposed framework is compared with Splunk ES, QRadar, Elastic Security, and Wazuh under a replay with two analyst groups, but the paper does not establish matched hardware, equivalent integrations, identical alert semantics, balanced analyst crossover, or equal automation and filtering policies. The 10,000-alert-per-second statement is difficult to reconcile with the reported 240-alert/hour analyst throughput and does not constitute a stress test of the complete pipeline. The paper provides no per-attack-category results, calibration analysis, precision-recall operating-point trade-offs, cost of false negatives, or incident-level outcome measurement. The risk-ranking evaluation appears vulnerable to circularity because expert judgments help define AHP weights and also provide the comparison notion of ranking quality; the paper does not provide an independent operational utility label or analyst decision-quality measure. The central multi-agent contribution is largely orchestration of hand-built rules and external queries, so the incremental value of each plugin, graph component, integrity check, and evidence branch is not isolated beyond coarse ablations. The claimed 0.4% high-risk filtering error depends on the authors' risk-gate evidence definitions and graph coverage, whose recall and adversarial robustness are not measured. Finally, chronological and triplet-isolated split claims are not reconciled clearly with the headline tenfold cross-validation results, leaving potential temporal, entity, or feature-construction leakage insufficiently resolved. Bottom Line: Practitioners working on SOC alert fatigue can gain a useful architecture and realistic evaluation checklist from this paper, but its large end-to-end improvements should not be accepted as evidence of algorithmic superiority until independently replicated with matched platform controls, transparent splits, and live incident-level outcomes.

Scaffolding Minds: Optimizing Latent Visual Target Representations for Multimodal Reasoning

H Kang, Y Chen, L Liu, JS Andersen, A Ogale, B Sun… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-stage latent-visual-reasoning framework that learns task-optimized latent targets from training-time helper images and applies reward-guided Gaussian exploration to the latent block. - Why it's important: It targets the information loss and inference cost of text-only visual reasoning while avoiding the substantial latency of generating intermediate images. - How it does it: A trainable copy of the vision encoder is optimized through the downstream answer loss, after which input-adaptive mean and variance heads sample residual latent actions during GRPO-style reinforcement learning. - The good: On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, the full method reaches 75.0% average FrozenLake accuracy versus 65.5% for VaLR, with the gap increasing to 19 percentage points on 32×32 grids; it also reaches 73.9% average accuracy across nine visual-centric benchmarks versus 68.7% for VaLR. - The missing: The evaluation does not establish robustness when helper images are unavailable, costly, automatically generated, or substantially different from the training distribution, and the visual-benchmark training setup includes held-out-benchmark data in some cases. - Read it or not: Researchers working on multimodal latent reasoning or efficient visual inference should read it for the target-optimization and latent-exploration ablations, while practitioners should wait for evidence beyond curated helper-image settings.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (82) are high because task-optimized latent targets and learned residual exploration form a coherent, nontrivial advance over fixed latent visual features. Rigor (76) benefits from extensive component ablations, multiple benchmark families, and latency analysis, but is weakened by benchmark-mixture training, privileged helper images, incomplete seed reporting, and no release artifact. Completeness (68) and Resilience (65) are constrained by uncertain out-of-distribution generalization and the possibility that helper-image information drives the gains, while Impact (72) reflects promising low-overhead inference without deployment or checkpoint evidence. The weighted composite is 0.20*78 + 0.25*76 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*72 = 74.05, rounded to 74.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Multimodal models often lose fine-grained spatial and perceptual evidence when they verbalize visual reasoning into text, while methods that generate intermediate images incur large inference-time costs. Existing latent visual reasoning methods insert continuous latent tokens into the reasoning chain, but generally supervise those tokens using frozen, general-purpose vision features from a training-time helper image. Such features are not optimized for the downstream decision and may preserve irrelevant perception while omitting reasoning-critical evidence. During reinforcement learning, prior methods either optimize only the text trajectory or use a deterministic fixed-variance Gaussian as a latent regularizer, limiting direct exploration of alternative continuous reasoning states. The affected domain is visual question answering and spatial planning, especially tasks requiring fine-grained localization, comparison, or multi-step spatial decisions. The framework assumes that suitable helper images exist during training but discards them at inference. Key Idea The central insight is to treat the latent target representation itself as a trainable task-dependent object rather than as a fixed projection of a generic vision encoder, and then to treat deviations from the resulting latent prior as explicit continuous actions that can be explored with reward feedback. The first idea addresses representation quality; the second addresses exploration. The two components are conceptually distinct but are presented as complementary: Stage 1 establishes a high-quality latent space, while Stage 2 samples and optimizes local residuals around the generated latent prior. Methodology The pipeline has two training stages and an inference-time latent-generation path. In the Stage 1 scaffolding phase, a trainable copy of the VLM vision encoder followed by a cross-attention pooling module maps a helper image h to K=4 target tokens z. The base VLM remains frozen, and the scaffolding encoder is optimized with the teacher-forced answer cross-entropy, L_scaffolding(ψ)=L_CE(y|x,z), so its output is useful to the downstream VLM rather than merely aligned with a generic vision-feature space. In the generation phase, the scaffolding encoder is frozen and the base VLM is fine-tuned to generate K latent tokens z from x alone using learnable latent embeddings processed in one forward pass. The objective is λ_latent/K times the sum of squared distances between z_k and z*_k plus λ_task L_CE(y|x,z), with the default weights 1.0 and 0.5. At inference, the helper image and scaffolding encoder are discarded. In Stage 2, the generated latent prior z_θ is perturbed by a diagonal Gaussian residual Δz sampled from N(μ(z_θ),σ(z_θ)^2), where two MLP heads predict input-adaptive mean and variance from shared latent-position hidden states. The sampled block z_θ+Δz replaces the deterministic latent block during rollout. GRPO then combines a block-level latent importance ratio for the sampled action with per-token text ratios, clipped at ε=0.2, and adds a KL penalty of 0.001 to the Stage 1 reference policy. Zero initialization of the mean head and σ=0.05 initialization of the variance head stabilize early exploration. The main design decisions—task-loss optimization of the scaffold, joint latent/task supervision, and learned residual sampling—are supported by ablations, although the choice of four tokens and helper-image construction is evaluated mainly on FrozenLake. Key Results On FrozenLake, the method uses 4,550 training examples from even levels 8–32 and 100 held-out examples per reported level. With Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Scaffolding Encoder+RL obtains 96.0%, 82.0%, 67.0%, and 55.0% at grid sizes 8×8, 16×16, 24×24, and 32×32, respectively, for a 75.0% average. This exceeds SFT at 52.0% by 23.0 points, SFT+GRPO at 53.8% by 21.2 points, and the strongest prior latent baseline VaLR at 65.5% by 9.5 points; the 32×32 advantage over VaLR is 19 points. It exceeds DiffThinker’s 64.3% average by 10.7 points, although the image-generation comparisons have different inference mechanisms. On nine visual-centric benchmarks—V★, BLINK, MMVP, MMStar, CVBench, HRBench-4K, HRBench-8K, MME-RealWorld-Lite, and Jigsaw—the full method scores 90.6%, 67.2%, 76.7%, 73.5%, 88.4%, 77.5%, 74.1%, 57.3%, and 59.7%, respectively, averaging 73.9%. This is 5.2 points above VaLR’s 68.7% and 6.2 points above the strongest listed thinking-with-images average of 67.7% (SkiLa), while it is 10.4 points above Vanilla SFT’s 63.5%. The largest gains over the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B are 20.7 points on MMVP, 17.6 on MME-RealWorld-Lite, and 13.9 on CVBench; the smallest are 8.9 on HRBench-4K and 9.3 on Jigsaw. Stage 1 alone improves FrozenLake from 58.0% for the prior mean-pooling latent setup to 72.0%; under a fixed Stage 1 checkpoint, latent sampling adds 3.0 points, versus 1.8 for VLPO and 0.6 for text-only RL. The method is tested at standard benchmark scale, not at production-scale model or workload scale. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new elements are the end-to-end task-optimized scaffolding encoder for producing latent targets and the explicit learned Gaussian policy over residual latent actions; the surrounding VLM fine-tuning, GRPO clipping, cross-attention pooling, and KL regularization are established ingredients combined for latent visual reasoning. The empirical contribution is evidence that target optimization contributes more than the objective change alone and that latent exploration improves a strong Stage 1 prior. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes useful component ablations: frozen versus tuned vision encoders, mean pooling versus attention pooling, three Stage 2 RL strategies, token-count sweeps, helper-image comparisons, loss-weight sweeps, model-scale tests, LoRA tests, and latency measurements. Reported main results include mean±values, and the appendix states that the 3B and LoRA experiments average three seeds; the paper does not clearly state the number of seeds for every main table, nor does it report statistical significance tests or confidence intervals beyond the displayed deviations. FrozenLake baselines are trained and evaluated by the authors under a shared backbone, dataset, and protocol, which improves comparability, but independent reproduction is not reported. Some visual-benchmark baselines use original checkpoints/code while others are re-implementations, so the comparison is heterogeneous. The paper does not mention a public code repository, dataset release, model-weight release, or URL for an implementation. A methodological concern is that the visual-centric mixture uses official training data where available and, notably for MMVP, trains on 70% of the released questions while evaluating on the remaining 30%; this is a benchmark-specific split rather than a clean evaluation on an untouched test distribution. Helper images include annotated crops, highlighted relationships, or value-function heatmaps that may encode substantial privileged information during training, and the paper does not measure how performance changes with noisy, incomplete, automatically generated, or unavailable helpers. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The inference path runs on commercially available hardware and is measured on one A100, with only the base VLM, four latent tokens, and two small MLP heads retained; training nevertheless uses eight 80-GB A100 GPUs for approximately 10 hours per configuration. Efficient: Single-query FrozenLake latency is 272 ms versus 260 ms for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, a 4.6% overhead, and is lower than the reported approximately 540–980 ms for listed image-generation or tool-calling systems, though it is slower than several latent baselines at 266–269 ms. Effective: The method improves exact-match path accuracy and multiple-choice benchmark accuracy, with gains of 9.5 points over VaLR on FrozenLake and 5.2 points over VaLR across nine visual benchmarks, but the evidence measures curated benchmark proxies rather than deployment-level reliability, calibration, or safety. Scalable: The paper tests 3B and 7B backbones, LoRA, and grid sizes through 32×32, but it does not test 10×–100× larger images, contexts, model sizes, datasets, rollout groups, or production workloads; scalability beyond these settings is therefore claimed only indirectly. The work delivers a trained-model method and implementation description, but no software artifact, public checkpoint, or repository is stated. Strengths - The Stage 1 ablation isolates two effects that are often confounded: changing from feature regression to task-loss optimization adds 4.3 points, while tuning the vision encoder adds a further 10.0 points, supporting the claim that target quality—not simply adding latent tokens—is the dominant factor. - The Stage 2 comparison directly tests text-only RL, VLPO-style deterministic regularization, and learned Gaussian sampling under the same scaffolding checkpoint; the reported gains are correspondingly attributable more plausibly to latent exploration than to generic RL. - The evaluation combines controlled spatial planning with nine heterogeneous visual-centric benchmarks, and the FrozenLake results show an increasing advantage as grid size rises, from 5 points over VaLR at 8×8 to 19 points at 32×32. - The method retains low inference overhead: four latent tokens and lightweight adjustment heads yield 272 ms per query on an A100, making the approach substantially cheaper than methods that repeatedly generate and re-encode images. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge that the framework requires intermediate helper images during training and do not solve settings in which those images are unavailable or expensive. They also state that they do not exhaustively search helper-image designs for FrozenLake and leave automatic helper-image proposal for new domains to future work. These limitations are stated directly, but their practical effect is not quantitatively evaluated. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The strongest generalization claim is weakened by training on mixtures covering the evaluated visual benchmarks and by using a 70/30 split of MMVP, rather than evaluating exclusively on untouched benchmark test data or a genuinely out-of-domain suite. - The helper image can contain privileged information such as an optimal-path overlay or value-function heatmap; the paper does not compare against equally privileged non-latent methods, quantify helper-generation cost, or test imperfect helpers, creating uncertainty about how much of the gain comes from the scaffold versus the information supplied by the helper. - The proposed Gaussian policy is described as input-adaptive, but the paper does not report learned variance statistics, exploration diversity, action-distribution diagnostics, reward calibration, or whether improvements arise from the mean shift, variance learning, or both. - The method is evaluated primarily with one backbone family, Qwen2.5-VL, and the model-scale evidence remains limited to 3B and 7B; there is no test against larger open models or a fundamentally different VLM architecture. - Main-result reproducibility is incomplete: seed counts, complete training-data construction for the nine benchmarks, implementation details for all reproduced baselines, and release artifacts are not clearly provided in the supplied paper text. - The paper reports single-query latency on one A100 but omits training FLOPs, parameter counts for the scaffolding and RL heads, memory consumption, batch-throughput measurements, and latency under realistic autoregressive answer lengths. - Exact-match FrozenLake reward is sparse and benchmark-specific; the paper does not establish whether the latent policy improves intermediate planning quality, robustness to distribution shifts, or behavior on tasks with dense or noisy rewards. Bottom Line This is a technically credible and empirically well-supported advance for latent visual reasoning, particularly because its controlled ablations show that task-optimized targets matter more than fixed vision features and that explicit latent exploration adds further gains, but its practical and scientific impact remains bounded by privileged helper images, benchmark-mixture evaluation, limited backbone diversity, and absent release artifacts.

UrbanGround: From Local Perception to Spatial Agency in a Real-Scale City (70 ▲ )

Tianjie Ju, Zheng Wu, Yueqing Sun, Yuhan Cui, Bobo Li, Shengqiong Wu, Pengzhou Cheng, Haodong Zhao, Zongru Wu, Xinbei Ma, Doris Zhang, Kunling Li, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu, Hao Fei, Qi Gu, Gongshen Liu, Zhuosheng Zhang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces URBANGROUND, a Unity-based, georegistered Hong Kong sandbox and five-level benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language model agents in closed-loop urban perception, navigation, planning, and dynamic-environment interaction. - Why it's important: Existing multimodal-agent evaluations often test isolated visual reasoning, bounded simulated spaces, or disconnected street-view observations, leaving unclear whether local perception supports reliable action across a physically constrained real-scale city. - How it does it: It streams territory-wide 3D geospatial data and a pedestrian network into a collision-enabled simulator, exposes first-person and interactive-map observations with structured actions, and evaluates agents from local recognition through long-horizon navigation and replanning. - The good: Across 810 manually verified instances and 10 contemporary MLLMs, the benchmark clearly separates local competence from sustained agency: for example, GPT-5.5 reaches 82.5% visual-recognition accuracy and 75.0% short-navigation success but 0.0% long-navigation success, while trajectory analyses show that 31.25% of its long-navigation runs make substantial progress and later lose it. - The missing: The study does not report multiple-seed or repeated-run variability, controlled ablations of map access, memory, prompting, action duration, or simulator realism, nor comparisons with specialized navigation agents or classical map-based planners. - Read it or not: Researchers working on embodied MLLM evaluation, urban navigation, or long-horizon agent memory should read it for the environment and failure taxonomy, while readers seeking a new navigation algorithm can skip it because the paper primarily contributes a benchmark and empirical diagnosis.
Why this rank
Scored using the Systems profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong: the real-scale, georegistered city benchmark exposes a meaningful gap between local perception and sustained spatial agency. Rigor (68), Completeness (68), and Resilience (62) are held back by missing repeated-run variability, specialized and oracle baselines, component ablations, simulator-fidelity measurements, and single-city coverage, while Impact (82) reflects the released simulator, native builds, benchmark, and evaluation code. Problem & Motivation: The work addresses whether an agent that recognizes landmarks and spatial relations from individual views can maintain a usable spatial frame while moving through a large, physically constrained urban environment. The target domain is multimodal-agent interaction with cities containing dense buildings, steep terrain, elevated walkways, road crossings, changing visibility, and moving pedestrians. Prior evaluations typically isolate local visual reasoning, use game-specific worlds, operate in bounded indoor spaces, or use street-view and aerial observations without continuous physical interaction in one geographic frame. The unresolved gap is the transition from local evidence to persistent, globally aligned, and adaptive action: an agent must retain earlier landmarks after they leave view, distinguish geometric proximity from traversable pedestrian routes, follow explicit or implicit goals, and revise plans when routes or environmental conditions change. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat spatial agency as a cumulative progression from grounding to persistence to adaptation, and to expose each transition in one georegistered, closed-loop city. Instead of judging agents only by answers or endpoint success, URBANGROUND measures whether local spatial evidence remains useful after viewpoint changes, whether route state survives extended interaction, and whether behavior changes appropriately when visibility, connectivity, or pedestrian traffic changes. Methodology: URBANGROUND loads Hong Kong’s territory-wide 3D Visualisation Map as textured Cesium 3D Tiles and combines it with the georeferenced 3D Pedestrian Network in a shared WGS84-derived coordinate frame. Unity streams visible tiles, uses their geometry for collision, instantiates a continuous first-person character, records pose/elevation/heading, and simulates time of day, weather, rain exposure, road closures, and Rocketbox pedestrians. An external MLLM receives RGB first-person observations, text task context, interaction history, and an optional interactive overhead map; it returns one structured action per turn from movement, sprinting, looking, jumping, map manipulation, or termination, with no route API, coordinate readout, shortest-path signal, or teleportation. Episodes are capped at 100 interaction steps, with movement actions limited to two seconds. The five-level ladder contains visual recognition, orientation understanding, and active exploration questions; short- and long-range, instructional, and constrained navigation; place-type search and implicit-intent inference; time-window and multi-stop planning; and dynamic road-closure replanning and navigation among pedestrians. Evaluation uses answer accuracy for question answering, a 15-meter endpoint tolerance for labeled navigation, task-specific completion rules for search and multi-destination tasks, pedestrian-network adherence (the fraction of action time on the registered network), safe-progress/closure measures, and pedestrian-collision rate. The georegistered physical simulation and fixed model-facing interface are well motivated for isolating spatial interaction, but the paper does not provide a formal learning objective because the evaluated agents are prompting-based, and it does not quantify the fidelity or geometric error of the reconstructed city and pedestrian network. Key Results: The evaluation covers 810 manually verified base instances: 220 Level-1 local-understanding tasks, 240 Level-2 explicit-navigation tasks, 120 Level-3 implicit-instruction tasks, 120 Level-4 multi-task-planning tasks, and 110 Level-5 dynamic-environment tasks, evaluated with 10 MLLMs including GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro, GLM-5V-Turbo, and Kimi-K3. Local recognition is substantially stronger than orientation: GPT-5.5 obtains 82.5% visual-recognition accuracy but 40.0% orientation accuracy; Claude Opus 5 obtains 91.3% and 58.3%, respectively; Gemini 3.6 Flash obtains 93.8% and 56.7%. Active-exploration accuracy remains moderate to high, ranging from 46.3% for Gemini 3.1 Pro to 82.5% for Claude Opus 5. Short navigation is possible for some models, with 75.0% for GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 and 67.5% for Kimi-K3, but long navigation is nearly absent: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.2, and Gemini 3.6 Flash obtain 0.0%, while the best result is 3.8% for Kimi-K3. Overall navigation success across eight subtasks peaks at 22.9% for Claude Opus 4.6 and 22.5% for Kimi-K3. Instructional navigation reaches at most 42.0% for Kimi-K3, while time-window scheduling reaches at most 3.3% and multi-stop planning at most 3.3%. In dynamic tasks, road-closure success is 0.0% for eight of ten models and 3.3% for Claude Opus 4.6 and Kimi-K3; pedestrian-navigation success is at most 3.8%, and collision rates remain high at 76.3%–90.0%. Pedestrian-network adherence is much higher than task success, often above 90%, demonstrating that locally compliant movement does not imply route completion or obstacle awareness. In matched condition tests, GPT-5.5 local QA decreases from 63.6% in clear conditions to 59.1% at dusk, while its short-navigation success remains between 72.5% and 76.3%; this divergence supports the claim that appearance robustness and route-state maintenance are distinct. For GPT-5.5 LongNav, 57.5% of episodes end closer to the goal than at the start, but 31.25% later lose substantial progress, 27.50% never achieve it, 22.50% stop outside the arrival radius, and 18.75% retain progress until timeout. These results are diagnostic rather than comparative evidence for a new algorithm, and the evaluated models are current vendor models, making their exact versions and availability important to interpreting reproducibility. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW BENCHMARK, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the genuinely novel contribution is the combination of territory-wide, georegistered real-city geometry, continuous collision-constrained first-person interaction, map-grounded navigation, and dynamic urban conditions in a single benchmark, while the agent protocol and underlying components largely combine established simulator, visual-language navigation, and game-agent evaluation ideas. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper releases a project page, code repository at https://github.com/UrbanGround/UrbanGround, and native application downloads at https://github.com/UrbanGround/UrbanGround/releases; it also gives task definitions and prompts in the appendices and bases the city on publicly released Hong Kong government geospatial datasets. Manual construction and two-round verification of all 810 instances, fixed prompts, explicit action schemas, hidden-state restrictions, endpoint tolerances, and matched weather/time conditions strengthen procedural reproducibility. However, the paper does not state the number of independent runs per model-instance pair, report multiple random seeds, provide significance tests for most comparisons, or quantify confidence intervals except for selected trajectory-level plots. No ablation isolates the effect of the map, frame buffer, prompt design, action granularity, memory length, collision model, or dynamic components. There is no comparison with specialized vision-language navigation policies, graph planners, oracle localization, or classical pedestrian routing, so the benchmark diagnoses general MLLM behavior but does not establish that its failures are specific to language-model reasoning rather than the interface or protocol. The manually authored Hong Kong-only tasks and evaluator-defined geographic labels also limit external validity, and some dynamic measures—particularly pedestrian collision rate—could be sensitive to avatar density, motion policy, and collision geometry that are not fully characterized. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, with an empirical benchmark evaluation. Practical: The released Unity application and native builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux indicate that it can run on commercially available desktop hardware, although the paper does not state minimum GPU, CPU, RAM, or inference requirements. Efficient: Runtime tile streaming avoids loading the entire territory at once, but compute, memory, bandwidth, rendering cost, and MLLM API latency relative to smaller simulators or specialized navigation systems are not measured. Effective: The evidence supports the benchmark’s ability to expose differences between local recognition, navigation, and adaptation, but it only indirectly measures real-world urban agency because success occurs in a reconstructed simulator and no physical-robot or human-navigation transfer study is reported. Scalable: The environment covers territory-wide Hong Kong geospatial data, but the agents are tested under a 100-step limit and the paper does not evaluate 10×–100× longer trajectories, additional cities, larger pedestrian populations, or substantially denser dynamic events. The work delivers a reusable software artifact, benchmark task suite, simulator, prompts, and evaluation code rather than a trained navigation model. Strengths: - The benchmark targets a consequential and under-measured failure mode: local spatial competence does not automatically compose into persistent, goal-directed behavior. - The georegistered combination of aerial/3D city geometry, pedestrian connectivity, continuous physical motion, and first-person/map observations gives the evaluation stronger spatial consistency than disconnected street-view or waypoint-only settings. - The five-level ladder and complementary metrics reveal several distinct failure modes, including directional-grounding weakness, geometric-proximity versus traversability errors, progress regression, route-obsolescence failures, and high pedestrian-collision rates despite high network adherence. - The retrospective checkpoint analysis is a useful diagnostic addition: for GPT-5.5, rescoring the closest checkpoint raises the fraction of episodes closer than the start from 57.5% to 98.7% and the fraction achieving at least 20% distance reduction from 34.6% to 67.9%, showing that endpoint failure partly reflects regression rather than inability to initiate useful movement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly frame URBANGROUND as a foundation for future work rather than a complete solution and acknowledge that current agents fail when local skills must compose into sustained exploration, that visibility changes affect local question answering, and that road closures and moving pedestrians expose weak online updating and constraint adherence. They do not provide a dedicated limitations section in the supplied text, and they do not explicitly discuss single-city coverage, simulator-to-reality transfer, model-run variability, simulator fidelity, task-author bias, or the absence of specialized navigation baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unacknowledged concern is that the paper attributes failures to spatial memory, orientation, and adaptation without experimentally separating those causes from interface and control issues. Agents must infer movement outcomes from screenshots, issue coarse up-to-two-second actions, maintain state in text interaction history, and use a manually designed map; no oracle-localization, finer-control, route-planner, or memory-augmentation baselines establish which bottleneck dominates. The evaluation also lacks per-instance repeated trials and uncertainty estimates for the main tables, so small task subsets—such as 30 constrained-navigation or 30 road-closure instances—can produce unstable percentages. A single Hong Kong reconstruction cannot establish general city-scale validity, and the paper does not report mesh/geolocation accuracy, map readability, pedestrian density, closure timing distribution, or whether landmarks and task locations leak geographic knowledge from model pretraining. The claim that the benchmark is physically grounded is credible within Unity but remains a proxy for real pedestrian behavior because no human-agreement, simulator-fidelity, or real-world transfer evaluation is supplied. Finally, comparing proprietary vendor models at unspecified inference configurations makes model-to-model differences difficult to reproduce and may confound model capability with API version, latency, context-window, or prompt-handling differences. Bottom Line: URBANGROUND is worth reading and likely useful as a benchmark release because its real-scale georegistered environment and failure analyses expose a genuine gap between visual recognition and sustained urban agency, but its scientific conclusions would be substantially stronger with repeated trials, specialized and oracle baselines, component ablations, simulator-fidelity measurements, and evaluation beyond Hong Kong.

EchoWM: Open and Enterable Omnimodal World Models (43 ▲ )

Songchun Zhang, Yaowei Li, Junhao Zhuang, Weiyang Jin, Haoyu Wang, Xin Lu, Yilang Sun, Shiyi Zhang, Haoran Li, Xiaoxiao Ma, Yuming Li, Yijun Liu, Yaofeng Su, Yanwen Ma, Haoyu Wu, Zihan Su, Yue Ma, Lvmin Zhang, Haoyang Huang, Zeyue Xue, Anyi Rao, Nan Duan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EchoWM, an interactive world model that generates 720p video, environmental sound, music, and speech while following continuous first-person or third-person camera trajectories across multiple turns. - Why it's important: Existing interactive video/world models generally provide silent visual rollouts or domain-specific controls, limiting their usefulness for enterable environments, games, simulation, and multimodal media interaction. - How it does it: It converts discrete controls and metric poses into a globally calibrated relative 6-DoF camera-intent trajectory, injects that trajectory through a relative-geometry UCPE attention branch, and trains the model with staged audio-visual, control, joint, and autoregressive objectives. - The good: On the reported public benchmarks, EchoWM obtains 81.7 average on the 158-case WBench Navigation split and reaches 83.91/83.96 VBench scores on the short SANA-WM-Bench simple/hard splits, while its four-step causal variant leads the evaluated causal models at 80.13/81.06 on the 961-frame protocol. - The missing: The paper does not report model size, training/inference compute, latency, throughput, or numerical ablation results sufficient to isolate the contributions of scale calibration, UCPE conditioning, progressive training, and self-gradient forcing. - Read it or not: Researchers working on interactive video generation, camera control, or multimodal world models should read it for the unified camera-intent formulation and system design, but practitioners should wait for stronger efficiency and reproducibility evidence before treating it as deployable.

Problem & Motivation The work targets interactive generative environments in which a user navigates a generated scene and receives synchronized visual and acoustic feedback. The intended domains include games, real-world and cinematic scenes, stylized environments, driving, robotics-related scenes, and embodied or social settings. Prior world models often generate only video, expose controls tied to a particular keyboard, controller, actor, or camera rig, or support only a single viewpoint convention. Joint audio-visual generators provide sound and speech but generally lack continuous geometric interaction. The specific gap is a single open-domain interface that supports continuous viewpoint evolution in both first- and third-person settings while retaining scene consistency and producing video, environmental sound, music, and speech together. The paper deliberately narrows the interaction problem to navigation and viewpoint-related motion rather than arbitrary actor actions such as attacking, jumping, manipulating objects, or issuing robot commands. Key Idea The central insight is to treat interaction as camera intent rather than device action or actor-specific control. A relative 6-DoF trajectory describes how the observer intends to move and view the world. In first-person scenes, this trajectory represents observer motion; in third-person scenes, the model learns from data how the same camera evolution should induce coordinated character motion, camera following, and scene framing. The representation is paired with a single robust dataset-level translation scale and relative UCPE geometry, allowing heterogeneous discrete commands, recovered video poses, and simulator poses to share one conditioning pathway. This is a meaningful unification, although the overall system also combines established ingredients—camera conditioning, joint audio-visual diffusion, causal teacher forcing, self-gradient forcing, and few-step distillation—rather than introducing a wholly new generative architecture. Methodology EchoWM starts from a pretrained joint audio-visual diffusion transformer identified as LTX-2.3-based. The data engine combines internally collected gameplay with action logs and native audio, human-played Internet gameplay, Unreal Engine simulation with ground-truth poses and keyboard controls, and general Internet video. Video and audio are quality-filtered; multimodal descriptions are generated using Qwen3-Omni and Gemini-3-Pro; and long continuous windows are processed for geometry before being sliced into aligned training clips. UE poses are used directly, while other poses are recovered with ViPE, VGGT-Omega, and MoGe-2, followed by filtering for reconstruction reliability, intrinsic stability, temporal smoothness, and plausible motion. Each pose sequence is converted to a relative transform \(\Delta T_t=T_0^{-1}T_t\). For clip \(i\), the maximum translation magnitude \(m_i\) is computed and a global scale \(s_{global}=Q_{0.9}(\{m_i\})\) is used to normalize translations; rotations remain unchanged. At inference, keyboard states are mapped to local \(se(3)\) increments, integrated with the exponential map, and converted to the same relative trajectory representation. The calibrated trajectory enters a lightweight relative-UCPE camera-attention branch parallel to video self-attention. The branch uses geometry-dependent QKV transformations, combines camera geometry with spatiotemporal RoPE, and merges its output through a zero-initialized projection; the branch is shared across first- and third-person data and operates only on video tokens. Audio receives no direct trajectory injection and is expected to couple through the existing audio-visual cross-attention. Training has four stages. AV-CPT updates the full backbone on an AV-rich mixture using video and audio losses, with empty, reference-frame, or synchronized-prefix contexts. Action-SFT freezes the backbone and trains only the camera branch using control-clean data, static text fields, reference images or empty context, and a video-only denoising loss; motion-bearing narrative descriptions are removed to reduce textual motion leakage. Joint-FT updates both backbone and camera branch at a reduced learning rate on a smaller balanced set with video and audio losses. Autoregressive post-training first uses chunk-level causal audio-visual teacher forcing, then short-horizon and long-horizon Self-Gradient Forcing with Distribution Matching Distillation to expose the model to its own generated histories and reduce multi-step denoising to a four-step sampler. Long rollouts use a sink-plus-FIFO KV cache, with separate video, audio, and camera-attention states. These design choices are plausible and internally coherent, but the paper gives limited quantitative justification for the particular 90th-percentile scale, the zero-initialized UCPE branch, the data-mixture proportions, cache sizes, or loss weights. Key Results On the 158-case WBench Navigation split, undistilled EchoWM reports an average score of 81.7, with Quality 81.5, Setting 79.4, Interaction 87.2, Consistency 89.8, and Physical 70.6. EchoWM-Flash, the four-step causal variant, reports 81.0 average, Quality 81.1, Setting 88.3, Interaction 87.9, Consistency 77.5, and Physical 70.1. The comparison includes HiDream-O1-World at 80.9, Alaya-EVOKE at 80.8, LingBot-World fast v2 at 79.4, and other recent systems; the baselines are relatively current, although several are preprints or vendor/technical reports and the paper does not establish identical model access or evaluation conditions for every system. On the 241-frame SANA-WM-Bench evaluation, EchoWM obtains VBench Overall scores of 83.91 on the simple split and 83.96 on the hard split. On the simple split it reports rotation error 0.523 degrees, translation error 0.160, and CMC 0.162, compared with SANA-WM's 0.489 degrees, 0.194, and 0.195. On the hard split, EchoWM reports 1.697 degrees, 0.256, and 0.266, while SANA-WM reports 1.248 degrees, 0.199, and 0.206; thus EchoWM's visual score is higher but its pose accuracy is worse on the difficult split. Under the undistilled 961-frame protocol, EchoWM obtains VBench 81.36 on the simple split and 81.72 on the hard split, with simple-split revisit PSNR 15.10 dB, SSIM 0.335, LPIPS 0.451, and temporal IQ degradation 0.02; hard-split rotation error rises to 12.05 degrees, exposing substantial accumulated pose drift. Under the 961-frame causal protocol, EchoWM-Flash reports VBench 80.13/81.06 on simple/hard splits, rotation errors 5.009/14.221 degrees, translation errors 1.592/1.735, CMC 1.611/1.829, revisit PSNR 14.41/14.04 dB, SSIM 0.2998/0.2910, LPIPS 0.4802/0.4893, and IQ degradation 2.09/1.30. It outperforms the listed causal baselines on the headline VBench and most trajectory/revisit metrics, but its hard-split rotation error remains materially larger than its short-horizon value. A user study uses a self-built 200-case benchmark with 100 game, 50 humanoid-robot, 20 outdoor, 15 indoor, and 15 driving cases; 132 are third-person and 68 first-person. EchoWM receives 46.50% overall-preference votes against LingBot-World-v2 versus 21.57% for the competitor, and 63.13% against HappyOyster versus 27.06%. Against HappyOyster, however, EchoWM receives only 13.63% of semantic-following votes versus 29.44% for HappyOyster, with 51.50% judged both good. Scene-level results are heterogeneous: against HappyOyster, EchoWM is strongly preferred in autonomous driving and multi-social scenes but is nearly tied in embodied-robot and natural-outdoor scenes. The paper provides qualitative examples of synchronized sound and speech, first-/third-person control, unseen robot and 2D/2.5D domains, and 3D reconstructions, but it reports no numerical audio synchronization, speech intelligibility, sound quality, latency, throughput, or physical-interaction metrics. Novelty Classification The contribution is best classified as NEW PROBLEM, NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the enterable omnimodal-world setting and camera-intent interface are the clearest conceptual contributions, while the implementation largely assembles relative camera geometry, staged multimodal fine-tuning, causal diffusion training, and self-gradient forcing into a unified system; the open-source implementation is linked at https://github.com/jd-opensource/JoyAI-Echo, but no new public dataset is released or described with sufficient statistics to classify it as a new dataset contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper is an arXiv preprint, listed as version 1 dated 24 August 2026, and should not be treated as peer-reviewed evidence. It evaluates on two public benchmarks, includes current named baselines, reports both short- and 961-frame horizons, distinguishes undistilled and causal variants, and includes a user study and qualitative stress cases. It also explicitly addresses possible motion leakage by removing narrative fields during control training and reports that WBench rescales trajectories, which can obscure absolute-scale errors. However, the supplied paper text does not provide numerical ablation tables despite describing ablations for scale calibration, viewpoint semantics, speed control, and AV mixtures; it therefore does not quantitatively establish which components drive the gains. It reports no error bars, random-seed variation, statistical significance, annotator agreement, or confidence intervals. The self-built user study has 7 annotators for the LingBot comparison and 8 for the HappyOyster comparison, but sampling, instructions, randomization, and adjudication details are limited. Dataset sizes, exact filtering thresholds, mixture proportions, model parameter count, training budget, hardware, inference latency, throughput, and memory use are not stated. The code URL is provided, but the paper does not specify whether training data, processed pose annotations, model weights, or exact evaluation scripts are released. Reliance on internally collected gameplay, proprietary or externally hosted annotation models, and self-recovered poses introduces potential data-selection and annotation bias; the public benchmark results reduce but do not eliminate this concern. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS, because the paper trains and evaluates a functioning generative system and provides a code repository. Practical: The method is conceptually runnable on commercial hardware, but hardware requirements and whether either model variant can run interactively on a single GPU are not stated; the claimed “high-throughput” or low-latency behavior is therefore not demonstrated operationally. Efficient: EchoWM-Flash reduces generation to four denoising steps and uses bounded sink-plus-FIFO caches, but the paper gives no absolute latency, throughput, memory footprint, parameter count, or compute comparison against the multi-step model or alternatives. Effective: Public benchmark results show strong visual quality, trajectory following, revisit consistency, and long-horizon behavior, but the evidence primarily measures generated-video proxies; synchronized audio, speech quality, and usefulness of multimodal feedback under interaction are shown qualitatively rather than measured with dedicated metrics. Scalable: The system is evaluated to 961 frames, approximately one minute in the cited qualitative and benchmark settings, but the paper does not test 10×–100× longer horizons; the authors acknowledge that drift remains and that the bounded cache has no explicit persistent 3D memory. The work delivers a software artifact through the JoyAI-Echo repository and a project page, but the paper does not establish that the full training data, trained weights, or production-ready inference stack are publicly available. Strengths - The camera-intent formulation gives one technically concrete interface for discrete navigation and continuous poses, first-person observer motion, and third-person camera–subject evolution, without introducing separate viewpoint-specific controllers. - The data-engineering strategy correctly recognizes that audio quality, action supervision, and metric geometry come from different sources; separating AV-rich, control-clean, and balanced mixtures is a sensible response to conflicting supervision rather than assuming one ideal corpus. - The relative pose representation, robust global translation calibration, and relative UCPE injection address a real failure mode in camera-conditioned generation: per-clip normalization can remove displacement magnitude, while absolute camera encodings are sensitive to coordinate-frame choices. - The evaluation covers short and long horizons, simple and hard trajectories, causal and noncausal inference, user preferences, and revisit consistency. The reported hard-split pose degradation and weak semantic-following results against HappyOyster are visible rather than completely hidden, which makes the empirical claims more credible. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that EchoWM only models navigation and viewpoint-related actions representable by relative 6-DoF trajectories, does not model arbitrary actor intent or conventional game-engine rules, lacks explicit persistent 3D memory, and can drift in geometry, identity, world state, and audio over repeated turns. They also state that the interaction range is limited by the global motion filter, that generalization to larger translations, higher speeds, or unusual rotations is unestablished, and that recovered Internet/gameplay poses remain imperfect and may correlate with scene content or motion blur. The paper confronts these limitations directly, particularly by reporting hard-split rotation drift, but it does not quantify the failure boundaries or provide controlled tests of the omitted interaction types. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper presents a large composite contribution but does not provide the numerical component ablations needed to distinguish the effect of global scale calibration, relative UCPE, camera-intent semantics, staged training, the data mixtures, causal teacher forcing, and long-horizon SGF. - It does not report audio-specific metrics or controlled audio experiments, so the claim of synchronized environmental sound and speech is supported mainly by examples and the inherited audio-visual backbone rather than direct measurement under navigation. - The model is trained substantially on internally collected gameplay and filtered/recovered trajectories, but the paper does not report corpus size, domain composition beyond a small summary, train/test separation procedures, or whether benchmark scenes overlap in visual assets, game environments, captions, or pose distributions. - The use of Qwen3-Omni and Gemini-3-Pro for structured annotation creates an unquantified dependence on proprietary or external annotators; annotation errors, agreement, and their influence on model behavior are not evaluated. - The paper compares favorably on public benchmarks, but several baselines are rapidly changing preprints, technical reports, or vendor systems, and the text does not establish equal checkpoint freshness, sampling budgets, hardware, or access to reference conditioning across all comparisons. - The global 90th-percentile translation scale discards trajectories above the retained range rather than modeling them; this may improve benchmark behavior while narrowing the supported motion distribution. The paper acknowledges the range limitation but does not report retention rates or performance as a function of trajectory magnitude. - The claim that audio remains synchronized through visual-only trajectory injection is mechanistically plausible through cross-modal attention but is not isolated from the possibility that audio simply follows text and scene context; an action-to-audio intervention or trajectory-conditioned acoustic metric is missing. - The self-built 200-case user study is useful for breadth but is not an independent benchmark, and the reported preference margins coexist with dimension-level weaknesses, especially semantic following against HappyOyster. More transparent protocols and significance tests are needed before treating the preferences as robust evidence. Bottom Line This is a technically substantial and practically relevant preprint for interactive video-generation researchers, with a credible camera-intent abstraction and strong reported benchmark performance, but its novelty is primarily in integration and formulation and its deployment or scientific ranking should remain provisional until compute, data, audio metrics, and component-level ablations are disclosed.

#33 — Innovative (74)

Mitigating Rubric Interference in LLM Judges via On-Policy Self-Distillation

D Yu, T Zhang, Y Mou, Y Zhang, W Ye, S Zhang · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Self-Anchored Rubric Alignment (SARA), an on-policy self-distillation method that trains LLM judges to produce more invariant per-rubric verdicts when evaluating multiple rubrics jointly. - Why it's important: Joint evaluation can reduce inference cost relative to one-call-per-rubric evaluation, but context-dependent verdict changes undermine the reliability of automated benchmarks and reward signals. - How it does it: SARA distills a slowly updated teacher's single-rubric analysis logits into the student's joint-mode analysis while separately preserving joint structural outputs, with rubric shuffling and irrelevant-rubric injection during training. - The good: Across three datasets and four open models, SARA substantially improves isolation–joint consistency; for example, Qwen3-8B on ResearchQA improves from 0.22 to 0.59 sample-level exact match and from 0.665 to 0.868 weighted Cohen's kappa. - The missing: The paper does not establish that isolation judgments are correct relative to human annotations, and it does not quantify the inference-cost or latency trade-off after SARA increases output length substantially. - Read it or not: LLM-evaluation researchers and practitioners building rubric-based judges should read it for the interference diagnostic and training recipe, but deployment decisions require stronger human-grounded accuracy and cost evaluations.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (82) and Non-Obviousness (80) are strong because the paper identifies rubric interference as a distinct reliability failure and proposes a targeted self-distillation remedy across multiple domains and models. Rigor (72), Completeness (70), and Resilience (68) are held down by weak human-grounded validation, narrow baselines, absent uncertainty estimates, and unmeasured latency/cost; Impact (65) reflects released code but no production artifact or demonstrated correctness gains.
empirical Novelty 82 Rigor 72 Non-Obv 80 Completeness 70 Resilience 68 Impact 65
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses reliability of LLM-as-a-judge systems that evaluate one generated response against several fine-grained criteria, particularly in medical, scientific, and general instruction-following settings. Evaluating each rubric in isolation provides relatively stable per-rubric judgments but requires multiple inference calls; evaluating all rubrics jointly is more efficient and can produce a coherent report, yet the verdict for a fixed conversation–rubric pair can change when other rubrics are added, removed, reordered, or replaced with irrelevant rubrics. The paper reports that only 36% of HealthBench samples receive a fully matching isolation-versus-joint verdict for Qwen3-32B, despite repeated evaluations showing at least 0.98 self-agreement across seeds. The specific gap is a largely unmeasured form of context sensitivity in joint rubric evaluation, distinct from position, verbosity, self-enhancement, and other biases concerning comparisons between responses. Key Idea: Treat the model's single-rubric judgment as a privileged, self-generated anchor and train the joint evaluator to reproduce the corresponding per-rubric reasoning without external labels. The central insight is that the model appears more invariant when the rubric is presented alone, so the difference between isolation and joint contexts supplies a self-supervised signal for correcting interference. SARA therefore attempts to suppress harmful cross-rubric information flow while preserving the structure and coherence needed for a single joint response; the paper does not prove that isolation is always preferable, and acknowledges that related rubrics may sometimes provide useful context. Methodology: SARA uses full-parameter fine-tuning with an on-policy student–teacher pipeline. First, the student model samples a structured joint evaluation y for a conversation and rubric set, consisting of per-rubric analysis segments and structural segments containing verdicts, formatting, transitions, and total scores. A parser creates analysis and structure masks. Second, an exponential-moving-average teacher evaluates each sampled analysis segment in isolation with only its target rubric, producing isolation-anchored logits; the same teacher also evaluates the complete sampled joint output under the full rubric set. Third, the student minimizes a symmetric Jensen–Shannon divergence between its joint-context logits and the teacher's isolation logits over analysis tokens, plus a preservation divergence between student and full-context teacher logits over structural tokens: L = L_distill + 0.4 L_preserve, with EMA decay 0.999 and JSD interpolation parameter 0.5. Finally, rubric order is randomly shuffled and, with a stated probability, unrelated rubrics are appended to expose the model to positional and content-based interference. The critical design decisions are the EMA teacher, which is supported by an ablation showing EM 0.48 without momentum versus 0.52 with the default; the separation of analysis and structural losses, which is necessary because removing preservation causes structural output failure within tens of steps; and on-policy sampling, which is motivated by reducing distribution shift but is not isolated against an equivalent off-policy distillation design. Instruct-mode segment extraction uses a predictable rubric-analysis-verdict format, whereas thinking-mode extraction relies on a coarse paragraph heuristic. Key Results: The experiments use 500 HealthBench samples with 2–32 rubrics per sample and binary verdicts, 1,740 FLASK samples with three fixed 1–5 rubrics, and 1,000 ResearchQA samples with 1–8 0–4 rubrics. They evaluate Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, using an 8:1:1 train/validation/test split and comparing mainly against the untrained base model and, for one Qwen3-14B ResearchQA experiment, isolation-output SFT (SFTiso). In overall isolation–joint consistency, SARA raises ResearchQA EM from 0.22 to 0.59 for Qwen3-8B, 0.23 to 0.52 for Qwen3-14B, 0.25 to 0.42 for Qwen3-32B, and 0.12 to 0.34 for Llama-3.1-8B; corresponding kappa changes are 0.665 to 0.868, 0.658 to 0.879, 0.651 to 0.851, and 0.608 to 0.800. On FLASK, EM changes are 0.41 to 0.52, 0.41 to 0.55, 0.41 to 0.59, and 0.24 to 0.41 for the same models. On HealthBench, EM changes are 0.22 to 0.34, 0.34 to 0.38, 0.36 to 0.36, and 0.08 to 0.18, showing limited benefit for Qwen3-32B where the binary baseline is already strong. For ResearchQA consistency-at-K, Qwen3-32B's MAD grows from 0.203 at K=2 to 0.362 at K=8, while SARA yields 0.124 and 0.108, respectively. Under five random rubric permutations, Qwen3-8B ResearchQA EM rises from 0.298 to 0.594; under 40% irrelevant-rubric noise, it rises from 0.255 to 0.620. Cross-dataset transfer of a Qwen3-14B model trained only on ResearchQA improves HealthBench EM from 0.34 to 0.34 relative to the base and FLASK EM from 0.41 to 0.55, with agreement gains on both datasets; the HealthBench transfer result is therefore an agreement improvement without an EM improvement. SARA generally maintains or slightly improves GPT-4.1 agreement on HealthBench, but GPT-4.1 is used as a reference judge rather than human ground truth. SFTiso is marginally better on ResearchQA isolation–joint agreement for Qwen3-14B (Agr 0.909, EM 0.54) than SARA (Agr 0.900, EM 0.52), while SARA better preserves agreement with the base model. SARA increases average joint output length, for example Qwen3-8B HealthBench from 405 to 611 tokens, which complicates the claim that joint evaluation is operationally cheaper. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The empirical identification and controlled measurement of rubric interference are the clearest conceptual contributions, while SARA is a targeted combination of on-policy self-distillation, EMA teachers, masked token-level distillation, and rubric augmentation applied to multi-rubric judging rather than a fundamentally new distillation primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides a four-operation diagnostic framework—expansion, subsetting, reordering, and noise injection—and reports agreement, Cohen's kappa, EM, MAD, RMSE, correlation, and aggregate total-score metrics. It includes ablations for EMA decay, JSD interpolation, and preservation loss, plus a limited attention analysis on 10 ResearchQA samples and a preliminary thinking-mode experiment. The released code is stated to be available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SARA-22E2/, and the paper states that datasets and models are publicly available under permissive licenses. However, the main comparison is often only against the untrained base model; SFTiso is evaluated on one model and one dataset, and there is no comparison against alternative consistency training, prompt-based debiasing, multi-pass aggregation, or a direct isolation deployment cost. The primary target metric measures agreement with the model's own isolation behavior, not correctness against human labels. GPT-4.1 agreement is reported only on HealthBench and is an imperfect external proxy. No error bars, multiple training seeds, statistical significance tests, or confidence intervals are reported. Checkpoint selection uses validation shuffle consistency, while the principal objective is broader isolation–joint consistency. Evaluation caps rubrics at 10 per sample despite HealthBench containing up to 32, and the attention interpretation is based on only 10 samples. These limitations weaken claims about correctness, statistical robustness, and deployment-scale generality. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a systems-oriented training procedure rather than a deployed production system. Practical: The models run on commercially available NVIDIA H20 GPUs, but SARA requires full-parameter fine-tuning and the reported experiments use 8 GPUs, so the training cost is material; inference hardware requirements are otherwise standard for the underlying models. Efficient: Joint evaluation can reduce the number of calls relative to isolation, but SARA increases output length substantially and the paper reports no end-to-end latency, throughput, memory, or dollar-cost comparison, so net efficiency is unestablished. Effective: The evidence strongly shows improved invariance to rubric composition, order, and noise, but it does not establish improved judgment correctness because isolation agreement and GPT-4.1 agreement are proxies rather than human-validated accuracy. Scalable: The method is tested on up to 32-rubric HealthBench samples but evaluations are capped at 10 rubrics and the controlled K experiments reach only K=8; behavior at 10×–100× larger rubric sets, longer contexts, production traffic, or larger models is not evaluated. The work delivers a released code artifact and trained model variants, but not a production library, CLI, hosted judge, or independently validated dataset. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete and practically relevant failure mode—verdict changes for the same response and rubric under altered co-rubric context—and separates it from response-comparison biases. - The four perturbation operations test different mechanisms rather than relying on a single isolation-versus-joint statistic; the scaling curves show that interference can increase sharply with rubric count. - SARA improves consistency across three domains, binary and ordinal scoring formats, two model families, and several model scales, with especially large gains in strict sample-level EM and scored agreement. - The method has a plausible mechanistic account: in a small attention study, within-output diagonal attention increases from 0.623 to 0.809, while off-diagonal output attention decreases from 0.039 to 0.014 after training. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that SARA depends on predictable segment boundaries in instruct mode and performs worse in thinking mode, where paragraph-level heuristics can misassign or entangle rubric reasoning; for Qwen3-14B ResearchQA, thinking-mode EM improves only from 0.22 to 0.29, versus 0.23 to 0.52 in instruct mode. They also acknowledge that isolation judgments are not infallible and that joint evaluation of related rubrics can sometimes provide beneficial context. They caution that consistency does not guarantee correctness and recommend retaining human oversight in high-stakes domains. These limitations are confronted directly, although the paper does not quantify the broader operational costs implied by longer outputs. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unacknowledged concern is objective validity: SARA is optimized to imitate isolation judgments, but the paper does not show that isolation is more accurate than joint evaluation against human annotations or adjudicated labels. The work also lacks a proper compute-efficiency analysis, despite motivating joint evaluation by efficiency and observing output-token increases of up to 220 tokens on HealthBench for Qwen3-8B and 259 tokens on ResearchQA on average. Baseline coverage is narrow: there is no strong comparison to prompt ensembles, majority voting across isolation calls, consistency regularization, RL-based judge training, or methods that explicitly model rubric dependencies. The evaluation truncation to at most 10 rubrics underrepresents the 32-rubric regime used to motivate HealthBench, and the transfer experiment uses only one source model and one source dataset. The attention analysis is small and correlational, so it does not establish that altered attention causes the consistency gains. Finally, the method may suppress legitimate cross-rubric reasoning and could preserve systematic isolation biases; the paper acknowledges the former in principle but does not measure the trade-off. Bottom Line: This is a useful and technically credible preprint for researchers building rubric-based LLM judges because it names and measures an overlooked failure mode and offers a reproducible mitigation, but its practical superiority remains unproven until human-grounded accuracy, stronger baselines, and end-to-end cost are evaluated.
