Problem & Motivation: The work addresses distributed autoregressive LLM inference on fleets of consumer Intel AI PCs with integrated GPUs, NPUs, and roughly 16–32 GB of shared memory per machine. The target users are organizations that already own such devices, require data locality, or want to serve models without cloud dependence. A single device cannot hold models such as Llama 3.1 70B, while naïvely splitting a model across networked nodes incurs per-token communication and pipeline-bubble costs. The paper identifies three specific gaps: OpenVINO's standard export path does not directly produce efficient layer-range shards for modern stateful transformers; stateful OpenVINO models lack the paged-attention or rewind APIs normally used by speculative decoding; and single-user pipeline inference leaves stages idle, limiting throughput. The paper focuses on closing these gaps for Intel GPUs and, secondarily, static NPU execution. Key Idea: The core insight is that several seemingly separate bottlenecks can be addressed at the graph and scheduling layers without changing model weights: a dummy runtime-identity Gather indexed by `beam_idx` activates an otherwise hidden OpenVINO GPU KV-cache fusion; rejected speculative tokens can remain physically in the cache if their positions are masked and logical positions are tracked correctly; and independent per-request state lets multiple users occupy pipeline bubbles. The contribution is therefore less a new inference algorithm than a platform-specific composition of compiler-pattern recovery, cache-state masking, and pipeline scheduling. Methodology: Offline, the system selectively loads contiguous transformer layers from Hugging Face safetensors, rewrites attention to use explicit KV tensors and externally precomputed rotary embeddings, traces each stage with `torch.jit.trace` using real tensors, converts each graph to OpenVINO IR, applies `make_stateful_transformation`, and compresses weights to symmetric INT4 with group size 128. A post-export graph pass inserts a `beam_idx` parameter and `Gather(ReadValue, beam_idx, axis=0)` before KV-cache consumers, causing the GPU plugin's IndirectKVCache fusion to fire; runtime `beam_idx=[0]` makes this an identity operation. Online, a coordinator hosts the tokenizer, generation loop, stage-0 shard, and a Llama 3.2 1B draft model; workers run later shards over persistent TCP daisy-chain connections carrying approximately 16 KB FP32 hidden states per token hop. Speculative decoding drafts K tokens locally and verifies K+1 positions in the target pipeline. Instead of `query_state()/set_state()` trimming, the runtime maintains a logical validity mask and sets rejected cache positions to zero in `attention_mask`, while `position_ids` follow logical rather than physical cache length. Micro-batching uses one independent `InferRequest` and compiled graph per user stream, preserving separate KV state and interleaving streams across stages. Critical design decisions are the beam-index graph surgery, the mask-based rewind, and per-stream graph isolation. The paper measures or verifies the first two directly, but provides limited justification for choosing fixed per-stream compilation over dynamic batching in the headline GPU experiments; it reports the memory cost of approximately 2 GB per additional Llama 8B stage per stream and approximately 6 GB per stream on Lunar Lake in the 3-stage setup. A separate NPU path removes stateful variables, fixes shapes, exposes KV as graph ports, and uses host-managed ring buffers and a block-diagonal `[1,1,S,T]` attention mask for packed multi-slot execution. Key Results: The paper is an August 2026 arXiv v1 preprint and evaluates three Intel AI PCs: two Lunar Lake ASUS Zenbook S 14 systems with Arc 140V GPUs and one Panther Lake HP OmniBook X 16 with an Arc B390 GPU, running Windows 11, OpenVINO 2026.1.0, and WiFi 802.11ax. For Llama 3.1 8B INT4 on Arc B390, the monolithic OpenVINO baseline reaches 24.54 tok/s over five paired runs; a naïvely exported one-stage shard reaches 21.26 tok/s, while the `beam_idx`-injected shard reaches 24.45 tok/s, recovering 15% and landing within 0.4% of the monolithic baseline. Splitting into 2 and 3 stages on one device reaches 20.56 and 21.56 tok/s, respectively, versus 24.28 tok/s for the paired monolithic reference. Physical KV trimming costs 45–50 ms per call for a 72-token cache, whereas mask construction costs less than 1% of step time at K=3; mask-based speculation produces a 1.33x mean speedup across eight prompt types, from 1.11x on creative writing to 1.50x on code completion, with 70.7% mean acceptance. On a 3-stage shard, speculation improves 21.56 to 28.38 tok/s, or 1.32x, and matches the target-only greedy output. Two-stream micro-batching raises 2-stage distributed Llama 8B throughput from 16.33 to 29.34 tok/s, or 1.80x. Adding K=3 speculation reaches 43.97 tok/s aggregate, 21.99 tok/s per stream, and 1.79x the 24.54 tok/s monolithic single-user baseline. A 3-stage deployment reaches 50.55 tok/s with two streams and K=5, and 64.67 tok/s with three streams, or 2.64x the monolithic baseline; each stream achieves 21.6 tok/s in the 3-stream case. In a deterministic injected-latency sweep, the 2-stage full stack produces 41.01 tok/s aggregate at LAN, 37.35 at 10 ms one-way hop latency, 18.25 at 50 ms, and 11.20 at 100 ms; per-stream throughput remains at least 5.6 tok/s, while naïve single-stream distributed decode falls from 14.51 to 2.77 tok/s. In a real Tiber Cloud path through a Tailscale DERP relay, top-1 token-plus-probability transmission improves 2-node 8B throughput from 2.80 to 22.88 tok/s, an 8.17x increase, but the compressed result remains 1.9x slower than the rainier LAN result. For Llama 3.1 70B INT4, four approximately 9 GB shards deployed across four Tiber Cloud nodes reach 1.74 tok/s target-only, 5.42 tok/s with K=10 speculation for one stream, and 6.43 tok/s aggregate with two streams; the 5.42 tok/s result is 3.11x the same-topology target-only baseline. At 4096 generated tokens it falls to 5.00 tok/s, while at 1024 tokens it reaches 5.72 tok/s. These 70B results are output-identical to the same four-stage target-only pipeline, not to an independently exported monolithic or Hugging Face reference. Gemma 4 E2B reaches 10.40 tok/s in a 2-stage multi-node FP32 configuration and 16.30 tok/s with two-stream micro-batching. The separate static NPU path reports 1.76 ms/token at 16 packed Qwen2.5-1.5B slots versus 10.57 ms/token at one slot, a 6.01x graph-level improvement, and 11.46 tok/s versus 3.55 tok/s for a 4-slot 2-stage Llama 3.1 8B NPU pipeline. Baselines are generally same-platform monolithic OpenVINO or same-shard target-only paths; the paper does not compare against Petals, Parallax, vLLM, or other serving systems on common hardware, so the comparative strength of the system against current distributed serving is unresolved. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING are justified: the technically distinctive elements are the use of a compile-time identity `beam_idx` Gather to recover OpenVINO's hidden IndirectKVCache optimization on independently exported shards and the mask-based rewind mechanism for speculative decoding on stateful OpenVINO; pipeline parallelism, speculative decoding, and micro-batching themselves are standard techniques composed for a new Intel OpenVINO edge setting rather than fundamentally new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports direct ablations for the beam-index injection, physical versus masked KV rewind, stage count, speculative K, activation/logit compression, stream count, device placement, and several failed optimizations. It checks numerical or token equality extensively, including maximum absolute differences below `5 × 10^-7` for the attention rewrite, zero logit difference in the trim comparison, and bit-exact greedy outputs for many headline configurations. However, many key measurements use one paired session: the beam-fusion table uses N=5, the 70B and several WAN studies use N=3 or fewer, and the latency sweep explicitly uses N=1 with no error bars. The paper provides some standard deviations, typically around ±0.3 tok/s for the 2-node Llama 8B session, but does not provide broad seed variation, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. It releases code, export scripts, raw JSON benchmark logs, VTune reports, and reproduction scripts at `https://github.com/labscommunity/pipeline-sharded-inference-paper`, including the `reproduction/` directory. The strongest methodological concern is the 70B reference: the monolithic 70B INT4 export failed because approximately 141 GB of FP16 calibration weights and NNCF workspace exceeded a 133 GB machine, so correctness is established only against another path using the same exported shards. The WAN headline is also partly synthetic: the sleep-based latency injection omits jitter, TCP slow-start, and congestion behavior, while the real-WAN comparison changes topology, hop count, relay behavior, and model configuration. The evaluation omits common cross-platform baselines and does not measure power, sustained thermal behavior, failures under node loss, authentication, encryption, or adversarial network conditions. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL — the paper runs compiled inference methods and evaluates a prototype distributed serving stack, although it also contains systems-engineering material. Practical: The GPU path runs on commercially available Windows 11 Intel AI PCs with Arc integrated GPUs and ordinary TCP networking, but requires compatible Lunar Lake-class hardware for the 70B deployment, approximately 32 GB system RAM, identical software stacks, and a trusted network; the NPU path has stricter fixed-shape and model-support constraints. Efficient: The beam surgery restores one-stage shard throughput from 21.26 to 24.45 tok/s, mask rewind avoids a measured 45–50 ms state-trim cost, and top-1 logits reduce a roughly 501 KB return payload to approximately 8 bytes, but stage splitting loses 11–15% on one device and per-stream compilation consumes about 2 GB per Llama 8B stage or roughly 6 GB per Lunar Lake stream in the reported 3-stage setup. Effective: The evidence supports exact greedy-output preservation and useful throughput on Llama 8B, Gemma 4 E2B, and a 70B deployment, but it measures throughput rather than quality, cost, energy, or service-level latency under realistic request arrival distributions; sampling and beam search remain unevaluated. Scalable: The experiments reach 3 nodes and 3 streams for 8B and 4 nodes for 70B, but provide no 10x–100x scale test, no fault tolerance, and no evidence that fixed per-stream compilation, TCP daisy chains, memory limits, or pipeline bubbles remain viable beyond the tested fleet sizes. The work delivers a reusable software artifact consisting of export tools, OpenVINO IR shard generation, coordinator and worker runtimes, benchmark drivers, and reproduction logs; it does not release new model weights or a general-purpose production serving framework. Strengths: - The beam-index discovery isolates a concrete compiler-pattern dependency and demonstrates a 15% throughput recovery without changing weights or model semantics; the resulting one-stage shard reaches within 0.4% of the monolithic OpenVINO baseline. - Mask-based cache rewind addresses a real API mismatch rather than assuming paged attention: it avoids a measured approximately 48 ms state mutation cost, preserves greedy outputs exactly in the tested cases, and exposes a plausible general primitive for cache deletion policies. - The paper evaluates composition rather than only isolated optimizations. The 2-node 8B progression from 16.33 to 29.34 to 43.97 tok/s quantifies the contributions of sharding, micro-batching, and speculation in one configuration. - The 70B deployment demonstrates a meaningful capability boundary: a model whose approximately 36 GB INT4 footprint exceeds one tested fleet member's capacity runs at 5.42 tok/s for one stream and 6.43 tok/s aggregate for two streams. The paper also documents negative results, hardware failures, NPU restrictions, and WAN measurement discrepancies instead of hiding them. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the main results to integrated GPUs, greedy decoding, trusted and reliable networks, identical software stacks, and Intel OpenVINO-compatible hardware. They state that sampling, beam search, in-generation cache compaction, multi-stage prefix-cache correctness certification, NPU execution for the 70B deployment, and composition of the NPU packed mode with speculative decoding remain unvalidated. They report no power or thermal measurements, no fault tolerance, authentication, or encryption, and acknowledge that prolonged laptop inference may throttle. They also acknowledge that the WAN latency simulator omits real TCP dynamics, that the 70B monolithic reference could not be built, and that the fixed-slot NPU layout trades context length against concurrency. These admissions improve credibility, although the paper still presents interactive-serving conclusions from limited duration and topology-specific measurements. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline comparison against a monolithic single-node baseline is not a serving-system comparison; there is no common-hardware evaluation against vLLM, OpenVINO ContinuousBatchingPipeline, TensorRT-LLM, Petals, or another distributed runtime, and the authors decline cross-system comparisons rather than supplying normalized cost, energy, or latency measurements. - The 70B correctness claim is circular at the most important scale: target-only and speculative paths share the same four exported shards, while an external Hugging Face or monolithic reference is unavailable. The paper therefore does not rule out a shared export or implementation error affecting both paths. - Throughput is emphasized over tail latency. TTFT is reported for the 2-stage 8B path but not separately for the 4-stage 70B deployment, and there are no p95/p99 token latencies, queueing delays, request-arrival traces, or load-shedding results. - The practical fleet claim lacks energy, thermal, reliability, and operational measurements. The authors note one Arrow Lake iGPU process death and possible thermal throttling, but do not quantify failure rates, recovery time, sustained throughput, or the cost of replacing failed nodes. - Generality remains narrow. Main measurements cover Llama 3.1 8B and 70B, Gemma 4 E2B, and a few small NPU tests; there is no systematic evaluation across model families, context windows, sampling distributions, prompt mixtures, or heterogeneous stage assignments. - WAN conclusions are difficult to compare because the headline simulator, queue proxy, and Tiber DERP experiment use different hop counts, payloads, topologies, and decoding modes. The paper reports this honestly, but does not provide one controlled end-to-end experiment varying only network conditions. - The fixed per-stream `compile_model()` strategy and static NPU slot count impose memory and admission constraints that may dominate real workloads; the paper does not compare them quantitatively with dynamic batching on the same distributed GPU pipeline or with a shared compiled graph. Bottom Line: This is a technically useful and unusually transparent OpenVINO systems preprint whose graph-fusion and mask-rewind techniques merit attention from edge-inference researchers, but its practical superiority over established serving stacks and its 70B correctness and scalability claims remain insufficiently established for a top-tier systems acceptance without stronger baselines, independent references, tail-latency and energy data, and larger controlled deployments.

RTPO: Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization for Stabilizing Agentic RL Training

Y Li, J Cao, J Qiao, S Hu · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Reverse-Turn Policy Optimization (RTPO), a multi-turn agentic RL algorithm that combines turn-boundary optimization, state-matched sibling rollouts, reverse-order updates, and on-policy downstream continuation. - Why it's important: Multi-turn tool-using agents can degrade as interaction horizons grow because training may optimize tokens under different contexts and policy versions from those used during rollout, while terminal rewards provide weak credit for individual turns. - How it does it: RTPO anchors training at sampled turn-boundary states, regenerates sibling trajectories under the current downstream policy, assigns each sibling a local return-relative-to-siblings advantage, and optimizes turn policies from the final turn backward while masking non-current-turn tokens. - The good: On Qwen3-8B, RTPO reports 61.66 average accuracy across eight math and knowledge benchmarks, versus 53.71 for GRPO and 57.68 for SeeUPO, while controlled experiments support separate benefits from turn-level credit and on-policy continuation. - The missing: The strongest convergence claims apply to a tabular finite-horizon formulation with frozen independent sub-policies, not the shared neural Transformer implementation, and the paper does not provide a fully compute- and token-matched comparison across all primary experiments. - Read it or not: Researchers working on long-horizon LLM-agent RL should read it for its concrete decomposition of context, credit, and policy-drift failures, but should treat the neural convergence claims and reported gains as preliminary because this is an arXiv v1 preprint with limited scale and only three evaluation runs.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses unstable reinforcement-learning post-training for multi-turn language-model agents that reason, call external tools, receive feedback, and continue over several turns. The affected domains are tool-augmented mathematical reasoning, web search, and stateful database interaction. The paper identifies three related problems in common PPO/GRPO-style flattened-trajectory training: rollout contexts may be truncated or summarized while training recomputes probabilities under full histories; one terminal or trajectory-level advantage is applied to all turns despite different causal contributions; and asynchronous short and long trajectories can be generated and optimized under different policy versions. Existing turn-level and tree-based methods improve granularity but, according to the paper, still retain context inconsistency, cross-state baselines, or stale downstream continuation. The stated gap is a training-pipeline formulation that addresses all three mechanisms together rather than treating them as independent numerical or reward-shaping problems. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat each interaction turn as a macro-action in a finite-horizon turn-boundary MDP and optimize those macro-actions by backward induction. At a fixed boundary state, RTPO compares sibling responses that share the same preceding state, so differences in expected terminal return are attributable to the current turn rather than to different upstream histories. It then generates the downstream continuation with the already-updated current policy, making the continuation on-policy and eliminating the need for a long-horizon importance-ratio product. The reverse ordering is therefore not merely an update schedule: it makes the downstream value target stationary in the idealized formulation while simultaneously providing state-matched credit and current-policy continuation. Methodology: RTPO first samples a complete trunk trajectory for each prompt and stores turn-boundary states, environment snapshots, the exact conditioning context c_k used by the model, and old-policy token log probabilities. For each turn k from K−1 down to 0, it restores the corresponding environment snapshot, generates G−1 sibling responses from the shared boundary state using the current downstream policy, and continues every sibling to termination under that same policy. With sparse terminal rewards, each sibling return R_j estimates the turn-level action value; the baseline is the sibling mean V-hat_k = (1/(G−1)) sum_j R_j, and the advantage is A^H_j,k = R_j − V-hat_k. The paper applies a token-level clipped PPO objective only to the current turn's response tokens, using the same c_k in rollout and training: J_k = (1/(G−1)) sum_j (1/T_j,k) sum_t min(rho_j,k,t A^H_j,k, clip(rho_j,k,t,1−epsilon,1+epsilon) A^H_j,k). After each phase, the current turn is treated as frozen and the algorithm proceeds to the preceding turn. Critical design decisions are: recording and replaying the exact rollout context, which directly fixes the denominator mismatch and is well motivated; state-matched sibling branching, which removes the upstream-state term from the baseline but can be sample-inefficient, especially with binary rewards; and on-policy continuation after every reverse stage, which makes the continuation importance weight exactly one but introduces synchronization and generation overhead. The theoretical analysis models the process as an H-MDP or finite-horizon semi-MDP with complete language-model responses as macro-actions, zero within-turn token rewards, and optional duration discounting. In practice, however, the implementation uses a shared neural language model rather than independent turn-specific policies, so masking tokens is only an operational approximation to the theoretical freezing assumption. Key Results: In the principal Qwen3-8B experiments, using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, 16 global rollouts per prompt, K=3 for math and K=6 for web search, RTPO obtains the following Pass@1 results on math tasks: 33.33% on AIME24, 26.67% on AIME25, 67.50% on AMC23, 86.20% on MATH500, 94.84% on GSM8K, and 55.49% on OE-Math. It obtains best-span F1 scores of 64.89% on HotpotQA and 64.35% on 2WikiMultiHopQA. The reported average is 61.66%, compared with 53.71% for GRPO and 57.68% for SeeUPO; the paper reports relative improvements over GRPO and SeeUPO of 21.50% and 10.76%, respectively. RTPO also reports fewer math tool calls than the baselines on most hard math tasks, but substantially more search calls on knowledge tasks: 613 versus 214 for SeeUPO and 867 versus 253 on 2Wiki, so its gains do not imply lower total inference cost across domains. In a controlled Qwen3-4B mathematical experiment using full histories for all methods, RTPO-CA reaches 79.13 average Pass@1 and 86.55 Pass@4, versus 78.15/83.23 for ARPO, 74.67/84.00 for TreeGRPO, and 76.33/84.18 for SeeUPO. For on-policy continuation, the default method improves output-hit rate over an off-policy RTPO variant by 5.83 percentage points on GAIA, 3.50 on WebWalkerQA, and 7.00 on XBench, but is 0.33 points worse on HLE. In the supplementary tau3-Airline study with Qwen3-1.7B, RTPO reaches 17.50% Pass@1 and 30.00% Pass@4 on 20 held-out tasks, versus 16.25%/25.00% for TreeGRPO and 11.25%/25.00% for GRPO; online success peaks at 56.25% at step 40 but falls to 40.63% at step 50. The main results average three runs, with standard deviations reported in the supplementary table, but the small AIME test sets make several percentage-point differences statistically fragile. The evaluation scale is standard benchmark scale rather than stress-scale deployment: one backbone family, primarily 4B and 8B models, horizons of 3 or 6 turns in the main experiments, and a small 1.7B stateful-agent study. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the unified RTPO training formulation that combines exact rollout-context replay, state-matched sibling advantages, reverse-order turn updates, and on-policy continuation; reverse-order optimization, tree rollouts, PPO clipping, and Monte Carlo returns individually draw on established ideas, so the novelty lies more in their coupling and formal diagnosis than in a wholly new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides formal assumptions and proofs for three claims: reverse-order optimization converges to recursive optimality in a finite tabular setting, sibling advantages remove the cross-state baseline term up to finite-group bias, and on-policy continuation gives an exactly unit continuation importance weight. The sibling analysis explicitly derives a multiplicative finite-group factor (G−2)/(G−1), and the paper reports a sibling-size study showing that G=3 is the minimum informative configuration under its estimator. Experiments include a context-control study, an on-policy/off-policy ablation, a stateful-agent supplement, cost measurements, and three-run means with standard deviations. The source code, installation instructions, training scripts, and pseudocode are stated to be included in the supplementary material, but no public repository URL is given. Important concerns remain: the convergence theorem assumes finite state and macro-action spaces, tabular values, infinite exploration, state coverage, exact downstream freezing, and context sufficiency; these assumptions do not hold literally for a shared autoregressive neural policy trained with PPO. The neural extension is not a direct convergence proof: it invokes universal approximation and standard stochastic-gradient arguments, which do not by themselves guarantee convergence to the required optimum in a nonconvex shared-parameter model. The primary comparisons use different algorithmic structures and potentially different token-generation patterns even when total rollout counts are matched; RTPO's extra continuation tokens and synchronization cost are not fully normalized in the main eight-benchmark comparison. LLM-as-Judge scoring is used for HotpotQA and 2Wiki, and output-hit scoring is used for deep-search tasks; judge reliability, prompt sensitivity, and inter-rater validation are not stated. There are no significance tests, broad seed curves, larger model scales, or experiments at 10×–100× the reported horizon. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS profile, because the paper runs a distributed implementation of RTPO and evaluates it experimentally, although it does not present a production deployment. Practical: The method runs on commercially available hardware; the reported setup uses 8× NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, VeRL, vLLM, FSDP, and environment snapshot restoration, so it is implementable but infrastructure-heavy. Efficient: RTPO costs more during training: in the tau3-Airline comparison it uses 21.48 versus 15.20 GPU-hours, 846,207 versus 604,532 generated tokens, and 41.3% more wall-clock/GPU time than GRPO; sibling size G=4 raises training-generation tokens by approximately 152.8% relative to G=3. Effective: The evidence shows improved benchmark accuracy, tool-execution success, and held-out success on several tasks, but it evaluates proxies for reliable agency rather than safety, factuality under distribution shift, or sustained real-world deployment; on-policy continuation is not uniformly beneficial, with a small negative result on HLE. Scalable: The paper tests K=3 and K=6 main-task horizons and a limited tau3-Airline setting, but does not measure behavior at 10×–100× horizon, model, environment, or branching scale; the reverse-stage synchronization and continuation cost are expected to grow with the number of turns. The work delivers a reproducible software implementation in the supplementary material, but no public URL, trained checkpoint, or standalone library release is specified. Strengths: - The paper identifies a coherent structural relationship between three failure modes that are often discussed separately: conditioning mismatch, state-confounded credit, and stale-policy continuation. - State-matched sibling comparison gives a clear causal interpretation to the turn-level baseline and yields an explicit finite-group bias analysis rather than only an empirical heuristic. - The ablations are directionally useful: full-history control isolates credit assignment, the off-policy variant isolates continuation freshness, and the supplementary stateful environment tests whether the method transfers beyond math and web search. - The authors quantify an important cost trade-off instead of presenting only accuracy: RTPO improves tau3-Airline success and tool execution while requiring about 41% more training time than GRPO, and its zero-advantage rate remains above 80% in the sparse binary-reward setting. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges dependence on trunk quality, because later sibling states inherit the trunk's visited regions and poor early decisions can produce uninformative downstream returns. It acknowledges the overhead of K sequential reverse phases, environment restoration, sibling continuation, and policy-engine synchronization. It also acknowledges low token utilization because only current-turn tokens receive gradients while trunk and downstream continuation tokens are discarded for optimization. The supplementary discussion further states that the strict theorem is tabular with exactly fixed downstream policies, that neural RTPO lacks a global convergence guarantee, that G=4 materially increases cost, that zero-advantage rates remain above 80% in tau3-Airline, that online success can decline after extended training, and that broader model scales, turn lengths, seeds, and intermediate synchronization schemes remain untested. These limitations are confronted directly, although their implications for the main accuracy comparisons are not fully quantified. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest gap is the mismatch between the theoretical object and the implemented learner: the proof freezes independent per-turn policies, whereas the experiment updates a shared Transformer whose parameters affect multiple turns and whose token masking does not prevent cross-turn interference through shared weights. The paper also treats context truncation or removal of internal reasoning traces as decision-sufficient under an assumption, but does not empirically compare alternative summaries, quantify information loss, or test cases where hidden reasoning affects future tool behavior. The main benchmark results do not report end-to-end generated-token, environment-call, wall-clock, or GPU-hour normalization for every baseline, making it difficult to determine whether accuracy gains reflect the algorithm or greater effective continuation computation. Stronger comparisons to sequence-level methods such as GSPO and to additional hierarchical or actor-critic baselines are absent from the main tables. The reported three-run evaluation is insufficient for reliable claims on 30-example AIME sets, and no confidence intervals or paired statistical tests are provided. Finally, the claimed elimination of policy drift is exact only for regenerated sibling continuations; trunk state coverage remains off-policy with respect to later reverse stages, and the paper does not measure how this state-distribution issue affects learning or how performance changes when trunks are systematically poor. Bottom Line: RTPO offers a technically coherent and empirically promising redesign of multi-turn agent RL, especially for long-horizon tool use, but its strongest value is the state-matched/on-policy training perspective and accompanying diagnostics—not the currently overstated neural convergence guarantee or conclusively established efficiency advantage.

AgentMercury: Your Agent Can Synthesize Verifiable Environments for Business Scenarios at scale (7 ▲ )

Minbyul Jeong, Chanwoong Yoon · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces AGENTMERCURY, a framework that converts high-level business scenarios into executable, stateful, multi-service environments with deterministic verification and uses them to train and evaluate agents. - Why it's important: Existing agent environments are commonly built around individual tasks or benchmarks, which limits world diversity and makes it difficult to generate realistic long-horizon workflows at scale. - How it does it: A PLANET authoring process factorizes scenario grounding into company identity, service graph, state schema, seeded state, and executable world invariants, after which tasks are sampled and graded against database-state assertions. - The good: Training Qwen3.5-4B on only 3,200 sampled tasks from the synthesized corpus raises ENTERPRISEOPS-GYM from 12.3 to 15.7 and AIME26 from 45.9 to 56.0, while construction-trace fine-tuning raises held-out world-authoring success from 3.3% to 83.3%. - The missing: The paper does not isolate AGENTMERCURY from the task distribution, reward implementation, model-specific training choices, or comparable synthetic-environment alternatives, so the source of the reported transfer gains remains uncertain. - Read it or not: Researchers building tool-use RL environments should read it for the world/task/verifier factorization and released artifacts, but readers seeking evidence of real-world business-agent deployment or causal generalization should wait for stronger controlled comparisons.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. AGENTMERCURY presents a genuinely useful world/task/verifier factorization (Novelty 82) with a strong non-obvious insight in separating persistent world construction from task generation (Non-Obviousness 84), plus substantial released-environment and model value (Impact 72). The transfer results are promising, but Rigor (68) and Resilience (65) remain below top-tier standards because matched task-centric baselines, reward and verifier ablations, compute accounting, realism validation, and contamination controls are missing; the paper's candid discussion of synthetic-world limitations supports Completeness (72). Problem & Motivation: Agent training environments are usually manually authored or synthesized around predefined tasks, user instructions, or benchmark specifications. This couples the world’s entities, services, state, and transition logic to a narrow task distribution and can increase task count without increasing meaningful world diversity. The target problem is to construct persistent, executable environments that represent evolving business workflows involving multiple services, tools, users, and cross-service state, while allowing many tasks to emerge from a shared world. The paper positions this as relevant to enterprise automation and long-horizon tool-use agents, where success depends on state tracking, service coordination, and satisfying constraints that are not reducible to a single textual answer. Key Idea: The central insight is to separate world construction from task construction: generate a persistent executable world from a high-level scenario first, then instantiate tasks and grading specifications within that world. AGENTMERCURY also separates world-level invariants from transition rules: invariants are checked after interaction through executable verification conditions rather than automatically enforced by the simulator, making cross-service workflow requirements observable as agent responsibilities. The PLANET abstraction is the paper’s main conceptual contribution, although the underlying components—programmatic environments, task generation, deterministic verifiers, and policy optimization—largely build on established approaches. Methodology: Given a scenario σ, PLANET samples a grounded company identity C, service graph G, state schema Σ, seeded initial state s₀, and invariant set R, yielding an executable world w = ⟨S, A, Ω, T, O, s₀, R⟩. The factorization is written as p(C|σ)p(G|C)p(Σ|G,C)p(s₀|Σ)p(R|G,Σ,s₀), with the service graph and schema inducing tools, state, observations, and deterministic transitions. TASK then samples task-specific state changes Δs₀, a natural-language instruction u, and rubric ρ from the world state and invariants. The agent interacts through MCP tools under partial observability; the environment applies deterministic transitions and returns tool observations. GRADE evaluates the final state, trajectory, task rubric, and hidden invariants, primarily through database assertions such as record existence, field equality, and field inequality. The policy experiments use GRPO with eight samples per prompt for the main 4B run and SAO for an additional 35B-A3B run; training uses a corpus of 43,300 tasks from 4,326 environments, although the reported 4B run gives gradients on 3,200 tasks over 200 steps. Critical design decisions include persistent multi-service worlds rather than task-specific simulators, post-episode executable verification rather than purely textual judging, and construction traces containing forward generation, intermediate completion, validator-guided repair, and intent-to-diff supervision. The separation and deterministic execution are clearly specified, but the paper does not quantitatively justify the particular scenario-generation distributions, task templates, invariant-generation process, or reward composition. Key Results: The corpus contains 4,783 synthesized environments spanning 14 industries and 50 countries; the RL subset uses 4,326 environments, 43,300 tasks, 2,287 industry descriptions, 842 tools, 222 state-table types, and 148 service combinations. Environments expose 10–26 tools, averaging 16.1, while tasks touch 1–5 services, averaging 2.9, and contain 2–10 programmatic assertions, averaging 5.4. On ENTERPRISEOPS-GYM, Qwen3.5-4B improves from 12.3±0.2 to 15.7±0.6 with GRPO, while Qwen3.5-35B-A3B improves from 24.8±0.6 to 28.1±1.4 with GRPO and 28.3±1.5 with SAO. The 4B model improves on AIME26 from 45.9±1.7 to 56.0±1.8, HMMT from 28.5±1.2 to 35.4±1.6, LiveCodeBench from 36.6±2.8 to 44.0±1.2, SciCode from 22.6±0.1 to 25.7±0.7, τ3-Airline from 48.8±2.1 to 58.7±0.8, τ3-Retail from 70.4±1.0 to 73.6±1.3, BFCL from 30.3±1.8 to 31.7±1.5, and GPQA-Diamond from 76.5±0.7 to 77.5±0.6; τ3-Telecom decreases from 92.5±1.0 to 91.9±1.3. At 35B-A3B scale with GRPO, AIME26 rises 91.0±0.3 to 91.9±2.1, HMMT 77.0±0.9 to 80.0±0.7, LiveCodeBench 74.3±2.2 to 79.0±0.5, and BFCL 31.1±1.3 to 42.5±0.3. These results indicate transfer across several held-out benchmarks, but the gains vary substantially and some benchmarks are near saturation or unchanged. For authoring, five API models obtain a reported zero-shot mean of 78.3% in the main table, while the appendix reports 80.7%; recipe conditioning lowers the corresponding appendix mean to 78.0%. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B rises from 3.3% to 83.3% on 30 held-out briefs after fine-tuning on 29,823 construction samples, passing an average of 11.5 of 12 validators; recipe conditioning then reduces the fine-tuned model to 10.0%, with 27 of 30 failures attributed to cross-service validation. All evaluations use three independent runs, but the authoring set contains only 30 briefs. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new element is the explicit scenario-to-persistent-world factorization with reusable tasks and executable world-level invariants, while MCP interaction, deterministic database verification, GRPO/SAO optimization, and supervised trace learning are standard components applied in this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports three independent evaluation runs with means and standard deviations, deterministic evaluation for AIME, HMMT, LiveCodeBench, SciCode, BFCL, GPQA-Diamond, and ENTERPRISEOPS-GYM, and a Fisher exact test for the authoring improvement with p = 1.2×10⁻¹⁰; it also reports a paired McNemar analysis for recipe conditioning and training diagnostics for reward, response length, truncation, and degeneration. However, the central policy-learning study lacks ablations that vary world diversity, number of worlds, number of tasks, task-template redundancy, invariant verification, reward judging, or training compute. It does not compare against policies trained on an equally sized task-centric synthetic corpus, existing environment generators, supervised fine-tuning, or RL with simpler verifiers. The paper itself finds that 8.3% of tasks have a TF-IDF nearest neighbor above 0.99, that task descriptions share templates, and that tool counts take only five values, which weakens the claim that the corpus provides unconstrained task diversity. The 4B RL run directly uses only 3,200 of 43,300 tasks and 2,313 of 4,326 environments, and the benchmark evaluation uses the same Qwen-family infrastructure and model-specific configurations. A DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge contributes to training rewards and τ3 evaluation, creating a possible judge-dependent optimization or measurement effect. The paper states that synthesized environments, tasks, construction code, and trained models are released, but gives no concrete repository URL in the supplied text; release completeness and independent reproducibility are therefore not verifiable here. The preprint is marked arXiv v1, dated 21 August 2026, and the cited surrounding literature is also dominated by recent preprints, so the evidence has not been established through peer-reviewed replication. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a substantial SYSTEMS artifact because the work executes local MCP-based environments and claims to release environment code and models. * Practical: The training setup runs on commercially available GPU hardware—a single node with eight GPUs for the 4B experiment—and environments execute locally in process, but the paper does not establish the hardware requirements or operating cost for the full 4,783-environment library or for production business systems. * Efficient: The method avoids network overhead and trains on only 3,200 sampled tasks in the reported 4B run, but it uses long contexts, up to 20 tool turns, up to 8,192 tokens per turn, asynchronous rollouts, eight GPUs, and an LLM-based reward judge; no cost or throughput comparison against alternative environment generators or RL pipelines is reported. * Effective: The evidence shows improvements on synthetic enterprise workflows and several external benchmarks, including +3.4 ENTERPRISEOPS-GYM points for Qwen3.5-4B and +10.1 AIME26 points, but it does not show reliable performance in live business software, human workflows, unseen real-world organizations, or consequential deployment settings. * Scalable: The corpus scales to 4,783 environments, 14 industries, 50 countries, 842 tools, and 43,300 tasks, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger corpora, longer-running worlds, more than five services per task, more than 26 tools per environment, or adaptive generation at deployment scale. The work delivers an executable environment library, business scenarios, task instructions, construction-code differences, construction traces, trained policy models, and claimed construction code; it does not yet deliver a learned closed-loop scenario selector or a world model that identifies policy gaps and generates the next training worlds. Strengths: - The world/task/policy/verifier decomposition addresses a real limitation of task-centric agent-environment construction and gives a reusable formal interface for persistent state and multiple objectives. - The environments support deterministic replay and post-episode verification of cross-service constraints, which is stronger than judging only the agent’s final text and makes reward generation auditable in principle. - The reported transfer spans enterprise workflows, mathematics, coding, scientific computing, knowledge reasoning, and tool calling; the 4B improvements are large on AIME26 (+10.1 points), HMMT (+6.9), LiveCodeBench (+7.4), and τ3-Airline (+9.9). - The authoring experiment measures executable structural validity rather than surface similarity, and the 3.3%→83.3% improvement after trace fine-tuning is substantial, even though it uses only 30 held-out briefs. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that AGENTMERCURY does not close the environment–agent loop: PLANET does not use a learned world model or policy failures to choose future scenarios. They also acknowledge that SAO is substantially less effective for the 4B model and that the current system remains an offline environment-generation process. The authoring analysis explicitly reports cross-service invariant failures, formatting failures under recipe conditioning, and the surprising collapse from 83.3% to 10.0% for the fine-tuned model under recipe prompting. These limitations are confronted rather than hidden, although the discussion does not fully address synthetic-world fidelity, benchmark contamination, or the causal interpretation of cross-domain transfer. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The paper lacks a controlled comparison against equally sized task-centric environments and prior generators such as AppWorld, MCPMark, Agent-World, EnvScaler, or EnvFactory under matched model, optimizer, token, and compute budgets; without this, the gains cannot be attributed to scenario-grounded world construction. - The training corpus is structurally narrower than the headline counts suggest: tasks use six main personas, 148 service combinations, five possible tool-count values, a fixed core tool set, and many near-duplicate textual templates. The paper documents this redundancy but does not test whether performance depends on repeated templates or familiar tool schemas. - The use of a model-based reward judge during RL is insufficiently isolated from the deterministic verifier. An ablation using only programmatic rewards, alternative judges, or independently generated validators is necessary to determine whether transfer comes from the environments or from judge-shaped language-model optimization. - The out-of-domain evaluation does not establish causal generalization. The paper reports improvements after RL but does not compare with equal-compute language-model continued training, tool-use supervised fine-tuning, generic RL, or training on simpler synthetic interaction data. - The authoring result is statistically strong for the stated 30-brief sample, but the held-out briefs are sampled from the same country–industry distribution as the library and the validators are adapted from the construction oracle. Independent scenarios, independently authored validators, and human or domain-expert assessments are missing. - The paper claims realistic business environments but provides no measurement of realism, semantic validity, workflow coverage, transition fidelity, or correlation with real enterprise-agent performance. Synthetic database consistency is not evidence that the modeled business processes are realistic. - The main results omit training compute, total tokens, wall-clock time, number of rollouts, reward-judge calls, and exact environment-generation costs, preventing a meaningful efficiency comparison. - The benchmark set includes very recent or future-dated evaluations and model releases, but the paper does not provide a contamination audit for the base models, training traces, or benchmark interfaces beyond noting that the target tasks were not used to construct the environments. Bottom Line: AGENTMERCURY is a useful systems-and-benchmark-construction paper whose strongest contribution is the executable separation of persistent world synthesis from task instantiation and grading, but its policy-transfer claims are not yet causally persuasive because the study lacks matched environment baselines, reward ablations, compute accounting, and evidence that synthetic business structure predicts performance in real workflows.

JIT-Agent: Scaling Harness Intelligence via Just-in-Time Harness Evolution (47 ▲ )

Guibin Zhang, Leo Lu, Fangzhou Xie, Kang Zhu, Junhao Wang, Zhifei Xie, Zhaochen Yu, Zihang Liu, Zhongxiang Sun, Qiankun Li, Yue Liao, Heng Chang, Xiaobin Hu, Qibing Ren, Wangchunshu Zhou, Shuicheng Yan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces JIT-Agent, a 27B-parameter meta-agent that generates, repairs, and evolves executable task-specific agent harnesses for frozen off-the-shelf LLM backbones. - Why it's important: Agent performance depends on memory, planning, tool orchestration, and control decisions as well as model weights, so adapting the harness could improve capability and reduce inference cost without retraining or replacing the backbone. - How it does it: JIT-Agent emits a protocol-compliant four-module program—memory, planning, action, and capability orchestration—then uses validation feedback and an archive of prior harnesses to repair and improve candidates. - The good: Across 24 matched backbone–benchmark comparisons against ReAct, generated harnesses improve performance by an average of 7.6 points, while controlled evaluations report 14.9–54.1% lower per-case cost than fixed harnesses. - The missing: The paper does not provide component or stage ablations, uncertainty estimates, training-data scale, or generator-overhead accounting, making it difficult to attribute gains specifically to JIT synthesis, repair, or Evo-GDPO. - Read it or not: Agent-systems researchers and practitioners interested in runtime adaptation should read it for the protocol and empirical evidence, but should treat the broad scalability and generality claims as provisional until stronger ablations and independent evaluations appear.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the manual, task-specific design of agent harnesses: the operational layer that determines what an agent remembers, how it decomposes a task, which tools it can invoke, how it executes actions, and how it verifies or recovers from failure. This problem affects general-purpose LLM agents operating over heterogeneous domains such as deep research, office automation, planning, coding, and workspace manipulation. Existing harness-optimization methods primarily construct or improve a durable ahead-of-time scaffold using an accumulated experience distribution. That approach can be poorly matched to a new task whose computational structure, evidence requirements, state representation, or failure modes differ from prior tasks. The paper seeks to close the gap between globally optimized fixed harnesses and instance-specific harness requirements by making harness construction conditional on the task and backbone at inference time. Key Idea The core insight is to treat a harness as a structured, executable four-tuple rather than as an unconstrained prompt or program: memory, planning, action, and capability orchestration. JIT-Agent generates an instance-specific combination and implementation of these modules, allowing the task to determine the control regime and state representation—for example, a dependency DAG and artifact store for production tasks, a fact graph and bounded delegation for uncertain research, or typed state and deterministic verification for numerical and file-editing tasks. The distinctive addition over ordinary modular agent design is that the generator itself is trained to customize, repair, and improve these executable harnesses from validation and execution feedback. Methodology The system defines a protocol-induced harness space with raw generations G, syntactically valid harnesses, protocol-compliant harnesses, and executable harnesses. Every harness has modules M, P, A, and F for memory view construction, local directive formation, action/control updates, and capability selection; runtime dependencies are described as M→P→F→A and share a frozen executor backbone. HarnessFactory reimplements 13 seed scaffolds, including ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, ReSum, Flash-Searcher, GAM, MemoBrain, AggAgent, OAgent, AgentFold, HiAgent, DeepAgent, ROMA, and AOrchestra. Stage I uses a stronger frozen teacher to generate task-conditioned harnesses from three task-type-matched seed scaffolds. It filters candidates through protocol and execution validation, trains with token-level supervised fine-tuning, and adds a preference objective that favors higher reward while not increasing latency or cost; the stated utility combines reward, latency, and monetary-cost gaps. Stage II converts invalid generations and structured diagnostics—compiler errors, interface mismatches, tool failures, and runtime exceptions—into teacher-generated patch trajectories, retaining only failures repaired within two rounds and training the model to imitate these revisions. Stage III introduces Evo-GDPO: groups of generated candidates are evaluated against an incumbent archive under the same backbone, budget, and seeds; reward, latency, and cost advantages are normalized separately, combined with reward-dominant weights, and optimized using a PPO-style clipped token objective with a KL penalty. Candidates enter the archive only if they preserve or improve the reward frontier and strictly improve reward, latency, or cost. At inference, static mode generates multiple candidates, validates and repairs them, and executes one selected harness; streaming mode carries an archive across tasks and updates it after completed rollouts. The important design decisions—fixed modular interfaces, bounded repair, and Pareto-style archive retention—are motivated operationally, but the paper does not quantify their individual necessity. Key Results The evaluation covers nine benchmarks across deep research, daily work, planning, and workspace tasks: BrowseComp-Plus, DeepSearchQA, xBench-DeepSearch, AgentIF-Oneday, PinchBench, DeepPlanning-Shopping, DeepPlanning-Travel, OfficeBench, and OdysseyBench. Main comparisons use GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and additional Qwen3.6 and Mimo-V2.5 variants; broad baselines include Qwen3.7-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K2.7 Code, GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Gemini 3.5 Flash. On GLM-5.2, JIT-Agent raises the nine-benchmark average from 74.1 to 81.8 (+7.7); on DeepSeek-V4-Flash it raises the average from 66.7 to 75.5 (+8.8). Reported individual gains include DeepSeek-V4-Flash on DeepPlanning-Shopping from 59.1 to 83.9 (+24.8), GLM-5.2 on DeepPlanning-Travel from 62.8 to 83.0 (+20.2), DeepSeek-V4-Flash on xBench-DS from 70.1 to 82.0 (+11.9), and on DeepSearchQA from 76.2 to 85.1 (+8.9). JIT-Agent-equipped systems are reported as the top result in eight of nine main benchmark columns; JIT-Agent + GLM-5.2 scores 93.9 on DeepSearchQA, 69.9 on AgentIF, and 93.3 on PinchBench, while JIT-Agent + DeepSeek-V4-Flash scores 83.9 on DeepPlanning-Shopping. In controlled comparisons against Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes, and NanoBot on DeepSearchQA, xBench-DS, and AgentIF, JIT-Agent wins four of six backbone–benchmark settings. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash it reaches 85.1 on DeepSearchQA and 82.0 on xBench-DS, versus the strongest fixed-harness scores of 80.4 and 78.0; on Qwen3.6-Flash it reaches 70.0 on xBench-DS and 58.3 on AgentIF. It uses the fewest tokens and lowest reported API cost in all six controlled settings, reducing cost relative to the cheapest fixed harness by 14.9–54.1%, with a stated mean reduction of 36.0%; one example reduces xBench-DS cost from $0.075 to $0.039 while increasing performance from 78.0 to 82.0. Across six backbones and four benchmarks, JIT-generated harnesses beat ReAct in all 24 matched comparisons, with a reported average gain of 7.6 points. Streaming archive updates finish above static JIT on ShoppingPlanning, TravelPlanning, and OfficeBench, but the paper gives no numerical endpoint values, confidence intervals, or statistical tests for these curves. The evaluation is standard-to-large for benchmark breadth but not a stress test of deployment scale; the stream lengths shown are roughly 100–240 tasks, and no 10×–100× scale experiment is reported. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper’s main conceptual contribution is framing task-conditioned executable harness generation as “harness intelligence,” and its main technical contribution is JIT-Agent’s combination of a four-module protocol, learned bounded repair, and archive-relative multi-objective evolution; however, individual ingredients such as modular harness search, teacher distillation, repair from failure traces, PPO/GRPO-style optimization, and Pareto retention are adaptations of existing ideas rather than wholly new primitives. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports controlled same-backbone comparisons, multiple model families, task-type diversity, token usage, API cost, and an online-versus-static streaming comparison. It provides links to a project website, GitHub repository (https://github.com/bingreeky/JIT), and Hugging Face model page (https://huggingface.co/JIT-Agent), so a software and model artifact is claimed to be available. However, the text does not state the number of training examples, teacher identity or cost, training compute, optimizer hyperparameters beyond the objective form, number of evaluation seeds, sample counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It contains no ablation isolating Stage I, Stage II, Stage III, protocol restrictions, archive retrieval, candidate parallelism, or repair. The teacher-generated data, task splits, harness-selection procedure, and full benchmark execution configuration are not described sufficiently to establish independence from evaluation tasks or to rule out benchmark-specific engineering. Several baselines are commercial or preview/vendor models and runtimes, which makes version stability and independent reproducibility uncertain. Reported cost excludes any clearly itemized cost for JIT-Agent generation, candidate generation, validation, repair, and archive maintenance; therefore the end-to-end cost advantage may be overstated. The broad claims rely heavily on self-reported benchmark numbers in a 2026 arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed or independently reproduced results. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper presents an executable harness-generation system and evaluates it with multiple agent backbones and external tools. - Practical: The design can in principle run with commercially available API-backed LLMs and ordinary tool runtimes, and code/model artifacts are linked, but the hardware and latency required to serve the 27B JIT-Agent generator are not stated. - Efficient: Executed harnesses use 14.9–54.1% less API cost than the compared fixed harnesses in six settings, but the paper does not include the generator, validation, repair, candidate-selection, or archive-management overhead in a complete end-to-end accounting. - Effective: Same-backbone comparisons show performance gains across 18 main matched pairs and 24 ReAct comparisons, including gains on research, planning, daily-work, and workspace proxies; real-world reliability, safety, and user-level utility are not evaluated beyond these benchmarks. - Scalable: Streaming experiments show improvement over task streams of approximately 100–240 cases, but the paper does not test 10×–100× longer streams, larger archives, more tools, more concurrent users, or substantially larger task and model distributions. The work delivers a GitHub software artifact, a Hugging Face model, and a HarnessFactory codebase according to the paper’s links; it is not only a paper-form proposal. The degree of completeness, licensing, exact release contents, and independent reproducibility are not stated in the paper. Strengths - It identifies a consequential systems-level bottleneck—harness design—as distinct from foundation-model capability and turns that observation into an explicit executable representation. - The four-module protocol gives heterogeneous harnesses a common interface while retaining meaningful variation in memory, planning topology, action semantics, and capability exposure; the qualitative examples show changes beyond prompt wording. - The same-backbone controls are stronger than comparisons based only on frontier model leaderboards: JIT-Agent beats fixed harnesses in four of six controlled settings and reduces measured execution tokens and API cost in every controlled setting. - The evaluation tests transfer across three model families and both stronger/weaker variants, and the streaming experiment directly probes whether archived experience can improve later task instances rather than only optimizing isolated tasks. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that production harnesses such as Codex, Claude Code, and DeepSeek Harness expose richer mechanisms than the deliberately compact four-module design. They position the protocol as a starting point and acknowledge that future production systems may retain a stable core while allowing only selected components to change. They also frame full just-in-time redesign as a deliberately radical form and identify model–harness co-design, verifiable runtime modification, and internalization of harness skills as future work. They do not provide a dedicated limitations section addressing evaluation variance, benchmark contamination, cost accounting, or scale limits. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No ablation demonstrates that learned JIT synthesis, bounded repair, or Evo-GDPO contributes beyond selecting or prompting existing seed harnesses; the full pipeline could be benefiting primarily from task-conditioned engineering or stronger hidden priors. - The paper does not report harness-generation overhead, so the claim of improved cost–performance applies mainly to downstream execution and not necessarily to the complete system. - Evaluation uses benchmark scores and vendor/preview model baselines without reporting seeds, uncertainty, statistical tests, per-task distributions, failure rates, or validity/repair success rates; large point gains could therefore reflect unstable averages or selective task subsets. - The training distribution, held-out task construction, teacher outputs, and archive retrieval policy are insufficiently specified to assess leakage, benchmark-specific adaptation, or whether generated harnesses generalize to genuinely unseen domains and tool registries. - The four-module protocol may constrain the comparison in favor of JIT-Agent because the seed and competing harnesses are reimplemented under the authors’ common kernel; fidelity to production runtimes such as Claude Code and Codex is not independently validated. - Streaming evolution is evaluated only over short, benchmark-specific streams and reports qualitative curve comparisons rather than archive size, retention rate, diversity, catastrophic regressions, or performance under distribution shift. - The method can generate executable code that controls tools, files, email, and delegated agents, yet the paper does not evaluate security, sandboxing, permission boundaries, malicious tool descriptions, prompt injection, or unsafe self-modification. Bottom Line This is a promising and practically relevant systems paper whose protocol and same-backbone cost/performance evidence merit attention, but its innovation and generality claims should not be accepted without stage ablations, complete cost accounting, reproducibility statistics, stronger independent baselines, and large-scale safety and distribution-shift evaluation.

RISE: Adaptive Imagination for World Action Models (24 ▲ )

Hongbo Lu, Liang Yao, Chenghao He, Hao Han, Fan Liu, Wenlong Liao, Tao He, Pai Peng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces RISE, a plug-in scheduler that makes sequential Roll/Stop decisions to select a scene-dependent imagination horizon for latent World Action Models, together with the CounterDrive counterfactual driving dataset. - Why it's important: Fixed future-rollout budgets waste inference time on scenes whose current observations already determine a safe plan and may under-allocate computation to ambiguous interactions. - How it does it: A Latent Evaluator predicts prefix risk and future planning-score gains, and a cost-conditioned Rollout Gate continues autoregressive latent prediction only when estimated downstream benefit exceeds computation cost. - The good: On NAVSIM, RISE reaches 91.5 PDMS and 90.8 EPDMS while averaging 2.40 rollout steps, and its CounterDrive-trained risk evaluator improves held-out counterfactual hazard AUC from 0.49–0.52 to 0.93–0.96. - The missing: The paper does not provide multi-seed variance or a direct comparison against the strongest fixed-depth baseline at matched latency and compute, so the claimed quality–cost advantage remains incompletely established. - Read it or not: Researchers working on latent world models, adaptive computation, or autonomous-driving planning should read it for the utility-based stopping formulation and dataset, but readers seeking evidence of deployment readiness can skip it because evaluation remains offline and short-horizon.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (74) come from treating imagination depth as a sequential utility decision and introducing counterfactual supervision for risk-aware stopping. Rigor (73) and Completeness (76) benefit from component ablations, transfer testing, released code and data, and explicit limitation discussion, but Resilience (68) is reduced by target circularity, synthetic counterfactual hazards, one-seed evaluation, and the lack of a matched fixed-depth control. Impact (70) is meaningful for offline driving research but does not yet establish closed-loop safety or broad scalability. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*73 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*76 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*70 = 72.95, rounded to 73.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses inference allocation in end-to-end autonomous-driving systems that use latent future prediction before trajectory generation. World Action Models must decide how much future evolution to imagine, but existing designs generally use no rollout or a globally fixed rollout depth. This creates a quality–latency trade-off: additional prediction can resolve interactions involving crossing vehicles, pedestrians, traffic lights, or construction, while it can be unnecessary or harmful on open-road scenes. The specific prior-work gap is the absence of a per-prefix signal that estimates whether another imagined step will improve the downstream plan enough to justify its cost. A second gap concerns supervision for safety-critical alternatives: factual logs expose only the future that actually occurred, not plausible hazardous counterfactuals. Key Idea: RISE treats imagination depth as a sequential utility decision rather than a fixed architectural hyperparameter. At every prefix, it estimates the planning-score improvement available from deeper rollout and stops when the best expected improvement after computation cost becomes non-positive. CounterDrive supplies paired factual/counterfactual futures so the same evaluator can learn when risk becomes observable, while a separate risk-guided latent refinement step adjusts imagined prefixes toward lower predicted risk before final planning. The central insight is useful, but the implementation combines familiar adaptive computation, learned stopping, auxiliary risk prediction, and latent optimization rather than introducing a new learning principle with theoretical guarantees. Methodology: The system encodes four front-camera frames with a frozen V-JEPA 2 ViT-L/16 encoder, producing two observed latent steps with 512 spatial tokens of dimension 1024. A 12-layer, 384-dimensional, 12-head causal Transformer autoregressively predicts future latent steps conditioned on relative ego-motion; the maximum rollout is four latent steps on NAVSIM and three on nuScenes. A 12-layer diffusion Transformer planner consumes the observed latent, a selected future prefix, observed ego-motion history, and current ego kinematics, and generates six trajectory modes of eight poses at 0.5-second intervals using 20 DPM-Solver++ steps. RISE adds a one-layer causal GRU Latent Evaluator that predicts a Risk Profile for available prefixes and a Future Planning Gain Profile for all valid continuations. The Rollout Gate receives pooled observed/predicted latents, evaluator outputs, normalized depth and cumulative cost, next-step cost, and a computation preference lambda; it rolls when its scalar output is positive and otherwise stops. Training has three stages: (1) train the predictor with normalized latent L1 loss on factual and accepted CounterDrive sequences, then train an initial variable-prefix planner with the stated trajectory losses; (2) train risk estimates using a fixed geometry-based risk evaluator on real prefixes, pairwise factual–counterfactual ranking after annotated incident onset, and pre-onset local calibration, then perform two norm-constrained gradient steps that minimize predicted prefix risk and train a final planner; and (3) enumerate all depths, compute planner scores q_h, form continuation targets y_h = I[max_j((q_j-q_h)-lambda(c_j-c_h)) > 0], and distill the Gate with binary cross-entropy. The key design decisions—utility-based stopping, counterfactual ranking supervision, and risk-guided latent refinement—are operationally specified and ablated, although the fixed downstream evaluator used to create both gain and gate targets introduces a strong dependence on the chosen planner and metric. Key Results: On nuScenes, RISE reports an average L2 error of 0.31 m and average collision rate of 0.10, compared with DAWN's 0.33 m and 0.11; the baselines include BEV-Planner, LAW, World4Drive, WorldRFT, and DAWN. On NAVSIM v1, RISE obtains 91.5 PDMS, exceeding the listed best baseline DriveFuture at 90.7, and improves EP to 98.3 and TTC to 98.6; on NAVSIM v2 it obtains 90.8 EPDMS versus 89.9 for DriveFuture and leads or ties on seven of nine component metrics. In the adaptive-strategy comparison, RISE averages 2.40 rollout steps and 287.429 ms latency, versus 2.03 steps and 264.075 ms for Random Stop and 2.98 steps and 308.532 ms for Latent Margin; its EPDMS is 90.8 versus 89.5 and 89.7. The Scheduler alone raises NAVSIM PDMS/EPDMS from 89.7/88.9 to 91.2/90.4, CounterDrive alone raises them to 90.5/89.8, and their combination reaches 91.5/90.8. On the held-out CounterDrive test set, adding CounterDrive raises hazard AUC at 1–4 seconds from 0.49–0.52 to 0.93–0.96 and accident-recognition accuracy from 0.51 to 0.96. Transferring the Scheduler to DAWN raises PDMS from 89.1 to 90.3. The fixed-depth analysis supports heterogeneity: 1,248 scenes prefer depth 0, 4,036 prefer depth 3, and 2,180 prefer depth 4; for the depth-0 group, EPDMS falls from 89.9 at depth 0 to 88.4 at depth 4, while for the depth-4 group it rises from 88.5 to 91.1. These results are promising, but the paper does not report confidence intervals, multiple seeds, matched-compute comparisons with fixed depth, or tests beyond the short maximum horizons of three or four latent steps. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new elements are the explicit Future Planning Gain formulation for sequential WAM stopping and the CounterDrive resource, while the predictor, planner, learned gate, auxiliary risk ranking, and latent refinement are standard components combined for autonomous-driving world-action planning. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations, comparisons with Random Stop and latent-convergence stopping, prefix-distribution studies, risk-refinement-step studies, lambda sensitivity, a transfer experiment to DAWN, and explicit training equations and algorithms. It uses a held-out CounterDrive split with 511 nuScenes and 1,000 NAVSIM clips, but the paper does not state the number of verified factual–counterfactual pairs separately from total clips, annotation agreement, class balance, generation acceptance rate, or geographic/scenario split details. All experiments use random seed 239, with no multi-seed results, error bars, statistical tests, or significance analysis. The paper releases code at https://github.com/COOWAI/RISE, CounterDrive at https://huggingface.co/datasets/COWARobot/CounterDrive, and a project page at https://cowarobot-ai.github.io/RISE/; model-weight availability is not stated. The main methodological concern is target circularity: the Latent Evaluator and Gate are trained from scores produced by the authors' own intermediate/final planner and a fixed geometry-based evaluator, so the improvement may partly reflect optimizing the benchmark proxy rather than independently measured driving quality. CounterDrive is generated by Wan 2.7 from VLM-written accident prompts and filtered by humans, making its high AUC potentially easier than performance on naturally occurring hazards. The comparison set is broad but heavily populated by recent preprints, and the paper does not compare against a carefully tuned full-rollout RISE backbone at equal measured latency or compute. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: The model runs in PyTorch on eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs for training and reports inference latency on the tested system, so the components are compatible with commercially available hardware, although real-vehicle integration is not evaluated. Efficient: RISE reports 287.429 ms at 2.40 average rollouts, outperforming the 308.532 ms latent-margin comparator but remaining slower than Random Stop at 264.075 ms; it does not report latency for the strongest fixed-depth WAM or break down scheduler, predictor, planner, and diffusion costs. Effective: Offline NAVSIM, nuScenes, and CounterDrive results show improvements in trajectory metrics, collisions, planning scores, and synthetic hazard ranking, but they do not establish closed-loop driving safety or performance under distribution shift. Scalable: The method is tested only at maximum horizons of four latent steps on NAVSIM and three on nuScenes, with no 10x–100x scale test, long-horizon evaluation, larger image/model setting, or evidence that sequential gating remains advantageous when predictor/planner parallelism or deployment batching changes. The work delivers released code and a released CounterDrive dataset; trained model weights and a vehicle-deployment artifact are not stated. Strengths: - The paper identifies a concrete systems problem—fixed imagination depth—and formulates continuation in the same planning-score space used to evaluate downstream trajectories, avoiding a purely representation-level stopping heuristic. - The sequential gate is trained from complete horizon-wise utility curves but operates online using only the current prefix, which gives a clear offline-distillation route to adaptive inference. - CounterDrive addresses a real supervision deficit in factual driving logs and includes temporal incident-onset labels, validity filtering, and factual–counterfactual pairing rather than treating generated videos as unquestioned ground truth. - The evaluation separates Scheduler and CounterDrive effects, tests alternative stopping signals, transfers the Scheduler to DAWN, and reports both planning quality and measured latency rather than only a single accuracy metric. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that experiments cover autonomous driving only, so generality to other WAM domains remains untested. They also state that CounterDrive does not provide one-to-one coverage of the NAVSIM training set because counterfactual generation and filtering are costly, and they plan to scale the dataset. They do not discuss the realism limits of Wan-generated counterfactual videos, possible prompt/model bias in incident construction, dependence on the geometry-based evaluator, absence of closed-loop validation, or the narrow rollout horizons. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The claimed cost-quality trade-off lacks the most important control: a fixed-depth baseline using the identical RISE planner and predictor, evaluated at matched latency or FLOPs. The reported Random Stop comparison is not an adequate substitute. - The Gate targets are derived from the final planner's own benchmark scores and the same fixed risk evaluator used to construct evaluator supervision. This can reward proxy optimization and does not independently validate that stopping decisions improve safety. - CounterDrive's synthetic accidents are generated from VLM prompts and Wan videos, yet the paper gives no human agreement, realism rating, acceptance/rejection statistics, or evaluation against real collision and near-miss data. AUC of 0.93–0.96 on this generated test set therefore provides limited evidence for real-world hazard detection. - The experiments use one seed, omit uncertainty estimates, and do not test sensitivity to scene distribution, weather, sensor corruption, unseen locations, longer horizons, or changes in compute hardware. - The paper calls RISE a plug-in framework, but the only transfer study modifies one reproduced DAWN implementation on the same benchmark; it does not establish plug-in behavior across substantially different latent representations, planners, or non-driving WAMs. - The paper does not report the fraction of scenes stopped at each depth under the learned Gate, the end-to-end cost distribution, peak memory, or whether sequential rollout can be efficiently served in a production batch/real-time stack. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers studying adaptive computation in latent driving world models because its utility-based stopping abstraction and released CounterDrive dataset are useful, but its central efficiency claim needs matched fixed-depth controls, independent safety evaluation, and repeated or closed-loop experiments before it merits strong deployment or top-tier novelty claims.
