Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses continuous-control RL for robotic locomotion, manipulation, humanoid whole-body control, and sim-to-real deployment. Classical SAC stabilizers—including parameter projection normalization and clipped double-Q—were designed for data-limited replay buffers, where state–action coverage is narrow and extrapolation error is a major risk. GPU-parallel simulators can instead collect transitions from 1,024 environments at high throughput, broadening replay coverage and shifting the bottleneck toward fitting and exploiting useful behavior. The claimed gap is that scalable off-policy pipelines commonly inherit conservative stabilizers unchanged, even though their benefits and costs may depend on the data-collection regime. Key Idea: The central insight is that stabilizers should be matched to replay coverage rather than applied uniformly. SWD is treated as regime-independent because it changes how the fixed update budget is allocated toward recent, more policy-relevant transitions. Parameter normalization and clipped double-Q are treated as conservative mechanisms whose value should decrease as replay coverage and data throughput increase. The resulting prescription is WarpSAC-L with SWD, normalization, and clipped double-Q for data-limited CPU-scale training, and WarpSAC-A with SWD, no normalization, and single-Q learning for data-abundant GPU-parallel training. This is primarily a new empirical design principle and a targeted recombination of existing mechanisms, not a fundamentally new RL objective or estimator. Methodology: WarpSAC builds on a FlashSAC-style SAC backbone with a tanh-squashed Gaussian actor, asymmetric actor/critic observations where applicable, distributional critics with 101 categorical value heads, target networks, entropy-temperature learning, and two critic updates per policy update. The critic is trained using the Bellman target, with clipped double-Q using the minimum of two target critics in the two-critic variants; the single-Q variant removes the second critic and the minimum operation. SWD assigns replay transition i the weight w_t(i) = max(w_min, 1 - A_t(i)/T_decay), where A_t(i) is transition age, w_min = 0.1, and samples according to normalized weights. The main CPU-scale configuration uses one environment, a replay capacity of 10^6, batch size 512, one gradient step per interaction step, float32 computation, and T_decay = 80,000; GPU-parallel configurations use 1,024 environments, a 10^7 replay buffer, batch size 2,048, two gradient steps per interaction step, bfloat16 computation, and T_decay = 2,000. Parameter projection normalization renormalizes linear kernels and normalization parameters after optimization; it is either enabled for both actor and critic or disabled. Three critical design decisions are therefore SWD, normalization on/off, and two-critic versus single-critic learning. The paper justifies these decisions conceptually through extrapolation and exploitation arguments and tests them through component ablations, but it does not derive an adaptive rule from measured coverage or establish why the selected decay horizons transfer across domains. Key Results: The paper reports mean normalized score–step AUC improvements over FlashSAC of 4.5% across nine CPU-scale environments and 23.1% across fourteen GPU-parallel environments, although the paper's environment-count descriptions are internally inconsistent with the appendix task listings. It reports a 19.1% improvement in mean normalized wall-time AUC on MuJoCo Playground and a UnitreeG1TransportBox-v1 success-rate increase from 19.8% to 96.4%. On the Unitree G1 sim-to-real case, WarpSAC reaches the target performance in approximately 35 minutes on one NVIDIA A800 GPU versus approximately 55 minutes for FlashSAC, a reported 36.4% reduction. CPU-scale experiments cover Gym–MuJoCo, DMC hard tasks, HumanoidBench, and MyoSuite, with one million environment steps; GPU-scale experiments cover MuJoCo Playground, IsaacLab, MJLab, and ManiSkill, generally with 50,000,896 steps and 1,024 parallel environments. Network-capacity ablations use one to three residual blocks. SWD's largest reported CPU-scale gains occur with one block: humanoid-run improves from 209.93 to 467.39, humanoid-walk from 627.07 to 924.39, h1-hurdle-v0 from 83.80 to 101.09, and h1-reach-v0 from 3018.97 to 3529.44. The results are not uniformly favorable: WarpSAC-A is less consistent on MJLab rough-terrain Unitree G1, and the paper states that the benefit of removing clipped double-Q remains task-dependent even within GPU-parallel training. Wall-clock comparisons are strongest for the Unitree G1 case and four measured IsaacLab environments; for several other domains, FlashSAC wall-time curves are placed on a WarpSAC-based speed proxy rather than measured with independent logged traces. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new claim is the experimentally supported regime dependence of normalization and critic conservatism, while the implemented method combines existing SAC, age-based replay weighting from SWD, parameter projection, and single- versus double-Q choices rather than introducing a new learning principle with theoretical guarantees. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study uses five seeds and reports mean curves with standard-deviation shading, includes component and network-capacity ablations, provides exact and bucketed SWD implementations, and releases code at https://github.com/wzhhasadream/warprl; a project page is provided at https://wzhhasadream.github.io/WarpSAC/. The controlled comparisons hold the stated backbone, optimizer, environment interface, and network size fixed within benchmark families, which supports attribution of effects to the three studied axes. However, the evaluation is dominated by comparisons with FlashSAC, a closely related and relatively recent baseline, rather than a broad set of strong alternatives such as TD7, REDQ, TQC, DrQ-style methods, or other high-throughput off-policy systems. The paper does not report confidence intervals for aggregate AUC differences, statistical significance tests, per-task aggregate tables in the supplied text, or systematic hyperparameter sensitivity for SWD's decay horizon and minimum weight. CPU-scale experiments use approximate bucketed SWD while GPU experiments use exact SWD, so the replay intervention is not computationally identical across regimes. The main wall-time comparisons also mix implementations and, in several domains, infer FlashSAC wall time from a WarpSAC two-critic run rather than measuring every method independently. Normalized scores use author-selected references, including near-asymptotic FlashSAC references in IsaacLab, which can make aggregate comparisons dependent on the chosen normalization. The paper is an arXiv preprint dated 25 August 2026, and peer-review status is not stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper provides and evaluates a runnable RL implementation but does not present a deployed software infrastructure system as its primary contribution. Practical: The method runs on commercially available hardware, with experiments on NVIDIA A800 GPUs and an implementation available in a public repository, although the main GPU-parallel recipe assumes a high-end GPU and 1,024 simultaneous simulated environments. Efficient: Removing the second critic reduces critic-side computation, while SWD introduces measurable replay overhead: exact sampling takes 3.263 ms versus 0.710 ms for uniform CPU sampling and 1.751 ms versus 0.267 ms for uniform GPU sampling; the 2,000-bucket CPU approximation reduces sampling to 0.959 ms. A synthetic full-update benchmark reports 7.895 ms for JAX/NNX bfloat16 versus 13.922 ms for compiled PyTorch FlashSAC with AMP, but this is an implementation comparison rather than an algorithm-only cost comparison. Effective: Evidence shows improved learning curves and selected success rates over FlashSAC across many simulated tasks and faster learning in one Unitree G1 sim-to-real pipeline, but it primarily validates a proxy objective—simulated return or benchmark success—and does not establish robust physical-world performance across multiple tasks or hardware conditions. Scalable: The method is tested at 1,024 environments, 50 million environment steps, and replay buffers of 10^7 transitions, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger actor counts, buffers, models, or training horizons; claims about B200-scale or broader deployment remain extrapolations. The work delivers a public software artifact and implementation code, not a new dataset or reusable proof technique. Strengths: - The component-wise comparison isolates three practically important choices—replay weighting, parameter projection, and critic multiplicity—rather than presenting an inseparable bundle of modifications. - The data-regime framing produces a useful and falsifiable explanation for why a stabilizer can help in narrow replay and hurt when data are abundant; the network-capacity ablations provide supporting evidence for the interaction between SWD, normalization, and model capacity. - The evaluation spans eight benchmark families, locomotion, humanoid whole-body control, dexterous manipulation, GPU-parallel simulation, and one real-robot transfer pipeline, making the engineering relevance broader than a standard MuJoCo-only study. - The paper measures implementation costs and provides both an exact sampler and a bucketed approximation, exposing the nontrivial CPU/GPU overhead of age-weighted replay rather than presenting SWD as cost-free. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the current method selects WarpSAC-L or WarpSAC-A offline and does not adapt when training moves between regimes, such as narrow-data pretraining followed by parallel fine-tuning. They propose future online adaptation based on replay coverage or value-extrapolation signals. They also limit the analysis to three axes and identify entropy weighting, target-network delay, gradient clipping, and replay-ratio schedules as unstudied stabilizers. These limitations are confronted directly in the conclusion, although the paper does not explicitly acknowledge the restricted baseline set, the wall-time proxy procedure, or the uncertainty in defining the regime boundary. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper's strongest generalization claim—that SWD is consistently useful and that the prescribed variants win across regimes—is not fully supported by the presented evidence because the aggregate task counts are inconsistent and several individual tasks show ties, task dependence, or instability. The CPU-versus-GPU distinction conflates hardware, number of environments, replay-device placement, batch size, precision, update ratio, decay horizon, and simulator backend; therefore the experiments do not isolate data coverage as the causal variable. The paper does not measure replay coverage, extrapolation error, critic bias, Q calibration, or uncertainty, so the proposed mechanism remains interpretive rather than directly verified. The comparison against FlashSAC may also favor WarpSAC because both are implemented within the authors' modified backbone and because wall-time baselines are sometimes estimated rather than independently logged. Strong contemporary off-policy baselines and tuned PPO/TD7-style alternatives are largely absent, and the reported state-of-the-art language is not substantiated by a broad leaderboard comparison. Finally, the fixed SWD hyperparameters and offline regime selection leave open whether the prescription requires per-domain tuning or whether an unseen intermediate regime would prefer a different combination of components. Bottom Line: This is a useful empirical and systems paper for practitioners working with GPU-parallel robot simulation, especially because it demonstrates that removing standard SAC stabilizers can improve throughput and learning, but its central regime-generalization claim should be treated as promising rather than conclusive until stronger baselines, direct coverage measurements, independent wall-time accounting, and controlled hardware/data-scale studies are added.

Problem & Motivation: Semantic ViT encoders provide strong image-text-aligned features for understanding but often discard or suppress fine-grained information needed for pixel reconstruction, high-fidelity generation, and reference-preserving editing. Existing unified multimodal systems therefore frequently combine semantic encoder tokens with separate VAE or other reconstruction latents, achieving architectural integration without a common visual representation. The paper targets the resulting problem for multimodal models that must simultaneously recognize reference images, preserve local details, generate images, and edit specified regions. The specific gap is whether a pretrained semantic ViT can expose reconstruction-relevant information without retraining its Transformer blocks or introducing a separate VAE pathway. Key Idea: The central insight is that poor reconstruction is attributed primarily to the pretrained semantic patch embedding rather than to an intrinsic inability of the frozen Transformer blocks to carry visual detail. Replacing only the patch embedding with a random projection improves last-layer SigLIP2 reconstruction PSNR from 20.96 to 24.66, motivating a learned reconstruction-aware input pathway that shares the frozen semantic backbone. The final representation explicitly preserves semantic tokens and compressed reconstruction tokens as separate channel groups instead of entangling them through an MLP, allowing the generative objective to assign direct weight to reconstruction-critical dimensions. Methodology: For an image I, the frozen semantic path computes Ts = Fϕ(Ps(I)), where Ps is the original pretrained patch embedding and Fϕ denotes the frozen ViT Transformer blocks. A second patch embedding Pr, initialized from Ps and trained for reconstruction, produces Tr = Fϕ(Pr(I)) through the same frozen blocks. A trainable projection Wr compresses Tr from d channels to dr = 128, and the unified token is Tu = Concat(Ts, WrTr); the resulting dimensions are 896 for SigLIP2/DINOv2 and 1280 for Qwen-ViT. A ViT-XL-scale decoder reconstructs the image from Tu using pixel L2, LPIPS, and later adversarial losses; only Pr, Wr, and the decoder are updated during tokenizer training. For generation, the method uses conditional flow matching from Gaussian noise Z0 to Tu, with a linear path Zt = (1−t)Z0 + tTu and velocity-prediction loss. The balanced objective normalizes semantic and reconstruction errors by their dimensions and weights the reconstruction component by λr = 0.75. UniSpace then uses PR-Qwen-ViT as its sole visual encoder-decoder interface inside a decoder-only Qwen3-8B Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts model: understanding uses next-token cross-entropy, while text-to-image and editing use the same balanced flow-matching loss over visual tokens. Token types are hard-routed to understanding or generation experts but interact through shared self-attention. Training progresses from 256 to 512 to 1024 resolution over approximately 510M sample instances and 470B multimodal tokens, with 256 Ascend 910B NPUs for the main stages and 128 for SFT. The key design choices—freezing Fϕ, explicit channel factorization, and λr = 0.75—are motivated by controlled diagnostics and ablations, although the broader UniSpace training mixture and architectural choices are not isolated by full factorial experiments. Key Results: On ImageNet-1K at 256×256, PR-SigLIP2 obtains 29.64 PSNR, 0.87 SSIM, and 0.18 rFID; PR-DINOv2 obtains 30.84 PSNR, 0.90 SSIM, and 0.14 rFID; PR-Qwen-ViT obtains 30.16 PSNR, 0.88 SSIM, and 0.17 rFID. Against matched RAE baselines, PR-SigLIP2 reduces rFID from 0.53 to 0.18 and PR-DINOv2 from 0.57 to 0.14; for DINOv2, PSNR rises from 18.86 to 30.84. In controlled LLaVA-v1.5/Vicuna-7B understanding experiments, PR-SigLIP2 scores 64.37 average versus 63.39 for original SigLIP2-B, and PR-Qwen-ViT scores 68.94 versus 68.29 for original Qwen-ViT. For ImageNet generation, PR-DINOv2 reaches gFID 2.10 without CFG and 1.87 with CFG, compared with RAE's 1.51 and 1.13 under the reported settings; thus the proposed representation improves reconstruction substantially but does not match the strongest generation quality. In an entangled diagnostic representation, real-latent reconstruction reaches rFID 0.069 and PSNR 33.83, but generated latents decode with FID 120.9 through the high-fidelity decoder, while approximately 95% of merger variation is attributed to the semantic pathway. At system scale, UniSpace scores 4.28 on ImgEdit, versus 3.90 for SenseNova-U1 and 3.20 for BAGEL, and 7.41/7.38 on English/Chinese GEdit, for a reported bilingual average of 7.39. It obtains 0.84 on GenEval, 0.561 English and 0.533 Chinese on OneIG-Bench, and 86.49 on DPG-Bench, including the highest reported relation score of 94.97 among the listed comparisons. These results are competitive rather than uniformly dominant: SenseNova-U1 scores higher on GenEval overall at 0.91, and UniSpace's GEdit perceptual-quality scores are weaker than its semantic-consistency scores. Several comparisons reproduce numbers from prior reports rather than evaluating all systems under a common pipeline. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the diagnosis that patch parameterization can determine whether frozen semantic ViT blocks preserve or suppress pixel detail, followed by explicit semantic–reconstruction channel factorization and balanced flow matching; the MoT backbone, flow matching, ViT decoder, and multimodal task mixture are largely established components applied to this representation design. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes useful controlled evidence: replacing only the patch embedding while freezing Transformer blocks, comparisons with matched semantic encoders, an ablation of reconstruction loss weight, an ablation of reconstruction-channel compression, and a diagnostic comparison between entangled and factorized representations. The λr sweep reports FID values from 8.99 at 0.25 to 7.10 at 0.75 and 7.39 at 0.92; increasing reconstruction dimensions from 128 to 768 improves rFID from 0.163 to 0.085 but worsens 40-epoch generation FID from 6.92 to 11.07. However, the paper does not report multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. The large-scale model is trained on internally curated, undisclosed datasets, preventing verification of data composition, duplication, filtering, and contamination. The released project, GitHub repository, and Hugging Face page are listed as https://yjb6.github.io/UniSpace/, https://github.com/yjb6/UniSpace, and https://huggingface.co/yjb6/UniSpace, but the text does not specify the exact completeness of code, training data, checkpoints, or evaluation scripts. System-level comparisons often rely on numbers reproduced from other reports, and UniSpace is not compared under a fully controlled compute, data, sampling, or evaluator protocol against the strongest specialized generation and editing systems. The paper is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 9 August 2026, not identified as peer-reviewed in the supplied text. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL, because the paper builds and evaluates an 8B multimodal system as well as smaller tokenizer and generation components. Practical: The model runs on commercially available accelerator-class hardware, but the reported training setup requires Ascend 910B NPUs and the paper does not state inference latency, memory requirements, hardware compatibility, or minimum deployment configuration. Efficient: A single visual space removes the separate VAE pathway, but the unified representation has 896–1280 channels and the training run consumed approximately 142K NPU-hours; no end-to-end inference or memory comparison against dual-space systems is reported. Effective: Controlled tokenizer results establish improved reconstruction and preserved encoder-level understanding, while benchmark results show useful editing and generation, but system-level understanding is explicitly not optimized and perceptual editing quality remains weaker on some GEdit categories. Scalable: The model was trained through 1024-pixel stages with 8B parameters, 470B multimodal training tokens, and 256 NPUs, but no 10×–100× scale experiment, larger model, longer-context stress test, or independent scaling law is provided. The work delivers a released trained model and associated code/tooling according to the listed GitHub and Hugging Face links, although dataset release and artifact completeness are not stated. Strengths: - The patch-swap diagnostic cleanly localizes a reconstruction bottleneck: changing only the input projection raises last-layer PSNR by 3.70 dB while retaining identical frozen Transformer blocks. - Explicit semantic/reconstruction factorization addresses a nontrivial modelability issue demonstrated by the entangled-latent experiment, where good real-latent reconstruction coexists with generated-latent FID 120.9. - The representation-level evaluation spans reconstruction, semantic understanding, and latent generation, making the claimed trade-off more credible than an evaluation on only one task. - The open release of a tokenizer/model implementation and the application to an 8B unified model provide a potentially reusable system design rather than only a representation analysis. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that UniSpace is primarily optimized for generation and editing and that its system-level understanding lags dedicated vision-language models. They also acknowledge that the shared encoder cannot be freely updated on understanding data without risking generative performance, limiting further understanding improvements. They do not claim uniform downstream gains. These limitations are addressed directly, although the paper does not discuss the consequences of undisclosed training data, high training cost, or evaluator/protocol dependence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central system-level advantage is difficult to attribute to Patch Reparameterization because UniSpace combines the representation with an 8B Qwen backbone, MoT routing, a large proprietary training mixture, curriculum design, and SFT without matched ablations against a VAE-based MoT model trained on the same data and compute. - The internal datasets are not disclosed, so data scale, quality, licensing, geographic/language composition, duplication, and benchmark contamination cannot be assessed; this is especially important because the reported training volume is approximately 470B multimodal tokens. - There is no direct end-to-end comparison of parameter count, latency, GPU/NPU memory, sampling steps, or throughput against BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, or dual-space alternatives, weakening the claim that eliminating a VAE is practically more efficient. - The representation uses concatenation rather than a mathematically shared single latent in the strongest sense: semantic and reconstruction information remain explicitly separated channel groups, so the paper demonstrates a common interface and decoder rather than complete information entanglement or task-indistinguishability. - Evaluation lacks seeds and uncertainty estimates, and several baselines are reproduced from prior reports or use different evaluators, resolutions, model sizes, and training protocols; the resulting rankings should therefore be treated as approximate. - Scalability beyond the tested 8B/1024-pixel configuration is claimed but not measured, and no analysis examines whether the 128-channel reconstruction bottleneck remains adequate at higher resolutions or for non-ImageNet image distributions. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for its controlled insight and practical factorized tokenizer design, but its strongest system-level claims require more convincing apples-to-apples, publicly reproducible experiments before it can establish that one visual space is superior to a carefully trained semantic-plus-VAE interface.

PILOT in the Loop: Live Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Agents (25 ▲ )

Yang Xiao, Yusong Sun, Haoyi Wu, Wenyang Hui, Wen Da, Zhaokai Luo, Mu Chuan, Yao Hu, Wenjie Li, Chengyue Jiang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PILOT, a supervisor–worker agent harness that redirects active long-horizon runs and updates persistent skills and memory during execution. - Why it's important: Long-horizon failures can waste substantial inference and execution time, while post-hoc self-improvement cannot recover the run that exposed the failure or immediately validate the learned correction. - How it does it: A separate supervisor monitors a worker through a two-way live channel, issuing steer/abort actions and distilling trajectory evidence into a persistent harness loaded by later workers. - The good: Across two frozen backbones and three benchmarks, PILOT ranks first in five of six backbone–benchmark configurations, including 71.9% versus 66.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 with GLM-5.1 and 65.1% versus 59.1% for the strongest listed baseline on SWE-bench Pro with Kimi-K2.6. - The missing: The paper does not provide component ablations, multiple-seed uncertainty, or a controlled comparison isolating live steering from live self-evolution and from the added supervisor inference cost. - Read it or not: Researchers and practitioners building long-horizon coding or terminal agents should read it for the runtime architecture and empirical protocol, but should treat the causal attribution and scalability claims as preliminary because this is an arXiv v1 preprint evaluated with only two runs per configuration.

systems Novelty 75 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 65 Resilience 62 Impact 80
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Long-horizon agents operating terminals and software repositories accumulate useful procedures, conventions, and failure information during execution, but conventional reflection, judging, and memory/harness evolution usually process that information only after a run completes. Such post-hoc methods cannot rescue the active trajectory, and newly extracted knowledge cannot be tested immediately on the run that generated it. Single-agent self-correction provides timely intervention but forces one context to execute and critique simultaneously; delegated subagents separate roles but generally expose results only after the subagent finishes. The target problem is therefore online recovery and reuse of experience in stateful, multi-step terminal and software-engineering tasks, where compounding errors, stalled branches, and repeated rediscovery create reliability and inference-cost problems. Key Idea The core insight is to combine two forms of online feedback in a single supervisor–worker loop: a supervisor with a separate context can intervene in an active worker trajectory, while the same supervision process can update persistent skills and memory before subsequent workers start. The contribution is not a new model-training method; it is an orchestration architecture that makes oversight both separate from execution and temporally live, with harness evolution coupled to the supervision stream. Methodology PILOT extends the Pi coding-agent runtime. A frozen language model serves as both supervisor and worker, while a persistent harness H contains a skill library K and memory M. For a task, the supervisor spawns one or more workers, each with an isolated context and the current harness; workers interact with the environment through a reason–act–observe loop and produce trajectories. The worker-to-supervisor channel carries notifications, questions, and automatic final-result events. The supervisor can inspect relevant trajectory segments, queue steering guidance for the worker's next turn, or abort an unproductive worker and spawn another. Separately, the supervisor writes procedures, project conventions, and failure modes into K or M, producing an updated harness H' that later workers in the same or later episodes load. The self-improvement evaluation runs 20 Terminal-Bench 2.0 iterations. All tasks in an iteration start from a shared harness state; task execution itself creates or revises skills and memory without access to verifier rewards, while verifier outcomes after the iteration determine which updates from successful runs are retained for the next iteration. All harnesses receive the same self-improvement instruction, differing only in native skill and memory paths. The one-shot evaluation resets harness state per task and measures live-steering performance. Key design decisions are the role separation between supervisor and worker, the two-way event channel with steer and abort operations, and retaining only updates from successful runs across iterations. The role separation is motivated conceptually and supported by trajectory examples, but the paper does not experimentally isolate its value; the channel semantics are specified clearly; and the success-conditioned retention rule is operationally defined but may confound learning quality with verifier-based filtering. Key Results On Terminal-Bench 2.0's 89 tasks, PILOT obtains 71.9% with GLM-5.1 and 71.3% with Kimi-K2.6, compared with the strongest average single-agent baseline, Pi, at 65.7% and 66.9%, respectively; its two-backbone average is 71.6% versus Pi's 66.3%. On Hard Terminal-Bench tasks it reaches 55.0% with both backbones, exceeding Pi by 5.0 percentage points with GLM-5.1 and 6.7 points with Kimi-K2.6. On SWE-bench Multilingual, PILOT scores 71.6% with GLM-5.1 and 73.7% with Kimi-K2.6, ranking first with the former and second with the latter. On SWE-bench Pro, it scores 54.7% and 65.1%, versus Pi's 51.8% and 59.1%, for a two-backbone average of 59.9% versus 55.5%. The study excludes 43 SWE-bench Multilingual tasks and 198 SWE-bench Pro tasks because their pinned environments cannot bootstrap the evaluated JavaScript runtimes, applying the exclusions to every harness. In the 20-iteration Terminal-Bench self-improvement setting, PILOT's best observed pass rate rises from 66.3% to 80.9% with GLM-5.1 (+14.6 points) and from 68.5% to 80.9% with Kimi-K2.6 (+12.4 points). The skill library grows from 62 to 83 skills for GLM-5.1 and from 50 to 81 for Kimi-K2.6. Mean output tokens per evaluated task decrease from 28.5K to 16.3K (-42.9%) and from 41.9K to 22.1K (-47.4%), respectively; best observed successful evaluations per million output tokens increase by 110.3% and 134.0%. Against Pi and OpenCode with GLM-5.1, PILOT improves from iteration 0 to its best observed result by 14.6 points, compared with 2.3 for Pi and 7.9 for OpenCode. These are best-so-far and repeated-iteration measurements, not independent held-out-task estimates, so they demonstrate adaptation on the repeated benchmark sequence more directly than generalization to unseen tasks. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper formulates live self-improvement as a loop coupling mid-run steering with persistent harness evolution and implements it as PILOT, while the underlying language-model agent, tool-use loop, skills, memory, and supervisor–worker pattern draw on existing agent and self-evolving-harness ideas. The strongest genuinely new element is the runtime integration and evaluation of intervention during an active worker trajectory rather than only after delegated execution completes; the paper does not establish a new learning algorithm or model objective. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides a high-level algorithm and pseudocode, specifies the five channel operations, names the Pi-based implementation, reports the GitHub repository as https://github.com/XiaoYang66/Pilot, and states that the same frozen backbone drives every harness within a condition. It compares against Pi, OpenCode, Terminus-2, Hermes, and Mini-SWE-Agent, with identical backbone models and isolated containers, and applies the same task exclusions to all harnesses. However, each configuration is run only twice, with no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed analysis. There are no component ablations for live steering, live self-evolution, supervisor context isolation, abort/re-spawn behavior, or success-conditioned retention. The self-improvement comparison is also not fully matched in computational budget: PILOT includes supervisor and worker output tokens, but the paper does not report wall-clock time, API cost, supervisor frequency, number of workers, or equivalent inference budgets for baselines. The repeated Terminal-Bench tasks and retention of updates from successful runs make the self-improvement results vulnerable to benchmark-specific memorization and selection effects, although verifier outcomes are not used to create updates during a run. Model weights are not released by the authors; the evaluated backbones are open-weight models referenced through their official model cards. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — PILOT is a built runtime extension evaluated through executable agent harnesses rather than a purely conceptual proposal. * Practical: It runs through the Pi coding-agent runtime on containerized terminal and repository environments, so it is compatible in principle with commercially available hardware, although the paper does not report hardware requirements. * Efficient: Iterative harness reuse reduces PILOT's mean output tokens per evaluated task by 42.9% for GLM-5.1 and 47.4% for Kimi-K2.6, but live supervision adds inference and coordination overhead; wall-clock time, monetary cost, memory use, and comparison against equal-budget alternatives are not reported. * Effective: Pass-rate improvements across Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro support effectiveness on the evaluated proxy tasks, but only 2.3% of successful GLM-5.1 runs and 10.6% of successful Kimi-K2.6 runs were manually classified as aided by live steering, so the overall gains cannot be attributed primarily to active intervention without further ablation. * Scalable: The experiments cover two backbones, up to 20 repeated iterations, and benchmark task sweeps, but do not test 10×–100× more tasks, workers, concurrent sessions, or longer horizons; scalability beyond the tested setting is claimed only indirectly. The work delivers a software artifact—an open-source PILOT implementation/repository—and a reusable supervisor–worker harness design, but not a trained model or a new model-level learning procedure. Strengths - It identifies a concrete architectural gap between self-correction and delegated oversight: existing designs typically sacrifice either role separation or the ability to intervene before a run ends. - The live channel is specified at an implementable level through notification, question, result, steer, and abort events, and the appendix supplies pseudocode rather than leaving the system as a high-level agent diagram. - The evaluation holds the frozen backbone constant across harnesses and spans terminal operation plus repository-level repair, reducing—but not eliminating—confounding from model capability and demonstrating transfer across two task domains. - The analysis connects repeated-run behavior to measurable skill growth, token reduction, difficulty-stratified gains, and trace-based correction cases; the two examples show technically plausible recovery from both a bad strategy and a distributed-linear-layer bias-placement bug. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that repeated iterative evaluation is expensive, restricting the study to three benchmarks and two open-weight backbones and leaving proprietary models and broader coverage for future work. They also acknowledge that using the same backbone for supervisor and worker reflects a common usage scenario but leaves heterogeneous supervisor–worker pairings and their trade-offs among oversight quality, task performance, and cost unexplored. These limitations are stated directly, but the paper does not acknowledge the lack of component ablations, uncertainty estimates, wall-clock/cost accounting, or the possible benchmark-specific effects of repeated task exposure. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central causal claim is under-tested: there is no factorial ablation comparing worker-only, post-hoc evolution-only, live steering-only, live self-evolution-only, and the full PILOT loop. - Two runs per configuration are insufficient to assess variance for pass rates near 50–80%, and best-so-far reporting over 20 iterations can overstate the reliability of the final improvement. - The self-improvement protocol repeatedly evaluates the same Terminal-Bench tasks and carries forward updates selected using verifier outcomes, but it does not include a held-out task split or cross-benchmark transfer test to determine whether skills generalize rather than encode benchmark-specific procedures. - The strongest live-steering evidence is based on manual classification of successful traces only; the study does not report failed interventions, interventions that increased cost, false-positive corrections, abort rates, or inter-rater reliability. - PILOT's added supervisor calls, context inspection, worker spawning, and possible parallelism are not compared under equal token, time, or dollar budgets, weakening the practical-efficiency conclusion. - The paper does not report the number of tasks remaining after SWE-bench exclusions in the main results, detailed per-task variance, or hardware and runtime statistics, limiting independent assessment of reproducibility and deployment cost. Bottom Line The paper offers a useful and implementable runtime pattern for long-horizon agent oversight, with credible but not yet causally isolated gains, so practitioners building coding or terminal agents should read it while treating the self-improvement and efficiency results as preliminary until matched-budget ablations and held-out evaluations are provided.

Problem & Motivation Scientific users who work primarily in Python lack direct access to the tested statistical implementations in R's recommended `KernSmooth` package and may otherwise resort to error-prone ground-up reimplementations. The specific technical gap is semantic rather than algorithmic: R and Python differ in FFT normalization, sample-variance conventions, integer widths, optional-argument handling, array memory order, prefix matching, and foreign-function-interface behavior. KernSmooth adds further complexity because its seven exported functions depend on 16 R-level functions and 13 Fortran 77 source files, including routines supplied by R's internal LINPACK implementation. The project therefore addresses reliable wrapper translation and distribution, not a new kernel-smoothing problem. Key Idea The central insight is to preserve the original numerical implementation and automate only the R wrapper layer, while converting language semantics into an explicit, machine-readable intermediate reference before translation. This separates numerical risk from interface-conversion risk: the Fortran routines remain unchanged, and a dependency graph plus call-site-specific guides constrain the AI conversion agents. The approach is primarily a structured engineering workflow rather than a new algorithmic idea. Methodology The workflow has seven reported phases. First, static analysis parses `KernSmooth/R/all.R`, identifies 16 functions, classifies language, internal, and Fortran dependencies, and derives a three-level call hierarchy. Second, Meson, meson-python, Ninja, NumPy/f2py, BLAS discovery, and cibuildwheel infrastructure compile 13 fixed-form Fortran files into `_KernSmooth`; two Netlib LINPACK QR routines are added because R's internal copies are unavailable outside R. Third, 509 R call sites covering 46 unique dependencies are catalogued and converted into guides, including explicit treatments for `fft`, `var`, `as.integer`, `missing`, `matrix`, and `match.arg`. Fourth, 16 wrappers are converted in dependency order and assembled into `__init__.py`; Fortran output arrays are preallocated and read in place. Fifth, manual auditing adds typed signatures, extracts duplicated bandwidth and argument-validation logic, removes dead lifecycle code, and corrects scalar handling. Sixth, the two shipped R tests are translated to `pytest` using live `rpy2` comparisons. Seventh, tests are generated for the seven documented exports, covering positive, negative, and edge inputs, and an iterative fix loop repairs failures. Important design decisions are well motivated locally, especially column-major allocation, explicit f2py signatures, and live R references; however, the report does not formalize an overall correctness criterion or quantify the AI agents' contribution separately from manual repair. Key Results The artifact contains seven documented R exports—`bkde`, `bkde2D`, `bkfe`, `dpih`, `dpik`, `dpill`, and `locpoly`—plus translated internal utilities. They also state that the planning documents describing the broader experimental design were unavailable while writing this record. Analyst-Identified Gaps The evidence does not establish that the workflow generalizes beyond this unusually self-contained recommended R package; no second package, package family, or controlled comparison with manual translation is evaluated. The report lacks performance and memory measurements despite motivating the port partly through performance and distribution concerns. It does not independently validate the statistical outputs against analytical results except for a small `bkde` sanity check, and live comparison with the same R implementation can reproduce shared assumptions or shared edge-case behavior. The 518-test result is largely generated and repaired by the same AI-assisted workflow, so test adequacy, oracle selection, and coverage of undocumented behavior remain unquantified; code coverage and mutation testing are not reported. The claimed cross-platform wheel matrix is configuration-level evidence rather than demonstrated build or installation evidence, and the use of a hard-coded `/usr/lib64/libopenblaso.so.0` fallback weakens the portability claim outside the documented HPC environment. Bottom Line This is a useful and technically credible case study and software artifact for R-to-Python porting, especially for engineers dealing with f2py and semantic equivalence, but it is not strong evidence for a general AI code-conversion method and offers no new statistical technique or demonstrated performance advantage.

Problem & Motivation: Security operations centers, vulnerability-management teams, incident responders, and threat-intelligence analysts face high alert volumes, heterogeneous evidence, evolving adversaries, and costly manual workflows. LLM agents potentially address these demands through iterative reasoning, tool invocation, planning, memory, and multi-agent coordination, but prior work is fragmented across offensive testing, threat intelligence, SOC automation, vulnerability analysis, and phishing detection. The specific research gap is not the absence of individual systems or surveys, but the lack of a cross-domain, methodology-driven, reader-auditable synthesis that compares agent architectures, knowledge augmentation, human oversight, and evaluation maturity. The paper also targets an evidence gap concerning whether these systems have been tested under production, adversarial, privacy-sensitive, or regulated conditions. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat architectural organization and evaluation maturity as separable analytical dimensions rather than equating the most prevalent design with the most effective one. The taxonomy distinguishes stateless or externally looped single-agent systems, ReAct-style tool-calling, plan-and-execute agents, centralized hierarchical teams, peer-to-peer pipelines, and debate/consensus teams, then cross-tabulates these with security function, knowledge augmentation, HITL posture, and evaluation level. This yields the review’s main synthesis: single-agent tool calling is most common at 30.5%, whereas centralized multi-agent orchestration has the largest reported gains in a much smaller evidence base; however, neither prevalence nor isolated effect sizes establish general superiority. Methodology: The review follows PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance and covers work dated January 2022 through April 2026. The primary retrieval used 59 structured web-search queries targeting scholarly hosts and named systems, with only the first results page assessed per query, followed by forward and backward citation chaining. From 584 returned results, 380 title-level unique records, 174 scholarly records, and 37 chained records, the authors screened 211 records and retained 59 primary studies after full-text eligibility assessment. Inclusion required an LLM-based agentic loop involving tools, iterative reasoning, planning, or inter-agent communication, a cybersecurity application, and an empirical contribution; purely conceptual papers, classifier-only systems, benchmark-only studies, and papers about attacking LLMs were excluded. Each study received codes along five dimensions: D1 security function; D2 architecture; D3 knowledge augmentation; D4 HITL posture; and D5 evaluation rigor. The authors also performed an independent search of ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and arXiv, and estimated the broader eligible literature using a random sample of 60 out-of-corpus records. Critical design decisions include using web-search-mediated retrieval to capture fast-moving preprints, retaining systems whose LLM component sits inside an external execution or verification loop, and coding primary rather than all secondary security functions for marginal distributions. These choices are explained, but the search-engine ranking dependence, first-page cap, single-reviewer screening, retrospective rather than preregistered protocol, and lack of formal risk-of-bias instrument weaken the methodological basis for population-level claims. The review performs descriptive synthesis rather than a quantitative meta-analysis; it does not normalize metrics or estimate pooled effects. Key Results: The 59-study corpus is dominated by penetration testing and red teaming: 30 studies, or 50.8%, versus threat intelligence at 13.6% (8), vulnerability assessment at 10.2% (6), incident response at 8.5% (5), and only 1.7% (1) for compliance and risk assessment. The most common architecture is single-agent tool calling, with 18 studies (30.5%), followed by stateless/external-loop single-agent systems with 16 (27.1%), centralized hierarchical multi-agent systems with 11 (18.6%), peer-to-peer or pipeline systems with 8 (13.6%), plan-and-execute systems with 3 (5.1%), and debate/consensus systems with 3 (5.1%). In-context learning is used by 32 studies (54.2%), RAG by 17 (28.8%), hybrid augmentation by 7 (11.9%), and fine-tuning by 3 (5.1%). Fully automated operation appears in 52 studies (88.1%); only 6 are human-guided, 1 uses human approval, and none is human-overseen. Evaluation is E3 controlled experimentation for 44 studies (74.6%), E2 public benchmarks for 14 (23.7%), E1 qualitative evaluation for 1 (1.7%), and E4 production deployment for 0. Representative reported outcomes include HPTSA’s 4.3x improvement over single-agent zero-day exploitation, MyAntFarm.ai’s 100% actionable incident-response rate versus 1.7% for the same TinyLlama-1B model deployed singly, Audit-LLM’s reduction of false-positive rate from over 30% to under 7%, CORTEX’s actionable-alert F1 improvement from 0.66 to 0.78 and false-positive reduction from 24.9% to 14.2% relative to a matched single-agent baseline, ChatAFL’s 6.1x faster coverage than AFLNet and discovery of 9 vulnerabilities, and PentestEval’s 31% end-to-end success rate for contemporary autonomous penetration-testing pipelines. CORTEX also reports a median 152.4 seconds per ticket, 3.4x the latency and 5.68x the token consumption of its single-agent baseline. The independent database search recovered 47 of 59 included studies (79.7%) and 44 of the 51 surfaced by the primary query set (86.3%); sampling suggested roughly 345 additional eligible studies in those databases, implying a total literature on the order of 400 rather than a census of 59. These results are heterogeneous, often based on different datasets, metrics, and self-reported experimental settings, so the architecture comparisons are directional rather than statistically established. The counter-intuitive findings are that orchestration can appear more important than model scale in isolated studies, heterogeneous teams do not consistently outperform homogeneous centralized teams, and the field’s most frequent architecture is not the one associated with the largest reported gains. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION; NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; NEW TAXONOMY/DATA RESOURCE—the paper’s genuine contribution is an auditable five-dimensional coding framework, openly released corpus and search record, and descriptive synthesis separating architectural prevalence from reported performance across eight functions, while the individual agent mechanisms and most underlying experimental results are standard systems and findings drawn from prior work rather than contributions introduced by this paper. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides the full 59-query search record, independent verification-search exports, per-record screening decisions, coding manual, full 59-study classification matrix, population-estimation sample, and regeneration scripts through Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22025510. The authors explicitly distinguish their own analysis from the reported results of the included studies and state that no new empirical cybersecurity data were generated. Reproducibility is stronger than in many narrative surveys because the coding and descriptive statistics can be inspected and regenerated, and the authors quantify retrieval coverage rather than claiming exhaustiveness. However, no second reviewer independently screened records, no inter-rater agreement statistic is reported, exclusion codings were generated through an AI-assisted pass and not individually re-verified by a human, the protocol was not prospectively registered, and no formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment was performed. The paper includes limited ablation evidence only insofar as it reports ablations from selected underlying studies; it does not conduct new ablations of the taxonomy or architecture categories. Cross-paper comparisons are vulnerable to benchmark contamination, inconsistent metrics, unequal baselines, varying model generations, and publication or reporting bias. The review also contains internal evidence limitations: it analyzes only 59 studies despite estimating roughly 400 eligible works, relies heavily on arXiv, and uses a web search whose ranking and first-page truncation make recall impossible to bound. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile, because the paper conducts an empirical systematic-review and coverage analysis, although it does not run a new cybersecurity agent. Practical: The review itself is executable with ordinary research-computing resources, and its Zenodo data/code artifact is reusable; the surveyed agents range from commercially available API models to open-weight models, but the paper does not deliver or evaluate a deployable agent. Efficient: The evidence shows substantial overhead in some systems—CORTEX uses 5.68x more tokens and is 3.4x slower than its single-agent baseline—while LLMDFA reports $0.04–$0.14 per task; production-scale cost, throughput, and rework rates are generally not measured. Effective: The included studies report promising task-specific gains, but all field-level evidence remains controlled or offline, and no production evaluation demonstrates that these systems improve operational security outcomes rather than laboratory proxies. Scalable: Scalability to 10x–100x the tested workload is not evaluated; the review instead identifies static benchmarks, English-only CTI, seconds-to-minutes latency, context limits, and absent enterprise-scale telemetry as unresolved barriers. The work delivers a reusable review dataset, coding matrix, protocol, search record, and analysis scripts, but no library, CLI, trained model, or operational cybersecurity tool. Strengths: - The five-dimensional taxonomy is more informative than a domain-only survey because it links security function to architecture, augmentation, oversight, and evaluation maturity. - The paper is unusually candid about incompleteness: it reports 79.7% recovery in the verification search, estimates roughly 400 eligible studies, and explicitly refrains from calling the 59-study corpus exhaustive. - The prevalence-versus-performance distinction is analytically valuable; it prevents the common error of inferring architectural superiority from frequency and highlights that the strongest reported multi-agent effects come from a small evidence base. - The review connects technical evidence to deployment constraints—prompt injection, RAG reporting gaps, privacy and residency, human approval, DORA, NIS2, and the EU AI Act—while generally labeling regulatory extrapolations as directional rather than measured findings. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge web-search-mediated retrieval, first-page result truncation, arXiv concentration, incomplete corpus coverage, single-reviewer screening, absence of inter-rater agreement, nonregistration, lack of formal risk-of-bias assessment, AI-assisted and partly unverified exclusion coding, the absence of production-grade E4 studies, model-generation drift after the April 2026 cutoff, and the fact that financial-sector conclusions rest on one banking-specific study that is also the sole compliance study. They also acknowledge domain-specific gaps including static rather than continuous threat-intelligence evaluation, English-only CTI, limited DAST, no live SOC integration for most systems, no hardened-target testing, missing multilingual and infrastructure-critical domains, incomplete HITL frameworks, and insufficient regulatory alignment. These limitations are confronted directly and materially reduce the strength of the paper’s claims rather than being hidden behind a generic limitations paragraph. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The review does not sufficiently control for confounding when associating architecture with performance: MA-CH systems may use stronger models, more tools, larger budgets, easier or harder environments, or different success definitions than single-agent baselines, so the reported 4.3x and 100%-versus-1.7% effects cannot be interpreted as architecture effects without matched multi-system experiments. The coding framework also treats evaluation rigor primarily as setting type—E2/E3/E4—rather than assessing dataset leakage, baseline quality, statistical power, seed variance, evaluator dependence, or security-specific validity. The population estimate from a 60-record random sample is useful but has wide uncertainty and may inherit the verification query’s vocabulary and database coverage biases. The paper reports many striking numbers from included studies without systematically separating peer-reviewed results from preprints, vendor-adjacent work, or studies with unclear artifact availability, and it does not provide a formal evidence-confidence grade for each headline conclusion. The taxonomy’s boundary around SA-IO systems embedded in external loops is defensible but potentially inconsistent across papers, especially where the external loop is not an agentic reasoning process. Finally, the regulatory discussion is valuable as an agenda but does not evaluate whether cited legal interpretations, proposed audit schemas, or EU AI Act applicability classifications hold for specific deployment contexts. Bottom Line: This is a useful, unusually transparent orientation survey and data resource for researchers entering LLM-based cybersecurity agents, but its claims about architecture effectiveness should be treated as hypotheses because the underlying evidence is small, heterogeneous, largely preprint-based, and entirely short of production deployment.

Problem & Motivation: BERT-family encoder models remain deployed for classification, ranking, retrieval, and question answering, where CPU inference can provide lower infrastructure cost and broader availability than accelerators. Their transformer linear layers are dominated by GEMM computation, making INT8 arithmetic attractive, but straightforward quantization and eager-mode TorchAO execution leave runtime overhead from activation scaling, tensor conversions, weight-layout transformations, unfused post-operations, and backend setup. The specific gap is an end-to-end, maintained, native PyTorch 2.x path that turns SmoothQuant-quantized encoder models into efficient Xeon CPU code across both older AVX512_VNNI-only systems and newer AMX systems. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat quantization and compilation as one backend-aware graph transformation rather than as separate model preprocessing and kernel execution stages: identify the INT8 GEMM–scaling–bias/activation subgraph, lower it to a fused operator with prepacked weights and cached metadata, and use shape-dependent compilation-time benchmarking to choose between oneDNN and generated ISA-specific kernels. Methodology: The pipeline starts with a pretrained model and TorchAO SmoothQuant calibration, which inserts observers, collects activation statistics, derives per-channel smoothing factors, and replaces linear layers with quantized tensor subclasses containing INT8 weights, scales, and smoothing metadata. The quantized forward graph executes INT8-by-INT8-to-INT32 GEMM through `torch._int_mm`, followed by scale application and higher-precision non-linear operations. TorchInductor then matches patterns such as `reshape -> int_mm -> dtype_convert -> mul -> mul -> reshape -> bias`, replaces them with `qlinear_pointwise`, folds weight conversion into constants, caches oneDNN setup data, and can further fuse operations such as GeLU. The CPP backend generates candidate oneDNN and template-based GEMM implementations, including AMX kernels for newer Xeons and AVX512_VNNI kernels for Ice Lake, compiles and microbenchmarks them, and retains the fastest choice for each shape. On Ice Lake, where the available instruction path requires unsigned activations, the method transforms signed activations using `Xu8 = uint8(int32(Xs8) + 128)` and precomputes the corresponding weight-sum compensation. The main design decisions—offline smoothing and static quantization, fused scale/post-operation handling, and runtime kernel selection—are technically plausible and supported by performance results, but the paper does not isolate their individual benefits with component-level ablations. Key Results: The experiments use BERT-large, DistilBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa with batch size 1 and sequence length 256 on a 3rd-generation Ice Lake Xeon 8358 with 64 physical cores and a 6th-generation Granite Rapids Xeon 6980P with 256 physical cores; throughput uses multi-instance execution with four cores per instance. Relative to FP32, dynamic/static SmoothQuant throughput speedups are 2.22×/2.58× for BERT-large, 1.90×/2.30× for DistilBERT, and 1.86×/2.17× for XLM-RoBERTa on Ice Lake; corresponding Granite Rapids speedups are 5.02×/5.82×, 4.24×/5.37×, and 4.17×/5.41×. Linear-block latency improves by 3.05–3.87× on Ice Lake and 7.58–9.92× on Granite Rapids. Against BF16 on Granite Rapids, static INT8 improves throughput by 1.59× for BERT-large, 1.24× for DistilBERT, and 1.29× for XLM-RoBERTa, while dynamic INT8 is slower than BF16 for DistilBERT and XLM-RoBERTa at 0.98× and 0.99×. On SQuAD 1.1 and MultiNLI, accuracy changes remain below 0.7 percentage points in the reported metrics, with the largest stated degradation being DistilBERT SQuAD exact match under static quantization, from 79.02 to 78.49. The roofline analysis estimates INT8-vs-FP32 end-to-end ceilings of 3.15× on Ice Lake and 7.06× on Granite Rapids; measured static throughput reaches 2.58× and 5.82× respectively. These results are meaningful at standard model scale but do not test larger batch sizes, longer sequences, service-level latency distributions, or multi-tenant deployment. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; the quantization method and basic INT8 arithmetic are established, while the paper's genuine contribution is their upstreamed integration with TorchAO/TorchInductor, fused Xeon-specific lowering, Ice Lake signed-to-unsigned compensation, and measured performance behavior across Xeon generations rather than a new quantization formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper specifies model names, hardware, batch size, sequence length, core allocation, thread settings, warm-up and measurement iterations, AOTI usage, quantization granularity, and calibration/evaluation datasets. It provides a benchmark repository at https://github.com/Xia-Weiwen/torchao_smoothquant_benchmark and states that the implementation was upstreamed to PyTorch and TorchAO, but it gives no exact upstream commit or version corresponding to all results. It reports no random-seed analysis, error bars, repeated-run variance, or statistical tests. There are no ablations separating graph fusion, prepacking, kernel selection, AMX/AVX512_VNNI kernels, or the Ice Lake compensation path. Performance baselines are limited to FP32 and BF16; the study omits direct comparisons with ONNX Runtime, IPEX, Intel Neural Compressor, vendor libraries, or alternative native PyTorch quantization paths. Throughput uses synthetic inputs and an aggressive multi-instance, weight-sharing configuration, whereas accuracy uses only six task-finetuned checkpoints and two datasets; this limits conclusions about production traffic, calibration robustness, and model diversity. The paper also reports relative speedups without absolute RPS, latency percentiles, memory footprint, compilation time, or calibration cost. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. * Practical: The workflow targets commercially available Intel Xeon CPUs and generates C++/AOTI code through PyTorch, but practical portability beyond the two tested Xeon generations and the exact software-version requirements are not stated. * Efficient: Static INT8 delivers 2.17–2.58× throughput gains over FP32 on Ice Lake and 5.37–5.82× on Granite Rapids, while outperforming Granite Rapids BF16 by 1.24–1.59× for static quantization; absolute memory use, compilation overhead, and end-to-end service latency are not measured. * Effective: The experiments show substantial GEMM and end-to-end throughput gains with less than 1% reported downstream accuracy loss on SQuAD and MultiNLI, but they evaluate only proxy workloads and do not establish benefits for real production request distributions or tail latency. * Scalable: The paper tests 64- and 256-core systems but only batch size 1 and sequence length 256, so behavior at 10×–100× model, sequence, batch, or concurrent-service scale is not evaluated; scalability beyond the tested Xeon configurations is claimed only indirectly. The work delivers a reusable software implementation integrated into PyTorch/TorchAO/TorchInductor, plus a public benchmark repository; it does not introduce a new dataset, trained model, or reusable proof technique. Strengths: - It addresses a concrete deployment gap between a correct PyTorch-native quantization workflow and a production-quality CPU execution path, rather than evaluating quantization in isolation. - The fused lowering removes several identifiable overheads—runtime weight layout conversion, separate scale operations, and repeated oneDNN setup—and aligns them with the actual Xeon instruction constraints. - Supporting both AMX-capable Granite Rapids and AVX512_VNNI-only Ice Lake, including the mathematically compensated signed-to-unsigned transformation, improves architectural coverage over a single-generation optimization. - The roofline/Amdahl analysis connects measured results to hardware bottlenecks and explicitly explains why INT8 gains over FP32 are much larger than gains over BF16 on Granite Rapids. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly note that the roofline ceilings are idealized, that quantization/dequantization, dynamic-scale search, Ice Lake compensation, and framework overhead reduce realized speedups, and that linear-block latency is only an approximation of pure GEMM latency because it includes post-operations and differs across fusion paths. They also restrict the study to representative BERT-family models, batch size 1, sequence length 256, two Xeon generations, and omit per-tensor weight quantization because its potential accuracy cost was not the focus. These limitations are discussed directly, although the paper does not fully discuss the consequences of synthetic performance inputs or the absence of external runtime baselines. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest missing evidence is a direct comparison with established CPU deployment stacks, especially ONNX Runtime, IPEX, Intel Neural Compressor, and optimized FP32/BF16 oneDNN paths under identical threading and instance configurations. The paper should report absolute throughput, median and tail latency, memory footprint, model conversion/calibration time, compilation time, and cold-start behavior, since relative warm throughput can obscure deployment costs. It also needs ablations to establish whether the gains come primarily from INT8 arithmetic, fusion, prepacking, kernel selection, or multi-instance cache sharing. The accuracy study is narrow, uses task-finetuned checkpoints selected by the authors, does not report calibration-set size or sensitivity, and includes an XLM-RoBERTa checkpoint fine-tuned on SQuAD 2.0 evaluated on SQuAD 1.1, which weakens interpretability. Finally, the claim of an out-of-the-box native PyTorch path would be more credible with exact PyTorch/TorchAO/oneDNN revisions, reproducible build instructions, and evidence from additional sequence lengths, batch sizes, socket configurations, and real request traces. Bottom Line: This is a useful systems and compiler-engineering contribution for practitioners deploying encoder NLP models on Intel Xeon CPUs, with credible measured speedups and an actionable upstream implementation, but its novelty and comparative strength are limited by missing absolute metrics, external baselines, ablations, and broader deployment evaluation.

VGI-BENCH: Probing Visual Intelligence in Video Generation Models (139 ▲ )

Xuan He, Cong Wei, Yuhao Cheng, Linrui Ma, Yuxuan Zhang, Zuojun Li, Yuhao Wen, Jize Jiang, Zeyi Liu, Yuren Hao, Songcheng Cai, Keming Wu, Penghui Du, Kai Zou, Rui Yang, Chenkai Sun, Ke Yang, Ping Nie, Kelsey R Allen, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao, ChengXiang Zhai · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces VGI-BENCH, a 27-task, 810-instance benchmark for evaluating whether image-to-video generation models can perform visually grounded, process-sensitive reasoning. - Why it's important: Existing evaluations can conflate reasoning with visual-domain mismatch or accept plausible final states without verifying the intermediate process, making model capability estimates unreliable. - How it does it: It combines photorealistic input scenes, three calibrated difficulty levels, a task-and-skill taxonomy, and a VLM evaluator that multiplies goal completeness by checklist-based process validity. - The good: Across nine video models, the strongest overall score is only 51.0%, while strict end-to-end success is 14.0%, and the evaluator reaches 0.803 ROC-AUC and 73.2% pairwise agreement with human preferences. - The missing: The benchmark relies heavily on a single VLM judge and a narrow, model-calibrated task suite, without fully establishing cross-judge validity, inter-human reliability, or performance at longer horizons and broader conditioning modes. - Read it or not: Researchers evaluating generative video reasoning should read it for the benchmark design and denoising analysis, while practitioners seeking a deployable reasoning system will find no new model or demonstrated downstream deployment.
