Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the problem of measuring visual intelligence in video generation models rather than only visual fidelity, motion realism, or prompt alignment. The target domain is generative video models used as visual world simulators or potential vision foundation models, especially in image-to-video settings where a model must transform an input scene through a valid sequence of actions. Prior benchmarks often use abstract or line-art inputs that may be distributionally mismatched with models trained predominantly on natural imagery; many permit answers that can be inferred from a static input or judged only from a final state; and some include tasks whose duration or non-visual knowledge requirements make failure difficult to interpret. The paper aims to close these evaluation gaps by requiring process-sensitive rollouts, using realistic-style inputs, and calibrating tasks near the current capability boundary. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat visual reasoning in a video generator as a constrained procedural rollout rather than as production of a plausible target frame. Each task requires both global progress toward a goal and preservation of local process rules, so the final score is the product of a completeness score and a rubric score. This design makes shortcuts such as teleportation, rule violations, object duplication, altered scene structure, or reaching a correct-looking state through an invalid trajectory count against the model. Methodology: VGI-BENCH contains 27 tasks and 810 instances distributed across Visual Organization (5 tasks), Physical Manipulation (7), Structured Puzzles (8), and Spatiotemporal Dynamics (7). Each task is tagged with one or more of seven skills—Planning, Spatial, Temporal, Attribute Grounding, Physics, Affordance, and Topology—and has approximately ten instances at each of Easy, Mid, and Hard levels. The model receives a 16:9 input image and an English prompt specifying the goal, allowed actions, prohibited shortcuts, object constraints, and scene-preservation requirements, then produces a 5–10 second video. Inputs come from web/existing datasets or image-generation systems; generated inputs are manually reviewed and iterated. Task proposals are prefiltered by testing two easy instances on several contemporary video models, retaining tasks solved by at least one model and failed by at least one, followed by manual checks for clarity, duration, and fidelity. Evaluation uses a VLM judge in two passes: Completeness samples the video at 2 fps and maps task-specific judgments to 0, 0.5, or 1; the Rubric pass samples at 4 fps, adaptively refines suspicious intervals to 8 fps, uses sliding focus windows, counts deduplicated checklist violations, and assigns each item a score of 1/(x+1). The final per-instance score is Completeness × Rubric. Critical design choices include realistic rather than abstract inputs, explicit process-sensitive rubrics, and multiplicative aggregation; the paper motivates each choice, but the precise rubric weights, inverse-decay function, and task-calibration procedure remain partly heuristic. An auxiliary 16-task image-output subset removes temporal-process requirements and measures binary static goal-state success. Additional analyses compare vanilla and oracle prompts, realistic and line-art inputs, VBVR fine-tuned versus base models, and decoded intermediate states across diffusion denoising steps. Key Results: On the primary video benchmark, Seedance 2.0 obtains the highest overall final score at 51.0%, followed by MiniMax-H3 at 44.4%, Kling 3.0 at 44.0%, Gen-4.5 at 36.6%, Sora 2 at 36.7%, Wan 2.7 at 35.7%, Veo 3.1 at 32.0%, Wan 2.2 at 21.6%, and HunyuanVideo-1.5 at 19.1%. Seedance 2.0 leads Visual Organization (60.8), Physical Manipulation (56.0), and overall performance, while MiniMax-H3 leads Structured Puzzles (50.6) and Spatiotemporal Dynamics is highest for Seedance 2.0 at 45.3. Structured Puzzles is the weakest domain for most commercial systems, and Topology and Temporal are identified as weak skill dimensions. Under the stricter criterion requiring perfect completeness and perfect rubric scores, Seedance 2.0 reaches only 14.0% overall, compared with 97.1% for the human reference study; MiniMax-H3 reaches 12.1%, VBVR-Wan2.2 11.0%, and the remaining models are at or below 9.5%. The judge agrees with human pairwise preferences at 73.2% accuracy and 0.803 ROC-AUC; removing adaptive sampling lowers these to 69.5% and 0.772, and removing focus windows lowers them to 68.3% and 0.753. On the auxiliary image subset, Nano-Banana-Pro scores 55.0% and Seedream 4.5 scores 23.8%; this comparison is not directly equivalent to the video metric because it evaluates static target states with a binary judge. Oracle prompts improve some models but do not reliably produce valid trajectories. Realistic versus line-art input changes rankings and often causes greater degradation for open-source models. Synthetic VBVR fine-tuning improves Wan2.2-I2V from 21.5 to 41.2 overall, with overlap-task performance rising from 15.3 to 55.8, semi-overlap from 17.8 to 34.9, and non-overlap from 29.2 to 35.4; however, Wan2.1 and LTX2.3 show smaller or negative changes on some groups. In the denoising analysis of 702 checkpoint transitions from 117 instances across four open-source models, wrong-to-correct transitions remain at or below 0.9%, whereas wrong-to-wrong transitions reach 23.1% from steps 4 to 10 and 24.8% from steps 10 to 20; readable states become stable in 90.6% of transitions from steps 20 to 40. The main results use half of the instances per task and difficulty; a limited six-task, five-model full-set check reports an average half-versus-full difference of 2.3 percentage points and preserved model rankings. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW EVALUATION FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The benchmark’s combination of realistic inputs, process-sensitive procedural tasks, difficulty calibration, hierarchical taxonomy, and adaptive VLM judging is the main contribution; the evaluator uses standard VLM-as-judge and frame-sampling ideas, while the denoising and synthetic-transfer findings provide new empirical analyses rather than a new generation algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes ablations for adaptive frame sampling and sliding focus windows, comparisons among several judge backbones, a half-versus-full instance stability check, human preference validation, oracle-prompt tests, visual-style comparisons, and base-versus-fine-tuned model analyses. It reports 0.803 AUC and 73.2% pairwise accuracy for the primary evaluator, but it does not report conventional error bars, multiple-seed generation estimates, confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement before filtering. The human preference pool contains 1,100+ filtered pairs from four co-authors, with contradictory pairs and preference cycles removed; this filtering may inflate apparent judge agreement and limits external validity. The benchmark data and evaluation code are stated to be released under a research-friendly license, and the first page displays Project Page, Data, and Code links, but exact URLs, release status, and model-weight availability are not stated in the provided text. Most benchmark scores rely on one Gemini-3-Flash-based judge, and the alternative judge results vary substantially, including 0.478 AUC for Claude-Haiku-4.5. The task acceptance criterion explicitly uses contemporary models, which makes the benchmark capability-boundary calibration useful diagnostically but also risks model-dependent selection and future saturation. Generated input images and extensive prompt constraints improve control but may introduce artifacts or bias toward behaviors anticipated by the authors. Comparisons with prior benchmarks are largely desiderata-based and partly inferred for unreleased datasets rather than controlled head-to-head evaluations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper evaluates existing commercial and open-source video/image models and does not introduce a deployed system. Practical: The benchmark can run on commercially available APIs or local NVIDIA H20 GPUs, but full evaluation is expensive and commercial video generation costs range from $0.08 to $0.20 per second, excluding judge calls. Efficient: The half-instance protocol reduces cost, and adaptive rubric sampling avoids dense evaluation of every frame, but each model-task cell still requires video generation plus multiple VLM judgments; no end-to-end wall-clock or total-budget measurement is reported. Effective: The process-sensitive scores, strict success rates, failure-mode analysis, and human comparison provide evidence that the benchmark distinguishes partial progress from valid completion, although the primary conclusions remain dependent on VLM-judge validity and proxy task design. Scalable: The study tests 27 tasks, 810 total instances, 5–10 second clips, 16:9 i2v inputs, and only a limited full-set slice; it does not test 10×–100× larger task pools, longer videos, text-to-video, multi-image, audio-conditioned generation, or long-horizon planning. The work delivers a benchmark dataset and evaluation code as claimed, but it does not provide a new model, library, or deployed reasoning artifact; exact artifact URLs and release verification are not stated. Strengths: - The benchmark targets a meaningful measurement gap by requiring valid intermediate trajectories rather than accepting only plausible final states. - The two-level taxonomy and four-domain organization support diagnosis beyond a single aggregate score, while the 27 tasks span spatial organization, physical interaction, puzzles, temporal dynamics, topology, and planning. - The completeness–rubric product is a clear operational response to the failure mode in which a model reaches a target-looking state through teleportation, scene alteration, or rule violations. - The paper combines broad model coverage with useful diagnostic experiments: visual-style sensitivity, oracle prompting, synthetic-to-real transfer, failure categories, and denoising-state transitions. The finding that wrong-to-correct transitions occur at no more than 0.9% is particularly informative for claims about self-correction in diffusion video generation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the benchmark to roughly 5–10 second image-to-video generation with fixed 16:9 inputs. Text-to-video, multi-image conditioning, audio conditioning, and longer-horizon procedures are out of scope. Prompts and rubrics are English-only, and the task suite is representative rather than exhaustive. The authors also acknowledge that performance transfer from synthetic fine-tuning is uneven, that overlap does not guarantee improvement, and that later denoising steps generally refine rather than correct early hypotheses. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The validity of the central score is not fully established: the primary judge is a single VLM configuration, human agreement is based on filtered pairwise preferences from four co-authors, and no independent annotator agreement or unfiltered agreement statistics are reported. - The adaptive rubric judge samples frames rather than evaluating continuous video, so brief physical violations, object identity failures, or temporal discontinuities can remain invisible; the paper reports lower human alignment for Physics and Topology but does not quantify missed-event rates. - Difficulty calibration is model-dependent because tasks are retained after testing contemporary generators. This may produce a benchmark that reflects the authors’ model panel and prompt design more than a stable, external capability scale. - The benchmark inputs are partly generated by image models and manually refined, while prompts contain highly specific scene-control instructions. The paper does not report the proportions of web, existing-dataset, scripted, and generated inputs, nor does it test whether results transfer to naturally occurring scenes with less curated structure. - The central model comparison uses one fixed random half of instances per task and difficulty. The limited six-task full-set check is reassuring but too small to establish uncertainty for all 27 tasks, domains, skills, and model rankings. - The paper presents aggregated model scores without per-task variance, generation-seed sensitivity, API sampling variability, or cost-normalized comparisons; these factors may materially affect rankings for stochastic commercial systems. - The denoising analysis labels decoded visual solution states using human or unspecified annotation procedures, but the reliability and reproducibility of these intermediate-state labels are not quantified. The inference that denoising transitions correspond to reasoning decisions therefore remains suggestive rather than causal. Bottom Line: VGI-BENCH is worth reading as a carefully motivated diagnostic benchmark and a useful empirical study of process failures in video generators, but its conclusions should be treated as benchmark- and judge-dependent until broader human validation, uncertainty reporting, and evaluation beyond the curated 5–10 second i2v regime are provided.

Problem & Motivation: Neuro-symbolic software development combines neural prediction with logic, rules, constraints, probabilistic programs, or other symbolic structures, but framework selection is complicated by incompatible modelling languages, semantics, solvers, training interfaces, and deployment assumptions. The problem affects AI researchers and software developers working across domains such as visual reasoning, structured NLP, probabilistic inference, planning, knowledge-graph management, and embedded AI. Existing surveys classify neuro-symbolic work by research area, application, or architecture, but do not sufficiently support developer-facing comparison of reusable open-source frameworks. The paper targets this gap by asking which frameworks are available, how their linguistic and reasoning commitments differ, how they integrate neural and symbolic components, and what engineering limitations affect adoption. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat a neuro-symbolic framework as a sequence of coupled design commitments: the symbolic language determines the semantics; the semantics determine the inference substrate and computational cost; the neural-symbolic pipeline determines how symbolic information interacts with learning; and these choices determine usability, scalability, and engineering requirements. The four-dimensional taxonomy is therefore more than a feature checklist: it is an interpretive map from modelling choices to developer-visible trade-offs. The paper’s most useful synthesis is that semantic fidelity, differentiability, expressiveness, and scalability cannot generally be maximised simultaneously. Methodology: The study conducts a systematic literature review following software-engineering systematic-mapping guidance. Searches in Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, and IEEE Xplore used a query combining neuro-symbolic AI, software/framework terms, and open-source requirements; the search ran in February 2026. From 1,040 initial records, deduplication produced 633 candidates for title-and-abstract screening, 72 full texts were inspected, and 42 articles were retained, representing 41 framework-level approaches. The review uses backward snowballing and separates application-specific systems from general-purpose frameworks. It then selects nine general-purpose frameworks with open-source artefacts and documentation sufficient to explain the modelling language, installation, and at least one example: PYLON, LTN/LTNtorch, DomiKnowS, Scallop, DeepProbLog, SLASH, Edward/Edward2, DeepStochLog, and NeurASP. The taxonomy records syntax, logical paradigm, expressiveness, solver, inference mechanism and strategy, loss computation, Kautz-style architecture, integration, scalability, suitable use cases, and limitations. Critical design decisions include restricting the detailed comparison to documented general-purpose projects, using observable framework commitments rather than author labels, and interpreting repository metadata and maintenance status as engineering evidence. These decisions are motivated, but the selection and qualitative coding remain partly judgment-dependent and are not validated through an independent user study or quantitative coding reliability for the taxonomy itself. Key Results: The review retained 42 articles published from 2017 through February 2026, corresponding to 41 framework-level approaches; 19 were classified as general-purpose and the remainder as application-specific at the framework level, although the article’s article-level tables report 21 application-specific and 21 general-purpose studies. Nine general-purpose frameworks were analysed in depth. Six of the nine selected frameworks were classified as primarily following Kautz’s Neuro | Symbolic pattern, in which neural outputs feed a symbolic reasoning component. Constraint- and fuzzy-oriented systems include PYLON, LTN/LTNtorch, and DomiKnowS; logic and probabilistic systems include Scallop, DeepProbLog, SLASH, DeepStochLog, and NeurASP; Edward/Edward2 represents probabilistic programming rather than logic-centred neuro-symbolic reasoning. The usability table labels accessibility as high for PYLON, Scallop, SLASH, Edward/Edward2, and DeepStochLog; medium for LTN/LTNtorch and DomiKnowS; and low for DeepProbLog and NeurASP, but these ratings are qualitative and not tied to measured installation time or developer studies. No accuracy, runtime, throughput, memory, parameter-count, speedup, error-bar, or significance results are reported, and no framework is experimentally compared against another on a common benchmark. The headline empirical result is consequently the composition and qualitative classification of the corpus, not a performance ranking. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION are the best-fitting categories: the genuinely new contribution is a developer-oriented four-dimensional taxonomy and its synthesis of 41 framework-level approaches, while the underlying frameworks, logical formalisms, Kautz architectural patterns, and repository metadata are existing material rather than newly invented methods or systems. Rigor & Reproducibility: The review reports a documented protocol, database sources, query strategy, inclusion and exclusion criteria, screening counts, backward snowballing, and inter-rater agreement of 80.6% for title-and-abstract screening and 84.7% for full-text screening using Krippendorff’s alpha, with disagreements resolved through discussion and an additional reviewer when needed. A replication spreadsheet is released at https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FDhApZAdCQRN8439wNBC2xpiRynM01W0bLOMlfVg4Y4/edit?usp=sharing and contains search results, decisions, the final corpus, extracted data, repository metadata, licenses, and last-commit information. There are no experimental ablations, random seeds, error bars, significance tests, or controlled performance measurements because the study is qualitative. The main methodological concerns are the narrow search string’s dependence on explicit neuro-symbolic and open-source terminology, exclusion of non-peer-reviewed material, subjective selection of nine frameworks based partly on documentation quality, and lack of quantitative validation that the taxonomy predicts adoption or performance. The paper also contains a minor reporting ambiguity: article-level counts show 21 application-specific and 21 general-purpose studies, whereas the framework-level discussion states 22 application-specific and 19 general-purpose frameworks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper gathers and analyses observations about published frameworks and their repositories, although it does not itself deploy a new system. Practical: The reviewed frameworks generally target Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, or accessible source repositories and can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but the paper does not provide a unified installation or hardware evaluation. Efficient: Relative compute and memory costs are not measured; the analysis only identifies likely bottlenecks such as grounding, possible-world enumeration, answer-set search, proof-space growth, compilation, solver calls, and fuzzy quantifier aggregation. Effective: The evidence establishes a useful qualitative map of framework capabilities and trade-offs, not that any framework improves task accuracy, reliability, interpretability, or total development cost. Scalable: The paper does not test 10×–100× scale; it infers scalability limitations from the underlying reasoning mechanisms and reports framework-specific mitigations such as SLASH pruning, Scallop top-k proof selection, and DeepStochLog tabling and derivation forests. The work delivers a reusable online spreadsheet and taxonomy, but no new library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or deployed software artifact. Strengths: - It frames framework choice around coupled semantic and engineering commitments rather than superficial feature lists, linking language and reasoning choices to grounding, solver, differentiation, and deployment consequences. - It covers a heterogeneous but relevant set of 41 framework-level approaches, including constraint-guided learning, fuzzy first-order logic, probabilistic logic programming, ASP, relational programming, and probabilistic programming. - It separates application-specific systems from reusable general-purpose frameworks, which directly serves the stated software-development and framework-selection use case. - The review reports screening counts, agreement statistics, threats to validity, repository metadata, and a replication spreadsheet, giving the qualitative synthesis a stronger audit trail than an informal survey. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge construct-validity problems in distinguishing frameworks, tools, and application-specific systems; internal-validity risks from screening and coding decisions; the time-sensitive nature of repository availability, documentation, dependencies, and maintenance; and conclusion-validity limitations caused by heterogeneous tasks and evaluation protocols. They also explicitly state that controlled comparisons on standard benchmarks, including runtime and output performance, are outside the present study and are planned as future work. The authors directly confront these boundaries rather than claiming that the taxonomy establishes performance superiority. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The study does not quantify the reliability or predictive usefulness of the proposed taxonomy beyond screening agreement, and it does not report independent validation by developers attempting to build the same applications with different frameworks. The database query may miss work that uses alternative terminology, especially newer foundation-model, program-synthesis, constraint-learning, or probabilistic-programming language without the exact “neuro-symbolic” and “open-source” wording. The nine-framework deep analysis is filtered by documentation quality, which is relevant to usability but may systematically exclude technically important projects with poor documentation. The usability and scalability labels lack operational definitions, measured workloads, resource budgets, or comparable baselines. Repository “last commit” is also an incomplete proxy for engineering maturity: it does not establish test coverage, issue resolution, release stability, API compatibility, security, or reproducible builds. Finally, the paper’s framework-count inconsistency should be corrected because the corpus composition is a central result. Bottom Line: This is a useful, reproducible qualitative map for choosing among neuro-symbolic frameworks and for identifying research gaps, but it does not support claims about comparative effectiveness or scalability; practitioners needing deployment evidence should wait for or conduct a controlled benchmark study.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses safety alignment for instruction-following language models in settings where harmful and benign requests can share surface transformations such as role-play, translation, academic framing, fictional framing, indirect formulation, or formatting constraints. The central failure is that prompt-level refusal supervision can make the wrapper itself predictive of refusal: transformed harmful prompts bypass safeguards, while similarly transformed benign prompts are rejected. The paper targets the gap between surface-form robustness and intent-sensitive behavior, especially the failure of training datasets that add transformed harmful examples without matched benign counterexamples. The affected users are developers of safety-tuned assistants who must balance harmful-request refusal with helpfulness on sensitive, dual-use, or benign requests. Key Idea: Treat a group of surface variants expressing one underlying intent—not an isolated prompt—as the supervision unit, and make wrapper form non-diagnostic by pairing harmful and benign intents under the same wrapper families. WIFA supplies this structure; A-GCRT then makes the model's refusal/compliance orientation consistent across variants of an intent and pushes harmful and benign group means to opposite sides of a margin. The conceptual contribution is a structured supervision principle, although the implementation combines matched augmentation, intent-analysis targets, LoRA SFT, and a logit regularizer. Methodology: WIFA begins with 250 harmful seeds in each model setting and a pool of Alpaca-style benign instructions. Each harmful intent receives seven manually designed wrapped forms plus two direct-form refusal anchors; each benign intent receives seven matched wrapped forms. The target is a unified format containing an [INTENT ANALYSIS] segment that restates the direct-form request, followed by either the base model's direct-form refusal or an audited helpful answer. This produces 2,250 harmful and 3,500 wrapped-benign examples, or 5,750 WIFA-SFT examples. WIFA-Boost applies LoRA-based SFT in two stages: first WIFA-SFT, then a 2,750-example calibration set containing the harmful examples and 500 plain benign examples. A-GCRT applies standard sequence-level SFT plus a group regularizer, \(L=L_{SFT}+\lambda_{gcr}(L_{var}+\gamma L_{anchor})\). For a group of wrapper forms, it computes a refusal-minus-compliance score at the first response token after the closing intent-analysis marker, using the maximum logit over fixed refusal-prefix tokens minus the maximum over comply-prefix tokens. \(L_{var}\) penalizes within-intent score variance; a hinge anchor loss pushes harmful group means above +m and benign group means below -m. Critical design choices are the matched wrapper construction, self-distilled intent-analysis targets, and the fixed prefix-logit score. The matched construction is supported by data ablations; the two-stage order is supported by ordering ablations; the logit score is only partially justified because free-generation calibration is weak, although target-forced diagnostics show the intended training behavior. Key Results: The paper is an arXiv v1 preprint dated 13 August 2026 and evaluates Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with AdvBench-style harmful seeds and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with HH-Inst harmful seeds. In Qwen, the base model scores 22.1% on SORRY-Bench SB-avg5, 25.7% OR-Bench over-refusal, 70.1% MMLU, and 89.39% GSM8K. WIFA-SFT reaches 63.6% SB-avg5 but 69.7% OR; WIFA-Boost reaches 63.7% SB-avg5, 59.3% misrepresentation-subset refusal, and 56.0% OR; A-GCRT-M5 reaches 46.7% SB-avg5, 20.9% misrepresentation refusal, and 17.4% OR, while A-GCRT-M10 reaches 52.0% SB-avg5 and 40.7% OR. Qwen A-GCRT-M5 retains 69.0% MMLU and 83.70% GSM8K, whereas WIFA-Boost scores 67.9% and 79.00%. In Llama, the base scores 31.2% SB-avg5 and 28.4% OR; A-GCRT-M5 reaches 50.8% SB-avg5 and 40.1% OR, so it improves safety but does not beat the base over-refusal rate. Llama A-GCRT-M5 retains 67.2% MMLU versus 67.4% for the base but falls to 68.16% GSM8K versus 85.52%. On 15 unseen Qwen attack families, WIFA-Boost has 9.5% average attack success rate versus 16.8% for A-GCRT-M5, but the authors explicitly do not evaluate adaptive attackers. Data ablations show WIFA-SFT outperforming harmful-only SFT (63.6% versus 38.7% SB-avg5), unmatched benign augmentation (40.8%), and wrapped-benign SFT without intent-analysis targets (43.6%). The baselines include three prompt-time defenses and three reproduced training-time defenses; they are relevant but not necessarily the strongest current alternatives, and the paper reports SIRL only as a non-reproduced external reference. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper formulates refusal supervision around matched harmful/benign intent groups and introduces a group-variance plus directional-anchor objective, while empirically showing distinct safety-first and low-over-refusal operating points; the implementation nevertheless uses standard SFT, LoRA, manually authored wrappers, and logit-based regularization rather than an entirely new learning framework. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study includes useful ablations for matched benign structure, benign-to-harmful ratios, two-stage order, learning-rate/stronger-SFT alternatives, variance-only and anchor-only losses, and margin/anchor settings. It reports benchmark sizes, optimizer settings, LoRA configuration, deterministic decoding, judging protocols, compute hardware, and a HarmBench exact/normalized-overlap check. A self-distilled-target audit samples 300 harmful and 300 benign examples; 232 harmful and 275 benign targets are valid, with 68 harmful format-invalid cases and 24 ambiguous benign cases. A cross-judge check using GPT-4o preserves the Qwen A-GCRT-M5 below-base OR result, although transformed SORRY-Bench subtype values are judge-sensitive. The experiments use seed 42 and do not report multiple-seed variance, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. An anonymous code and sanitized-artifact URL is mentioned: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WIFA-1C32/. The evaluation remains vulnerable to benchmark and source-distribution limitations: only 250 harmful training intents per setting, fixed manually designed training wrappers, one principal Qwen setting, and no adaptive red-team loop. The authors acknowledge that exact overlap is absent but semantic overlap remains possible. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, with a training-time method rather than a deployed safety system. Practical: The method runs with LoRA adapters on commercially available NVIDIA A100 GPUs, but the reported main runs used an eight-A100 node and no cost or latency measurements are provided for deployment. Efficient: LoRA avoids full-parameter fine-tuning, but the method adds grouped multi-form batches and extra logit-based losses; compute, memory, training-time, and inference overhead relative to baselines are not quantified. Effective: The evidence demonstrates improved benchmark refusal/over-refusal operating points, particularly Qwen A-GCRT-M5 and WIFA-Boost, but it does not establish real-world safety, semantic intent understanding, or robustness to adaptive attackers. Scalable: The method is tested only on 7–8B text-only models and 250 harmful intents per setting; behavior at 10×–100× data or model scale, in other languages, multimodal systems, tool use, or production traffic is not evaluated. The work delivers training code and sanitized artifacts if the stated anonymous release is accessible, but it does not deliver a standalone runtime guard, classifier, or deployment system. Strengths: - The matched harmful/benign wrapper construction isolates an important causal factor: Table 17 shows that adding unmatched benign data does not reproduce the transformed-harmful refusal gains, while matched wrapped benign examples and intent-analysis targets substantially improve them. - The paper separates two operational goals rather than reporting one ambiguous safety score: WIFA-Boost prioritizes transformed-harmful refusal, while A-GCRT targets the low-over-refusal region. This produces a more informative safety–helpfulness frontier than a single tuned model. - The A-GCRT ablations are diagnostically useful: neither variance-only nor anchor-only regularization reproduces the 17.4% Qwen OR result, and stronger SFT does not explain it; the full objective is necessary within the tested configuration. - The authors are unusually explicit about limits: the decision score is not a calibrated inference classifier, the unseen-attack suite is not adaptive, Llama does not achieve below-base OR, and GSM8K capability degradation remains substantial. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the methods are training-time techniques rather than complete deployment safeguards; experiments cover fixed wrappers, two 7–8B models, two harmful-source settings, and no larger models, other languages, multimodal or tool-use contexts, or adaptive attackers. They acknowledge that operating points may change with benign/harmful mixtures, that GSM8K capability declines, and that the A-GCRT decision score should not be used as an inference-time classifier. They also discuss the risk that safety training increases benign denial and report residual target-format noise. These limitations are confronted directly, although the conclusion still generalizes the intent-group lesson beyond the tested scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main claims rely on a single training seed and lack uncertainty estimates, so differences such as 17.4% versus 25.7% OR are not accompanied by statistical reliability. The manually designed seven wrapper families and the use of a required intent-analysis output format leave open whether gains reflect genuine latent intent invariance or improved compliance with a learned format. The low-OR Qwen result is not replicated on Llama, where A-GCRT remains above the base OR, and no larger, multilingual, multimodal, tool-use, or production-scale tests assess external validity. The harmful and benign source pools are small and partly benchmark-adjacent; exact overlap with HarmBench is checked, but semantic overlap and contamination with other evaluation sets are not fully ruled out. The comparison omits a directly reproduced SIRL result and does not establish superiority over the strongest contemporary safety-tuning systems under a common protocol. Finally, no human evaluation assesses refusal quality, helpful redirection, severity-weighted harm, or whether reduced OR reflects appropriate compliance rather than unsafe permissiveness. Bottom Line: This is a worthwhile preprint for researchers designing intent-aware refusal datasets or studying safety–over-refusal trade-offs, with credible Qwen ablations and a useful two-operating-point framing, but its novelty and deployment significance should be discounted until multi-seed, larger-scale, human, and adaptive-attack evaluations confirm that the gains are not format- or benchmark-specific.

Annotations as Rollouts: Efficient and Scalable Reinforcement Learning for Video MLLMs (88 ▲ )

Yunheng Li, Guohong Mu, Hao Li, Shengsheng Qian, Dingwen Zhang, Qibin Hou, Ming-Ming Cheng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OraRL, a reinforcement-learning post-training method that treats each ground-truth annotation as an oracle rollout alongside sampled policy rollouts for unified video multimodal language models. - Why it's important: Fine-grained video perception requires precise intervals, boxes, masks, trajectories, and spatial judgments, but standard group-based RL often receives no high-quality positive rollout and becomes expensive when using chain-of-thought generation. - How it does it: OraRL computes policy advantages only from on-policy rewards, separately injects a gap-calibrated detached oracle advantage, and retains a sign-balanced subset of positive and negative rollouts for the update. - The good: In controlled three-task experiments, OraRL reaches a 62.7 average versus 60.3 for GRPO and 57.8 for the SFT initialization, while reducing step time from 92.5 to 62.4 seconds and peak memory from 62.4 to 50.9 GB. - The missing: The study does not report multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests, and its data-mixture changes and difficulty-based prompt selection leave some of the gains potentially confounded with the RL algorithm itself. - Read it or not: Researchers working on RL post-training for multimodal or structured-output models should read it for the advantage-inversion analysis and reproducible implementation; readers seeking evidence under noisy labels, learned oracles, or much larger models should wait for broader validation.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. Novelty (76) and Non-Obviousness (78) are strong because the annotation-as-rollout formulation and explicit advantage-inversion diagnosis address a concrete weakness of group RL for structured video outputs, while the evaluation is broad and the artifact is released. Rigor (63) and Resilience (62) prevent a higher score: the preprint reports no seed variance or significance testing, and gains remain confounded by task-mixture changes, difficulty filtering, hand-tuned components, and cross-model comparisons; the weighted composite is 0.20*76 + 0.25*63 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*78 = 69.95, rounded to 70.
empirical Novelty 76 Rigor 63 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 68 Resilience 62 Impact 78
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Unified video MLLMs are expected to perform fine-grained temporal localization, spatial grounding, segmentation, tracking, spatial-temporal grounding, video question answering, and spatial reasoning in one model. Existing SFT treats annotations as maximum-likelihood targets and does not explicitly distinguish near-correct from incorrect predictions, while GRPO-style RL samples several on-policy responses and uses annotations only to score them. Because sampled responses frequently miss exact temporal boundaries, boxes, masks, or trajectories, many groups lack a reliable positive target; chain-of-thought increases rollout and inference cost without consistently improving structured perception. The paper targets the resulting sample-efficiency and scalability gap for post-training video MLLMs. Key Idea: The central insight is annotation-as-rollout: serialize the paired annotation into the model's output format and use it as a known-correct oracle response without replacing the exploratory on-policy samples. Directly mixing this oracle into GRPO normalization is shown to cause “advantage inversion,” in which useful on-policy rollouts above the on-policy mean receive negative advantages because the high-reward oracle raises the group baseline. OraRL therefore separates policy-relative comparison from oracle guidance rather than treating all responses as one normalized group. Methodology: For each query, the policy samples eight on-policy rollouts, evaluates them with a task-specific scalar reward, and appends a ninth rollout obtained by serializing the annotation. The method first computes unnormalized on-policy advantages A_i^(0)=r_i−μ_op, where μ_op is the mean reward of only the policy rollouts. It then computes a bounded directional gain g_q from the ratio of augmented to on-policy reward dispersion, applies that gain only to above-mean policy rollouts, and re-centers the resulting policy advantages. A separate detached oracle advantage uses a squared normalized reward gap w_q and is capped relative to the strongest positive policy advantage; this makes oracle supervision decay as the policy approaches the annotation. For efficiency, the method retains the oracle plus the strongest positive and negative policy rollouts under a sign-balanced quota; with eight policy rollouts and κ=0.5, it backpropagates through four of the nine responses. A post-selection moment correction restores zero mean, constrains the oracle advantage to be nonnegative, and rescales the retained advantages toward the pre-pruning on-policy RMS. The final update is the standard clipped PPO/GRPO token-level objective applied to the retained responses. Task adapters serialize intervals, boxes, trajectories, segmentation hints, answer tokens, or numerical answers and use temporal IoU, box IoU, tracking overlap, a mask-aware segmentation reward, exact match, or mean relative accuracy. The key design decisions are technically motivated by the inversion analysis, but the fractional exponents, clipping constants, oracle cap, and reward-gap exponent are hand-designed and not theoretically derived. Key Results: In the authors' broad seven-family evaluation, Video-ORA-9B reports temporal-grounding mIoU of 61.8, 63.6, and 72.5 on the Charades-TimeLens, ActivityNet-TimeLens, and QVHighlights-TimeLens splits, versus 58.6, 58.6, and 70.2 for TimeLens2-8B; it reaches 78.2 AO on GOT-10k versus 73.0 for OneThinker-8B; 61.3 J&F on MeViS and 63.7 on ReasonVOS versus 52.7 and 54.9 for OneThinker-8B; and 40.0 tIoU@0.5, 41.7 mean tIoU, 27.4 sIoU@0.5, and 28.4 mean sIoU on STVG. It obtains 79.4/72.6/75.1 cIoU on RefCOCO/RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg and a 66.8 macro accuracy across seven Video QA benchmarks, ranking first among the reported open-source models on five. Its VSI-Bench average is 73.1, compared with 57.9 for Qwen3.5-9B and 55.0 for GPT-5 in the paper's comparison, although its corrected ReVSI score falls to 58.2 at 128 frames and remains below Gemini-3-Pro. In matched three-task experiments, OraRL scores 62.7 versus 60.3 for GRPO, 60.7 for Dr. GRPO, 60.5 for CPPO, 60.4 for GDPO, 61.2 for reward-shaped oracle injection, and 57.8 for the SFT initialization. Naive oracle mixing instead falls to 55.4. Across 92,024 rollouts, naive mixing flips 22.4% of rollouts that GRPO considers positive, affects 42.5% of groups, and removes all positive rollouts in 8.3% of groups; OraRL reduces the rollout-level rate to 1.9% before pruning and 0.3% among gradient-bearing rollouts. Pruning at κ=0.5 reduces step time from 92.5 to 62.4 seconds and memory from 62.4 to 50.9 GB at a 0.4-point average-score loss. Answer-only OraRL reaches 61.4 temporal mIoU in the CoT ablation versus 58.7 for answer-only GRPO and 58.5 for CoT GRPO, while requiring 62.4 versus 93.9 and 135.6 seconds per step. Video-ORA-9B has 24.30-second median end-to-end latency on ten-minute, 2-fps videos versus 29.03 seconds for Qwen3.5-9B with reasoning, with P90 latency of 25.15 versus 62.67 seconds. Experiments span 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B models and up to 100,032 RL prompts, but not 10x–100x larger models or substantially larger rollout groups. Several comparisons involve newer model reports and vendor model cards, so cross-model rankings should be treated cautiously. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION; the genuinely new contribution is the annotation-as-rollout formulation together with the explicit diagnosis and correction of oracle-induced advantage inversion, while the underlying clipped policy objective, group-relative RL, reward shaping comparisons, and rollout pruning are established techniques adapted to unified video perception. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides controlled comparisons using shared initialization, data, rollout budget, and optimization schedules, plus component ablations, pruning trade-offs, data scaling, model scaling, backbone transfer, CoT comparisons, a second backbone family, and a ReVSI robustness check. The ablations support the claimed roles of directional gain, detached oracle advantage, reward-gap weighting, sign balance, and moment correction: removing these components reduces the reported three-task average by 1.1–1.5 points, while removing pruning improves the average by 0.4 points at higher cost. However, no multiple random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. The RL and SFT mixtures differ substantially—RL increases structured-task share from 18% to 63%—and the RL subset is selected using SFT-checkpoint difficulty, so some gains may reflect task reweighting or curriculum effects rather than OraRL alone; the controlled three-task table mitigates but does not eliminate this concern. Evaluation uses public benchmarks, and the authors state that overlapping training examples were removed, but detailed split-level leakage audits and annotation-quality analyses are limited. Code is listed at https://github.com/HVision-NKU/OraRL, data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/OraRL/OraRL-Data, and models at https://huggingface.co/OraRL/models; the project page is https://orarl.github.io/. The document is an arXiv preprint, dated August 24, 2026 in the paper metadata and marked arXiv:2608.20492v1, so the results are not presented as peer-reviewed findings. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL — the paper evaluates a trained multimodal model and its post-training method rather than proving a theorem or primarily reporting a deployed production system. Practical: The method runs on commercially available NVIDIA H20 GPUs using bfloat16, veRL, vLLM, and FSDP, although the full 9B RL run uses 64 H20 GPUs and therefore has substantial infrastructure requirements. Efficient: Sign-balanced pruning reduces controlled step time by 32.5% and peak per-GPU memory by 18.4% relative to full-group optimization, while answer-only decoding reduces Video-ORA-9B median latency to 24.30 seconds on ten-minute videos; the method still requires eight policy rollouts plus an oracle during training and reports no complete training-cost or energy accounting. Effective: The evidence demonstrates improvements on the paper's structured perception and spatial-intelligence proxies, including a 2.4-point gain over GRPO in the matched three-task average and broad benchmark gains, but it does not establish reliability in open-ended deployment, noisy annotations, or safety-critical perception. Scalable: Results scale from 0.8B to 9B parameters and from 6.4k to 100k prompts, with improvements at each tested scale, but no evidence covers 10x–100x larger models, longer training, larger rollout groups, higher-resolution videos, or distributed serving under production load. The work delivers a reusable training implementation, released data, and trained model checkpoints rather than only a paper-form algorithm. Strengths: - The advantage-inversion diagnosis is concrete and measurable: it derives the inversion band analytically and quantifies 22.4% rollout-level inversion and 42.5% group-level incidence under naive oracle mixing. - The method directly exploits existing annotations as positive policy targets, avoiding teacher-trace generation and avoiding CoT rollout overhead while preserving sampled policy exploration. - The controlled ablations connect individual mechanisms to task-specific behavior; for example, removing the detached oracle costs 2.5 temporal points, while removing directional gain costs 2.7 tracking points. - The evaluation covers seven task families, two backbone families, four model scales, up to 100k prompts, training efficiency, inference latency, and corrected spatial-intelligence evaluation, making the empirical case broader than a single-task RL improvement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that OraRL assumes each annotation can be serialized into a valid response and evaluated by a scalar reward. They do not evaluate ambiguous, partial, noisy, or learned-oracle supervision, and they cover only seven task families and two backbone families. They also acknowledge that complex spatial-reasoning tasks still underperform some proprietary models and identify backward relative-direction questions as a weakness: Video-ORA-9B obtains 91.5% on forward ReVSI questions but only 8.3% on backward questions. These limitations are confronted with a ReVSI experiment and qualitative analysis rather than minimized, although the proposed future work is not experimentally tested. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The main unresolved issue is confounding between algorithm and data construction: the RL stage uses a different task mixture, difficulty-filtered subsets, and a larger structured-task proportion than SFT, while the strongest headline comparisons often use different model architectures, frame budgets, or training recipes. The paper does not provide seed variance or significance testing, so improvements of 0.5–2 points on several benchmarks may be within run-to-run noise. It also does not compare against a clean oracle-supervised SFT or DPO-style baseline using the same serialized annotations, nor does it isolate each of the many hand-tuned clipping and scaling constants through sensitivity analysis. The scalar rewards and exact-format validation may favor datasets whose annotations map cleanly to deterministic strings, and the strong VSI-Bench result is substantially reduced on ReVSI, exposing benchmark-specific overfitting or template bias. The method's behavior when annotations are inconsistent, incomplete, multiple-answer, or unavailable remains unknown. Finally, the reported latency experiment uses only ten videos and does not report throughput, concurrent-serving behavior, preprocessing cost, or end-to-end training cost. Bottom Line: This is a technically useful and unusually well-instrumented preprint for researchers designing RL post-training with structured multimodal annotations, but its central performance claims need stronger seed-controlled, data-mixture-matched comparisons before OraRL can be regarded as a generally superior RL recipe rather than an effective video-perception training system under a favorable annotation regime.

FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion (130 ▲ )

Liangcai Su, Zhaopeng Feng, Zhuo Chen, Zhen Zhang, Xiang Lin, Ruilin Li, Handuo Zhang, Ning Wang, Kailong Wen, Yueqi Guo, Feng Xing, Yiling Guo, Chenxiong Qian, Simon Shaolei Du, Lidong Bing, Xinyu Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 27 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FRONTIERCHALLENGE, a cross-domain benchmark of end-to-end scientific workflows that evaluates whether agents produce complete, mutually consistent bundles of code, tables, figures, simulation outputs, and reports. - Why it's important: Scientific handoffs fail when an agent produces plausible partial results but omits or contradicts required artifacts, so answer-level evaluation can substantially overestimate reliability. - How it does it: The benchmark fixes each task's inputs, environment, workflow contract, and executable grader, then separates strict full completion from graded partial progress using Pass Rate and Avg. Score. - The good: Across 97 released tasks and 12 frontier models, the best configurations completed only 20.6% of tasks, while analytical chemistry reached at most 4% Pass Rate and electrochemistry/environment reached 0% despite Avg. Scores as high as 94.9. - The missing: The study reports single runs without seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or controlled scaffold comparisons, and it does not establish that its task contracts and judge-based criteria generalize beyond the curated release. - Read it or not: Researchers building scientific-agent benchmarks should read it for its contract-level evaluation design and failure evidence; readers seeking a new agent method or a broad causal comparison of models can skip it.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. The artifact-contract framing is a strong benchmark contribution (Novelty 80) and exposes a genuinely important, non-obvious gap between high partial scores and complete scientific handoffs (Non-Obviousness 78). The cross-domain tasks and executable graders provide useful evidence, but Rigor (62) and Resilience (65) are reduced by single-run results, absent uncertainty estimates and scaffold controls, unvalidated judge criteria, and lack of held-out-task evidence; Completeness (72) benefits from explicit scope and limitation statements. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*62 = 69.95, rounded to 70.
empirical Novelty 80 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 72 Resilience 65 Impact 62
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Scientific agents increasingly need to process heterogeneous data, use specialized domain software, execute dependent analyses, validate intermediate results, and hand off consistent code, tables, figures, and prose. Existing benchmarks commonly evaluate a final answer, a single program, an interaction trace, a replication task, or one scientific discipline, which leaves open whether an agent can satisfy a multi-stage deliverable contract. The target capability is deliberately narrower than autonomous discovery: given a fixed objective, fixed inputs, and a defined environment, can an agent complete the specified workflow and deliver all required artifacts? The intended users are researchers and practitioners evaluating agents for reproducible scientific and engineering analysis across quantum chemistry, molecular dynamics, materials characterization, analytical chemistry, life science, and electrochemistry/environment. Key Idea The central insight is to make the complete artifact bundle, rather than the final textual answer, the unit of evaluation. Each task specifies a contract containing required files, numerical outputs, visualizations, executable code, reports, and cross-artifact consistency conditions; a strict Pass Rate counts only submissions meeting the full contract, while Avg. Score records partial progress. This reframes scientific-agent evaluation from plausibility or local task competence to verifiable completion of a dependency-aware handoff. Methodology The authors curate 300 workflows and release 97 non-GPU tasks for evaluation, retaining 203 as an internal held-out set. Each packaged task contains an objective, fixed inputs and context, available tools and environment, an output contract, reference or expected-output material, a stepwise rubric, and an executable task-specific Grader. Workflows span 21 families across six domains and can require domain software such as ORCA, CP2K, LAMMPS, AmberTools, and PLUMED. The study evaluates 12 named frontier models through 13 model–scaffold configurations: Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol or GPT-5.6 Terra (max), Claude Code with 10 models, and Frontier Agent in an Agent Team configuration with Apodex 1.1. Each Grader checks files, numerical results, formats, figures, code execution, and cross-artifact consistency; semantic criteria may be delegated to GPT-5.6 Sol as a Judge, run three times and averaged. For task score s_mi in [0,100], full completion is defined as s_mi >= 99.9, and the reported metrics are Pass Rate = N^-1 sum_i 1[s_mi >= 99.9] and Avg. Score = N^-1 sum_i s_mi. The key design decisions are the strict contract threshold, task-specific executable grading, and separation of public agent-visible inputs from evaluator-side references and checks. These choices are well aligned with the stated goal, although the paper gives limited evidence about inter-rater validity, rubric calibration, or the sensitivity of conclusions to contract design and the 99.9 threshold. Key Results On 97 released tasks, Pass Rate ranged from 3.1% to 20.6% across configurations, while Avg. Score ranged from 67.5 to 87.9. GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex achieved the highest Avg. Score, 87.9, and a 20.6% Pass Rate; Grok 4.6 with Claude Code matched the 20.6% Pass Rate with Avg. Score 86.6. Kimi K3 and Claude Opus 5 each reached 17.5% Pass Rate, and GPT-5.6 Terra (max) reached 15.5%. Medium-task Pass Rates ranged from 4.3% to 43.5%, while Hard-task Pass Rates ranged from 1.4% to 14.9%. Domain results were highly uneven: Grok 4.6 with Claude Code reached 60% Pass Rate in quantum chemistry; three configurations reached 38% in molecular dynamics; no configuration exceeded 9% in materials characterization; analytical chemistry reached a maximum of 4%; and electrochemistry/environment reached 0% for every configuration despite a maximum Avg. Score of 94.9. The largest quantitative finding is the separation between partial and complete delivery: eight configurations had Avg. Scores above 80, but none exceeded 20.6% full completion. In 970 Claude Code trajectories, 641 of 849 non-passing runs, or 75.5%, ended with lexical completion language, whereas 90.1% of passing runs did so. At least one tool error appeared in 80.7% of non-passing and 94.2% of passing trajectories, with median error rates of 4.4 and 5.6 per 100 tool results, respectively. Reported input use ranged from 2.183 million to 13.730 million tokens per task, and mean execution time ranged from 21.8 to 112.8 minutes; the authors correctly avoid treating provider-specific token counts as hardware-normalized efficiency measurements. These are benchmark measurements, not evidence that any model has reliable scientific autonomy outside the fixed task setting. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL: the main contribution is a publicly released benchmark and evaluation package that combines fixed cross-domain scientific workflows, heterogeneous artifact contracts, executable grading, and strict complete-task scoring; the contract-level framing and the finding that high partial scores and completion language poorly predict complete delivery are useful empirical additions, but the underlying agent scaffolds, language models, domain software, and grader/Judge mechanisms largely combine existing evaluation practices rather than introduce a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports a substantial benchmark package and links to a leaderboard, GitHub evaluation repository, and Hugging Face dataset, but the parsed paper does not provide the exact URLs or confirm whether all task data, grader code, hidden checks, reference artifacts, traces, and model outputs are publicly available. The task packaging and executable graders support reruns under fixed environments, and three Judge passes reduce—but do not quantify—semantic-scoring variance. The study does not report multiple seeds, repeated independent trajectories per model–task pair, error bars, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or bootstrap uncertainty for Pass Rates; the conclusion that configurations differ may therefore be sensitive to the 97-task sample, especially in small domains such as life science with 10 tasks and electrochemistry/environment with 6. The benchmark uses GPT-5.6 Sol as the Judge while also evaluating GPT-5.6 Sol as a model, which creates a potential evaluator/model interaction that requires dedicated calibration and blinded cross-model validation. The comparison also confounds model and scaffold in most cases, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that the Apodex scaffold comparison does not isolate scaffold effects. The public release is a randomly selected non-GPU subset of a 300-task collection, while 203 tasks—including GPU-dependent workflows—remain internal, so leaderboard results may be exposed to benchmark-specific adaptation and do not establish generalization to the held-out set. Avg. Score is explicitly heterogeneous and uncalibrated across task rubrics, making aggregate comparisons descriptive rather than statistically comparable. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluated workflows run in defined software environments without requiring GPUs for the 97 released tasks, so the released subset appears runnable on commercially available hardware, although exact hardware, setup effort, licensing constraints, and domain-software installation requirements are not stated. Efficient: Mean runtime spans 21.8–112.8 minutes per task and reported input use spans 2.183–13.730 million tokens, with long tails such as 272.2 minutes at the 90th percentile for Frontier Agent; the paper does not provide comparable dollar cost, peak memory, CPU/GPU utilization, or a controlled efficiency analysis. Effective: The strict evidence shows low complete-delivery reliability—at most 20.6% of tasks passed—and demonstrates that high partial scores and self-reported completion do not guarantee contract satisfaction, but it does not measure downstream scientific validity or usefulness to working scientists beyond the task rubrics. Scalable: The study evaluates 97 tasks and trajectories averaging up to 112.8 minutes, but it does not test 10×–100× larger workflows, larger datasets, more artifacts, longer dependency chains, or the 203 held-out tasks. The work delivers a benchmark dataset, evaluation code, task-specific graders, and associated leaderboard artifacts if the linked repositories are complete; it does not deliver a new agent algorithm or trained model. Strengths - The benchmark evaluates a scientifically meaningful failure mode—missing, inconsistent, or non-reproducible deliverables—that answer-level and single-program benchmarks can miss. - The combination of fixed inputs, multi-artifact contracts, executable checks, and cross-artifact consistency makes the evaluation target more operationally precise than subjective judgments of final reports. - The cross-domain release covers 97 tasks across six domains and 21 workflow families, including specialized workflows such as quantum-chemistry calculations, molecular-dynamics analysis, image-based wound-healing assays, TLC reaction monitoring, and reaction calorimetry. - The failure analysis yields actionable evidence: 75.5% of non-passing Claude Code trajectories used completion language, while raw tool errors occurred in 94.2% of passing trajectories, showing that status language and error counts are poor substitutes for artifact validation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that the six domains are descriptive slices rather than probability samples and that domain differences should not be interpreted as intrinsic disciplinary difficulty. They limit conclusions to the 97 released tasks, evaluated model–scaffold configurations, the Claude Code trajectory subset used for failure analysis, provider-specific resource accounting, and single runs. They also state that failure signatures are descriptive rather than causal, that the Apodex scaffold comparison does not isolate a pure scaffold effect, and that provider-specific tokenizers, caching, and reporting conventions prevent hardware-normalized efficiency comparisons. The paper directly acknowledges these boundaries rather than presenting the benchmark as a complete measure of autonomous scientific research. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not quantify grader validity: it provides no expert–Judge agreement, false-pass/false-fail analysis, rubric inter-rater reliability, or sensitivity analysis for semantic criteria delegated to GPT-5.6 Sol. - Single-run evaluation prevents reliable uncertainty estimates and makes the reported rankings difficult to distinguish from task-level variance, especially for domains with 6–10 tasks. - The 99.9 full-completion threshold is reasonable for the stated scoring rule but is not stress-tested against alternative contract policies, weighted deliverables, or the possibility that one minor formatting failure invalidates an otherwise scientifically correct handoff. - Model and scaffold effects remain confounded for most configurations, so the results cannot support strong claims about which agent architecture improves workflow completion. - The study does not report per-task difficulty calibration, contract size, artifact-count distributions, grader false-positive rates, or correlations between task complexity and failure, limiting interpretation of the domain gaps. - The authors claim a 300-workflow collection but evaluate only a non-GPU random subset of 97 and keep 203 tasks internal; without held-out results or a blind evaluation protocol, robustness to benchmark overfitting and release-selection effects remains untested. - The benchmark starts from fixed objectives and inputs, so it does not evaluate problem formulation, experimental design, literature synthesis, open-ended discovery, or whether the generated scientific conclusions are substantively correct beyond rubric compliance. Bottom Line This is a worthwhile benchmark paper for researchers studying reliable scientific agents because its strict artifact-contract framing exposes a real failure mode and produces clear evidence that partial progress is not completion, but its empirical ranking claims should be treated as preliminary until repeated trials, grader validation, controlled scaffold comparisons, and held-out-task results are reported; readers focused on general scientific-agent evaluation should also compare it directly with stronger alternatives such as ScienceAgentBench, CORE-Bench, PaperBench, ScienceBoard, and AstaBench rather than treating FRONTIERCHALLENGE as a definitive replacement.

GEAR: Generative Expansion and Real Anchoring for Two-Stage Distillation of Tabular Foundation Models

Q Qin, J Zhu, D Chen, Y Zhang, JX Han, Y Su, P Zhang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GEAR, a two-stage protocol that distills context-dependent tabular foundation models into context-free MLP or gradient-boosted-tree predictors using synthetic teacher-query expansion followed by real-data anchoring. - Why it's important: Removing the TFM and labeled context table from inference can make tabular prediction practical on commodity CPUs, reducing deployment latency, memory use, and dependence on retaining training records. - How it does it: Stage 1 trains a student on frozen-TFM soft predictions at generated covariate locations, while Stage 2 initializes from that student and optimizes a mixture of real labels and out-of-fold teacher predictions on the observed data. - The good: Across TALENT and TabArena, the reported two-stage MLPs improve over supervised MLPs by 1.81–2.00 AUC points on binary tasks and 1.19–1.35 points on multiclass tasks, while reducing median prediction time by 57–2,866× versus direct TFM inference. - The missing: The study does not establish end-to-end deployment cost or scalability because it reports inference efficiency but does not quantify the substantial cost of generating synthetic queries and repeatedly querying the TFM, and it provides limited evidence beyond the selected benchmarks. - Read it or not: Researchers working on tabular foundation-model compression or small-data tabular learning should read it for the staged query-expansion/anchoring design and ablations, while practitioners should treat the deployment claims as incomplete until training and distillation costs are measured.
