Problem & Motivation: The work targets high-throughput, low-latency multi-tenant inference for hybrid Transformer–Mamba LLMs, as well as pure Transformer and Mamba workloads, on large heterogeneous chiplet packages. Transformer attention is dominated by matrix computation and growing KV-cache traffic, whereas Mamba uses recurrent state and more sequential, element-wise, and nonlinear computation; prefill is generally compute-intensive while decode exhibits different memory and parallelism demands. Asynchronous arrivals, variable input and output lengths, dynamic batching, and shifting prefill/decode mixtures make fixed task mappings and static performance models inaccurate. Existing chiplet DSE frameworks cited by the paper generally focus on homogeneous or static workloads, microarchitectural rather than macroarchitectural choices, or do not model runtime dynamics. The claimed gap is therefore joint architecture–placement–runtime exploration for heterogeneous hybrid LLM serving under package area, memory, and NoI constraints. Key Idea: The central insight is to treat the dominant runtime control variable as the aggregate allocation of compute chiplets between prefill and decode, rather than the detailed ordering of individual tasks. HYDRA uses this abstraction in a Markov/fluid estimator while using a more detailed simulator to account for queueing, memory management, NoI contention, and transient scheduling effects. At the system level, the other key design principle is to separate HBM capacity partitioning from compute placement: first balance HBM capacity between Attention and Mamba state/weights, then place compute chiplets near their dominant memory partners. Methodology: HYDRA consumes model/block descriptions annotated with compute, memory, and communication requirements; datasets and request traces; a chiplet library; NoI topology and bandwidth; interposer dimensions; and area constraints. Its macroarchitecture selects counts of four accelerator classes—prefill- and decode-oriented Attention chiplets (Ap, Ad) and Mamba chiplets (Mp, Md)—plus HBM chiplets and D2D bandwidth. Placement first places HBM on an outer interposer ring and partitions it between Attention and Mamba by maximizing the smaller estimated concurrency, using remaining capacity after weights for KV cache or recurrent state. It then places compute chiplets using Manhattan distance and communication volume as a locality objective, resolving conflicts by placing larger groups first. Runtime batching maintains a continuously changing active batch, admits requests subject to maximum batch size and a token budget, uses virtualized memory blocks similar to vLLM, and preempts the request with the fewest generated tokens when memory is insufficient. Scheduling first constructs a preferred task-to-chiplet mapping by minimizing the maximum cumulative compute-plus-communication load, then selectively reassigns ready tasks to underutilized compatible chiplets while considering communication distance. The estimator models a state s in {0,...,N}, where s is the number of compute chiplets assigned to prefill; state-dependent prefill and decode capacities are Gp(s) and Gd(s), and expected throughput is the occupancy-weighted sum of Gd(s). A fluid queue approximation estimates state occupancy and TTFT rather than solving the full CTMC analytically. The major design decisions—two-stage placement, locality-aware rather than purely load-based stealing, and low-dimensional phase-allocation modeling—are plausible, but the paper gives limited formal justification for the concurrency heuristic, the token-budget rule, preemption policy, state abstraction, or transition-rate construction. Key Results: The evaluation uses Nemotron-H-4B, LLaMA3-7B, and Mamba2-2.8B; ArXiv-4K, Bilingual Web Books, LongWriter-6K, and LMSYS-Chat-1M; a 2D mesh NoI; 24 total compute chiplets; 2–16 HBM3 chiplets; 256–640 GB/s D2D bandwidth; 2–64 maximum batch sizes; 2700–3000 mm² interposer area; and approximately 121 mm² per chiplet. An in-house event-driven simulator runs each configuration for 100 seconds of workload time and models chiplet queues, computation, memory, NoI communication, and contention. Relative to a static placement/scheduling/batching baseline, the complete HYDRA stack reports 1.55× average throughput, 43.7% lower average TTFT, and up to 2.3× throughput. Dynamic batching alone is reported to improve throughput by 15% and reduce TTFT by 23% on average. Communication-aware placement improves throughput by 3%–100% across the reported workloads; in a Nemotron-H ArXiv case it provides 1.3× throughput with a 1.06× TTFT increase, and across four Nemotron-H workloads it improves TP/TTFT by 1.29× and throughput by 1.22× over round-robin placement. Elastic scheduling improves TP/TTFT by 1.40×–2.04× and maximum throughput by 1.17×–1.73× over static mapping; relative to FCFS it improves the target metric by 1.04×–1.30× and generally outperforms work stealing. The Markov estimator reduces exploration from 2 days 8 hours, 3 days 1 hour, and 8 days 8 hours for LLaMA3, Mamba2, and Nemotron-H exhaustive searches to 4, 4, and 15 minutes, respectively. It recovers 93% of exhaustive-search maximum throughput on average, compared with 74% for a roofline approach, and reduces simulated design points by 2520–8520×. The estimator reports average cosine similarity of 0.9 with full simulation, but selected examples still show 8% and 12% throughput gaps. In cross-model generalization, the all-model design limits worst-case degradation to 14% for the balanced objective; for maximum throughput it reaches normalized values of 0.99, 0.96, and 0.84 on Jamba, Zamba, and Nemotron-H, respectively. The baselines are useful internal controls—round-robin, random placement, FCFS, work stealing, roofline, and exhaustive simulation—but the study does not compare against a real GPU serving stack, a modern production scheduler, or an independently implemented chiplet DSE framework. All headline results are simulator-derived rather than measured on fabricated or emulated hardware. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The main contribution is a system-level formulation and framework that couples heterogeneous chiplet macroarchitecture with placement, dynamic batching, and elastic scheduling, plus a Markov/fluid estimator for runtime-aware DSE; individual ingredients such as continuous batching, virtualized memory, work stealing, Manhattan-distance placement, queueing models, and Pareto search are established techniques combined for this chiplet-based hybrid-LLM setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component ablations for communication-aware placement, elastic scheduling, and dynamic batching across 12 model–dataset pairs, plus placement and scheduler comparisons on Nemotron-H workloads and validation of estimator-selected points against exhaustive simulation. It also tests specialization versus generalization across three hybrid models. However, it reports no error bars, repeated trials, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite stochastic arrivals and dynamic scheduling. The exhaustive-search comparison is valuable, but the simulator itself is the evaluation oracle and is not independently validated against hardware or a deployed serving implementation. Latency values are assembled from prior MARCA/TSTC characterizations, vendor specifications for B200-like designs, and custom RTL simulation, creating heterogeneous fidelity across chiplet types. The paper states that the framework is available on GitHub, but no repository URL, commit, dataset release, simulator validation suite, model weights, or exact request-trace-generation procedure is provided in the text. Important implementation details—Markov transition rates, fluid-model update equations, scheduler thresholds, token-budget derivation, preemption overhead, and the exact exhaustive-search algorithm—are insufficiently specified for faithful reproduction. The comparison against roofline is informative but weak as a runtime-DSE baseline, and several reported gains are measured against static or round-robin policies rather than the strongest available serving systems. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — HYDRA is a built simulation and DSE framework evaluated through experiments, but not through deployment on physical chiplet hardware. Practical: The modeled design targets commercially plausible components such as HBM3, UCIe-like links, and 2D interposers, and its DSE software can run on a commodity AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7985WX, but the actual accelerator package, runtime scheduler, and simulator-to-hardware correspondence are not demonstrated. Efficient: The estimator reduces reported exploration time from 2–8 days to 4–15 minutes and retains 93% of exhaustive-search maximum throughput on average, but it introduces approximation errors of up to roughly 12% in the examples reported and does not quantify runtime overhead, memory use, or scheduler hardware/software cost. Effective: The simulator shows consistent improvements from placement, elastic scheduling, and dynamic batching on the selected workloads, but evidence establishes performance within the authors' modeled system rather than end-to-end user-visible performance on real serving infrastructure; quality, SLA-tail latency beyond TTFT, fairness, and request-level throughput under realistic admission policies are not evaluated. Scalable: The framework explores systems with up to 24 compute chiplets and reports a 2520–8520× reduction in simulated design points, but it does not test 10×–100× larger packages, richer chiplet libraries, alternative NoI topologies beyond the modeled 2D mesh, or whether the low-dimensional estimator remains accurate at those scales. The work delivers a claimed GitHub software artifact consisting of the HYDRA DSE framework, simulator, and estimator, but the paper provides no URL or enough release metadata to verify availability; it does not deliver silicon, a deployable accelerator, or a production serving library. Strengths: - It identifies a meaningful systems-level interaction among hybrid-model heterogeneity, prefill/decode phase imbalance, HBM capacity, NoI locality, batching, and scheduling rather than optimizing a single accelerator kernel. - The estimator has a useful practical objective: it is explicitly positioned as a pruning/ranking mechanism and is checked against exhaustive simulation, achieving 93% average maximum-throughput recovery while reducing search time by orders of magnitude. - The ablations separate the effects of placement, elastic scheduling, and dynamic batching; the reported gains are not attributed solely to an undifferentiated framework. - The specialization–generality study provides a deployment-relevant result: designs optimized for one hybrid model can transfer poorly, while mixture-aware DSE substantially improves worst-case cross-model performance with limited loss on in-target workloads. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit the current objective to throughput and TTFT and state that power, thermal behavior, and reliability are not modeled. They propose extending HYDRA with power and thermal models. They also acknowledge that the Markov estimator abstracts fine-grained queueing effects, transient contention, and scheduling decisions, explaining observed discrepancies of approximately 8%–12% in an example workload. These limitations are stated directly, but the paper does not similarly discuss simulator validation, model-library narrowness, or deployment overhead. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strongest validity gap is the absence of hardware or independent simulator validation. The reported 1.55× throughput and 43.7% TTFT reduction are predictions from an in-house simulator whose chiplet performance inputs mix prior-work measurements, vendor specifications, RTL estimates, and analytical NoI models. - The baseline set is incomplete for the stated serving problem. There is no comparison with vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve, DistServe, Vidur-derived policies, disaggregated prefill/decode systems, or a strong architecture-search method using comparable hardware assumptions. - The Markov model's central abstraction is under-specified and potentially fragile: the paper does not provide transition-rate equations, calibration methodology, estimator error distributions, confidence bounds, or sensitivity to workload burstiness, phase correlation, heterogeneous chiplet affinities, and NoI hotspots. - The placement objective appears to use simplified Manhattan-distance and communication-volume proxies, while the simulator models contention more fully; the paper does not quantify when the heuristic fails or compare it with optimization, simulated annealing, integer programming, or learned placement. - The dynamic batching policy uses a median per-request token cost and a user-defined maximum batch size, but the paper does not evaluate heavy-tailed lengths, adversarial arrivals, tail TTFT, starvation, fairness among tenants, preemption cost, or SLA violations. - The design space is narrower than the framework's generality claims suggest: evaluation uses a single 2D mesh topology, HBM3 memory, four accelerator classes derived mainly from MARCA and TSTC, and at most 24 compute chiplets. The cited library options such as B200-like or GDDR7 designs are not clearly included in the reported experiments. - The experiments simulate only 100 seconds per configuration without reporting warm-up removal, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to trace length and random arrival seeds, so stochastic variability and steady-state reliability remain unclear. - The study optimizes throughput and TTFT but omits energy, power density, thermal constraints, cost, reliability, model quality, interconnect power, and tail latency, all of which can change the preferred chiplet composition in a real package. Bottom Line: HYDRA is a worthwhile systems-architecture paper for its runtime-aware chiplet DSE formulation and fast estimator, but its practical claims should be discounted until the simulator, baselines, stochastic methodology, and hardware correspondence receive substantially stronger validation.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Best Practice Critic Optimization (BPCO), a single-rollout actor–critic recipe for language-model reinforcement learning that combines bounded value prediction, Monte Carlo critic targets, unnormalized advantages, length-adaptive GAE, and optional privileged critic inputs. - Why it's important: Replacing 16-response group sampling with one response per prompt could reduce rollout cost and provide token-level credit assignment, but only if critic training remains stable and its extra computation is worthwhile. - How it does it: BPCO aligns the critic’s output range and training target with bounded outcome rewards, preserves the magnitude of policy advantages, and uses length-adaptive bootstrapping while applying DPPO to the policy update. - The good: Across a 1.5B model, two 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts models, 40.3K mathematical problems, and rubric-based rewards, BPCO consistently improves the paper’s critic baseline and generally matches or exceeds a 16-sample Dr. GRPO baseline. - The missing: The paper does not report wall-clock, GPU-memory, or end-to-end compute comparisons, so its claimed efficiency relative to group sampling is not established despite the critic’s additional training cost. - Read it or not: Researchers implementing LLM RL or studying critic stability should read it for the controlled recipe and ablations, while readers seeking a fundamentally new estimator or broad evidence beyond math and rubric rewards can treat it as an engineering-oriented synthesis.

Problem & Motivation: LLM reinforcement learning needs reliable token-level credit assignment from sparse outcome rewards. Group-based methods such as GRPO avoid a learned value function by sampling multiple completions per prompt, but they incur repeated rollout cost and assign one response-level advantage to every token. Critic-based methods can use one completion and estimate prefix-specific values, yet long-response training is vulnerable to policy-ratio instability, critic extrapolation outside the reward range, bootstrapping bias, length-dependent attenuation of terminal rewards, and batch advantage normalization that amplifies residual noise near convergence. The target domain is mathematical reasoning and open-ended instruction following with rubric or judge rewards. The paper also addresses whether training-only evaluative information—such as an answer, solution, or rubric unavailable to the policy—can make critic approximation easier without changing deployment inputs. Key Idea: The central insight is that critic-based LLM RL becomes more reliable when the critic’s input, output parameterization, regression target, and induced policy signal are made mutually consistent with the bounded outcome reward. Concretely, the critic is constrained to the reward interval, trained against the observed Monte Carlo outcome rather than a self-referential bootstrapped target, and used through raw, length-adaptive advantages; optional reward-defining information is supplied only to the training critic. The individual ingredients are mostly drawn from or closely related to prior work, so the main conceptual contribution is their integration and controlled diagnosis rather than a wholly new estimator. Methodology: For each prompt, the policy generates one response, receives a scalar terminal reward, and computes token-level GAE advantages using a frozen critic. The policy is updated with DPPO, whose clipping threshold is expressed as an absolute sampled-token probability change: the ratio bounds become \(1 \pm \epsilon/\mu(y_t|s_t)\), equivalent to constraining the sampled token’s probability shift by ε. The critic uses a value head parameterized by a scaled arctangent, \(V_φ(s)=R_{min}+(R_{max}-R_{min})(1/2+\arctan(z_φ(s))/\pi)\), which keeps predictions inside the known reward interval. Critic training uses λV=1 and therefore regresses directly to the observed terminal reward under the paper’s γ=1, outcome-only setting; policy advantages use a separate λπ. Rather than batch-normalizing advantages, BPCO feeds raw GAE estimates to the policy objective. For response length L, it sets λπ(L)=1-1/(\alpha L), with α=0.4 in the main study, approximately preserving the terminal-residual weight across lengths. Optional privileged inputs concatenate or otherwise expose a reference answer, official solution, or rubric to the critic while leaving the policy input unchanged. The key design decisions are well motivated analytically and tested individually, although the selected hyperparameter α and interactions among components receive limited systematic study. Key Results: In the 1,460-example sanity test with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, 1,024 trajectories per iteration, and 1,500 iterations, standard PPO with λ=1 collapses after initially increasing reward, while DPPO remains stable; DPPO with fixed λ=0.99 becomes unstable until the later BPCO changes are added. Bounded values keep binary-reward predictions in [0,1] instead of the observed approximately -8 to +8 range and restore training reward toward 1. Using the Monte Carlo critic target improves stability relative to the bootstrapped target, whose explained variance approaches 1 despite inaccurate return prediction. Removing advantage normalization prevents the advantage range from expanding to roughly ±60 in the sanity test and improves held-out AIME 2025 avg@32. Length-adaptive GAE with α=0.4 reaches a better validation trade-off than fixed λ=0.99 or λ=1. On the approximately 40.3K-example DeepScaleR dataset, with 24,000-token maximum generations, BPCO variants reach roughly 0.32–0.34 AIME 2025 avg@32 versus roughly 0.29–0.30 for the critic baseline and about 0.29–0.31 for the group baseline in the plotted curves; exact tabulated scores are not provided. On DAPO-Math-17K with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base and Qwen3-30B-A3B, using up to 12,000 generated tokens, BPCO reaches approximately 0.35–0.38 and 0.58–0.62 AIME avg@32, respectively, while the critic baseline remains around 0.28–0.30 and 0.47–0.52; it is comparable to the group baseline on the base model and better on the instruct/model variant. On OpenRubrics with Qwen3-4B-Base and a frozen Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 judge, BPCO learns faster than both baselines, but the group baseline eventually reaches comparable validation reward near 0.94–0.96. These results are shown as curves with shaded variability, but the paper does not state the number of seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The experiments are standard-to-large for research-scale LLM RL, but do not constitute a 10×–100× stress test or a production deployment evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new contribution is the BPCO recipe and its controlled evidence that bounded value heads and raw advantages improve critic-based LLM RL; DPPO, decoupled Monte Carlo targets, length-adaptive GAE, and privileged training information are individually based on prior or closely related ideas, making the work primarily a non-obvious integration and empirical validation rather than a new theoretical estimator. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper provides useful component-wise sanity-test ablations for DPPO, value bounding, critic targets, advantage normalization, privileged inputs, and length-adaptive GAE, followed by larger-scale ablations of value bounding, normalization, and privileged information. It controls total trajectories per iteration when comparing one-response critic methods with 16-response Dr. GRPO, and uses a shared DPPO policy objective to isolate advantage estimation. However, the principal baseline is an author-described critic recipe that already includes decoupled GAE, Monte Carlo targets, and length-adaptive GAE but retains the two components BPCO emphasizes; comparisons against broader contemporary critic implementations, PPO variants, or carefully compute-matched alternatives are limited. The paper reports curves and shaded variation but does not state seeds, error-bar construction, statistical tests, or exact final values. Code is stated to be available at https://github.com/QPHutu/golden_critic; data and model weights are not stated as released. The group comparison is trajectory-matched, not compute-matched, and the authors explicitly acknowledge that critic computation and memory are omitted from the comparison. Evaluation relies heavily on the same mathematical training ecosystem and AIME validation metric, creating some risk that recipe choices are tuned to this benchmark family. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL. Practical: The method uses standard transformer policy/critic training and can run on commercially available accelerator hardware, although the paper does not provide hardware requirements or an implementation cost breakdown. Efficient: It samples one response per prompt instead of 16 for the group baseline, but adds critic forward/backward passes and memory, and no wall-clock, throughput, GPU-memory, or total-FLOP measurement establishes a net efficiency gain. Effective: Evidence shows improved training reward, critic explained variance, and AIME 2025 avg@32 over the selected critic baseline, with competitive or better results than Dr. GRPO; rubric-task gains are mainly faster learning because the group baseline eventually becomes comparable, and the study does not measure solution quality beyond these proxies. Scalable: The recipe transfers from 1.5B to 30B-A3B models and from 1,460 to approximately 40.3K problems, but it is tested only up to 24,000-token generations and does not establish behavior at 10×–100× scale or under substantially different reward distributions. The work delivers a reusable training implementation through the linked code repository, but no separately packaged library, CLI, trained model, or dataset is stated. Strengths: - The controlled sanity test is well chosen: fitting a deliberately solvable 1,460-problem set exposes optimization failures independently of model capacity or reward scarcity. - The paper identifies a real diagnostic failure in explained variance: a bootstrapped target containing the old critic can be fit well while remaining inaccurate with respect to observed returns. - The ablations isolate several interacting stability factors rather than attributing all gains to an opaque end-to-end recipe; value bounding and removal of advantage normalization remain beneficial on the larger dataset. - The evaluation spans mathematical rewards, judge-based rubric rewards, a 1.5B dense model, and 30B-A3B MoE models, providing stronger transfer evidence than a single-model demonstration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly limit evidence to mathematical and rubric rewards, assume a known reward range, note that privileged variants require evaluator information, and acknowledge that critic training adds computation and memory not captured by trajectory-matched comparisons. They also show that privileged information can cause earlier validation decline in the small-data setting and that its benefit is task dependent. These limitations are confronted directly, although the computational trade-off is not quantified. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not report exact numerical tables, seeds, statistical significance, or reproducibility details sufficient to determine whether several plotted differences are robust. It does not provide an end-to-end compute or latency accounting, so the central practical comparison with multi-sample group methods remains unresolved: fewer rollouts may not imply lower total training cost when a large critic is trained. The evaluation omits non-mathematical verifiable tasks, preference rewards, noisy or unbounded rewards, and settings where the reward range must be estimated rather than known. The baseline set is narrow and partly constructed so that BPCO differs from the critic baseline mainly in the authors’ favored components; stronger current critic and group implementations, matched tuning budgets, and equal wall-clock comparisons would make the claim more convincing. The paper also does not test sensitivity to α, reward scaling, critic capacity, critic update frequency, or privileged-input encoding, and it does not establish whether improved explained variance causally predicts policy quality across tasks. Bottom Line: This is a useful, reproducible recipe paper for practitioners struggling with unstable single-rollout LLM RL, but its main practical claim should be treated as incomplete until compute-matched and more diverse evaluations show that critic training actually beats group sampling in total cost and robustness.

WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution (9 ▲ )

Liyan Tang, Cyrus Rashtchian, Chun-Sung Ferng, Andrew Tomkins, Da-Cheng Juan, Tu Vu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 28 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WikiSkill, a skill-evolution framework that separates immutable execution traces, a persistent structured wiki, and executable agent skills, then uses the wiki to guide iterative skill updates. - Why it's important: Persistent procedural knowledge could reduce repeated rediscovery during agent optimization and let skills transfer across models instead of remaining tied to one optimization run or model. - How it does it: A Wiki Maintainer consolidates sampled successful and failed trajectories into pattern pages and evolution logs, a ReAct Skill Proposer reads that accumulated state to generate one skill change, and validation gating accepts only changes that improve validation accuracy. - The good: Across 5 benchmarks and 5 models, WikiSkill has the highest reported macro-average in every model block, including 63.3% versus 53.3% for the strongest competing method on Qwen-3.6-27B and 68.1% versus 56.1% for Gemini-3.5-Flash. - The missing: The paper does not isolate WikiSkill from differences in optimizer compute, prompt budgets, proposal-generation behavior, or validation reuse, so the gains cannot be attributed cleanly to persistent knowledge alone. - Read it or not: Agent-learning and prompt/skill-optimization researchers should read it for the persistent-memory design and transfer experiments, but practitioners should wait for cost-normalized, longer-horizon, retrieval-based evaluations before treating it as a deployable solution.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. Novelty (76) and Non-Obviousness (74) come from separating persistent experience compilation from executable skills and demonstrating meaningful cross-model transfer. Rigor (70) benefits from five benchmarks, five models, ablations, and multiple runs, but Completeness (65) and Resilience (62) are reduced by validation overfitting risk, compute confounds, unfactorized wiki ablations, and lack of long-horizon retrieval tests; Impact (55) is limited because no reusable implementation is confirmed. systems Novelty 76 Rigor 70 Non-Obv 74 Completeness 65 Resilience 62 Impact 55
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: LLM agents often need domain-specific procedures for tool use, search, spreadsheet manipulation, document navigation, and embodied interaction, but manually authored skills are costly and existing automatic skill-evolution methods primarily retain proposals, feedback, or locally extracted lessons rather than a separate, structured representation of accumulated knowledge. The target problem is therefore continual improvement of reusable procedural skills from agent execution experience while avoiding repeated rediscovery of failure modes and preserving knowledge across iterations. The paper focuses on five benchmark domains—mathematical reasoning, web search, spreadsheet manipulation, long-context document QA, and interactive embodied tasks—and evaluates skill quality with all active skills directly injected into the inference prompt rather than addressing skill retrieval. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat accumulated experience as a persistent intermediate knowledge layer rather than directly editing the executable skill after every rollout. Immutable raw traces provide evidence, wiki pattern pages and logs compile recurring successes, failures, rejected proposals, and acceptance outcomes, and the proposer converts that persistent record into one targeted skill update; the skill can be rolled back while the wiki is never reset. This is a meaningful architectural distinction from prior skill-evolution pipelines, although the underlying operations—trajectory analysis, LLM-generated edits, and validation-based selection—remain standard. Methodology: WikiSkill initializes an empty skill set and empty wiki, evaluates the no-skill agent on a validation split, and repeats an evolution loop for up to 8 iterations (the reported update-stage grouping uses iterations 0–7). First, an Inference Agent runs every training task using the current skills but cannot access the wiki; each rollout produces an immutable trace containing reasoning, tool calls, observations, and the final answer. Second, the Wiki Maintainer receives the existing wiki and up to 8 stratified traces per iteration—at most 5 failures and 3 successes, with each trace capped at 15,000 characters—and performs LLM-based root-cause analysis, creating or patching Markdown pattern pages, updating an index, and appending an evolution log. Third, a ReAct Skill Proposer reads the wiki index, skill-impact history, training outcomes, selected pattern pages, and on-demand raw traces through `read_file`; it proposes one atomic skill creation or patch. Fourth, the candidate skill is evaluated on the validation split and accepted only if its score strictly exceeds the best validation score so far; rejected skill changes are discarded, but their diffs and outcomes remain in `skill-impact.md`. Skills are injected in full into the inference system prompt, eliminating retrieval and triggering as confounds. The major design decisions are persistent rather than rollbackable wiki state, restricting wiki access during inference rollouts, and full-batch training-trace processing with a ReAct proposer. The paper gives a qualitative rationale for each, and the wiki-access ablation supports the first two, but it does not provide a cost-matched or component-level comparison of alternative maintainer/proposer prompts, trace budgets, or acceptance rules. Key Results: On the five test sets, WikiSkill obtains the best reported average for every inference model: Qwen-3.5-4B 38.5% versus 35.2% for SkillOpt; Qwen-3.5-9B 47.4% versus 42.3% for EvoSkill; Qwen-3.6-27B 63.3% versus 53.3% for EvoSkill; Gemma-4-31B 54.9% versus 49.1% for SkillOpt; and Gemini-3.5-Flash 68.1% versus 56.1% for EvoSkill. Relative to no skills, the reported average gains are +12.3, +17.5, and +23.9 points for Qwen-3.5-4B, Qwen-3.5-9B, and Qwen-3.6-27B, respectively. The largest individual gains include Gemini-3.5-Flash on LiveMath, 33.0% to 72.6%, Qwen-3.6-27B on SpreadsheetBench, 40.8% to 81.7%, and Qwen-3.6-27B on ALFWorld, 52.8% to 77.6%. Qwen-3.5-9B with WikiSkill reaches 47.4% average versus 39.4% for Qwen-3.6-27B without skills. Cross-model transfer is sometimes stronger than self-evolution: Qwen-3.5-9B reaches 70.2% on ALFWorld with a Qwen-3.6-27B-derived skill versus 63.4% with its own skill, and Gemma-4-31B reaches 73.7% on LiveMath with a Qwen-3.6-27B-derived skill versus 56.7% with its own. Transfer is not uniformly robust: Qwen-3.5-4B-derived skills reduce Gemini-3.5-Flash SpreadsheetBench performance from 50.5% to 18.1%. In the Gemini ablation, removing wiki access from the proposer and maintainer reduces the average from 63.7% to 48.7% when the inference agent also lacks wiki access, while granting wiki access to the inference agent reduces the default configuration from 63.7% to 60.9%. Results average three independent full evolution runs and use 1,000-iteration paired bootstrap tests at p < 0.05, but the paper does not report confidence intervals, per-run variance, exact p-values, or the number of statistically significant pairwise comparisons. Benchmark sizes are small to moderate: 124–280 test examples, 16–80 training examples, and 10–40 validation examples per benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the persistent wiki as a separate, compounding representation of experience and the evidence that skills can transfer across model families and outperform self-evolved skills are the substantive contributions, while the maintainer–proposer–gating loop combines established LLM reflection, trace analysis, patching, and validation techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study covers 5 benchmarks, 5 models, 3 independent runs per method, three named skill-evolution baselines, no-skill controls, cross-model transfer, and a wiki-access ablation. It reports a stratified trace-sampling protocol, dataset split sizes, exact system prompts for the inference, maintainer, and proposer agents, and an explicit algorithm. The ablation supports the claimed role of the persistent wiki, but it does not separate the effects of persistent pattern pages, rejection history, skill-impact logs, raw-trace access, and the ReAct proposer. The strict validation rule repeatedly uses small validation sets—10 to 40 examples—and selects skills based on validation improvement, creating a plausible risk of validation overfitting; the paper does not report validation/test correlation, repeated validation splits, or an untouched second validation set. Three runs are limited for a stochastic multi-agent optimizer, and error bars are absent. The baselines are recent dedicated skill-evolution systems, but the comparison excludes general prompt optimizers such as GEPA and does not provide compute- or token-budget-matched results. The paper states that exact prompts are provided in the appendix, but it does not state that code, datasets, evolved skills, model weights, or a runnable WikiSkill implementation are released; no software URL or repository is mentioned. Because this is arXiv:2608.27454v1 dated 27 August 2026, the results should be treated as preprint evidence rather than peer-reviewed findings. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS, because the paper specifies a built multi-agent skill-evolution workflow and evaluates it as an agent framework, although it does not report deployment in a production environment. * Practical: The open-weight experiments use Qwen and Gemma models deployed with vLLM, so the inference components can run on commercially available accelerators, but the paper does not report hardware type, memory, latency, wall-clock time, or the feasibility of running the full evolution loop. * Efficient: WikiSkill uses full-batch processing and approximately 10–20 ReAct proposer turns plus one maintainer call per iteration, giving 11–21 optimizer LLM calls per iteration in the reported setting; this is asymptotically O(1) in training-set size under full batching, but the paper does not report token counts or total cost and compares against baselines under different batching and optimizer-call regimes. * Effective: Test accuracy improves over no-skill and competing skill-evolution methods on the reported benchmarks, but the evidence measures benchmark correctness rather than production reliability, intervention safety, task completion cost, or performance under changing environments. * Scalable: The largest reported training split has 80 examples, the longest reported evolution is 8 iterations, and the active skills are fully injected into the prompt; no experiment tests 10×–100× more tasks, substantially longer evolution, large skill libraries, context pressure, hundreds of environment actions, or online within-rollout adaptation. The work delivers a specified filesystem-style skill and wiki architecture, prompt specifications, an algorithm, and benchmark-generated skill artifacts in principle, but the paper does not state that a reusable software artifact or repository is publicly released. Strengths: - The separation of raw traces, persistent structured knowledge, and executable skills gives a clear state representation and a concrete mechanism for retaining rejected proposals and recurring failure patterns instead of treating each update as an isolated edit. - The evaluation spans five qualitatively different task types and five model configurations, including open-weight and closed models, which makes the repeated performance pattern more informative than a single benchmark result. - The cross-model transfer matrix exposes an important distinction between discovering procedures and executing them: skills from Qwen-3.6-27B improve Qwen-3.5-9B ALFWorld from 34.7% to 70.2%, while some skills produce severe negative transfer, such as 50.5% to 18.1% for Gemini-3.5-Flash on SpreadsheetBench. - The ablation tests a central causal claim rather than only reporting end-to-end gains: removing persistent wiki maintenance lowers the Gemini average from 63.7% to 48.7% when inference-time wiki access is absent, and allowing the inference agent to use the wiki during training lowers the default average to 60.9%. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that direct skill injection leaves skill retrieval and triggering unevaluated; strict validation gating rejects neutral updates that could enable later gains; the wiki has no automated pruning mechanism; and the benchmark suite lacks very long-horizon tasks spanning hundreds of actions or multiple hours. They also identify online within-rollout skill adaptation as future work. These limitations are clearly stated, but the paper does not acknowledge the associated validation-overfitting risk, the absence of compute-normalized comparisons, or the lack of a public implementation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central improvement is confounded by additional optimizer computation and a different proposal interface. WikiSkill’s proposer performs roughly 10–20 ReAct turns and dynamically reads traces, while baselines use different batching, reflection, and call budgets; no equal-token, equal-call, or equal-wall-clock comparison shows that persistence rather than extra optimization effort drives the gains. - The validation gate uses only strict score improvement on small fixed validation sets, and the same validation score controls many sequential accept/reject decisions. The paper does not quantify selection bias or test whether the final skills generalize to a fresh validation split. - The ablation removes the Wiki Maintainer together with proposer wiki access, so the reported 15.0-point average drop cannot uniquely establish that persistent knowledge, rather than an additional analysis agent or changed prompt context, is responsible. - The evaluation injects every active skill in full, avoiding the retrieval problem but also avoiding the context-length and interference costs that motivate persistent, modular skills. The paper does not test dozens or hundreds of skills, skill selection errors, context overflow, or competing skills. - The benchmarks are mostly static, have small training and validation sets, and use task-specific scaffolding such as oracle reference pages for OfficeQA. The paper does not evaluate distribution shift, adversarial tasks, changing tools, contaminated live data, or long-horizon accumulation beyond eight iterations. - The optimizer-call complexity analysis is asymptotic and excludes rollout inference, validation inference, tool costs, ReAct token usage, and maintainer/proposer context length. Its claimed efficiency advantage therefore does not establish lower monetary or latency cost. - Statistical reporting is incomplete for a stochastic system: the paper provides three-run means and bootstrap testing but no standard deviations or confidence intervals, and it does not clarify whether bootstrap comparisons account for shared task instances and independent evolved skills across runs. Bottom Line: This is a useful and empirically substantial preprint for researchers studying self-improving agents because it makes persistent experience compilation and cross-model skill transfer concrete, but its headline gains are not yet sufficient for a top-tier systems claim without cost-matched baselines, factorized ablations, fresh validation splits, public artifacts, and evaluation with realistic skill retrieval and long-horizon workloads.

The Evaluation Context Protocol (ECP): A Portable Contract for AI Agent Evaluation

A Wattamwar, M Anandani, M Kakirwar · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes the Evaluation Context Protocol (ECP), an open-source JSON-RPC contract and reference implementation that exposes an agent’s user-visible output, tool calls, and evaluator-safe audit context for portable, trajectory-aware evaluation. - Why it's important: Outcome-only scores can miss unauthorized actions, fabricated reasoning, benchmark shortcuts, and unreliable behavior in agents that modify external systems. - How it does it: ECP separates the evaluation plane from the execution/orchestration plane through three protocol methods—`agent/initialize`, `agent/step`, and `agent/reset`—plus schema-validated result fields and pluggable graders. - The good: The paper delivers a runnable implementation with Python and early TypeScript support, adapters for LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and PydanticAI, CI integration, JSON Schemas, reports, and a conformance harness. - The missing: It provides no controlled evidence that ECP detects more defects than outcome-only evaluation, that independent implementations produce matching verdicts, or that its overhead is acceptable at production scale. - Read it or not: Agent-evaluation and observability researchers should read it as a concrete protocol proposal and implementation case study, but readers seeking validated performance improvements or a mature standard can defer it.
Why this rank
Profile: systems. The protocol-and-tool contribution is reasonably novel (Novelty 72) and non-obvious as an interoperability boundary (Non-Obviousness 60), with strong practical value from the released runtime, adapters, schemas, and CI tooling (Impact 78). However, the absence of ECP-specific defect-detection, portability, overhead, and baseline comparisons substantially lowers Rigor (45) and Resilience (45), despite candid limitation disclosure supporting Completeness (78). systems Novelty 72 Rigor 45 Non-Obv 60 Completeness 78 Resilience 45 Impact 78
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation The work addresses the difficulty of evaluating autonomous and multi-step AI agents whose behavior includes planning, memory use, tool invocation, environmental feedback, and side effects rather than a single text response. This matters to developers and operators in software engineering, CloudOps, healthcare, finance, legal services, and other domains where an agent can modify data or trigger external actions. The paper identifies a gap between static or final-answer benchmarks and operational reliability: current evaluations often fail to expose unauthorized tool use, benchmark exploitation, context-rot-induced fabrication, policy violations, run-to-run instability, and the difference between best-case capability and consistent success. It also argues that evaluation infrastructure is fragmented across orchestrators and proprietary observability platforms, making evaluation definitions difficult to transfer across frameworks and CI environments. Key Idea The central insight is to treat agent evaluation as a portable contract layer orthogonal to the agent’s execution layer. Instead of standardizing how an agent calls tools, as the Model Context Protocol does, ECP standardizes what an agent returns to an evaluator: the public result, the environmental actions taken, and evaluator-safe evidence about those actions. These fields can then be asserted independently by deterministic or model-based graders. The idea is conceptually straightforward and related to existing trajectory logging and observability practices; the paper’s distinctive contribution is packaging this separation as a small transport-level protocol with schemas, adapters, CI behavior, and conformance tooling. Methodology ECP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 with stdio as the default transport and Streamable HTTP as an alternative. An evaluator starts an agent process, sends `agent/initialize` with the evaluation configuration, repeatedly sends `agent/step` for scenario turns, inspects the returned envelope, and calls `agent/reset` between scenarios. The envelope currently contains `public_output`, `tool_calls`, `evaluation_context`, and optional `logs`. A manifest specifies scenarios, expected outputs or tool behavior, and checks; JSON Schemas validate manifests and result artifacts before execution. The reference runtime provides `text_match`, `tool_usage`, and `llm_judge` graders, combines declared checks with a logical AND, emits JSON/HTML reports, and returns a nonzero process status on failure so CI can block a build. Framework adapters translate native execution events from LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and PydanticAI into the common result object; examples also cover plain Python, asynchronous Python, and HTTP serving. Three important design decisions are only partly justified: separating public output, actions, and audit evidence is well motivated by the cited failure modes; using evaluator-safe evidence rather than raw chain-of-thought is appropriately motivated by disclosure and intellectual-property concerns, but its semantics and reliability remain underspecified; and keeping the protocol surface minimal supports independent reimplementation, although the current omission of tool results, cost, latency, delegation identity, and structured evidence limits what can actually be evaluated. The paper does not define a formal objective function or optimization loss because ECP is an evaluation protocol rather than a learning method. Key Results The paper does not report primary experiments evaluating ECP. It reports implementation scope rather than measured performance: three JSON-RPC methods, two transports, three grader families, four named framework adapters, published schemas, a conformance harness, CLI commands (`ecp run`, `ecp init`, `ecp validate`, `ecp doctor`, and `ecp conformance`), pytest integration, JSON/HTML reports, a CI exit-status gate, and an early TypeScript SDK. The quantitative findings in the paper come from cited external work, not from ECP experiments: the cited pass@3 versus pass^3 example gives approximately 97% versus 34% success; MAESTRO is described as covering 12 multi-agent frameworks; the AIDev study reports human intervention in 52.17% of agent-authored pull requests versus 83.59% of human-authored pull requests and 58.02% of intervention effort spent on guidance-level work; a healthcare scoping review reduced 1,070 records to 43 relevant studies; and the paper claims evaluation can consume 10–15% of an organization’s production LLM budget. These numbers motivate ECP but do not establish that ECP improves detection, reliability, portability, cost, or deployment outcomes. No ECP benchmark, baseline comparison, sample size, latency measurement, defect-detection rate, or stress-scale evaluation is provided. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW FORMULATION, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a secondary POSITION/VISION contribution: ECP formulates a portable evaluation-plane contract and implements it as a JSON-RPC runtime, schema set, adapters, graders, and CI workflow. The underlying ingredients—trajectory logging, tool-use checks, LLM judging, JSON-RPC, schema validation, and CI gates—are established, so the genuine novelty lies in their proposed cross-framework contract and reference implementation rather than in a new evaluation algorithm or empirically demonstrated finding. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper is unusually explicit that ECP is unvalidated and provisional, but it does not provide the experiments needed to support adoption claims. There are no ECP-specific ablations, repeated-seed studies, confidence intervals, significance tests, fault-injection results, portability agreement measurements, or overhead measurements. The implementation, specification, examples, and SDKs are said to be open source, with the repository listed as https://github.com/evaluation-context-protocol/ecp and the specification at https://www.evaluationcontextprotocol.io/spec; the paper does not provide a commit hash, release version, or evidence that the linked artifact is independently reproducible. The conformance harness checks protocol behavior but does not establish semantic equivalence across implementations. The current `evaluation_context` may be concatenated reasoning text rather than structured evidence, the TypeScript SDK is not at Python parity, the export path is tied to one external platform, and the protocol lacks native repeated-run `pass^k`, policy/authority, deterministic execution, signed provenance, redaction, and delegation mechanisms. Several numerical claims about judge bias, calibration thresholds, evaluation cost, and external benchmark behavior rely on heterogeneous references—many documentation or vendor sources—and are not independently verified in this paper. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with an empirical implementation component but no primary deployment evaluation. Practical: The stdio/HTTP design, Python runtime, CLI, pytest plugin, and CI exit codes can run on commercially available developer or CI hardware, although model-judge cost and framework-specific instrumentation are not quantified. Efficient: The paper gives no measured runtime, memory, token, storage, or monetary overhead relative to native framework evaluation; it acknowledges that trajectory grading may add substantial inference and telemetry cost and only proposes caching, sharding, tiered graders, and budget ceilings as future mitigations. Effective: The implementation can check outputs, tool names/arguments, and declared audit evidence, but the paper does not measure whether these checks detect more real or injected failures than outcome-only grading, and evaluator-safe evidence may be incomplete or misleading. Scalable: The protocol is architecturally transport-portable, but the paper tests neither 10×–100× scenario volume nor long-horizon, high-cardinality multi-agent workloads; storage, judge cost, delegation, and telemetry scalability remain unestablished. The work delivers a software artifact—reference runtime, SDKs, adapters, schemas, CLI, reports, and conformance harness—but not a validated production-scale platform, benchmark, or observability backend. Strengths - It identifies a concrete interoperability boundary between tool execution and evaluation, rather than proposing another framework-specific tracing dashboard. - The result envelope and CI lifecycle make the proposal operationally legible: checks become versioned machine-readable contracts and failed behavioral checks can block a build. - The paper responsibly distinguishes evaluator-safe evidence from raw chain-of-thought and acknowledges that current adapters often cannot provide the intended structured evidence. - It documents important missing capabilities—delegation attribution, tool results, latency/cost, reliability statistics, signed provenance, redaction, versioning, and independent implementations—instead of presenting the early protocol as complete. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that ECP is an early-stage, experimental proposal rather than a settled standard. They acknowledge the absence of controlled defect-detection comparisons, independent interoperability evidence, and deployment-scale validation. They also identify the provisional nature of the evaluation surface; free-text and inconsistently structured `evaluation_context`; missing tool observations, latency, cost, and delegation semantics; under-specified paused execution; provider-specific LLM-judge credentials; unsigned reports; incomplete TypeScript parity; limited export generality; evaluation cost and telemetry storage overhead; and the need for domain experts and calibrated judges. The paper confronts these limitations directly and presents them as a roadmap for future work. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper claims a portable contract but does not test semantic portability: equivalent agents across the four adapters could emit different evidence, tool traces, failure semantics, or verdicts even if they pass the protocol schema. - It does not compare ECP against strong existing alternatives such as OpenTelemetry-based tracing, LangSmith, Phoenix, Langfuse, Braintrust, or framework-native evaluation pipelines on identical tasks and injected failures. - The proposed `evaluation_context` is a potentially gameable, agent-controlled evidence channel; the paper does not analyze whether agents can produce plausible justifications that conceal incorrect internal state or whether evaluators can verify evidence against tool observations. - The logical-AND verdict policy is not evaluated and may trade false positives for safety without measuring missed failures, annotation burden, or usability. - The paper advocates trajectory evaluation but the current protocol omits returned tool observations, side effects, timing, cost, and first-class multi-agent identity, limiting its ability to validate several stated motivations. - The cited quantitative claims are not methodologically synthesized: source quality varies from peer-reviewed papers to vendor documentation and blog-like reports, and no systematic review protocol or provenance analysis supports the literature-wide conclusions. - Security properties are asserted more strongly than implemented: current unsigned JSON/HTML reports, lack of sealed manifests, and absence of authority semantics do not yet provide cryptographically secure accountability or contamination control. Bottom Line This is worth reading as a concrete, candid early software-and-protocol proposal for researchers and teams designing framework-neutral agent evaluation infrastructure, but it is not yet evidence that ECP is better than existing observability and evaluation systems or ready to serve as a standard.

MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks (21 ▲ )

Yi Zhu, Xiongwei Wu, Qiyi Wang, Tingyu Qu, Jiajun Liu, Sihan Cao, Long Chen, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Steven Hoi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 25 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MobilePA-Bench, an interactive stateful benchmark and executable mobile sandbox for evaluating LLM planner agents across tool use, sub-agent collaboration, memory retrieval, and reusable skill execution. - Why it's important: Reliable mobile assistants must operate under API dependencies, permissions, mutable application state, personalization requirements, and runtime failures rather than merely emit correct function-call strings or click screen coordinates. - How it does it: It represents direct tools, memory queries, sub-agent dispatches, and skill loading as structured actions in a closed-loop simulator whose databases mutate and return execution feedback, then verifies each task by tool-call, state-change, or agent-behavior criteria. - The good: The benchmark exposes substantial weaknesses in current models: the best reported overall score is 75.52%, memory success peaks at 64.63%, and no evaluated model leads across all capability dimensions. - The missing: The paper does not provide component ablations, human validation of task realism or behavior-based judgments, or comparisons against strong integrated mobile-agent systems and real-device execution. - Read it or not: Researchers building mobile or tool-using agents should read it for its stateful evaluation design and failure taxonomy, while readers seeking evidence of real-world deployment should treat the simulator results as preliminary.
Why this rank
Profile: empirical. MobilePA-Bench offers a useful stateful, executable benchmark formulation (Novelty 75) and a reasonably non-obvious integration of tools, memory, skills, delegation, and heterogeneous verification (Non-Obviousness 70). Rigor (62), Completeness (62), and Resilience (58) are held back by the simulator-only setting, arbitrary weighting and routing choices, absent ablations and strong integrated baselines, limited human validation, and minimal stability testing; its released benchmark nevertheless gives it moderate impact (60). empirical Novelty 75 Rigor 62 Non-Obv 70 Completeness 62 Resilience 58 Impact 60
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Mobile personal assistants need to translate underspecified natural-language requests into multi-step actions over a dynamic operating system. The affected domain includes mobile communication, scheduling, settings, travel, media, security, and productivity, where actions depend on permissions, prior state, runtime feedback, user preferences, and sometimes visual interaction. Existing GUI-centric benchmarks emphasize screen perception and pixel-level manipulation, while static function-calling benchmarks test offline schema or string matching without executing calls in a mutable environment. The stated gap is a unified evaluation of high-level mobile planning that combines structured API orchestration, runtime error recovery, persistent memory, reusable procedures, and delegation to specialized sub-agents. The paper frames these requirements as four dimensions: Basic Tool Use, Sub-agent Collaboration, Memory Usage, and Skill Usage. Key Idea The central insight is to evaluate the planner as an orchestrator in a lightweight stateful operating-system sandbox rather than as either a screen-clicking agent or an offline function-call generator. The benchmark exposes heterogeneous capabilities through one structured action space, while separating capability labels from evidence-aligned success criteria: exact tool trajectories for deterministic tasks, terminal database deltas for path-equivalent tasks, and observable interaction behavior for open-ended delegation or clarification tasks. This combination is the paper's main conceptual contribution; the underlying ingredients—function calling, simulators, memory retrieval, skills, and sub-agents—are largely established individually. Methodology Each task is modeled as a user query q, initial state S0, optional dialogue history H0, and active candidate action set A0. At each step, a planner selects an action from retrieved direct-tool schemas, sub-agent entry points, memory tools, or skill loaders; the sandbox executes it, mutates persistent domain databases, records operation logs, and returns structured feedback containing status, error type, and payload. The trajectory continues until a Finish action or a maximum of 15 steps. The initial action set contains the top-N recalled tools with N=15 plus query-relevant skill loaders; loading a skill expands the active action set with its concrete procedures. The sandbox covers 212 tools in 13 domains, including communication, settings, media, scheduling, travel, connectivity, security, and productivity. Basic Tool Use tasks test grounding, dependencies, reference tracking, intent revision, boundary detection, and recovery from missing parameters, permission blocks, or ambiguities. Sub-agent tasks test route selection and completeness of handoff payloads to one of six specialized agents, including GUI, image, search, and monitoring agents. Memory tasks require retrieval of annotated memory IDs and successful downstream use, with a conjunctive gate requiring both retrieval and primary-task success. Skill tasks require loading the annotated gold skill and completing the resulting procedure, evaluated under Skill-Only Routing and Mixed Tool-Skill Routing. Verification uses three fixed buckets: exact tool names, order, and arguments; terminal database state changes; or task-specific behavior rubrics. Overall score is a fixed weighted sum: 50% Basic Tool Use, 10% Sub-agent Collaboration, 20% Memory Usage, and 20% Skill Usage. The state-transition and verification design is explicit, but the paper does not adequately justify the 50/10/20/20 weighting, the top-15 tool-recall policy, the 15-step budget, or the choice of gold skill and memory gates. Key Results The evaluation covers 1,705 tasks: 1,040 Basic Tool Use, 89 Sub-agent Collaboration, 376 Memory Usage, and 200 Skill Usage tasks; Skill Usage reports a denominator of 400 trajectories because it pools Skill-Only and Mixed Tool-Skill settings. Thirteen proprietary and open-weight LLMs are evaluated. Claude-Opus-5 obtains the highest overall score, 75.52%, with 83.85% Basic Tool Use, 62.92% Sub-agent Collaboration, 58.51% Memory Usage, and 78.00% Skills. Claude-Fable-5 reaches 75.31%, Kimi-K3 73.01%, and Qwen-3.8-Max 72.51%; the lowest overall score is 55.63% for Kimi-2.6. Basic Tool Use ranges from 68.94% to 83.85%, with Claude-Opus-5 succeeding on 872/1,040 tasks and a 13-model mean of 76.58%. Sub-agent performance ranges from 43.82% to 77.53%, led by Gemini-3.1-Pro. Memory ranges from 33.78% to 64.63%, led by Qwen-3.8-Max at 243/376 tasks, with a 13-model mean of 50.98%. Skills range from 46.50% to 78.00%, led by Claude-Opus-5 at 312/400 and with a mean of 66.77%. The reported pattern is that skill invocation often outperforms memory use and may reduce long-horizon error accumulation, while capability leadership is fragmented across models. A three-run stability check using Qwen3.6-27B produces an overall range of 57.22%–57.63% and standard deviation 0.22 percentage points, but this tests only one model and repeated stochastic generation under identical benchmark conditions. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a secondary NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING classification: the paper packages stateful mobile tool execution, explicit memory and skill gates, sub-agent routing, and three verification modes into one benchmark, whereas the individual mechanisms are standard combinations of existing agent-evaluation ideas rather than a new planning algorithm or formalism. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports a large task count, immutable full-denominator scoring, explicit formal definitions for state transitions and memory/skill gates, and one three-run stability experiment. It does not report ablations isolating the effects of statefulness, runtime friction, memory gates, skill loading, candidate-tool recall, or verification buckets; it also provides no confidence intervals across models, significance tests, per-category error bars, inter-annotator agreement, or detailed error breakdown by task type. The authors state that all 1,705 tasks, evaluation datasets, and the sandbox infrastructure are open-sourced at https://github.com/Tongyi-MAI/MobilePA-Bench, but the paper does not document release versioning, licenses, exact prompts, model API settings, latency/cost, or enough implementation detail to independently assess fidelity. The benchmark is a simulated environment with authored schemas, databases, gold trajectories, gold memory IDs, and gold skills, so its scores may reflect familiarity with the benchmark's interface and annotation conventions. Behavior-based verification is described as task-specific but its rubric construction and judge reliability are not reported. The paper also distinguishes a 1,530-query scenario-analysis snapshot from the 1,705-task evaluation denominator, but does not fully explain the relationship between these sets. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL, because the paper evaluates LLM planners and delivers an executable benchmark rather than a deployed mobile-agent system. * Practical: The sandbox itself should run on commercially available hardware because it directly executes structured database operations without full OS rendering, although hardware and runtime requirements are Not stated. * Efficient: The authors claim high-throughput, RL-friendly execution by avoiding screenshot rendering and VM/VNC overhead, but provide no throughput, latency, memory, energy, or cost measurements relative to AndroidWorld, OSWorld, or real-device alternatives. * Effective: The evidence shows that the benchmark discriminates among planner capabilities and reveals failures on its simulator's tasks, but it does not establish that the measured scores predict successful operation on real phones, third-party applications, or safety-critical user workflows. * Scalable: The benchmark scales to 1,705 tasks and 212 tools in the reported experiments, but the paper does not test 10×–100× larger tool catalogs, longer horizons, larger persistent memories, concurrent users, or more complex state transitions; scalability beyond the implemented sandbox is claimed rather than measured. The work delivers a reusable software artifact consisting of a benchmark dataset and stateful sandbox, with the claimed repository at https://github.com/Tongyi-MAI/MobilePA-Bench; it does not deliver a trained planner or a new planning algorithm. Strengths - The benchmark evaluates execution in a closed loop with mutable databases and structured runtime errors, avoiding the main validity problem of static function-call matching. - The separation of capability dimensions from verification buckets is a useful design choice: exact trajectories, terminal state, and interactive behavior require different notions of correctness, and the paper does not force one metric onto all tasks. - The benchmark integrates memory retrieval, skill loading, and delegated execution into mobile workflows instead of evaluating each only as an isolated algorithmic capability. - The empirical results identify a concrete systems-level finding: direct tool competence does not imply reliable personalization or coordination, and the strongest model differs across Basic Tool Use, Memory, Skills, and Sub-agent Collaboration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper does not present a dedicated limitations section. It acknowledges that current results are insufficient for fully autonomous mobile operating systems, that models exhibit hallucinated or premature tool calls under ambiguity and errors, and that the benchmark decouples central planning from low-level GUI execution by delegating visual interaction to specialized sub-agents. It does not explicitly acknowledge the simulator-to-real-device gap, possible annotation or checker bias, arbitrary aggregate weighting, limited sub-agent sample size, or the absence of human validation. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The environment is described as realistic but appears to be a hand-built simulator over structured databases rather than a real mobile OS or live application ecosystem; no transfer study to Android, iOS, or real APIs tests ecological validity. - The benchmark's gold memory IDs and gold skill IDs can reward retrieving or invoking the annotation's preferred artifact even when an alternative memory record, procedure, or valid plan would satisfy the user, potentially conflating benchmark conformity with capability. - The fixed 50/10/20/20 aggregate is not grounded in deployment risk, user utility, or a sensitivity analysis; changing the weights could alter the ranking substantially. - Sub-agent Collaboration has only 89 tasks, behavior rubrics lack reported human agreement, and the paper does not show whether the central planner is being evaluated independently of the downstream sub-agent's competence. - The paper reports aggregate scores but omits per-domain, per-horizon, per-error-type, and per-verification-bucket results, making it difficult to determine whether failures arise from reasoning, tool retrieval, schema design, error handling, or checker strictness. - There are no strong baseline agents, simple scripted planners, retrieval-only or skill-only controls, or ablations showing that stateful feedback and composite skills improve performance relative to otherwise matched alternatives. - The stability experiment uses only Qwen3.6-27B and three runs; it does not establish robustness across model families, prompt variants, temperature settings, task seeds, or benchmark regeneration. - The paper claims usefulness for reinforcement learning but reports no training experiment, reward-design study, rollout throughput measurement, or evidence that benchmark trajectories improve a planner after fine-tuning. Bottom Line MobilePA-Bench is a useful and potentially reusable diagnostic benchmark for researchers studying stateful mobile tool orchestration, but its contribution is primarily infrastructure and task design, and the absence of real-device validation, ablations, human rubric validation, and stronger controls limits the strength of its claims about dependable real-world mobile agents.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a narrative review of type I, II, and III interferon signaling in lupus nephritis (LN), evaluates biomarker evidence, and maps direct interferon- and upstream nucleic-acid-sensor-targeted therapies. - Why it's important: LN frequently causes irreversible renal damage, kidney failure, dialysis, or transplantation, while current immunosuppression does not reliably provide organ-specific control or individualized treatment. - How it does it: The review connects interferon activity in blood and renal tissue to damage in podocytes, mesangial cells, tubular epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells, then compares receptor, JAK–STAT, and pattern-recognition-receptor interventions. - The good: It clearly separates the commonly used blood interferon gene signature from actual interferon activity and shows why renal-tissue or urine-derived measurements may be more informative for LN. - The missing: The review provides no systematic search or quantitative synthesis, and no clinical trial has yet established that interferon blockade improves renal outcomes in LN; the pivotal phase III IRIS trial remains ongoing. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on lupus nephritis biomarkers, renal immunology, or interferon-targeted therapeutics; readers seeking new experimental data or definitive treatment recommendations can skip it.
