Problem & Motivation: District-heating operators need short-term forecasts of aggregate network heat demand to schedule production, exploit volatile electricity prices, operate electric boilers and heat pumps, manage storage, and participate in reserve markets. The research gap is a controlled comparison of classical statistical, machine-learning, deep-learning, and foundation forecasting models across multiple district-heating networks, together with an assessment of whether detailed meteorological inputs provide value beyond temperature and calendar information. The application is Finnish district heating, with five operational networks of approximately 1–10 MW peak demand and hourly observations. The motivation is practical, but the link from lower point-forecast error to reduced operating cost, emissions, or dispatch risk is not directly measured. Key Idea: The core insight is empirical rather than architectural: under the study's controlled feature comparison, future temperature supplies most of the useful weather signal, while a pretrained covariate-aware foundation model, Chronos-2, transfers substantially better than locally trained alternatives. The work does not introduce a new forecasting algorithm; it applies existing models and constructs a multi-model, multi-network, multi-covariate comparison. Methodology: The target is hourly heat demand for each network, forecast at horizons h ∈ {8, 24, 48}. The six covariate configurations progress from univariate demand history, to calendar variables, to temperature, all twelve meteorological variables, selected engineered weather features, and a full combination. Weather variables include temperature, wind, humidity, pressure, dewpoint, precipitation, snow accumulation, cloud cover, solar radiation, UV index, wind-related features, and daylight indicators; the study uses retrospective ERA5-Land values extracted through Open-Meteo, so future weather is effectively known. The benchmark includes Seasonal Naïve, AutoETS, AutoTheta, MSTL with AutoARIMA, LightGBM, XGBoost, NBEATSx, NHITS, HourlyOLS, TimeGPT zero-shot and fine-tuned, and Chronos-2 in 120M- and 28M-parameter versions. Tree models use recursive one-step prediction; NBEATSx and NHITS are trained independently per network with 1,000 steps, batch size 32, and input size twice the horizon; HourlyOLS fits 24 separate OLS models with lags {1, 2, 6, 12, 24} and a 30-day training cap; Chronos-2 is run locally zero-shot, while TimeGPT uses a remote API and 50 fine-tuning steps. Evaluation uses five temporally ordered rolling windows per horizon and four truncations at 70%, 80%, 90%, and 100% of each series. MASE is the primary metric, supplemented by RMSE, sMAPE, CRPS, Winkler interval score, and empirical 90% interval coverage. Critical design decisions are the oracle-weather setup, the per-network scale normalization, and the exclusion of imputed values in favor of long contiguous segments. The first isolates model and feature effects but weakens operational validity; the second enables cross-network comparison but uses a full-series denominator; and the third avoids injecting unreliable synthetic targets but discards data and may bias evaluation toward unusually clean periods. The paper does not provide a formal objective for every model, and the probabilistic evaluation is not tuned consistently across models. Key Results: Chronos-2 is the best model at all three horizons: MASE 0.421 at 8 hours, 0.487 at 24 hours, and 0.514 at 48 hours, using all-weather features at 8 and 24 hours and engineered features at 48 hours. Chronos-2-small is close behind at 0.423, 0.513, and 0.574. The best non-Chronos scores are MSTL 0.493 at 8 hours, NHITS 0.638 at 24 hours, and NBEATSx 0.697 at 48 hours. Relative to the best non-Chronos model, the reported Chronos-2 advantage is 14.6%, 23.7%, and 26.3% at 8, 24, and 48 hours. At 8 hours, the remaining ranking includes LightGBM at 0.496, HourlyOLS at 0.524, NHITS at 0.525, XGBoost at 0.531, and NBEATSx at 0.541. At 48 hours, HourlyOLS reaches 0.713, NHITS 0.706, XGBoost 0.885, LightGBM 0.886, TimeGPT fine-tuned 0.916, and TimeGPT zero-shot 0.921. The best seasonal-naïve MASE values are 1.110, 1.194, and 1.411 at the three horizons under the paper's nonstandard full-series scaling, so MASE is not equal to one for that model by construction. Temperature provides most of the improvement over univariate or calendar-only inputs: for example, Chronos-2 improves from 0.497 to 0.430 at 8 hours and from 1.249 to 0.536 at 48 hours, while additional weather features produce only small or inconsistent gains. A notable exception is HourlyOLS, for which larger feature sets often worsen performance, consistent with overfitting from only 30 days of per-hour training data. Chronos-2 beats the other evaluated models on each of the five networks when each model's best feature configuration is selected. The probabilistic results are materially weaker: empirical nominal-90% interval coverage is 0.859 for Chronos-2, 0.854 for Chronos-2-small, 0.630 for TimeGPT zero-shot, 0.629 for TimeGPT fine-tuned, 0.568 for NHITS, and 0.533 for NBEATSx; LightGBM and XGBoost reach 0.940 and 0.912, respectively, but interval sharpness and proper scoring results are not headlined. On one consumer workstation, mean training times range from 139 ms for HourlyOLS and 183 ms for LightGBM to 5.8–5.9 seconds for NBEATSx and NHITS; inference is 772 ms for Chronos-2, 262 ms for Chronos-2-small, and 12.3 seconds for remote TimeGPT, although the TimeGPT measurement includes network latency. These results are from five short, mostly winter Finnish records rather than a broad stress-scale benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; NEW BENCHMARK/COMPARATIVE STUDY; ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely useful contribution is the cross-model comparison on five previously unavailable operational district-heating series and the finding that Chronos-2 dominates under oracle weather inputs while temperature captures most feature value; the models, losses, and feature engineering are standard existing components rather than a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: The temporal ordering of the rolling evaluation is appropriate, and the paper tests multiple horizons, four data fractions, five networks, six covariate configurations, and two Chronos-2 sizes. It also explicitly evaluates imputation methods before excluding unreliable gaps, reports compute hardware and runtimes, and acknowledges the oracle-weather limitation and possible foundation-model leakage. However, no error bars, multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, pairwise statistical tests, or significance procedures are reported despite the claim that Chronos-2 models “significantly” outperform the alternatives. The five test windows per horizon are few, adjacent and concentrated near the ends of relatively short series; the data span roughly September 2025–February 2026 for four networks and about one year for the fifth, limiting seasonal and regime coverage. The MASE denominator is computed from each network's full available series before truncation, including observations outside the training period, which does not alter predictions but uses future target values in metric normalization and complicates the paper's claim of no leakage. Model comparisons are also not fully symmetric: some statistical models cannot use covariates, foundation models are evaluated zero-shot or with different adaptation mechanisms, and feature configurations are selected per model and horizon after evaluation. Several baselines use default library hyperparameters, while neural models receive some hyperparameter exploration; modern competitors such as Toto-2.0 are absent because they were released after the experiments. The DHN data are confidential and cannot be shared; no code, trained weights, or reproducible repository is stated, although public Nixtla libraries and the Open-Meteo/ERA5-Land source are identified. Chronos-2 is locally available, but TimeGPT relies on a closed remote API, and possible TimeGPT pretraining contamination cannot be ruled out. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The locally run models can operate on commercially available hardware, and the full Chronos-2 model was tested on an RTX 3070 with 8 GB memory, but deployment still requires acquiring operational weather forecasts, integrating a private model/data pipeline, and addressing confidential-data and API constraints. Efficient: Chronos-2 inference averaged 772 ms per reported run and Chronos-2-small 262 ms, but the study does not provide end-to-end throughput, memory consumption, retraining frequency, energy cost, or a fair comparison at production batch sizes; TimeGPT inference averaged 12.3 seconds including network latency. Effective: The evidence supports lower retrospective point-forecast error on five Finnish networks, not improved dispatch decisions, cost, emissions, peak management, or service reliability; the poor or unexamined calibration of several probabilistic outputs is a serious operational issue. Scalable: No 10×–100× scale test is conducted: the study evaluates only five independent series with records of at most approximately one year, and it does not test more networks, longer histories, changing seasons, extreme weather, or large deployment concurrency. The work delivers an experimental benchmark and scripts/pipeline implied by the implementation, but no public software artifact, dataset, trained model release, or deployable service is stated. Strengths: - Evaluates multiple forecasting paradigms under a common rolling-window protocol rather than comparing a single new model against weak baselines. - Tests feature value explicitly across six nested-ish configurations and shows that temperature, not extensive hand engineering, supplies most of the measured weather benefit. - Uses five independent operational networks and reports per-network results; Chronos-2's lead persists across all five rather than arising from one favorable series. - Confronts two practical data issues—missing-value reconstruction and uncertainty calibration—instead of silently assuming clean data and reliable intervals. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that retrospective weather observations create an oracle setting and make reported errors a lower bound for deployment. They acknowledge that probabilistic outputs are default-setting exploratory results and that many neural models are overconfident. They note that the benchmark is not exhaustive, that newer foundation models such as Toto-2.0 are missing, that fine-tuning may overfit short histories, and that real weather-forecast error and sensitivity were not evaluated. They also discuss possible data leakage risks for proprietary TimeGPT and recommend operational-weather evaluation, calibration, and periodic rebenchmarking. These limitations are addressed directly and generally improve the paper's credibility, although some consequences are still understated in the headline operational recommendations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The evaluation does not use weather forecasts, which is the main deployment-time input and could materially change both model rankings and the relative value of weather features. - The dataset is too short and seasonally narrow to support conclusions about year-round Finnish operation, unusual cold events, summer behavior, network changes, or robustness to distribution shift. - The paper reports statistical significance without presenting tests, uncertainty estimates, seeds, or per-window distributions, so the reliability of close rankings and percentage improvements cannot be assessed. - Selecting the best feature configuration for each model and horizon from the same benchmark risks optimistic model/configuration selection unless a separate validation protocol is used. - The full-series MASE normalization uses target observations beyond individual training cutoffs and makes the seasonal-naïve reference differ from the nominal MASE=1 interpretation; a strictly training-only scale or an explicitly relative out-of-sample metric would be cleaner. - The operational conclusion is based on point MASE rather than asymmetric generation costs, peak errors, ramp errors, reserve-market value, or closed-loop dispatch outcomes. - The foundation-model comparison lacks the newest strong baselines and cannot exclude pretraining contamination for TimeGPT; Chronos-2's strong result is therefore a time-stamped benchmark finding rather than evidence of durable superiority. - The paper does not report complete RMSE, sMAPE, CRPS, Winkler-score, model-memory, or per-window results in the extracted headline results, limiting independent assessment of tradeoffs beyond average MASE. Bottom Line: This is a useful applied benchmark showing that Chronos-2 is a strong candidate for Finnish heat-demand forecasting under retrospective weather inputs, but its practical recommendation is premature until evaluated with real weather forecasts, statistically supported uncertainty estimates, broader seasonal data, current foundation-model baselines, and operational cost metrics.

MissDiag: Diagnostic Evaluation of Incomplete-Knowledge Robustness in KGQA and KG-RAG

H Wang, H Dong, L Liu, C Ren · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MissDiag, a paired evaluation framework that measures incomplete-knowledge robustness through typed evidence-removal interventions and degradation profiles for KGQA and KG-RAG systems. - Why it's important: Aggregate performance drops cannot distinguish whether failures result from losing answer-supporting evidence, system behavior, or answer-matching artifacts, limiting the reliability of robustness claims. - How it does it: It holds the question, gold answer, source entities, and node inventory fixed while removing support edges using random, source-context, relation-level, or answer-adjacent operators at controlled severity levels. - The good: Across 12 systems and 1,050 paired development examples, answer-adjacent removal consistently caused the largest degradation, ranging from 10.3 to 21.3 F1 points, while source-context removal was sometimes neutral or beneficial. - The missing: The study uses one benchmark's development split and synthetic edge-removal operators, without reported error bars, multiple-seed variability, statistical tests, or experiments showing that the intervention types correspond to naturally occurring KG incompleteness. - Read it or not: Researchers evaluating KGQA, KG-RAG, or structured-reasoning robustness should read it for the diagnostic protocol, but practitioners seeking a deployed robustness solution will find an evaluation framework rather than a system that improves answers.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Novelty (78) and Non-Obviousness (75) are the strongest dimensions because the paired typed-degradation formulation exposes failure structure that scalar robustness scores conceal. Rigor (58), Completeness (55), and Resilience (52) are pulled down by reliance on one development split, synthetic interventions without ecological validation, absent uncertainty and significance analysis, no released code, and no evidence that the diagnostic profiles predict real deployment failures; Impact (35) is limited because the work diagnoses systems rather than improving or releasing one.
empirical Novelty 78 Rigor 58 Non-Obv 75 Completeness 55 Resilience 52 Impact 35
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: KGQA and KG-RAG systems depend on local graph evidence, yet real knowledge graphs are sparse, outdated, and unevenly populated. Existing incomplete-knowledge evaluations generally remove or corrupt evidence and report a single change in answer quality. That measurement does not identify whether the degradation comes from the structural type of evidence removed, the system's inability to exploit retained evidence, changes in candidate construction or search space, or the answer-matching metric. The problem affects researchers and developers assessing factual grounding, structured reasoning, and reliability in knowledge-graph question answering and graph-grounded generation. The paper targets the attribution gap between observing a score change and explaining its cause; it does not attempt to improve the underlying QA systems. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat robustness as a typed degradation profile rather than a scalar property. By comparing each system on the same question-answer instance with complete support and with equal-budget removals targeted at different graph structures, MissDiag makes evidence type an explicit experimental factor. The most consequential comparison is between source-context removal and answer-adjacent removal: the former tests source-side contextual evidence, whereas the latter targets edges incident to or within one hop of aligned answer entities. Methodology: Each instance is represented as a question, gold answer set, and local support graph, with source entities and graph-aligned answer entities identified when possible. The graph may contain original support edges and deterministic source-anchored context edges. For severity \(\alpha\), the nominal removal budget is approximately \(\alpha |E|\), bounded to leave at least one edge; each operator selects and orders candidate edges, then removes the first edges within the shared budget. Random missingness uniformly permutes all edges; source-context missingness removes edges incident to source entities but not answer entities, ordered by source depth; relation-level missingness removes relation-type blocks ordered by frequency; and answer-adjacent missingness removes edges with endpoint distance at most one from aligned answer nodes, ordered by answer distance. The same system then processes complete and incomplete graphs, and paired degradation is computed as complete-support macro set-level F1 minus incomplete-support F1, with negative values indicating improvement. The key design decisions—paired fixed-input comparison, a shared severity budget, and explicit metric indexing—are sensible and directly support causal attribution, although the paper does not empirically validate that the operators isolate only the intended mechanisms. Graph distances are computed on the undirected projection, which simplifies structural targeting but can ignore relation direction and query semantics. Trained models are trained only on complete-support data and reused without retraining; LLM-based methods serialize retained triples into prompts and use deterministic greedy decoding with fixed budgets. Key Results: On 1,050 KGQAGen-10k development examples feasible for all four operators at severity \(\alpha=0.3\), answer-adjacent degradation was largest for every evaluated system: ReaRev 11.9, NuTrea 12.2, NSM 12.1, MindMap 12.7, StructGPT 13.8, KG-GPT 10.3, ToG 11.4, PoG 11.6, GoG 19.8, Qwen2.5-7B 21.3, Qwen2.5-14B 17.0, Llama-3.1-8B 15.8, and Mistral-7B 13.3 F1 points. Complete-support F1 ranged from 45.7 for KG-GPT to 90.0 for Qwen2.5-14B. Source-context removal produced small or negative changes for many systems, including -24.1 for NSM, -9.9 for NuTrea, and -1.2 for ReaRev, whereas random and relation-level removal generally produced intermediate degradation. For Qwen2.5-7B, degradation at severities 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5 was approximately 5.5, 11.1, and 19.0 for random removal and 14.0, 21.3, and 36.0 for answer-adjacent removal; for Llama-3.1-8B, the corresponding curves were approximately 2.5, 6.1, and 11.0 versus 10.0, 15.8, and 30.5. Exact versus semantic F1 changed magnitudes modestly but preserved the answer-adjacent ordering. In structural slices averaged over four direct LLMs, the answer-adjacent-minus-random degradation gap was 19.9 points for multi-answer questions versus 7.6 for single-answer questions, and 14.2 for small-support graphs versus 4.5 for large-support graphs. The systems and baselines span older trained KGQA models, graph-prompting methods, KG agents, and contemporary open-weight LLMs, but the evaluation remains at standard benchmark scale rather than deployment or stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new contribution is the formulation and implementation of incomplete-knowledge robustness as typed, paired diagnostic attribution; the evaluated systems themselves combine existing KGQA, prompting, agent, and LLM techniques, and the empirical finding is that answer-local evidence loss consistently dominates several other synthetic removal conditions while source-context loss can improve scores. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paired fixed-input protocol, deterministic non-random ordering, fixed decoding budgets, pinned official implementations for trained models, and shared Qwen2.5-7B backbone for graph-prompting and agent systems improve internal comparability. However, the paper reports no confidence intervals, standard deviations, multiple independent random seeds, significance tests, or per-instance uncertainty. Random missingness uses a fixed seed, but sensitivity to alternative random realizations is not evaluated. No ablation isolates the effects of the shared budget, distance definition, candidate ordering, context-edge construction, or feasibility filtering. The primary evaluation uses only the KGQAGen-10k development split and one benchmark; the paper does not report results on LC-QuAD, GrailQA, KQA Pro, or naturally incomplete real-world graphs. Semantic F1 is evaluated only for direct LLM baselines. Code is not currently released; the authors state that it will be released after the review process, and no repository or URL is provided. The design controls many confounds within an instance, but synthetic interventions and exclusion of infeasible instances may affect external validity and comparability. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The evaluation can run on commercially available hardware in principle, but the reported experiments used NVIDIA GH200 GPUs and the computational cost of evaluating 12 systems across multiple interventions is not quantified. Efficient: MissDiag multiplies inference by complete and several incomplete conditions, so it is more expensive than ordinary single-condition evaluation; no runtime, memory, or cost comparison is reported. Effective: The evidence supports the narrower claim that typed removals reveal different score responses, but it does not establish improved robustness, better answers, or better correlation with failures in naturally incomplete graphs. Scalable: The study tests 1,050 benchmark instances and severity levels up to 0.5, not 10×–100× larger graphs, datasets, model sizes, or production retrieval workloads; scalability is not evaluated. The work delivers a methodological evaluation framework, with code promised but not yet released, rather than a released library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or deployed service. Strengths: - The paired protocol cleanly holds the question, gold answer, and system fixed, making differences across removal types more interpretable than unrelated complete/incomplete benchmark comparisons. - The shared removal budget provides a quantity-matched comparison among structurally different interventions, reducing the obvious confound that one condition simply removes more evidence. - The framework reveals behavior that aggregate scores would hide: source-context removal can improve trained KGQA performance, while answer-adjacent removal harms every evaluated system and is especially damaging for multi-answer and small-support cases. - The study examines system families with substantially different mechanisms—trained graph reasoners, prompting methods, graph agents, and direct LLMs—and checks severity and metric sensitivity rather than reporting only one table. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Not stated. The provided paper does not include a dedicated limitations section or explicitly discuss threats from synthetic missingness, single-benchmark evaluation, feasibility filtering, lack of uncertainty estimates, graph-alignment assumptions, or the fact that semantic-metric analysis is restricted to direct LLM baselines. It does state that code will be released after the review process and notes that operators can be infeasible when required source or answer alignments are unavailable. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The central missing validation is ecological: the paper does not show that random, source-context, relation-level, and answer-adjacent removals model the distributions or causal failure modes of real KG incompleteness. Operator definitions are not independent—source and answer neighborhoods can overlap structurally, relation-level removal can preferentially remove frequent or important relations, and undirected distance can label edges as answer-adjacent despite their directed role in a query. The fixed budget does not guarantee equal semantic difficulty or equal impact on reachable answer paths across instances. Results rely on one benchmark's development split, with no held-out test or cross-dataset replication, and feasibility-based exclusion could bias the evaluated population. The direct LLM baselines may answer from parametric memory despite graph restriction, but this leakage or no-evidence behavior is not measured. The headline claims lack uncertainty estimates and formal tests, and severity results are shown for only two representative LLMs. Finally, the framework diagnoses score changes but does not demonstrate that its profiles predict real deployment failures, improve system selection, or lead to actionable interventions. Bottom Line: This is a useful evaluation formulation and a credible first diagnostic study for KGQA robustness, worth reading for researchers designing structured-evidence stress tests, but its novelty and practical value remain limited until it validates the operators on multiple datasets, natural missingness patterns, and statistically supported deployment-relevant outcomes.

SplitScaling: Adaptive Scaling for Disaggregated LLM Serving Against Traffic Bursts via DRL

W Xiao, X Huang, W Shi, B Zhao · ijcai-preprints.s3.us-west-1.amazonaws.com · inference optimize llm faster inference throughput - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SplitScaling, a DRL-based autoscaling framework that independently adjusts Prefill and Decode instance pools in disaggregated LLM serving and reschedules queued tasks when capacity becomes available. - Why it's important: Bursty request rates and changing prompt-to-generation ratios can leave one PD pool overloaded while the other is idle, increasing GPU cost and causing tail-latency SLO violations. - How it does it: A Soft Actor-Critic controller observes traffic, queue, workload, and pool-pressure features, selects continuous scale-out/scale-in magnitudes for the two pools, and uses a global atomic queue to avoid head-of-line blocking during scaling delays. - The good: In a Splitwise-based simulator using BurstGPT traces, it reduces average instance count to 22.44 versus 30.00 for the optimized static configuration and 31.28 for HeteroScale, while reporting P99 TTFT slowdowns of 1.94 versus 2.43 and 8.59. - The missing: The evaluation lacks real-cluster deployment, hardware measurements, multiple workload families and seeds, and ablations isolating the DRL controller from the global-queue rescheduling mechanism. - Read it or not: Read it if you study LLM-serving control planes or RL-based autoscaling; skip it as evidence for production readiness because all primary results come from a simulator and the paper does not quantify scaling churn or model-loading overhead.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. The phase-specific autoscaling formulation and global-queue mechanism provide meaningful novelty (72) and non-obviousness (70), but the underlying SAC control and queueing ingredients are largely established. Rigor (55), Completeness (58), and Resilience (52) are pulled down by simulator-only evidence, narrow traces, absent hardware validation, no DRL-versus-simple-controller ablation, and unsupported production-level guarantees. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: The work addresses cluster-level resource provisioning for disaggregated Prefill-Decode LLM inference services. Production operators face simultaneous burstiness in request arrivals and in the ratio of prompt tokens to generated response tokens: prompt-heavy periods stress compute-bound Prefill pools, while generation-heavy periods stress memory- and bandwidth-bound Decode pools. Fixed Prefill/Decode ratios waste resources or create bottlenecks, CPU- and memory-based HPA signals do not reliably identify LLM phase-specific saturation, and rigid coordinated-scaling policies such as HeteroScale can misallocate capacity. Scaling latency creates a second problem: tasks already trapped in overloaded local queues may continue to violate SLOs even after new instances start. The paper targets lower resource cost and queueing latency while satisfying TTFT, TBT, and end-to-end latency SLOs. Key Idea: The central insight is to combine decoupled control-plane actions for Prefill and Decode with a global queue that delays joint allocation until both sides are available, allowing queued work to be rebound immediately to newly started or newly released instances. The DRL component is a learned policy for mapping phase-specific pressure and workload dynamics to independent pool sizes; the global-queue rescheduling mechanism, rather than DRL alone, addresses the scaling-lag and head-of-line-blocking failure mode. Methodology: The system has a global-queue Atomic Scheduler, a DRL Scaling Controller, and a Scaling Manager. Incoming requests enter the scheduler, which jointly checks suitable Prefill and Decode capacity and leaves a task pending if either side is unavailable; streamed KV-cache transfer then connects the selected Prefill and Decode instances. At fixed intervals, the controller observes request rate, request-rate change, temporal information, scheduler queue length, allocation-rejection status, active Prefill and Decode counts, Prefill backlog, token lengths, and token arrival intensity. A Soft Actor-Critic policy emits a two-dimensional continuous action \(a_t=[\alpha_{p,t},\alpha_{d,t}]\), with each value in [-1,1] mapped to discrete pool scale-out or scale-in operations. The reward combines SLO utility and penalties for TTFT/TBT violations, an all-SLO bonus, and a cost term proportional to active instances: \(R=w_s(\text{latency utilities}+\mathbf{1}_{all}B)-w_c(n_p+n_t)\). The manager models instance startup delay, registers ready instances with the scheduler, and uses connection draining for scale-in. Critical design choices are the two-dimensional decoupled action space, the global queue with immediate rescheduling, and the multi-objective reward; the paper motivates each qualitatively but provides limited quantitative justification for action discretization, observation intervals, reward weights, or the policy architecture. Key Results: Evaluation uses a high-fidelity discrete-event simulator based on Splitwise and replays BurstGPT traces from Microsoft Azure OpenAI workloads, preserving timestamps and input/output token lengths. Against an exhaustive-search Optimal Static Ratio and HeteroScale, the extreme-burst experiment reports 22.44 average instances for SplitScaling, comprising 19.79 Prefill and 2.65 Decode, versus 30.00 (23+7) for Static and 31.28 (20.27+11.01) for HeteroScale. The corresponding P99 TTFT slowdown is 1.94 for SplitScaling, 2.43 for Static, and 8.59 for HeteroScale; average queue wait is 14.20 ms, 17.15 ms, and 96.38 ms; and average queued request tokens are 60.05, 202.36, and 2,097.46. The paper summarizes these as cost reductions of 25.2% versus Static and 28.3% versus HeteroScale, with queue-wait reductions of 17.2% and 85.2%. On an unseen temporal trace, the trained policy uses 20.27 average instances versus 26.00 for Static and 28.87 for HeteroScale, and obtains P99 TTFT slowdowns of 1.25, 1.49, and 29.59, respectively; average queued tokens are 2.14, 55.73, and 12,672.74. Training curves show a selected learning rate of \(7\times10^{-4}\), and feature-removal experiments show lower or less stable reward for most ablations, but numerical variance, confidence intervals, seed counts, and statistical tests are not reported. The experiments are simulator-scale rather than a physical-cluster stress test, and the paper does not state model size, GPU type, network configuration, trace duration, or absolute request throughput. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper combines SAC-based independent Prefill/Decode autoscaling with global-queue rescheduling for bursty disaggregated LLM serving, while the underlying PD architecture, SAC algorithm, queueing concepts, and many system components are established techniques applied to this control problem. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper reports feature ablations, learning-rate sensitivity, reward-weight sensitivity, an exhaustive static-baseline search, an extreme-burst test, and a temporal zero-shot trace test. However, it does not ablate the rescheduling mechanism separately, compare SAC against simpler controllers such as PID, MPC, threshold rules, or a non-learning policy under matched tuning, report multiple random seeds or error bars, or quantify policy-training variability. The strongest baseline, HeteroScale, is described as a recent heuristic method, while HPA and other autoscaling approaches are discussed but not evaluated. The work uses a simulator derived from Splitwise rather than a deployed serving system, and the paper does not establish simulator fidelity against hardware measurements. Code is stated to be publicly available at https://github.com/Onlytonight/SplitScaling; data availability, trained policy weights, exact simulator configuration, and full hyperparameter details are not stated. The optimized static baseline may be favorable to the proposed method for changing workloads only if its single configuration is evaluated across the same trace, but the paper does not provide enough protocol detail to assess all tuning and trace-splitting choices. The reported generalization result uses one training trace and one unseen temporal trace, which is insufficient to establish broad distributional robustness. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile, with a proposed systems architecture evaluated only in simulation. Practical: The controller and queueing design could in principle run on commercially available GPU and virtual-machine infrastructure, but the paper provides no physical deployment or end-to-end integration measurements. Efficient: DRL inference is claimed to operate at microsecond scale and scaling occurs at minute-level intervals, but the paper does not measure controller overhead, model-loading cost, network cost, or the cost of maintaining excess warm instances relative to alternatives. Effective: The simulator evidence shows lower instance counts, queueing, and P99 TTFT slowdown on two BurstGPT-derived traces, but it establishes effectiveness primarily for simulated Splitwise behavior and proxy SLO metrics rather than production service quality. Scalable: The paper imposes hard minimum and maximum node limits but does not test 10x–100x larger clusters, higher request rates, larger models, multiple tenants, control-plane failures, or concurrent scaling events. The work delivers a source-code artifact for the simulator/framework, but no validated production service, library interface, trained model release, or hardware benchmark is reported. Strengths: - It identifies a concrete failure mode in PD serving—phase imbalance combined with scaling lag—and addresses both resource allocation and transition-time queue placement rather than treating autoscaling as a static ratio-selection problem. - The independent Prefill and Decode actions match the architectural asymmetry between compute-bound prompt processing and memory-bound generation, making the control formulation more appropriate than a single aggregate utilization signal. - The global queue and connection-draining design exposes operational details often omitted in autoscaling proposals, including how to use newly ready capacity and avoid abrupt scale-in interruption. - The evaluation uses timestamped, variable-length production-derived traces and includes a held-out temporal workload, with large reported gaps over HeteroScale in the tested simulator scenarios. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly identify resource thrashing as an unresolved problem: frequent scaling switches can cause model-reloading overhead and redundant energy consumption. They state that future work will add stabilization mechanisms. They also describe hard node limits, boot-up delay modeling, and multi-replica scheduler redundancy, but these are design claims rather than independently evaluated limitations or resilience results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not isolate the value of DRL from the Atomic Scheduler/rescheduling mechanism, so the source of the reported gains remains unclear. It omits physical-cluster experiments and therefore does not validate simulator assumptions about GPU service rates, KV-cache transfer, startup time, model loading, VM availability, or network contention. It does not report scale-out frequency, time spent in warm-up, resource thrashing, energy, or total cost including cold-start overhead, despite acknowledging thrashing as important. Evaluation covers only BurstGPT-derived traces and apparently two temporal segments; there is no cross-model, cross-hardware, multi-tenant, adversarial-burst, long-horizon, or failure-injection evaluation. The paper gives no random-seed variability, confidence intervals, statistical tests, detailed SAC architecture, control interval, action-to-instance mapping, SLO violation rate distribution, or exact simulator parameters. Claims such as “strictly guaranteeing” SLOs and “zero service interruption” are not supported by formal guarantees or hardware fault tests. Baseline coverage is narrow: HPA and other contemporary autoscalers are not measured, and the static baseline's offline oracle tuning may not represent an online deployable competitor. Bottom Line: The paper offers a useful systems-control formulation and a plausible queue-rescheduling design for bursty PD serving, but its evidence is not strong enough to support production or broad novelty claims until component-level ablations and real-cluster, multi-trace evaluation quantify cold-start cost, scaling churn, and simulator-to-hardware validity.

Developing a System Dynamics Framework for Sustained Digital Transformation

Q Battle · stars.library.ucf.edu · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper develops the Digital Transformation Sustainability Framework (DTSF), an evidence-grounded system-dynamics framework comprising an integrated causal-loop diagram, a six-stock model, and a three-scenario simulation of sustained, eroding, and governance-interrupted digital transformation. - Why it's important: Organizations invest heavily in digital transformation but often fail to sustain adoption, capability development, learning, and leadership support long enough to realize value. - How it does it: It synthesizes a PRISMA-guided review, twelve case studies, causal-loop modeling, expert review, and normalized stock-and-flow simulation around reinforcing and balancing feedback loops. - The good: The framework makes a useful systems-level distinction between an R1 acceleration loop and a B9 erosion pathway, with simulation showing adoption declining before capability and leadership commitment under adverse conditions. - The missing: The quantitative model uses illustrative, non-calibrated parameters and does not provide sensitivity analysis, longitudinal validation, formal measurement instruments, or predictive evidence. - Read it or not: Read it for a structured conceptual synthesis of digital-transformation dynamics and system-dynamics modeling; skip it if you need validated causal estimates, generalizable intervention effects, or deployment-ready decision support.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the organizational problem of sustaining enterprise-wide digital transformation across technology, data, strategy, structure, workforce capability, culture, and learning. Organizations pursuing AI, cloud, analytics, platform, and enterprise modernization initiatives face delayed value realization, legacy-system constraints, fragmented governance, capability gaps, employee resistance, technology overload, and uneven adoption. The claimed gap in prior work is that digital-transformation mechanisms are usually studied as isolated factors or through static and sequential change-management frameworks, with limited modeling of how they interact, accumulate, and erode over time. The relevant users are organizational leaders, transformation offices, change managers, and researchers in digital transformation, management, information systems, and engineering management. Key Idea: The central insight is that digital transformation follows competing feedback trajectories rather than a fixed sequence of implementation stages. In the reinforcing R1 trajectory, leadership commitment supports capability development, capability enables adoption, adoption produces organizational learning, learning builds dynamic capabilities, and dynamic capabilities renew leadership commitment. In the balancing B9 trajectory, delayed value realization weakens sustainability and learning, which reduces dynamic capabilities, leadership commitment, capability development, and adoption, further delaying value. This is a systems-dynamics reframing of familiar organizational factors; the main potentially distinctive elements are their integration into a cross-domain feedback structure and the treatment of dynamic capabilities, adoption, learning, and leadership as accumulating or depleting stocks. Methodology: The six-phase design begins with a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review across Web of Science, ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus. From 4,532 records, the authors report 112 included peer-reviewed studies and 771 coded mechanisms, organized into six domains: leadership and capability development; strategic alignment and governance; organizational structure and dynamic capabilities; cultural and behavioral dynamics; technology and data integration; and enterprise-wide learning systems. Phase 2 grounds the review in twelve cases: seven published cases, two artifact-based institutional cases, and three interview-based institutional cases. Hybrid deductive-inductive coding reduces the evidence to 20 variables using cross-source support, causal directionality, and feedback-loop participation. Phase 3 constructs fishbone diagrams, six domain-level causal-loop diagrams, and an integrated CLD containing eight reinforcing loops, ten balancing loops or links, and nine cross-domain links. Phase 4 uses structured review by three practitioners from healthcare, higher education, and supply-chain/logistics contexts to assess face validity, structural validity, boundary adequacy, and behavioral plausibility. Phase 5 translates the CLD into six normalized stocks—Digital Leadership Commitment, Transformation Capability, Adoption and Engagement, Organizational Learning, Dynamic Capabilities, and Transformation Sustainability—with twelve flows and four exogenous auxiliary variables. Stock dynamics use gap-closing inflows and governance-dampened outflows, with Euler integration at a 0.25-year time step over ten years. Phase 6 compares the framework with Kotter, Lewin, McKinsey 7-S, and ADKAR. Critical design decisions include collapsing several CLD constructs into Governance Effectiveness and Value Realization auxiliaries, explicitly modeling only selected loops in the stock-and-flow equations, and assigning illustrative 0–1 parameters from case narratives and system-dynamics conventions rather than observed time series. These decisions improve parsimony but are only partially justified empirically and materially limit causal interpretation. Key Results: The literature review reports 64% of coded mechanisms as enabling, 30% as constraining, 4% as moderating, and 1% as context-specific. It classifies 69% as digital-transformation-specific, 27% as hybrid, and approximately 3% as traditional, although another passage describes 96% as DT-specific or hybrid; the discrepancy is not resolved. Capability development appeared in 14 of 112 studies, leadership commitment in 11, structural change in 8, data assetization and visibility in 7, governance in 6, and behavioral resistance or hindrance appraisal in 6. Across the twelve cases, data integration appeared in 10 cases, governance in 8, data assetization in 8, strategic alignment in 9, and capability development in 6 according to the presence matrix. In the normalized Scenario 1 acceleration simulation, Transformation Sustainability rises from 0.550 to 0.632 over ten years, Organizational Learning from 0.600 to 0.771, and Transformation Capability from 0.700 to 0.730; Adoption and Engagement nevertheless declines from 0.700 to 0.627 and Dynamic Capabilities from 0.700 to 0.657, an internally important tension that weakens the paper's description of uniformly sustained momentum. In Scenario 2, Adoption and Engagement falls from 0.300 to approximately 0.001 by Year 3, Transformation Capability reaches 0 by Year 3, Digital Leadership Commitment falls from 0.450 to 0.006 by Year 4, and Transformation Sustainability falls from 0.200 to 0.010 by Year 2 and remains at its floor. In Scenario 3, higher governance and value-signal parameters raise Digital Leadership Commitment from 0.450 to 0.577 and Organizational Learning from 0.300 to 0.320, but Adoption and Engagement falls to 0.025, Transformation Capability to 0.085, and Dynamic Capabilities to 0.148; Transformation Sustainability remains flat at 0.250. The results therefore show that governance can preserve commitment and learning under the chosen parameters but cannot independently restore adoption, capability, or dynamic-capability growth. The baselines are conceptual comparisons with established change frameworks rather than empirical or quantitative model baselines, and no strong predictive benchmark is used. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The work's genuine contribution is an integrated, evidence-traceable system-dynamics formulation of digital-transformation sustainability that links leadership, capability, adoption, learning, governance, and delayed value across feedback loops; most individual mechanisms, case observations, system-dynamics techniques, and change-management critiques are established ideas recombined for this setting rather than fundamentally new theory or algorithmic methodology. Rigor & Reproducibility: The study provides a transparent search flow, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, a coding scheme, case-selection criteria, variable-downselection rules, equations, parameter tables, scenario settings, and a ten-year simulation trace. The SLR uses a substantial corpus, and the case analysis combines published cases, artifacts, and interviews. However, the paper reports no inter-coder reliability, independent replication of the coding, effect sizes, uncertainty intervals, multiple simulation seeds, statistical tests, formal sensitivity analysis, extreme-condition testing, historical-data comparison, or parameter-identification procedure. The model's validation is primarily structural and face-validity assessment, not dynamic or predictive validation. The simulation parameters are deliberately selected to produce qualitatively anticipated trajectories, so reproduction of the R1 and B9 patterns is not independent evidence that the causal structure is correct; it is partly a test that the equations implement the authors' assumptions. Several CLD loops are not modeled endogenously but are collapsed into scenario-level auxiliaries, particularly structural agility, strategic coherence, legacy constraints, technology overload, and data-to-value dynamics. This creates substantial room for parameterization to determine the result. The document mentions Insight Maker but does not state that a model file, code repository, data, or trained artifact is publicly released, and no URL for reproducible simulation assets is provided. There are also internal reporting inconsistencies: the study alternately describes expert validation as involving three experts and, in the proof-of-concept limitations, as relying on a single subject-matter expert; the classification percentages do not align across sections; and the narrative claims Scenario 1 stocks generally increase even though Adoption and Engagement and Dynamic Capabilities decline. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL profile, because the work combines case evidence and a simulation rather than presenting proofs or a deployed infrastructure system. Practical: The model can run on commercially available hardware through the web-based Insight Maker platform, although applying it requires system-dynamics expertise and organization-specific measurement of its abstract stocks and auxiliaries. Efficient: The six-stock, twelve-flow model is computationally trivial relative to enterprise analytics or optimization systems, but its organizational data-collection and calibration cost is not evaluated. Effective: The evidence supports a plausible explanatory vocabulary and identifies simulated trajectory patterns, but it does not establish that the framework improves transformation outcomes or that adoption decline is a validated early-warning indicator. Scalable: The paper claims transferability across sectors but tests neither 10×–100× organizational scale nor larger model dimensions; external market, regulatory, funding, leadership-turnover, ecosystem, and organizational-restructuring effects are excluded or treated as fixed conditions. The work delivers a conceptual stock-and-flow model and causal diagrams in paper form; a reusable Insight Maker model, diagnostic instrument, dataset, or decision-support tool is not stated as released. Strengths: - The study integrates literature synthesis, case evidence, causal mapping, expert review, and simulation into a traceable modeling pipeline rather than presenting an unsupported conceptual framework. - The R1 acceleration and B9 erosion structures provide a readable systems explanation for why transformation can compound positively or deteriorate gradually, especially through delayed value realization and adoption decline. - The framework treats adoption, learning, capability, and leadership as dynamic accumulations with inflows and outflows, which is more informative for temporal reasoning than a static list of success factors. - The inclusion of hindrance appraisal, technology overload, data assetization, legacy constraints, and knowledge loss broadens the analysis beyond technology deployment and generic leadership prescriptions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the parameters are illustrative rather than calibrated to longitudinal organizational data, that the four auxiliary variables lack validated measurement instruments, and that the framework is not predictive. They acknowledge the small expert-validation base, the need for a larger Delphi-style panel, the exclusion of external factors such as leadership turnover, policy changes, funding shifts, and market conditions, and the specialist expertise required to use stock-and-flow models. They also identify the need for longitudinal calibration, formal sensitivity analysis, predictive scenario testing, and a practitioner-oriented diagnostic instrument. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest gap is that the quantitative results are generated by hand-selected scenario values that encode the intended case narratives, so the simulation demonstrates model behavior but does not independently validate the proposed mechanisms. The model omits a direct endogenous representation of several constructs central to the qualitative argument: data integration and data-to-value dynamics, strategic coherence, structural agility, legacy systems, technology overload, and employee value perception. Treating these factors as fixed auxiliaries prevents the simulation from testing their claimed feedback relationships and makes Scenario 3's governance effect difficult to disentangle from the jointly changed parameters. The framework also lacks operational definitions and measurement models for normalized stocks such as Transformation Sustainability, Dynamic Capabilities, and Organizational Learning. The case evidence is heterogeneous and includes vendor or educational case materials, retrospective published narratives, artifacts, and interviews, but the paper does not establish source independence, coding reliability, negative-case analysis, or systematic comparison of successful and failed initiatives. The claim that adoption declines one to two years before leadership-level erosion is a practical early-warning result, but the model only produces that ordering under one illustrative parameterization and does not measure it in observed organizations. The review's search strategy restricts inclusion to English-language peer-reviewed journal articles while also using several recent and non-journal case sources for grounding, creating possible selection and source-quality asymmetries. Finally, the comparison with Kotter, Lewin, McKinsey 7-S, and ADKAR is a qualitative author-constructed mapping rather than a head-to-head evaluation of intervention outcomes. Bottom Line: This is a useful conceptual system-dynamics synthesis and a reasonable starting point for researchers or transformation offices, but its normalized simulation should not be treated as evidence of causal effects, early-warning performance, or cross-organization predictive validity until the model is measured, calibrated, sensitivity-tested, and externally validated.

InfinityEdit: Infinite Video Editing with a Lightweight Edit-Ignition Adapter (31 ▲ )

Yunze Tong, Mushui Liu, Canyu Zhao, Shiyi Zhang, Didi Zhu, Peng Zhang, Wanggui He, Jinlong Liu, Ying Chen, Hao Jiang, Pipei Huang, Bo Zheng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 24 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces InfinityEdit, a lightweight adapter that enables a frozen streaming video generator to apply successive natural-language edits while generating future video segments beyond the source clip. - Why it's important: Existing video editors rewrite fixed windows, so they do not support interactive editing of open-ended streams such as live game footage or ongoing shots. - How it does it: It injects history conditioning, causal temporal propagation, and edit-text cross-attention into each transformer layer, activates the adapter only at edit boundaries, and then continues with the frozen generator using a reset anchor and sliding history window. - The good: On a 200-video, three-round benchmark, it substantially improves VLM-judged edit faithfulness, preservation, and coherence, while maintaining nearly constant performance across rounds. - The missing: The paper does not report component ablations, training-set size or composition, statistical uncertainty, inference latency, adapter parameter count, or a controlled evaluation of truly unbounded edit sequences. - Read it or not: Researchers working on streaming video generation or interactive video editing should read it for the task formulation and inference design, but deployment-oriented readers should wait for stronger efficiency, reproducibility, and long-horizon evidence.
Why this rank
Scored using the systems profile, given the streaming-generation system and deployment-oriented inference design. Novelty (72) and Non-Obviousness (70) are relatively strong because the paper defines a meaningful forward-only sequential editing problem and an event-triggered ignition mechanism, but Rigor (55) and Completeness (58) are reduced by missing component ablations, uncertainty, training-set details, and unclear artifact contents. Resilience (55) and Impact (55) are limited by the three-round synthetic benchmark, qualitative long-horizon evidence, absent latency and memory measurements, and no real interactive deployment; weighted composite: 0.15*72 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*55 + 0.30*55 = 59.5, rounded to 60.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation Existing instruction-based video editors primarily perform in-place transformation: they preserve frame-level correspondence and produce an edited clip over the same finite temporal window. This does not define how an edit should affect frames that have not yet arrived in an open-ended stream. The target setting is interactive editing of live or continuously generated video, where a preceding segment and an edit request must produce a subsequent segment that both realizes the request and remains a coherent continuation. The central research gap is therefore the combination of source-grounded editing, forward temporal continuation without aligned target frames, and resistance to error accumulation under repeated edits. The paper identifies applications including live-game restyling and camera control over ongoing shots, but it does not evaluate a real deployed stream or user interaction loop. Key Idea The core insight is to treat each edit as an event that must be ignited once, rather than conditioning every future chunk on a persistent editing module. InfinityEdit applies a learned adapter to the first chunk after an instruction arrives; the frozen streaming backbone then propagates the edited state through subsequent chunks. History cross-attention anchors the new chunk to recent content, causal temporal self-attention propagates the change forward within the chunk, and edit cross-attention injects the instruction. A moving anchor frame and bounded sliding history are reset at each edit to prevent the backbone from reverting toward the original source. The individual mechanisms are familiar attention and autoregressive-generation techniques; the more distinctive contribution is their event-triggered composition for sequential, forward-only editing. Methodology The data pipeline samples source clips from UltraVideo, groups them by captioned entities, expands abstract edit types into detailed instructions with Gemini 3 Flash, and synthesizes future target segments with Wan2.2-I2V-A14B. For appearance edits, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 modifies the final source frame before image-to-video generation; camera and motion edits preserve that connection frame directly. Videos are resized and temporally clipped to match Helios-Distilled, then manually filtered by 20 labelers on instruction alignment, source-target consistency, rationality, and source visual quality using 1–4 ratings. The model freezes the 14B Helios-Distilled autoregressive video diffusion transformer and inserts trainable adapter blocks after every transformer layer. Each block leaves history tokens unchanged and applies three residual operations to current-chunk tokens: history cross-attention updates only the first L_a frames; framewise temporal causal self-attention allows information to move from earlier to later frames; and edit cross-attention conditions all current tokens on the instruction. The adapter is trained with a flow-matching objective, L = E[w(σ)||v_θ(z_σ,σ,c)−(ε−z_0)||²], using corrupted histories to reduce exposure bias, a Gaussian-mixture noise sampler aligned with inference noise levels, and a two-phase curriculum that shifts toward lower-noise detail refinement and upweights later frames. At inference, the first chunk of each edit round uses a single-stage Euler schedule and the adapter, while later chunks use the original pyramid scheduler and frozen backbone. The system adds a near-zero-noise step for detail completion, slides a constant-size history window, resets the anchor to the first frame of the newly edited chunk, and replaces the scene prompt with the current edit instruction. The paper gives plausible motivations for these decisions, but it does not isolate their causal contributions through ablations. Key Results The authors construct an OOD benchmark with 200 source videos from five entity categories, 15 edit types across entity transformation, stylization, camera movement, and motion transfer, and three sequential edit rounds per sample; each segment contains four chunks, for 12 generated chunks per sample. At 384×640 resolution and 16 fps, InfinityEdit obtains VBench scores of 0.7654 for camera motion, 0.9833 for motion smoothness, 0.9660 for temporal flickering, and 0.7400 for dynamic degree. Its camera-motion score exceeds the strongest listed baseline, Helios-Base at 0.5494, by 0.2160; motion smoothness is below Helios-Base's 0.9869 but above the other listed editing baselines; temporal flickering is slightly above Helios-Base's 0.9641 and below no listed method. On Gemini-3.5-Flash VLM judging, InfinityEdit scores 3.828/5 for edit faithfulness, 3.765 for visual quality, 3.815 for scene preservation, and 3.840 for cross-edit coherence, versus the strongest non-ours scores of 3.303, 3.093, 3.060, and 3.480 respectively. Across rounds, its edit-faithfulness scores are 3.860, 3.805, and 3.820 with standard deviation 0.023, while competing methods have standard deviations from 0.039 to 0.715. VBench aesthetic quality is visually reported as nearly flat for the method, whereas source-conditioned baselines decline by approximately 0.02–0.04 after the first round. A separate qualitative/long-video demonstration exceeds 1,000 frames and shows persistence of earlier edits, but it provides no quantitative scores, failure rates, or repeated-edit count beyond the three-round benchmark. The comparisons are useful but imperfect: two prompt-switching baselines do not receive the source video, in-place editors solve a different temporal task, and several cited baselines are recent preprints or systems whose exact implementation and tuning parity are not documented in the paper. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM, NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/ BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper formalizes sequential forward-only or “infinite” video editing, introduces a synthetic benchmark and data-construction pipeline for it, and proposes an event-triggered adapter-plus-anchor inference scheme; the attention modules, flow matching, history corruption, and sliding-window memory are standard ingredients, so the main novelty lies in their task-specific integration rather than a fundamentally new learning primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports comparisons on 200 held-out source videos and evaluates both automatic metrics and VLM judgments, including round-level stability and a 1,000-plus-frame qualitative stress case. However, no ablation separates the effects of the three attention modules, history corruption, mixture-Gaussian sampling, curriculum, low-noise step, anchor resetting, or adapter-only training. The paper gives no confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, inter-rater agreement, human-versus-VLM judge validation, judge prompts, or significance tests. It also does not state the training-set size, retained-triplet count after filtering, label-selection thresholds, adapter parameter count, training duration, or inference latency. The benchmark instructions are generated by Gemini and the targets are synthesized by large proprietary models, creating possible evaluator and data-generation bias; the claimed OOD status means source videos and instruction wording are disjoint from training, but the edit taxonomy is derived from prior instruction sets and may still overlap conceptually. A project page and GitHub URL are provided—https://yunzetong.github.io/InfinityEdit and https://github.com/YunzeTong/InfinityEdit—but the paper does not state what code, weights, data, benchmark, or scripts are released. The method is therefore only partially reproducible from the paper. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL and SYSTEMS — the paper trains and runs a video-generation system, although it does not present a production deployment. Practical: The system runs on NVIDIA H20 GPUs, which are commercially available, but evaluation and training use 32 GPUs and the 14B Helios-Distilled backbone, so single-device or consumer-hardware operation is not demonstrated. Efficient: The frozen-backbone adapter avoids full 14B fine-tuning and uses bounded history memory, but the paper reports neither adapter size nor latency, throughput, memory consumption, denoising-step counts, or cost relative to Helios, in-place editors, or prompt-switching alternatives. Effective: Evidence on the authors' 200-sample benchmark shows improved proxy metrics and VLM-judged faithfulness, preservation, and coherence, but it does not establish performance on real live streams, human editing workflows, reference-guided edits, or edits outside the four synthetic categories. Scalable: The system retains constant-size history and qualitatively reaches more than 1,000 frames, but the benchmark uses only three edit rounds and the paper does not measure 10×–100× longer sequences, many more edits, diverse edit orderings, or failure accumulation under adversarial instructions. The work delivers a claimed software artifact through the project page and GitHub link, plus a proposed benchmark and data pipeline; release contents and whether the dataset or trained model are downloadable are not stated. Strengths - It identifies a meaningful gap between finite-window video editing and forward continuation of an open-ended stream, with a task definition that makes temporal alignment and accumulation behavior explicit. - The “ignite then continue” inference design preserves the long-video prior of the frozen backbone while limiting edit-specific intervention to boundary chunks; this is a nontrivial systems choice that directly targets prompt-induced drift and edit suppression. - The evaluation measures several distinct requirements—camera control, temporal stability, edit faithfulness, preservation, coherence, and round-level variance—instead of reporting only a generic video-quality score. - The method achieves a large reported margin on VLM-judged preservation and coherence and remains stable across three edit rounds, while the long-video example extends beyond 1,000 frames rather than stopping at a single short clip. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the current system accepts only natural-language instructions and lacks image or video reference guidance. They also acknowledge that transitions at edit boundaries can be abrupt and identify smoother successive-edit transitions as future work. They do not explicitly acknowledge the limited number of evaluated edit rounds, dependence on synthetic data and VLM judging, absence of quantitative efficiency measurements, or lack of component ablations. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper calls the task “infinite” and claims unbounded editing, but the principal quantitative test contains only three rounds; the >1,000-frame result is qualitative and does not establish indefinite stability. - The central architectural and inference choices are not supported by ablations, so the paper cannot show whether the gains come from the three attention modules, the reset anchor, prompt replacement, history corruption, or simply additional edit conditioning. - The benchmark and training targets depend on Gemini-generated instructions, Wan-generated videos, Qwen-generated boundary frames, manual filtering, and Gemini-based judging; this creates correlated model bias and does not measure performance against human-authored edits or real video continuations. - Baseline comparability is incomplete: prompt-switching methods lack source-video input, in-place editors optimize a different objective, and the paper does not report implementation details, compute matching, or hyperparameter tuning for any baseline. - The study omits latency, throughput, memory, adapter size, training cost, and hardware-normalized comparisons despite positioning the adapter as lightweight and the application as streaming. - The reported automatic measures are limited proxies: Dynamic Degree is explicitly not an edit-fidelity metric, temporal flickering can reward overly static outputs, and the camera metric covers only camera-type edits. - The paper does not report per-edit-type performance, failure cases, instruction ambiguity, boundary-transition quality, human preference studies, or robustness to conflicting edits and edits that should selectively preserve different attributes. Bottom Line This is a useful task formulation and a credible initial system result for streaming video editing, but practitioners should treat the strong claims as benchmark-specific until longer-horizon, human-evaluated, ablated, and efficiency-matched experiments establish that the adapter remains effective beyond three synthetic edit rounds.

On-policy Distillation with Verifiable Reward (12 ▲ )

Wenze Lin, Jiale Zhao, Xitai Jiang, Songde Rao, Yining Li, Shenzhi Wang, Bingxiang He, Gao Huang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 26 Aug 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OPDVR, a ReLU-gated sampled-token on-policy distillation objective that conditions teacher guidance on verifier-identified trajectory correctness, and GRPD, its GRPO-style extension. - Why it's important: Reasoning-model post-training must combine sparse but task-aligned outcome rewards with dense token-level supervision without destabilizing optimization or tuning an additional loss-balancing coefficient. - How it does it: It treats the teacher–student token log-probability ratio as an implicit reward and zeroes updates whose sign conflicts with the binary verifier outcome or group-relative advantage. - The good: Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, OPDVR raises mean avg@16 accuracy from 47.8% to 49.1% in same-architecture distillation and from 20.9% to 22.8% in cross-architecture distillation relative to sampled-token OPD. - The missing: The evaluation lacks multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, compute comparisons, and direct comparisons with the recent OPD–RLVR integration methods cited in the paper. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM post-training or on-policy distillation and want a simple, reproducible gating baseline; skip it if you need evidence of broad task generality, large-model scaling, or superiority over the strongest contemporary RLVR hybrids.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. The verifier-conditioned ReLU gate is a clear but relatively incremental formulation, yielding Novelty (65) and Non-Obviousness (60), while Rigor (62) is limited by single-run results, absent uncertainty estimates, omitted contemporary OPD-RLVR comparisons, and no analysis of unbounded log-ratio rewards. Completeness (55) and Resilience (55) fall because the claims are restricted to mathematical reasoning yet are not tested under verifier noise, longer-trace credit assignment, or broader domains; Impact (58) reflects an available code artifact without released models or demonstrated efficiency gains.
