Problem & Motivation: The work addresses automatic translation of informal problem specifications into complete ASP programs for combinatorial reasoning and optimization. The affected users are researchers and engineers who use ASP but must currently inspect, execute, diagnose, and revise LLM-generated encodings manually. The central gap is that existing LLM–ASP systems mainly extract facts or use feed-forward translation pipelines, while general-purpose coding agents provide execution feedback without explicitly separating construction from semantic validation. ASP is especially difficult because small syntax errors, unsafe rules, incorrect aggregates, or mismatches with stable-model semantics can invalidate an otherwise plausible encoding; solver execution alone can expose some errors but does not establish that the encoding matches the natural-language specification. Key Idea: The core insight is to separate ASP program construction from specification-level validation while giving both agents access to a shared persistent program state. The Modeler performs edits and solver calls, whereas a fresh Validator invocation independently inspects and executes the candidate and converts observed or inferred defects into feedback for the next Modeler pass. The formal functional model—LLM-driven decisions over tools, memory, and environment state—is useful as an organizing abstraction, but the main algorithmic novelty lies in the role-specialized construct–validate loop rather than in a new ASP-solving technique. Methodology: ALM–ASP starts with a natural-language prompt and an empty persistent ASP program. The Modeler, initialized with a role prompt and long-term interaction memory, repeatedly chooses among add-rules, replace-rules, remove-rules, inspect, solve, or termination actions. The environment stores the program and invokes CLINGO under a specified computational budget, returning the current program, answer sets, or diagnostic errors. After the Modeler terminates an internal episode, the Validator receives the original prompt and the shared program, uses only inspect and solve, and returns either acceptance or textual feedback; feedback becomes the next Modeler input. The outer loop stops at Validator acceptance or after five refinement iterations, followed by lightweight removal of redundant or unused rules. The architecture is implemented using LangGraph for stateful orchestration and MCP for tool exposure. There is no learned objective or explicitly defined training loss; the system relies on stochastic LLM prompting at temperature 0, role prompts, deterministic CLINGO execution, and textual feedback. Critical design choices include persistent Modeler memory, Validator read-only access, and solver-backed tool interaction. The paper motivates these choices conceptually, but does not experimentally establish that each is necessary or optimal. Key Results: On the 10-instance CP–Bench Hard subset, ALM–ASP solved 10/10 instances versus 9/10 for CP–Agent in ASP mode. It used fewer tokens than CP–Agent on many cases—for example, 43.7k versus 156.0k on Guard App, 37.5k versus 161.2k on Add Corners, and 77.3k versus 408.3k on the 2023 Student Exercises contest problem—but often required more wall-clock time because of validation overhead; on Crossfig it used 603.3k tokens, 31 tool calls, and 3146.9 seconds versus CP–Agent's 220.6k tokens, 8 calls, and 1023.1 seconds. ALM–ASP converged in one refinement iteration on 9 of the 10 CP–Bench cases and needed two on Crossfig. In the LP/CP contest totals, it solved 20/50 instances in 2021 versus CP–Agent's 10/50, 40/50 in 2022 versus 38/50, and 10/25 in 2023 versus 15/25. Direct GPT-5 prompting solved 10/50, 30/50, and 5/25, respectively, while gpt-oss:120b solved 0/50, 0/50, and 5/25. ALM–ASP solved Buttons & Scissors and RoBeep!, which CP–Agent failed, but failed on Street Builder, which CP–Agent solved. The comparisons use GPT-5 for both agentic systems and direct prompting, with a local 120B open-weights model only evaluated for direct prompting. The CP–Bench Hard subset is small and deliberately selected from cases requiring many CP–Agent tool interactions, so the results do not estimate performance on the full benchmark. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper formalizes tool-using agents with persistent state and instantiates the abstraction as a Modeler–Validator ASP synthesis system, while the empirical contribution is evidence that a specialized ASP agent can improve success and token usage over a general ReAct-style agent in selected difficult cases; the underlying ingredients—LLM prompting, ReAct-style tool use, persistent execution, solver feedback, and iterative repair—are established techniques combined in an ASP-specific architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation includes a direct-prompting baseline, a general-purpose agent baseline, an open-weights model for direct prompting, CLINGO execution, token counts, tool calls, wall-clock time, and contest-scale tests. However, no ablations test the Validator versus a single agent, persistent versus reset Modeler memory, Validator memory policy, role prompts, five-iteration limit, solver budget, or postprocessing. Results use temperature 0 and do not report multiple seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The CP–Bench Hard subset is selected by CP–Agent's tool-interaction traces, creating a benchmark-selection risk and making the comparison asymmetric; direct prompting is excluded from that subset by construction. The paper does not report exact prompts, model API versions or decoding details beyond GPT-5 and temperature 0, computational hardware, CLINGO budgets per task, annotation procedures for semantic validation, or independent human verification protocols. No code, dataset, model weights, or repository URL is stated. The contest comparison is informative but not a controlled benchmark: human teams had different time limits across years, and the reported metric mixes problem-level success with instance counts in a way that requires careful interpretation. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper implements and runs an agentic system, although its evaluation is experimental rather than a production deployment. Practical: The prototype can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but it depends on access to GPT-5, LangGraph, MCP, and CLINGO, and the paper does not provide deployment requirements or an artifact. Efficient: It can reduce token consumption substantially on some tasks, such as 77.3k versus 408.3k on Student Exercises, but validation can increase runtime dramatically, reaching 3146.9 seconds and 603.3k tokens on Crossfig and approximately 877k tokens with 37 tool calls in a reported 2021 outlier. Effective: The reported evidence shows improved solution rates over CP–Agent on the 10-instance hard subset and in 2021–2022 contest totals, but not reliable semantic correctness independent of benchmark test outcomes or a human audit. Scalable: The largest reported evaluation is 100 contest instances in 2021, 100 in 2022, and 25 in 2023, with a maximum of five outer refinement iterations; behavior at 10×–100× more instances, larger programs, longer solver budgets, or more difficult specifications is not evaluated. The work delivers a prototype architecture and software system on paper; a publicly reusable library, CLI, or released implementation is not stated. Strengths: - The paper gives a precise functional decomposition of LLM reasoning, tool actions, persistent environment state, and memory, making the agent loop easier to compare with other tool-augmented systems than an informal prompt description would. - The Modeler–Validator separation is well matched to ASP: CLINGO can diagnose syntactic and grounding failures, while an independently prompted Validator can identify specification-level issues that successful execution alone cannot prove. - The evaluation goes beyond familiar toy encodings by including low-resource ASP tasks from three programming contests, and it documents both success and resource costs rather than reporting accuracy alone. - The failure cases reveal an important trade-off: the architecture can improve token efficiency and recover cases missed by CP–Agent, but the extra validation loop can substantially increase latency and cost. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the Validator does not guarantee correctness, that final encodings still require human verification, and that agentic loops do not eliminate ASP's difficulty. They acknowledge slow convergence and expensive retries, including an approximately 877k-token, 37-tool-call outlier, and emphasize that ALM–ASP does not aim to outperform all existing agentic systems. They attribute remaining performance limitations partly to ASP's low representation in LLM pretraining data and propose fine-tuning, controlled natural-language intermediates, and reusable ASP templates as future directions. They do not explicitly acknowledge the benchmark-selection bias, lack of ablations, lack of repeated trials, or incomplete reproducibility details. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The strongest unaddressed issue is causal attribution: the experiments do not show whether gains come from the second agent, ASP-specific prompts and tools, additional token budget, persistent memory, or simply more opportunities to retry. The CP–Bench Hard set is selected from CP–Agent traces, and the evaluation uses only 10 instances, so the reported 10/10 result may not generalize to the full benchmark or to independently sampled hard tasks. The paper does not compare against recent ASP-specific synthesis methods under the same GPT-5 and execution conditions, nor against simpler one-agent CLINGO-feedback loops with equal budgets. Validator acceptance is treated as a termination signal even though it is an LLM judgment; the paper does not measure false acceptance or false rejection rates through expert review. It also lacks per-task variance, cost-normalized success curves, explicit solver timeouts, hardware and API cost reporting, exact prompts, and released code. Finally, the conclusion attributes the Python–ASP gap primarily to training-data representation bias, but the experiments do not isolate pretraining exposure from language expressivity, prompt quality, solver interfaces, or task distribution. Bottom Line: The paper provides a useful ASP-specific agent architecture and credible initial evidence that role-separated solver-grounded refinement improves selected hard modeling tasks, but its novelty and practical conclusions remain limited until controlled ablations, unbiased evaluation, human semantic audits, and reproducible artifacts establish that the Validator—not merely extra interaction budget—drives the gains.

Problem & Motivation Smart-glasses research is fragmented across augmented reality, egocentric vision, multimodal models, wearable HCI, privacy, agentic tool use, and embodied intelligence. Existing work commonly evaluates recognition, question answering, memory, interaction, or action in isolation and often abstracts away camera placement, sensor dropout, latency distributions, battery and thermal limits, network failures, feedback bandwidth, privacy, bystanders, model drift, and action consequences. The paper addresses the resulting gap: there is no sufficiently unified way to determine which capability claim a particular glasses-based system can support under a specified hardware route, task, temporal horizon, participant structure, operating environment, risk level, and evidence base. The intended users include researchers and practitioners building consumer assistants, accessibility systems, industrial and healthcare tools, educational systems, spatial services, collaborative interfaces, and human-to-robot data pipelines. Key Idea The central idea is claim-conditioned capability: a smart-glasses capability is not a device or model attribute but a claim conditioned on task scope, hardware and runtime, input/output channels, temporal validity, state persistence, action authority, stakeholders, operating conditions, system version, and risk. This idea is operationalized through a closed-loop perspective in which first-person observations are transformed into contextual state, feedback, persistent memory, and optionally authorized digital or physical action. The L0–L5 framework then distinguishes recording and relay, reactive perception, contextual assistance, persistent state, governed action, and embodied coupling; L5 is treated as an orthogonal cross-embodiment extension rather than simply a higher wearer-facing capability level. Methodology This is a conceptual literature survey and framework paper rather than an algorithmic or experimental study. It formalizes a first-person observation stream containing egocentric visual observations, audio, motion/localization, spatial and interaction cues, explicit user interactions, and device/privacy state. A system mapping produces feedback, updated working/spatial/personal state, and optional actions under latency, energy, thermal, privacy, and social-cost constraints. The survey then synthesizes seven capabilities: first-person perception, multimodal context modeling, persistent spatial state, auditable personal memory, situated agentic action, embodied data interfaces, and cross-cutting deployment constraints. It groups hardware into eight axes—vision capture; audio sensing/output; spatial and motion sensing; near-eye feedback; hands-free control; computing/connectivity; data/reproducibility interfaces; and deployment/trust signals—and maps representative products into route-aware profiles. It organizes prior work into nine application scenes and proposes nine deployment dimensions: hardware/form factor, runtime/resources, perception/inference, persistent state/memory, feedback/intervention, external-system orchestration, reliability/recovery, privacy/security/governance, and developer interfaces/reproducibility. Critical design decisions include separating prerequisites from demonstrated capabilities, treating deployment constraints as cross-cutting rather than a final pipeline stage, and requiring stronger evidence as persistence, action authority, risk, or stakeholder count increases. These decisions are well-motivated conceptually, but the paper does not empirically validate their necessity, weighting, or consistency across reviewers. Key Results The paper reports no new experimental results, benchmark scores, ablations, statistical tests, user studies, hardware measurements, or end-to-end deployments. Its substantive outputs are qualitative and organizational: a formalism for smart-glasses data flow and constrained utility; eight hardware capability axes; seven foundational capabilities; the L0–L5 framework; a matrix covering representative commercial, developer, and research platforms; application-centered evidence maps across daily assistance, accessibility, industrial workflow, healthcare/caregiving, education, mobility safety, social collaboration, spatial intelligence, and embodied intelligence; and a standardized evaluation protocol with an evidence ladder from documentation and laboratory measurement through replay, fault injection, end-to-end studies, longitudinal deployment, and privacy/security audit. The paper characterizes camera/audio-first consumer glasses as generally supporting evidence for L2 contextual assistance, camera-and-display systems as possible entry points toward L3, true-AR/developer platforms as prerequisites for L4 research, and platforms such as Project Aria and Pupil Labs Neon as supporting L5 data or partial-L5 claims rather than wearer-facing autonomous action. These ratings are based on publicly documented evidence and are not experimentally verified in the paper. The cited baselines span strong recent datasets and systems such as Ego4D, Ego-Exo4D, HoloAssist, WearVQA, SuperGlasses, EgoSAT, EGOSTREAM, and IPIBench, but the survey does not quantitatively compare them or establish that they jointly cover complete smart-glasses deployment. Novelty Classification NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: The genuinely novel contribution is a proposed conceptual and evaluation framework that connects hardware profiles, compositional capabilities, application risk, and evidence conditions; the literature synthesis, product mapping, and recommended measurements mostly reorganize existing work rather than introduce a new dataset, algorithm, or experimentally established finding. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper is a preprint dated August 2026 (arXiv:2608.24877v1), and its conclusions should be treated as an unreviewed synthesis. It cites 215 references, distinguishes direct smart-glasses evidence from neighboring-domain proxies in many tables, and explicitly warns against interpreting product specifications, component benchmarks, or vendor demonstrations as evidence of deployment readiness. However, it does not state a systematic search strategy, databases searched, date cutoffs beyond the document date, screening procedure, inclusion/exclusion criteria for individual papers, quality assessment rubric, duplicate-resolution process, or inter-rater agreement. The product matrix uses public documentation and a qualitative star scale, but the rating procedure and independent verification are not reported; the parsed table also contains ambiguous star glyphs. There are no ablations, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or quantitative validation of the proposed L0–L5 boundaries. A project resource is linked at https://github.com/zhangzjn/awesome-smart-glasses, but the paper does not clearly state whether the taxonomy, product matrix, evaluation templates, or extraction data are released there. Because many cited works and products are recent preprints, announcements, or vendor pages, evidence quality is heterogeneous and some product claims may be version-, region-, or availability-dependent. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: Not applicable—this is a conceptual survey/framework paper, not an empirical method, theoretical proof paper, or evaluated systems artifact. - Practical: Not evaluated; the paper proposes deployment criteria but does not implement or run a complete smart-glasses system. - Efficient: Not evaluated; it recommends measuring latency, energy, thermal behavior, and duty cycle but reports no new resource profile. - Effective: Not evaluated; the framework argues that end-to-end utility should be measured, but provides no causal evidence that its protocol improves task outcomes or safety. - Scalable: Not evaluated; the paper discusses all-day operation, longitudinal memory, version drift, and 10×–100×-type deployment concerns conceptually but presents no scale experiment. The paper delivers a conceptual taxonomy, evaluation protocol, design checklist, product evidence map, and public project link; it does not deliver a new library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or validated end-to-end system. Strengths - The claim-conditioned view usefully prevents unsupported transfer from a model or benchmark to a product-level deployment claim. - The separation between L0–L4 wearer-facing progression and L5 embodied coupling avoids conflating persistent assistance, external action, and human-to-robot data transfer. - The framework treats memory provenance, correction, deletion, state freshness, permission gates, rollback, and bystander governance as technical system properties rather than peripheral ethics requirements. - The application-centered organization connects capabilities to stakeholders, failure consequences, and evidence thresholds, which is more useful for deployment planning than a device feature list or undifferentiated benchmark catalog. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors repeatedly acknowledge that current evidence is fragmented, that most benchmarks measure localized components rather than complete wearable systems, and that no cited benchmark combines sustained wear, memory editing, tool rollback, product-version drift, and end-to-end validation. They explicitly note that human egocentric data do not by themselves establish robot policy competence, that medical and safety applications require stronger evidence than ordinary assistance, that vendor specifications do not establish sustained capability, and that future work needs longitudinal data, field studies, privacy audits, and downstream robot validation. They also state that the product matrix is not a universal ranking and that L0–L5 levels are task- and evidence-conditioned. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The survey does not establish that its taxonomy is complete, non-overlapping, or more reliable than existing AR, wearable-agent, embodied-AI, or responsible-AI taxonomies. - It lacks a reproducible systematic-review methodology, making coverage and selection bias difficult to assess despite the large reference list. - The eight hardware axes, seven capabilities, nine deployment dimensions, and L0–L5 levels are proposed without formal weighting, operational scoring rules, inter-rater agreement, or empirical validation on a set of real systems. - The product matrix mixes commercial documentation, planned or unreleased products, research platforms, and academic evidence; these sources have materially different verification quality, but the synthesis does not quantify uncertainty or independently audit the entries. - The constrained objective includes latency, energy, thermals, privacy, and social cost, but these quantities are not defined operationally and no method is provided for estimating or optimizing them jointly. - The paper recommends claim-specific thresholds but does not provide concrete minimum thresholds for latency, false recalls, unsafe actions, deletion effectiveness, bystander comprehension, or longitudinal adherence. - Application coverage is broad but often relies on proxies from non-eyewear, third-person, simulated, or offline settings; the paper identifies this limitation but does not quantify how much transfer error those proxies introduce. - The framework emphasizes governance and effective forgetting but provides no reference implementation or test harness for provenance graphs, correction propagation, deletion audits, authorization, rollback, or fault attribution. Bottom Line This is a useful position-and-survey paper for establishing a shared vocabulary and evaluation agenda for first-person wearable agents, but its high-level framework should be treated as a strong design proposal rather than validated scientific evidence or a substitute for quantitative system studies.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the burden of preparing cybersecurity conformity evidence for SMEs placing products with digital elements on the EU market under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA). The immediate domain is industrial IoT, exemplified by PATROLIoT, a wildfire-monitoring system with sensors, cameras, local machine-learning processing, and backend connectivity. Relevant evidence is distributed across design documents, test reports, audit records, and other heterogeneous artefacts, making manual mapping from CRA requirements to assurance arguments slow and dependent on specialist knowledge. Prior LLM-based assurance-case systems often instantiate templates or rely on parametric model knowledge rather than product-specific evidence; existing automated evaluators also lack external technical context or require unavailable labelled datasets. The paper targets the gap between syntactically valid assurance structures and verifiable, local, product-specific traceability, while also addressing confidentiality concerns associated with sending industrial documents to cloud LLM services. Key Idea The core insight is to treat assurance-case construction and its evaluation as a grounded, iterative retrieval-and-reasoning problem rather than as one-shot template completion. A ReAct agent searches heterogeneous local documentation, uses retrieved material to refine later searches, and converts the accumulated context into a CAE tree whose evidence nodes carry provenance. The same grounded structures then serve as synthetic training data for an NLI model, allowing semantic-support evaluation to be learned without a large manually labelled CRA dataset. The contribution is therefore more than ordinary RAG generation, but the experiments do not isolate the value of agentic iteration from conventional grounded retrieval. Methodology The pipeline begins with a CRA requirement and a product-context JSON string of fewer than 1,800 characters containing product type, deployment, firmware/OS, protocols, security features, and certification scope. Industrial artefacts are ingested with Docling, split into 3,000-character chunks with 500-character overlap, embedded using BGE-M3, and stored in ChromaDB. A LangChain ReAct agent alternates between semantic search using L2 distance, lexical constraints, filename and metadata filtering, and query refinement; it stops when it judges that sufficient support has been collected. It then emits a hierarchical JSON CAE structure in which claims map to CRA identifiers, arguments decompose claims through AND/OR/ARG relations, and terminal evidence nodes include descriptions, epistemic fields, confidence information, and provenance metadata; malformed JSON is repaired with a JSON-repair library. For evaluation, each parent-child CAE edge becomes an entailment pair, while unrelated nodes provide non-entailment pairs. The Agentic-RAG-generated corpus contains approximately 4.2k chain instances or 2.7k non-chain instances from 40 assurance cases covering four CRA requirements. A BERT-large model is fine-tuned and a 1B Llama model is evaluated with in-context learning; both are tested on 30 chain and 24 non-chain pairs derived from independent auditor tables covering three unseen requirements. A Vanilla-LLM synthetic-data condition provides an ungrounded comparison, and a real-to-real condition provides a limited supervised baseline. Token-level explanations are assessed on 60 NLI instances by the PATROLIoT product owner using four 1–5 Likert questions and a technical-agreement question, with Qwen2.5-32B also used as an automated judge. The use of local execution is well motivated by confidentiality; the choice of a requirement-wise split directly tests regulatory-article transfer; and the chain versus non-chain comparison is useful, although the paper does not fully justify the stopping criterion, retrieval parameters, negative-pair construction, or model-training details. Key Results For RQ1, 70 generated assurance cases spanning seven CRA requirements contained 356 evidence nodes, of which 307 had direct artefact references, yielding 86.2% citation coverage and approximately 4.4 referenced artefacts per case. The references came from 42 unique source entries, only 22 of which had formal file extensions. This metric measures provenance attachment, not whether the cited artefacts actually support the claims or whether the resulting assurance cases satisfy CRA law. For RQ2, on the unseen auditor dataset, fine-tuned BERT trained on Agentic-RAG synthetic data achieved 0.83 accuracy and 0.82 F1 in the Chain setting, and 0.88 accuracy and 0.85 F1 without explicit intermediate chains. The Vanilla-LLM synthetic baseline achieved 0.70/0.69, while the real-to-real BERT baseline achieved only 0.53/0.23 for Chain and 0.54/0.23 without Chain. The 1B Llama ICL model was substantially weaker: Agentic-RAG training produced 0.53/0.37 for Chain and 0.54/0.38 without Chain. The authors correctly note that the BERT-versus-Llama comparison confounds architecture, model size, and adaptation method. For RQ3, the product owner gave BERT’s non-chain explanations a mean plausibility score of 3.06/5, with 50.0% technical agreement for Chain and 41.7% for non-chain; Llama scored 2.17 and 1.94 mean plausibility, with 16.7% and 25.0% agreement. The LLM judge assigned higher scores to most configurations, including a 3.38 mean for BERT non-chain and 3.27 for Llama non-chain, while its agreement rates diverged sharply from the human ratings, indicating that automated judging overestimated explanation quality. The experiments are standard-case scale rather than stress-scale: one product, seven requirements, 70 generated cases, and fewer than 30 held-out real instances per reasoning configuration. Novelty Classification The contribution is primarily NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, with a narrower NEW FORMULATION in the synthetic-to-real evaluation setup: it combines ReAct-style local RAG, CAE assurance-case generation, and multi-hop NLI explanation auditing for CRA compliance, while the underlying components—RAG, ReAct, CAE/GSN argumentation, NLI, and token attribution—are established techniques. The most substantive empirical finding is that grounded synthetic CAE data transfers better to unseen audit artefacts than ungrounded synthetic data in this case, and that human experts rate fine-tuned BERT explanations more favorably than small-model ICL explanations. Rigor & Reproducibility The requirement-wise split across four training and three unseen test requirements is a meaningful attempt to avoid testing only on familiar regulatory language, and the paper includes comparisons against ungrounded synthetic data, limited real-data training, two reasoning representations, and two evaluator architectures. However, no confidence intervals, multiple random seeds, statistical significance tests, or variance estimates are reported. The 24–30 held-out test pairs are very small, and the synthetic training and real test data both concern the same PATROLIoT product, so the result does not establish cross-product or cross-organisation generalisation. The study lacks ablations isolating ReAct iteration, filename filtering, lexical constraints, metadata search, chunking, embedding choice, prompt components, and provenance enforcement. It also does not compare against a conventional non-agentic RAG pipeline despite explicitly acknowledging that grounding effects are not separable from agentic iteration. Citation coverage can be measured reproducibly, but it is not a correctness or compliance metric. The expert evaluator is the product owner and a paper co-author, creating a substantial risk of confirmation bias; the independent LLM judge does not adequately remove that concern and demonstrably disagrees with human technical judgements. The NLI training code and evaluation interface are publicly available at https://github.com/farizikhwantri/exclaim, but the Agentic-RAG implementation, generated outputs, source documentation, and technical datasets remain proprietary because of industry confidentiality. The paper is an arXiv preprint (v1, dated 19 August 2026 in the supplied text), so the results should not be treated as independently peer-reviewed. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS, with empirical evaluation; the paper implements a locally executed generation and evaluation workflow but does not report production deployment. Practical: The models and retrieval stack can in principle run on commercially available hardware, and local execution avoids transmitting proprietary documents, but the paper does not report hardware, latency, throughput, memory use, or operational integration costs. Efficient: The framework’s compute and memory cost relative to ordinary RAG, manual assurance work, or cloud inference is not measured; iterative agent calls and local 30B/32B-class models may impose substantial resource requirements. Effective: The evidence supports provenance attachment and NLI classification on a narrow audit-derived proxy, but it does not demonstrate that generated evidence is correct, that assurance arguments are complete, or that a legal auditor would accept the resulting CRA documentation. Scalable: The paper claims support for fragmented industrial repositories and iterative refinement but tests only one product, 70 assurance cases, 42 source entries, and seven requirements; behaviour at 10×–100× the document, product, organisation, or regulatory scale is not evaluated. The work delivers publicly available NLI training code and an evaluation interface, but the central Agentic-RAG implementation, proprietary documents, generated assurance cases, and datasets are not reusable artifacts. It therefore provides a partially reproducible research prototype rather than an independently deployable certification tool. Strengths - It identifies a concrete industrial failure mode—LLM-generated assurance arguments that lack product-specific evidence—and connects generation directly to provenance-bearing local artefacts. - The requirement-wise synthetic-to-real split is better aligned with the claimed cold-start scenario than random instance splitting and tests transfer to unseen CRA requirements. - The paper distinguishes citation coverage and semantic consistency from evidence correctness and formal legal compliance, avoiding the strongest possible overclaim. - The human-versus-LLM explanation comparison exposes a useful and non-obvious result: an automated judge can rate linguistically plausible explanations above human-preferred explanations and therefore cannot be assumed to validate technical faithfulness. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that domain experts did not validate legal CRA compliance, that the system cannot guarantee audit success, that the expert evaluator is also a co-author and may introduce confirmation bias, and that external validity is limited by the single-product case study. They also acknowledge that higher security levels require stronger real-world implementation evidence rather than merely refining assurance arguments. These limitations are confronted directly in the threats-to-validity section, although the conclusion still describes the framework as effectively addressing the industry problem despite the narrow evidence base. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The study does not evaluate whether retrieved documents genuinely entail the generated claims; 13.8% unsupported evidence nodes and 86.2% citation coverage reveal retrieval/provenance gaps but do not measure semantic correctness. - It omits a conventional non-agentic RAG baseline, so the incremental value of ReAct-style iteration, query refinement, and filename-aware retrieval remains unknown. - The held-out evaluation is extremely small—30 chain and 24 non-chain pairs—and no seed variation or uncertainty estimates establish that the reported 0.88 accuracy and 0.85 F1 are stable. - Both synthetic training data and auditor test data come from the same PATROLIoT context, leaving open whether the model learns general compliance logic or product-specific vocabulary and documentation conventions. - The expert study uses one product owner, who is also a co-author, and the LLM judge’s disagreement with human agreement rates shows that the proposed automated cross-check is not an independent validity substitute. - The paper does not report retrieval recall, generation latency, token/API-equivalent cost, hardware requirements, failure cases, duplicate or irrelevant citations, assurance-tree completeness, or comparison with established assurance-case tools and human effort. Bottom Line This is a useful early systems paper for researchers studying grounded assurance-case generation and synthetic-data evaluation, but practitioners should not rely on it for CRA certification until multi-product evaluations, independent legal and engineering review, evidence-correctness tests, stronger baselines, and operational cost measurements are provided.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the difficulty of extending and maintaining manually authored rules in interpretable, multilingual data-to-text generation. This problem affects developers of symbolic NLG systems for domains requiring controllability and traceability, including potentially regulated or safety-relevant applications. Existing neural D2T systems offer fluency but can hallucinate and are difficult to inspect, whereas logic-based systems provide explicit reasoning and semantic control but require substantial linguistic and domain expertise to engineer. The specific gap is assistance with higher-level semantic equivalences and context-sensitive linguistic transformations—such as alternative comparison formulations, temporal complements, and syntactic variants—that ordinary grammars and manually maintained rewriting systems do not readily scale to. Key Idea: Treat LLMs as candidate-knowledge discovery tools rather than as text generators: they suggest alternative conceptual structures and linguistic rules, but a symbolic rewriting engine and human reviewer determine what becomes executable. The central insight is that semantic equivalence can be expanded before surface realization, allowing one conceptual input to yield more varied text while preserving an explicit transformation trace. Methodology: The baseline represents concepts as finite rooted trees and transforms them through stratified Prolog rewriting stages: semantic equivalence, syntactic-role organization, lexical realization, agreement propagation, CLP-based inflection and ordering, and syntactic refinement. The proposed pipeline adds three agents. The Writer consumes a target phenomenon, input tree, or existing rule descriptions and produces representative natural-language examples or candidate abstractions. The Planner consumes those examples and produces structured specifications describing semantic conditions, transformations, and linguistic choices. The Developer consumes the specifications and the Concept2Text rule interface and emits Prolog predicates conforming to the rule/5 schema. A human user inspects, filters, and refines candidates before they are added to the rule set; the paper explicitly notes the need to avoid cyclic rule dependencies. Two modes generate semantic equivalences: a tree-driven mode that is more context-specific and a rule-driven mode that is more general but requires stronger validation. The paper also applies the approach to language-specific ordering constraints represented as CSPs solved through CLP. Important design decisions are the separation of LLM suggestion from symbolic execution, staged abstraction from examples to code, and heterogeneous model assignment: GPT-5 Mini for planning and abstraction, and Gemini Flash variants for example and code generation. These choices are described operationally but are not supported by controlled model-selection ablations. No explicit training objective or learned loss is used; the method relies on prompted proprietary LLM calls and symbolic rule execution. Key Results: The paper claims that LLM-generated rules increase syntactic and lexical variation, reduce manual rule-specification effort, support English/French multilingual adaptation, and preserve explainability. Demonstrations include temporal-complement rules selecting “for” for durations and “since” for calendar start points, and comparison transformations such as “A is greater than B,” “A surpasses B,” and reciprocal “B is less than A.” Table 1 reports token counts and estimated costs for selected tasks: complement generation costs €0.0006 for the Writer, €0.0141 for the Planner, and €0.0072 for the Developer; equivalence generation costs €0.0054 or €0.0096 for the two Writer modes, €0.0075 for planning, and €0.0082 for development. However, the paper provides no numerical count of generated variants, no grammar or semantic-accuracy score, no measured percentage reduction in human effort, no latency, no rule-acceptance rate, and no comparison with alternative prompting or rule-engineering methods. The “experiments” are primarily qualitative examples and cost accounting, tested on a small set of linguistic phenomena rather than a standard D2T benchmark or stress-scale workload. The baselines are limited to the authors’ manually defined Concept2Text pipeline; no neural D2T baseline, competing LLM-assisted rule-generation system, or current symbolic NLG baseline is quantitatively evaluated. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the paper combines prompted LLM agents, human validation, and Prolog/CLP rewriting to generate symbolic D2T rules, with the potentially useful empirical observation that LLMs can suggest non-lexical semantic equivalences; the underlying components—LLM prompting, agent decomposition, symbolic rewriting, human review, and constraint-based linearization—are largely established ideas applied in a specific explainable D2T setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes illustrative rule-generation traces, representative Prolog fragments, prompt templates, model assignments, token/cost accounting, and a link to Python and Prolog materials at https://ahead-lab.unipr.it/dalpalu-cilc2026/. It does not report ablations isolating the Writer, Planner, Developer, human supervision, model choice, or tree-driven versus rule-driven generation. It reports no multiple runs, seeds, error bars, significance tests, evaluator protocol, annotation agreement, acceptance/rejection statistics, semantic-equivalence verification procedure, or systematic error analysis. The implementation link improves reproducibility, but the experiments depend on proprietary and apparently time-specific models (GPT-5 Mini and Gemini Flash variants), and the paper does not state whether all prompts, API versions, generated candidates, accepted rules, datasets, or model outputs are archived. The evaluation uses the authors’ own Concept2Text rule framework and selected examples, creating a narrow assessment scope and potential benchmark-selection bias. Claims that explainability is preserved are structurally plausible for accepted rules, but the paper does not measure whether human reviewers detect all incorrect or overgeneral rules. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper describes and evaluates a built LLM-assisted rule-development pipeline integrated with a Prolog/CLP generator. Practical: The symbolic components can run on ordinary hardware, and the LLM stages can be accessed through commercial APIs, but local hardware requirements, API dependencies, operational latency, and deployment configuration are not stated. Efficient: The reported selected-task API costs range from €0.0006 to €0.0141 per agent call, but the paper gives no end-to-end cost, latency, memory use, reviewer time, or comparison with manual engineering and alternative models. Effective: Qualitative examples show plausible temporal, comparative, and ordering transformations with explicit traces, but the evidence does not establish grammatical accuracy, semantic preservation, coverage, or improvement in final text quality at a system level. Scalable: The architecture is modular and the authors claim easier domain and language extension, but it is tested only on a few phenomena and languages; behavior at 10×–100× the rule-base size, language count, candidate volume, or input complexity is not evaluated. The work delivers a Python/API orchestration example and Prolog implementation rather than a mature library, benchmark, trained model, or production-ready tool. Strengths: - It identifies a meaningful division of labor: LLMs search for linguistic knowledge, while Prolog performs the inspectable transformation and execution. - It targets semantic and structural equivalences, not only lexical paraphrases, with concrete examples such as relational, attributive, and reciprocal comparison representations. - It preserves compatibility with the existing staged rewriting architecture and uses CLP constraints for multilingual ordering rather than replacing declarative control with fixed neural outputs. - It exposes enough prompts, rule schemas, generated-code fragments, and cost data to make the proposed workflow conceptually reproducible and inspectable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that LLM candidates can be inconsistent or overly general and that human supervision is required to filter invalid rules. They also identify a precision–generality trade-off: tree-specific rules are narrower but more precise, while abstract rules cover more cases and require stricter validation. The paper notes the risk of cyclic dependencies among Prolog rules and identifies incomplete multilingual coverage, incomplete automatic selection of representative complement rules, and the need to expand semantic-equivalence coverage as future work. These limitations are acknowledged directly, but their frequency and practical impact are not measured. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal gap is the absence of quantitative evidence for the paper’s central claims about expressivity and reduced manual effort. The evaluation lacks standard datasets, objective grammaticality and semantic-preservation metrics, reviewer-time measurements, rule-coverage statistics, rejection rates, and comparisons with strong LLM-based or symbolic baselines. The paper does not establish that generated rules are correct beyond selected hand-picked examples, nor does it test interactions among many rules despite identifying cyclic and overgeneralization risks. The multilingual experiment is described mainly through simplified ordering constraints and mentions English and French without reporting language-specific test sets or scores. The reliance on proprietary model names and unspecified prompt/API details also weakens repeatability. Finally, “full explainability” is asserted for the symbolic execution trace, but the opaque LLM proposal process and the human validation process are not themselves audited for provenance, completeness, or reviewer consistency. Bottom Line: The paper offers a sensible and potentially useful workflow for LLM-assisted expansion of explainable Prolog-based D2T grammars, but practitioners should treat it as an early system design and qualitative feasibility report rather than validated evidence that it reduces engineering cost or improves generation quality.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprise AI agents operate in non-stationary environments where customers, regulations, policies, workflows, tools, and market regimes change. Conventional continual-learning objectives treat retention of prior knowledge as beneficial and catastrophic forgetting as the central failure, while memory systems commonly accumulate information through an implicit update such as M_t+1 = M_t ∪ ΔM_t. This can expose the agent to obsolete or harmful knowledge and produce negative transfer. The paper targets the unresolved lifecycle-management problem of deciding which knowledge should influence current behavior, which should remain recoverable but suppressed, and which should be retired under governance constraints. It distinguishes this problem from machine unlearning, where designated information must be removed, and from concept-drift detection, which detects environmental change without specifying how individual memories should be managed. Key Idea: The core insight is to treat agent memory as a governed lifecycle rather than a retention-versus-deletion binary: obsolete knowledge moves from active to dormant, remains recoverable with provenance, and can return to active use when contextual evidence and counterfactual utility justify reactivation. Hysteresis and persistence counters prevent repeated state oscillation, while shadow-mode reactivation tests whether restoring a memory improves behavior before it affects production decisions. This is a specific controller design hypothesis, but the paper does not demonstrate that the combination is superior to simpler memory policies. Methodology: The proposed pipeline receives a changing environment through a shift detector, computes a relevance score for each memory, and passes the evidence to HRMC. The conceptual relevance score is R_t(m_i) = αS_t(m_i) + βU_t(m_i) + γC(m_i) − δA_t(m_i) − λH_t(m_i), where similarity, utility, contextual compatibility, staleness, and harm are candidate signals. HRMC exponentially smooths this score as R̄_t = ρR̄_t−1 + (1 − ρ)R_t, moves active memories to dormant after L↓ consecutive scores below τ↓ or after a policy block, and reactivates dormant memories after L↑ consecutive scores above τ↑ plus shadow gain above ε, with τ↓ < τ↑. Dormant memories can become retired after T_retire only with policy or owner approval; transitions append the memory identifier, old and new states, reason, time, and evidence to a ledger. Three critical design decisions are hysteresis, temporal persistence, and shadow-tested reactivation; the paper motivates each qualitatively to control state flapping and false restoration but provides no calibration procedure, estimator specification, optimization objective, or validated parameter-selection method. It also proposes layer-specific interventions—retrieval filtering for episodes, versioning for facts and policies, preference decay for tools, workflow retirement, and parameter adaptation for model behavior—but leaves the mapping from relevance evidence to these interventions domain-specific. Key Results: Not evaluated. The paper reports no experiments, implementation measurements, datasets, accuracy or utility results, latency, memory overhead, ablations, or statistical comparisons. Finance serves only as an illustrative scenario: knowledge M1 is active in regime R1, becomes dormant during crisis regime R2 while M2 is active, and is reactivated when regime R3 resembles R1. The paper proposes, but does not run, comparisons against retain-all, fixed-window, least-recently-used, permanent-delete, and oracle-context baselines. Consequently, it provides no evidence that HRMC improves current-context utility, lowers harmful-retention cost, recovers prior utility after recurrence, or reduces transition flapping relative to those baselines. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION, NEW METHOD, and NEW EMPIRICAL-FINDING agenda rather than demonstrated finding: the paper formulates obsolete knowledge suppression as reversible lifecycle management and specifies HRMC with state transitions, hysteresis, shadow reactivation, policy gates, and transition logging, but much of the underlying machinery combines established ideas from concept drift, threshold controllers, memory management, governance, and machine unlearning without experimental validation of a new effect. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is an arXiv preprint, identified as version 1 dated 18 August 2026 in the supplied text, and presents a conceptual framework rather than a validated system. It includes pseudocode and a relevance-score template but leaves relevance estimators, thresholds, persistence lengths, shadow-gain computation, policy definitions, memory representations, and evaluation environments unspecified. No ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, implementation, code repository, dataset, model weights, or software artifact are reported. The proposed ablations and baselines are part of a future benchmarking agenda, not completed evidence. The framework also risks evaluator circularity because the same relevance proxies and policy signals could determine both state transitions and measured utility unless future studies use held-out environments or independently labeled obsolescence. The paper appropriately states that its advantages are design hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL in the supplied taxonomy, although the paper is better characterized as a conceptual systems proposal because it contains neither proofs nor experiments. Sound: The state machine and control rules are internally understandable, but no formal safety, convergence, false-suppression, or recovery guarantees are proved, and the assumptions behind relevance and shadow-gain estimates remain unspecified. General: The framework is intended for facts, episodes, tools, workflows, policies, and model parameters, but its applicability across these memory layers is asserted through design patterns rather than tested under realistic distribution shifts or compliance regimes. Tight: Not evaluated; the paper gives no bounds or quantitative trade-off between current utility, harmful retention, transition cost, dormant storage, and reactivation failure. Implementable: The pseudocode is implementable in principle on commercially available infrastructure, but domain-specific estimators, policy engines, shadow evaluation, access control, and storage semantics are missing, and no implementation or follow-up operationalization is provided. The work stops at paper form and does not deliver a library, CLI, tool, dataset, trained model, or reusable proof technique. Strengths: - It identifies a consequential failure mode that standard continual-learning framing underemphasizes: retaining knowledge can be harmful when the environment changes, even when that knowledge remains historically correct. - It makes a useful conceptual distinction between dormant suppression and retirement or legal erasure, avoiding the unsafe implication that recoverable dormancy satisfies deletion obligations. - The combination of asymmetric thresholds, persistence counters, shadow-mode reactivation, policy-gated retirement, and a transition ledger creates a concrete, falsifiable design target rather than only a high-level call for adaptive memory. - It proposes evaluation dimensions that separate current-context utility, harmful-retention cost, reactivation recovery, transition cost, unsupported suppression, policy violations, audit completeness, and actual deletion; this is a stronger evaluation framing than reporting retention alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the relevance score is illustrative rather than validated, that its proxies and thresholds require calibration by memory layer and policy domain, and that HRMC's claimed advantages are design hypotheses rather than demonstrated benefits. They acknowledge premature suppression, false shift detection, unbounded dormant storage, failed reactivation, adversarial feedback, and compliance conflict. They also explicitly note that dormancy cannot satisfy legally mandated erasure and that actual deletion requires separate unlearning or records-management procedures. The paper confronts these limitations directly, but it does not quantify their severity or provide mitigation experiments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The largest gap is the absence of any implemented controller or empirical test despite presenting algorithmic pseudocode. The paper does not define how contextual utility, harm, reliability, staleness, or shadow gain are measured; how obsolescence labels are obtained; how thresholds are selected; or how policy conflicts are resolved. It provides no comparison with retrieval-time filtering, version-aware retrieval, decay-based memory policies, machine-unlearning methods, concept-drift adaptation, or contemporary agent-memory systems beyond naming simple proposed baselines. It does not test whether dormant storage grows without bound, whether reactivation leaks obsolete information during shadow evaluation, whether an attacker can manipulate relevance evidence, or whether policy gates create unacceptable latency and human-review burden. The finance example is illustrative rather than a finance dataset or deployment, so the paper does not establish domain impact. The distinction between suppressing retrieved memories and changing model parameters is also underspecified: these interventions have different reversibility, attribution, and safety properties. Finally, the proposed oracle-context baseline may be difficult to construct without privileged knowledge of the correct regime, and the paper does not discuss how to avoid using future regime information when evaluating reactivation. Bottom Line: This is a useful position and design paper for researchers framing obsolete knowledge as a distinct problem from catastrophic forgetting, but it does not yet provide research evidence that HRMC works, and a practitioner should prefer an implemented, experimentally evaluated memory-management or version-aware retrieval system for deployment decisions.

Problem & Motivation: Automated pipeline design for digital circuits commonly treats partitioning as a clock-frequency optimization problem, typically balancing logic across stages while handling data dependencies separately. The paper targets gate-level pipelining with forwarding, where recurring read-after-write dependencies between latch inputs, latch outputs, and successor logic can cause stalls. Its central problem is that stage assignment changes the distance between communicating nodes even when the forwarding structure and nominal clock frequency remain fixed; therefore, partitioning can alter CPI as well as timing. The affected users are EDA researchers and hardware designers seeking higher throughput without manually analyzing increasingly large circuits. The claimed gap is the absence of a partitioning method that explicitly optimizes both timing and stall-related CPI while preserving functional correctness. Key Idea: The core insight is that pipeline stage distance between selected dependency-critical nodes is a usable proxy for forwarding-induced stall cost, so stage partitioning should minimize these distances rather than merely distribute logic evenly. EvoPartition restricts evolutionary search to a small set of critical nodes, inserts virtual nodes between critical inputs and their direct successors to prevent invalid stage-order interactions during search, and combines this CPI-oriented objective with a timing-oriented critical-path objective. The insight is plausible and supported by a reported Pearson correlation of 0.86 between stage-difference measurements and actual CPI on sampled circuits, but the paper does not establish that this proxy remains reliable across broader circuit classes or pipeline configurations. Methodology: The input is an unpartitioned circuit represented as an And-Inverter Graph, with a target number of pipeline stages. First, the method identifies critical nodes consisting of latch-input nodes, corresponding latch-output nodes, and direct successor AND nodes; it inserts virtual nodes between critical input nodes and their successors, then initializes an evolutionary population by perturbing an even partition based on the longest critical path. Second, each individual encodes stage assignments for critical nodes. Evolution repeatedly samples individuals, selects two low-fitness candidates, combines assignments around a split point, perturbs selected assignments, and uses simulated-annealing-style acceptance to retain some worse candidates and preserve diversity. The stated fitness is the product of the root-mean-square stage-distance term over critical input/output relationships and the maximum critical-path length across stages: F = sqrt((1/N) sum_i sum_j (1/M_j) sum_k (P(LO_i) - P(LI_jk))^2) × max_s P_s. This scalarization implicitly weights CPI and timing through multiplication, but the paper does not justify its normalization, weighting, or sensitivity. Third, post-processing removes virtual nodes, assigns each affected successor to the maximum stage of its virtual predecessors, computes logic levels for critical nodes, topologically traverses non-critical nodes, and assigns them using an even distribution guided by the resulting levels. The critical-node restriction reduces search cost, but its sufficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated with a full quantitative comparison; the virtual-node correctness argument and the effect of post-processing on the optimized objective also receive limited formal validation. Key Results: The authors evaluate using Yosys preprocessing and Design Compiler synthesis with a 65 nm standard-cell library, on two Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPUs. The main comparison covers ISCAS85 and EPFL circuits in single-function and constructed multi-function settings, against the automated EDA flow and Cheng et al. (2024), which the paper treats as the state-of-the-art baseline. Relative to Cheng et al. (2024), EvoPartition reports 7.26% lower average CPI and 6.97% higher throughput for single-function circuits, 7.42% lower CPI and 7.46% higher throughput for multi-function circuits, and an aggregate 7.34% CPI reduction with 7.22% throughput improvement. Average clock frequency is 98.25% of the Cheng baseline for single-function cases and 100.10% for multi-function cases; relative throughput is 106.97% and 107.46%, respectively. Average stall-cycle reduction is reported as 16.23%, approximately 150 cycles, with EPFL/div showing a roughly 30% CPI reduction and 708 fewer stall cycles. Against human-designed partitions, average CPI falls from 1.94 to 1.74 for single-function circuits and from 2.10 to 1.82 for multi-function circuits; EvoPartition improves CPI on 47 of 52 circuits. Against simulated annealing, Kernighan–Lin, and METIS, reported average CPI reductions relative to the strongest of those baselines range from 12.08% to 17.45% across four benchmark groups, including OpenCores and RTLLM. The evaluations use standard circuit suites but remain small relative to production-scale designs, and the paper gives no circuit-gate counts, target-stage scaling study, or optimization-time measurements. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the explicit claim and implementation that stage partitioning affects forwarding-induced CPI, operationalized through a critical-node stage-distance proxy and an evolutionary search with virtual-node handling; the evolutionary operators, simulated annealing, graph partitioning framing, and timing metrics are established techniques combined for this setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes comparisons with an automated EDA flow, Cheng et al. (2024), three conventional partitioning algorithms, human-designed partitions, and additional OpenCores/RTLLM circuits. It also reports a proxy-to-CPI Pearson correlation and 1,000 simulation runs for stall-cycle measurements. However, it provides no ablation isolating critical-node selection, virtual-node insertion, the multiplicative fitness, simulated annealing, evolutionary operators, or post-processing; no population sizes, mutation probabilities, temperature schedule, iteration budgets, stopping criteria, or runtime results are stated; and no error bars, random-seed analysis, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Code, data, trained models, and implementation URLs are not mentioned. The strongest automated comparison is primarily against one recent method, while the EDA baseline optimizes a different single objective, making the trade-off informative but not a controlled comparison of equally constrained multi-objective systems. The constructed multi-function benchmarks may also inherit assumptions from the prior method. The use of Design Compiler and a 65 nm library improves timing realism, but the paper does not report synthesis constraints, forwarding implementation details, functional-equivalence checks, or whether all compared methods use identical synthesis and simulation conditions. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL — the paper proposes and evaluates an algorithmic EDA method rather than a deployed infrastructure system. Practical: The search runs on commercially available Intel Xeon CPUs and consumes standard AIG inputs, but the absence of reported runtimes prevents judging whether it is practical within an EDA design loop. Efficient: The critical-node restriction and proxy fitness are intended to avoid repeated CPI simulation and reduce search cost, but no computational complexity, memory use, runtime, or comparison with full-node evolution is measured. Effective: On the reported benchmarks, the method improves CPI and throughput relative to the cited baselines, although it sacrifices clock frequency relative to the single-objective EDA flow and evaluates functional correctness mainly by construction rather than by reported equivalence experiments. Scalable: The paper claims applicability to large circuits but tests only standard benchmark suites and gives no 10×–100× scale experiment, node-count scaling curve, or behavior under many pipeline stages. The work does not explicitly deliver a released software artifact, library, CLI, dataset, or trained model; it stops at a preprint description of a method using Yosys and Design Compiler. Strengths: - It identifies a non-obvious interaction between stage partitioning and CPI in forwarding-based gate-level pipelines, rather than treating timing and hazard behavior as separable. - The virtual-node construction gives the evolutionary search a mechanism for avoiding certain topological assignment conflicts without evaluating every candidate through a full correctness checker. - The evaluation measures the intended mechanism directly through stall cycles and reports a strong correlation of 0.86 between the proposed stage-distance proxy and actual CPI. - The reported gains persist across standard ISCAS85/EPFL settings, constructed multi-function cases, human partitions, and additional OpenCores/RTLLM circuits, although the breadth and controls are limited. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Not stated. The paper does acknowledge a trade-off in which EvoPartition’s clock frequency is lower than the EDA baseline because it optimizes CPI and frequency jointly, but it does not present this as a formal limitations section or discuss runtime, benchmark scale, proxy failure cases, or reproducibility constraints. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The principal gap is insufficient evidence that the scalar fitness and critical-node abstraction faithfully optimize synthesized CPI across arbitrary circuits. The post-processing step can change assignments after evolution, yet its impact is not ablated or quantified. The claim of guaranteed functional correctness is argued from topological decoupling but is not backed by formal proof, equivalence checking results, or exhaustive simulation details. The study omits optimization runtime and scaling, which are essential for an evolutionary EDA method; omits random-seed variability and statistical uncertainty; and does not compare against a strong controlled multi-objective optimizer or a full-node version of its own method. The human-design baseline is not characterized, and the paper does not explain how its partitions, stage count, forwarding rules, synthesis constraints, or simulation workloads were matched. The headline averages also aggregate circuits with very different baseline CPI and frequency, so per-circuit distributions and weighted application-level impact would be more informative. Finally, the document is explicitly a preliminary preprint marked “DO NOT CITE,” with the final IJCAI-ECAI 2026 version not yet available; the reported results therefore have lower confidence than peer-reviewed, version-of-record evidence. Bottom Line: The paper offers a useful and plausibly important CPI-aware reframing of automated pipeline partitioning, but practitioners should treat it as an early method result until runtime, correctness, ablation, reproducibility, and large-scale validation are added.
