Problem & Motivation The work addresses the deployment of AI coding assistance in enterprises that handle proprietary intellectual property, including financial, medical-device, and trading software. Cloud assistants expose code or code-derived context to third-party infrastructure, creating confidentiality, compliance, and possible model-training risks. Existing local wrappers such as Ollama and LocalAI are characterized by the paper as lacking repository-specific semantic retrieval, optimized multi-GPU serving, and systematic productivity evaluation. The resulting gap is not merely code-generation capability but an integrated system that preserves organizational data boundaries while providing interactive latency and evidence of developer impact. Key Idea The core insight is to split retrieval and generation across two trusted local tiers: repository indexing, embedding, and semantic retrieval remain on each developer workstation, while computationally expensive generation runs on dedicated infrastructure inside the organization. A tiered embedding choice—SiamBERT for resource-constrained machines and CodeSage for machines with more than 16 GB RAM—attempts to adapt retrieval quality to workstation resources without moving source code to an external service. This is primarily an integration and deployment architecture rather than a new retrieval or inference algorithm. Methodology The proposed pipeline uses JetBrains and VSCode plugins connected to administrative, AI-tool backend, suggestion/chat, messaging, database, and monitoring services. On the client, repository code is divided with a 512-token sliding-window chunking strategy, embedded using either SiamBERT or CodeSage, and stored in a local FAISS vector index. A query retrieves semantically relevant code context locally; generation is then performed by an on-premise LLM server, described as an NVIDIA A100 80 GB machine running vLLM and supporting quantized models. The paper also benchmarks vLLM, TensorRT/TRT-LLM, LMDeploy, and TGI using LLaMA-3-8B, LLaMA-3-70B, and Mistral-8x7B, measuring throughput, time-to-first-token (TTFT), and inter-token latency (ITL) under varying user loads. For productivity, it compares Jira mean cycle time—from “In Progress” to “Resolved”—for more than 2,500 tasks in the three months after deployment against the preceding three months, filtering by similar Story Point complexity, and supplements this with developer surveys covering coding scenarios. The critical design decisions are the local retrieval boundary, the workstation-dependent encoder selection, and the choice of vLLM for serving; the paper gives rationale for these choices but does not provide retrieval-quality ablations, security threat modeling, or controlled evidence that each design decision improves end-to-end outcomes. Key Results In the single-GPU framework benchmark, LLaMA-3-8B achieved throughput of 1,250 tokens/s with vLLM, 1,320 with TRT, 1,260 with LMDeploy, and 1,240 with TGI; corresponding TTFT values were 20, 50, 22, and 110 ms, and ITL values were 17, 14, 13, and 18 ms. For LLaMA-3-70B, throughput was 720, 680, 750, and 745 tokens/s, with TTFT of 70, 130, 65, and 460 ms and ITL of 43, 35, 35, and 45 ms. For Mistral-8x7B, throughput was 820, 930, 790, and 810 tokens/s, with TTFT of 100, 100, 1,450, and 480 ms and ITL of 39, 35, 60, and 39 ms. A separate load table reports LLaMA-3-8B TTFT under 100 users as 70 ms for vLLM, 1000 ms for TRT-LLM, 170 ms for LMDeploy, and 550 ms for TGI; for LLaMA-3-70B under 100 users it reports 750, 6500, 450, and 6300 ms, respectively, but this table uses a different framework set and is not reconciled with Table 1. In the developer study, overall Jira mean cycle time decreased by 15.4% relative to the prior three-month baseline. Surveyed or categorized task-level perceived gains were approximately 50% for boilerplating, 60% for code explanation, 70% for documentation and random-data generation, 40% for regular-expression generation, 20% for Bash generation, 70% for code translation, 50% for Text2SQL, and 30% for CSS generation; usage counts ranged from 16 cases for translation to 66 for code explanation and random-data generation. The strongest counterpoint to the large subjective gains is the much smaller aggregate objective reduction, which is consistent with non-coding overhead but does not establish that the plugin caused the difference. No code-completion accuracy, generated-code acceptance rate, defect rate, security rate, or comparison with a cloud assistant is reported. Novelty Classification The contribution is best classified as NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the paper assembles a privacy-oriented IDE plugin with local tiered RAG and on-premise serving and reports deployment-oriented latency and productivity measurements. The architecture combines existing components—FAISS, SiamBERT, CodeSage, quantized LLMs, and vLLM—rather than introducing a new retrieval objective, model, serving algorithm, or formal privacy mechanism; the most distinctive claim is the empirical evaluation of an integrated private deployment, although the paper does not substantiate its assertion that this is the first systematic evaluation. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper provides no component ablations comparing SiamBERT with CodeSage, RAG against no-RAG, local retrieval against alternative retrieval schemes, or vLLM against other serving configurations in an end-to-end assistant. It reports point estimates without error bars, confidence intervals, multiple runs, statistical tests, or seed information. The productivity study is a before-versus-after observational comparison with no randomized assignment, concurrent control team, or accounting for developer learning, project changes, seasonality, task mix, or adoption intensity; Story Point filtering alone does not establish comparability. Survey methodology, response rates, participant demographics, usage logs, task-level sample sizes beyond selected counts, and the mapping from responses to percentage improvements are insufficiently specified. The framework evaluation is internally inconsistent: the text names TensorRT, while Table 1 labels TRT and Table 2 includes MLC-LLM and TRT-LLM; hardware configuration, batch size, prompt/output lengths, quantization, concurrency methodology, and reproducibility scripts are not stated. The linked C4 design page is provided at https://vasilkrikunov14.github.io/C4_llm_plugin/, but the paper does not state that source code, data, model weights, benchmark harnesses, or anonymized Jira data are released. The privacy claim is architectural rather than experimentally verified: no threat model, telemetry audit, access-control analysis, retention policy, or leakage test demonstrates that code never leaves the organization. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — the paper both describes a built IDE-integrated system and reports framework and developer-study measurements. Practical: The system can run on commercially available JetBrains/VSCode clients and an NVIDIA A100-class server, but the required dedicated GPU infrastructure and enterprise integration costs are not quantified. Efficient: vLLM and LMDeploy report low TTFT for LLaMA-3-8B, but the paper does not report total cost, GPU memory utilization, indexing cost, model quantization settings, energy use, or comparison with cloud and workstation-only alternatives; larger-model latency degrades sharply at 100-user load in the reported table. Effective: The evidence supports interactive serving and an association with a 15.4% reduction in Jira cycle time, but it does not demonstrate improved code correctness, defect reduction, retrieval quality, or causal productivity gains. Scalable: The benchmark tests up to 100 users and models up to LLaMA-3-70B on a single GPU, but there is no 10×–100× stress test, multi-GPU experiment, distributed-serving evaluation, or measured behavior for larger repositories and organizations. The work presents a system architecture and apparent plugin implementation, but it does not state that a reusable plugin, server codebase, benchmark suite, dataset, or trained model is publicly released. Strengths - It targets a concrete enterprise constraint—keeping proprietary code within an organizational boundary—rather than treating coding-assistant quality as the only deployment objective. - The separation of client-side retrieval from on-premise generation is a clear architectural boundary that can accommodate low-resource developer machines while centralizing expensive inference. - The serving benchmark reports latency, inter-token latency, throughput, and user-load behavior across multiple model/framework combinations instead of relying only on a single latency figure. - Combining Jira-derived cycle-time data with subjective task-level feedback is directionally stronger than evaluating perceived productivity alone, and the gap between 50–70% perceived task gains and 15.4% aggregate cycle-time reduction is an informative observation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The paper explicitly notes that self-reported productivity is biased and attempts to mitigate this with Jira analytics. It also explains that aggregate productivity is lower than task-level perceived gains because meetings, reviews, design, requirements, collaboration, and debugging contribute to cycle time. Beyond these points, no explicit limitations section is provided. The paper does not directly acknowledge the lack of randomization, uncertainty estimates, generated-code quality evaluation, detailed privacy verification, or the limited hardware/scale evaluation. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central 15.4% productivity claim is vulnerable to temporal and organizational confounding because the comparison uses three months before deployment rather than a randomized or concurrent control group; the paper does not report team-level trends or adoption dosage. - The evaluation measures Jira cycle time and perceptions, not whether the assistant produces correct, secure, maintainable code or reduces defects and review burden. This leaves the principal safety and quality trade-off unevaluated. - The paper claims that RAG improves grounding and code-assistance quality but reports no retrieval recall, completion accuracy, task-success rate, or no-RAG baseline, so the contribution of Personal CodeRAG is unverified. - Privacy is asserted from data-flow design without testing leakage through logs, prompts, telemetry, authentication services, monitoring tools, model outputs, or administrative components. “No code leaves the organization” is not equivalent to a formal confidentiality guarantee. - The framework tables contain naming and result inconsistencies, and the experimental protocol omits prompt lengths, output lengths, batch/concurrency settings, hardware details beyond a single A100 reference, quantization configurations, and repetition methodology. - Comparisons omit relevant end-to-end baselines, including a local model without retrieval, workstation-only inference, a conventional cloud assistant, and contemporary optimized serving configurations; the four-framework comparison therefore establishes relative latency only under an incompletely specified setup. - The developer sample is described only as 100 Java and Python developers. Organization, team allocation, seniority, prior assistant use, task distribution, survey instrument, and statistical uncertainty are not stated, limiting external validity. Bottom Line The paper is useful as a preliminary enterprise deployment report and architecture reference, but its strongest research claim— that private LLM coding assistance improves productivity by 15.4%—is not yet supported with the controls, quality metrics, security analysis, or reproducible protocol expected for a top-tier empirical systems paper.

#175 — Moderately Innovative (47)

Formation Control of a Multi- Agent System

B Banh, P Lancaster, D Sims · scholarcommons.scu.edu · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a ROS2-based three-robot prototype that performs decentralized aggregation and desired-distance formation control using Raspberry Pi 5 computers, mecanum-drive robots, peer odometry, and namespaced DDS communication. - Why it's important: Physical multi-robot coordination fails for reasons absent from ideal simulations—localization drift, wireless discovery problems, sensor noise, command-routing errors, and drivetrain mismatch—so a working deployment pipeline is necessary before evaluating swarm-control behavior. - How it does it: Each robot discovers peer `/robotX/odom` topics, waits for readiness messages, computes centroid-tracking and pairwise distance-error forces, converts world-frame velocity to body-frame commands, limits speed, and publishes only to its own `/robotX/controller/cmd_vel` topic. - The good: The project integrates theory, simulation, hardware bringup, localization, communication, actuation, diagnostics, and safety procedures, and it explicitly documents the transition failures and scope reductions encountered on real robots. - The missing: The paper reports no quantitative formation-control results—such as convergence time, distance error, repeatability, latency, packet loss, collision rate, or comparison with centralized and alternative decentralized controllers—and provides no statistical multi-trial evidence. - Read it or not: Robotics students and practitioners building small ROS2 multi-robot testbeds may find the deployment lessons and code structure useful, but control researchers seeking a validated algorithmic contribution can largely skip it.

Problem & Motivation The work addresses the practical problem of coordinating multiple small mobile robots so that they aggregate or maintain prescribed relative distances while operating with decentralized information in a shared indoor environment. The intended users are robotics researchers, student developers, and operators working with ROS2-based multi-robot platforms. The specific gap is between formation-control models that assume direct access to accurate positions, ideal single-integrator motion, and reliable communication, and physical deployments that must estimate state, discover peers, isolate commands by namespace, tolerate wireless and sensor failures, and control imperfect mecanum drivetrains. The application scope includes cooperative robotics, warehouse automation, environmental monitoring, search and rescue, and distributed exploration, although the demonstrated system remains a supervised laboratory prototype rather than an autonomous field platform. Key Idea The central idea is to turn a standard artificial-potential-field formation controller into a deployable ROS2 multi-robot workflow by combining peer odometry discovery, readiness handshaking, namespaced command routing, centroid tracking, body-frame conversion, speed limiting, and yaw-drift correction. The underlying control law is not conceptually new: it uses pairwise distance errors to attract robots that are too far apart and repel robots that are too close. The main contribution lies in integrating this conventional control structure with the operational infrastructure required for physical execution. Methodology The project follows a staged simulation-to-hardware pipeline. First, MATLAB/Simulink models represent robots with single-integrator dynamics, \(\dot{x}=u\), and explore aggregation, centroid tracking, desired-distance formation, and obstacle-repulsion concepts. Second, the physical ROS2 stack launches LiDAR, encoder odometry, IMU filtering, RF2O laser odometry, EKF filtering, AMCL localization, pose normalization, and controller interfaces under robot-specific namespaces. Third, `formation_control_3.py` discovers active `/robot\w+/odom` topics, sorts the discovered namespaces, creates one driver per robot, subscribes to local and peer odometry and readiness topics, and publishes readiness repeatedly to avoid transient-message loss. During its nominal 20 Hz loop, each driver computes a centroid term, \(G_{TRACK}(c-x_i)\), and pairwise formation terms based on \(e_{ij}=\|x_i-x_j\|-d_{ij}\); the final code uses a linear force, approximately \(-G_A e_{ij}\hat{u}_{ij}\), rather than the earlier singular inverse-square repulsion. The resulting world-frame velocity is normalized to a capped 0.3 m/s magnitude, transformed into the robot body frame, independently limited on each axis, augmented with bounded yaw correction, and sent to `/robotX/controller/cmd_vel`. Finally, component diagnostics, host/controller checks, drivetrain motion tests, sensor checks, odometry calibration utilities, communication checks, and supervised multi-robot trials are used to assess whether the pipeline operates. Critical design decisions include decentralized peer-state processing rather than a central controller, use of a shared ROS2/DDS graph with CycloneDDS static peers, and use of AMCL/EKF/odometry-derived poses; the architecture justifies these decisions operationally, but does not provide formal stability or estimator analyses. Key Results The paper claims that the system demonstrates the core deployment pipeline for three physical robot agents: bringup, namespaced ROS2 communication, peer discovery, readiness exchange, odometry sharing, velocity generation, command routing, and supervised indoor motion. It also reports successful qualitative or diagnostic checks for Raspberry Pi and RRC Lite operation, LiDAR and IMU topic availability, controller subscribers, mecanum forward/lateral/rotational commands, ROS2 graph visibility, and peer odometry discovery. The implementation specifies a 0.05 s control period, 0.3 m/s linear-speed cap, three-agent distance matrices such as 0.5 m pairwise spacing in the final code, and a 0.05 m per-pair goal tolerance in the listed implementation; another evaluation excerpt reports 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 m distances with a 0.40 m tolerance, indicating configuration inconsistency. No measured accuracy, F1-like metric, convergence time, formation-error trajectory, throughput, CPU/memory cost, packet-loss rate, latency, number of trials, success rate, error bars, or significance tests are reported. The simulations show qualitative aggregation and formation trajectories, but the paper gives no numerical simulation outcomes. Baselines are effectively absent: the work does not compare against centralized control, consensus, leader-follower control, alternative potential fields, or an uncontrolled hardware pipeline. The tested scale is small—apparently two or three physical robots, with a three-agent implementation—and no stress-scale experiment is provided. Novelty Classification NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION, and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the deliverable is a documented ROS2 multi-robot prototype and associated setup, diagnostic, launch, calibration, and control code, while the empirical contribution is the qualitative observation that conventional formation-control logic encounters substantial localization, DDS discovery, namespacing, and mecanum-actuation barriers on the target hardware; the controller itself is a standard artificial-potential-field and desired-distance formulation combined with established ROS2 components rather than a new control method. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper includes substantial implementation detail, source listings, launch files, topic conventions, hardware descriptions, configuration examples, calibration utilities, UML diagrams, and setup/build scripts. The project-specific package is described as Apache-2.0, and the appendix includes code, but no public repository URL is given; proprietary vendor images and packages cannot be redistributed. Component and integration checks are described, but they are mostly topic-visibility tests, short motion commands, visual inspection, and qualitative demonstrations rather than controlled experiments. No ablations isolate centroid tracking, yaw correction, readiness signaling, pose source, speed limiting, or the linear APF change. No multiple-seed or repeated-trial protocol, confidence interval, error bar, statistical test, packet-loss benchmark, latency measurement, or independent ground-truth localization evaluation is reported. The system is also evaluated largely on the authors' own hardware and controlled enclosure, with no strong algorithmic baselines. The paper contains potentially important reproducibility hazards: final tested parameters are inconsistent across listings, the distance matrix is hard-coded and indexed by sorted discovery order, vendor dependencies are unavailable, and the reported physical success criteria are not operationalized as numerical thresholds beyond code-level tolerances. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: SYSTEMS — the paper builds and evaluates a physical ROS2 robotic toolchain, although its evidence is primarily prototype integration testing rather than deployment-grade validation. - Practical: The system runs on commercially available Raspberry Pi 5 computers and small off-the-shelf-style mecanum robots, but requires ROS2 Jazzy, vendor-specific hardware/software, careful Wi-Fi/DDS configuration, SSH or terminal operation, and supervised indoor testing. - Efficient: The controller is computationally lightweight and runs at 20 Hz, but the paper does not measure CPU utilization, memory consumption, network load, battery impact, or cost relative to centralized or alternative implementations. - Effective: Evidence supports functioning topic discovery, command routing, sensor bringup, and observable coordinated motion, but does not establish accurate or robust formation maintenance because no quantitative formation-error or repeatability results are reported. - Scalable: The architecture is designed around additional namespaces and peer discovery, but testing is limited to a small group of two or three robots; behavior at 10×–100× scale, communication-load growth, and topology changes are not evaluated. The work delivers a reusable project-specific ROS2 package, launch files, diagnostic and calibration scripts, configuration artifacts, and selected source code, but not a general-purpose released library, benchmark dataset, trained model, or validated safety subsystem. Strengths - The strongest execution strength is the end-to-end integration of simulation, ROS2 middleware, state estimation, DDS networking, hardware control, and physical robot testing rather than stopping at a simulated controller. - The paper identifies practical failure modes that many idealized formation-control studies omit, including multicast/DDS discovery, namespace collisions, stale readiness messages, map quality, odometry drift, wheel slip, floor dependence, and mismatch between command and physical motion. - The final code addresses concrete integration bugs, including routing commands to `/robotX/controller/cmd_vel`, subscribing to the correctly namespaced joystick input, repeatedly broadcasting readiness, and replacing an unstable singular repulsion term with a bounded linear distance-error law. - The source listings and operational artifacts provide useful continuity for future student teams, even though proprietary dependencies limit exact external replication. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state that the system is not field-ready and that localization/odometry accuracy, ROS2/DDS communication reliability, sensor noise, mecanum drivetrain error, asynchronous updates, computational resources, and simulation-to-hardware mismatch constrain performance. They acknowledge that physical obstacle avoidance, dynamic leader switching, adaptive formation switching, formal automated logging, larger-scale trials, and statistical performance evaluation were not completed. They also acknowledge the absence of a certified hardware emergency stop, reliance on operator supervision, proprietary vendor software restrictions, and the limited validation scale. These limitations are confronted directly throughout the thesis and are generally not presented as completed capabilities, which improves the credibility of its scope claims. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper does not provide the quantitative measurements needed to substantiate its central formation-control claim: no formation-error curves, convergence statistics, recovery-after-disturbance tests, ground-truth position comparison, or repeated-trial success rates are shown. - There is no comparison against even a simple centralized controller, open-loop or teleoperated baseline, standard consensus/leader-follower controller, or the earlier aggregation implementation, so the contribution of the proposed integration choices cannot be separated from the capability of the underlying platform. - The paper does not report network latency, packet loss, stale-message behavior, control-loop jitter, or failure recovery, despite identifying communication as a major risk and relying on wireless DDS for the control loop. - The algorithmic formulation and implementation are not fully consistent: the text describes separate attraction and repulsion gains, while the final code uses a linear symmetric error term and leaves `G_R` unused; parameter values and distance/tolerance configurations differ across sections and listings. - The design is not genuinely decentralized in every respect: one primary robot receives joystick input and integrates the shared centroid, discovery assumes a shared ROS2 graph, all robots use a common hard-coded distance matrix, and sorted namespace order determines formation-agent identity. - Safety claims are limited by the lack of a hardware emergency stop, watchdog timeout, communication-loss fail-safe, collision guarantee, or formal hazard validation; publishing zero velocity or interrupting a process may not stop a robot reliably under network or software failure. - Scalability and resilience remain architectural claims rather than measured properties, and the use of a small, bounded, known indoor setup leaves performance in cluttered, dynamic, or communication-impaired environments untested. Bottom Line This is a useful senior-design systems report and a potentially practical starting point for educators or engineers assembling a small ROS2 multi-robot testbed, but it offers little publishable algorithmic novelty and insufficient quantitative evidence for a top-tier robotics research claim.

Digital transformation for sustainable business performance in small and medium enterprises

RK Letshaba, LT Mosupye-Semenya · sajbm.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results

Problem & Motivation The study addresses how SMEs can achieve durable financial viability while also improving environmental and social outcomes through digital transformation. The problem is particularly relevant to SMEs in South Africa and other emerging economies, where limited finance, skills, infrastructure, managerial capacity, and volatile markets constrain movement from isolated technology adoption to integrated transformation. Prior work has often examined digital adoption, readiness, efficiency, or competitiveness, while direct empirical links between digital capabilities and multidimensional sustainability outcomes remain less developed in resource-constrained SME settings. The paper also identifies a conceptual gap: digital transformation is frequently treated as a single construct rather than being separated into technological intensity and transformation-management capability. The stated application is SME strategy and policy, although the evidence comes from one municipality and is dominated by very small firms. Key Idea The central insight is an asymmetry between having digital resources and managing transformation: digital intensity may produce direct performance benefits in SMEs, whereas managerial transformation effort may not generate measurable outcomes unless it is supported by sufficient digital infrastructure and skills. The paper operationalises digital transformation through two separate constructs—DI and TMI—and tests each against the triple-bottom-line dimensions of financial, environmental, and social performance. This decomposition is the paper's main conceptual move; the underlying RBV framing and direct-effect hypotheses are established approaches. Methodology The authors conducted a quantitative, cross-sectional survey of SME owners and managers in the City of Matlosana Municipality, North West Province, South Africa. They distributed 300 questionnaires, received 232 responses, and retained 213 complete and consistent cases, reported as a 71% response rate. The sampling frame came from publicly available SME directories and municipal local economic development listings; the paper describes the selection as simple random sampling. Respondents rated items on a five-point Likert scale. DI and TMI were derived from a 20-item digital-transformation scale adapted from He et al. (2023), while financial performance, environmental performance, and social performance were measured using a 14-item scale adapted from Jabbour et al. (2020) and Huo et al. (2019). The authors used reflective measurement-model assessment with Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, average variance extracted, Fornell–Larcker comparisons, and HTMT, followed by SmartPLS partial least squares structural equation modelling. The structural model estimates six direct paths: DI to each of FP, EP, and SP, and TMI to each of FP, EP, and SP. Critical design choices include treating DI as a technological resource, treating TMI as an organisational capability, and using self-reported perceptual measures for both predictors and outcomes. The RBV rationale is stated, but the paper does not explain item wording, construct specification in sufficient detail, control-variable selection, bootstrap settings, power analysis, missing-data treatment, common-method-bias tests, or why direct effects are preferable to interaction or mediation models. The very high reliability values—α from 0.911 to 0.968 and composite reliability from 0.933 to 0.975—along with high loadings suggest possible item redundancy rather than unambiguously strong construct validity. Key Results The sample is heavily weighted toward micro-enterprises: 172 firms (80.7%) employed fewer than five people and 41 (19.2%) employed fewer than 20; no respondent reported a firm with 50 or more employees. Community, social, and personal services represented 17.3% of firms; agriculture and catering/accommodation/other trade each represented 15.4%; manufacturing represented only 5.1%, mining 2.8%, and electricity, gas, and water 1.4%. The measurement model reported AVE values of 0.736 for DI, 0.826 for EP, 0.736 for FP, 0.888 for SP, and 0.774 for TMI. The structural paths were DI → FP, β = 0.762, t = 7.533, p = 0.000; DI → EP, β = 0.777, t = 7.389, p = 0.000; DI → SP, β = 0.616, t = 6.258, p = 0.000; TMI → FP, β = −0.033, t = 0.282, p = 0.778; TMI → EP, β = −0.043, t = 0.335, p = 0.715; and TMI → SP, β = 0.162, t = 1.485, p = 0.138. Figure 2 reports R² values of 0.539 for FP, 0.549 for EP, and 0.575 for SP, although the text does not clearly identify whether these are endogenous-construct R² values or provide their inferential uncertainty. The paper's narrative correctly describes the three DI paths as statistically significant and the three TMI paths as nonsignificant, but Table 7 incorrectly labels the DI → EP and DI → SP paths as “supported but insignificant” despite reporting p = 0.000 and t-statistics well above 1.96. The results are associations among perceptual constructs, not measured changes in profitability, emissions, waste, employment, privacy, or community outcomes. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING; NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely distinctive contribution is the context-specific comparison of digital intensity and transformation-management intensity across financial, environmental, and social outcomes in South African SMEs, including the finding that DI is positively associated with all three outcomes while TMI has no significant direct association. The RBV framing and the use of PLS-SEM, Likert scales, and triple-bottom-line outcomes are standard, and the decomposition of digital transformation into technological and managerial dimensions builds on existing digital-transformation literature rather than introducing a new formal model. Rigor & Reproducibility The paper reports internal-consistency, convergent-validity, and two forms of discriminant-validity assessment. However, the validity evidence is not fully persuasive: HTMT for environmental and financial performance is 0.925, exceeding the stated conservative 0.90 threshold, and DI–TMI HTMT is 0.873 while several outcome constructs are highly correlated. The extreme alpha values and loadings above 0.94 for several social-performance items raise item-redundancy concerns that the paper mentions but does not investigate through item reduction or alternative measurement specifications. No ablations are relevant to this survey model, and the paper reports no multiple seeds, bootstrap confidence intervals, standard errors, effect-size measures such as f², predictive-relevance measures such as Q², collinearity diagnostics, robustness checks, subgroup analyses, or sensitivity to controls. The authors state that model-fit indices were acceptable but do not report the indices or thresholds. The analysis uses one respondent per firm and common self-report scales for predictors and outcomes, creating substantial common-method and same-source bias risks. The claimed probability sample is restricted to one municipality and may not represent South African SMEs nationally; the large concentration of micro-enterprises further limits generalisation. Data are not openly available but can be requested from the corresponding author; no code, analysis scripts, trained model, or software artifact is released. The paper is published as a 2026 open-access journal article, but the supplied document gives no independent replication or external validation. Deployability (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: The study's survey and SmartPLS analysis can run on commercially available hardware, although the paper delivers no operational digital-transformation tool for SMEs. Efficient: Computational cost is modest for 213 observations and five latent constructs, but the paper does not compare the cost or information value of PLS-SEM with covariance-based SEM, regression, or longitudinal designs. Effective: The evidence supports statistical associations between perceived digital intensity and perceived performance, not demonstrated improvements in audited financial results, environmental measurements, or social outcomes. Scalable: The study tests only 213 firms in one municipality and does not evaluate performance at 10×–100× the sample, across regions, sectors, firm sizes, or more digitally mature SMEs; scalability is therefore untested rather than established. The work stops at paper form and does not deliver a library, CLI, decision-support system, dataset, or trained model. Strengths - It addresses an underrepresented empirical setting: SMEs in a South African municipality, with a sample dominated by micro-enterprises that are often missing from large-firm digital-transformation studies. - It separates DI from TMI rather than treating digital transformation as a single undifferentiated predictor, enabling the informative finding that technological intensity and managerial effort do not have equivalent observed effects. - It evaluates three outcome dimensions—financial, environmental, and social—rather than reducing sustainability to profitability or a single ESG score. - It reports substantial positive DI path coefficients and R² values between 0.539 and 0.575, while also reporting null TMI effects instead of presenting all hypotheses as confirmed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly acknowledge the single-municipality scope, cross-sectional design, reliance on self-reported data, predominance of service-oriented firms, limited generalisability, and inability to support causal inference. They recommend longitudinal or mixed-methods research, broader regional and sectoral samples, and investigation of moderators and mediators such as innovation capability, leadership style, government support, digital literacy, and culture. They also discuss contextual barriers including unreliable connectivity, inadequate infrastructure, low digital awareness, financial constraints, skills shortages, high data costs, and resistance to organisational change. These limitations are directly stated, although their implications for measurement bias and the interpretation of large path coefficients are not fully developed. Analyst-Identified Gaps The paper does not test whether TMI moderates, mediates, or conditions the effect of DI, despite its RBV argument that managerial capabilities may matter primarily when paired with digital resources; a DI × TMI interaction or staged capability model would be more diagnostic than six independent direct paths. It omits firm age, sector, size, education, ownership, formalisation, infrastructure access, prior performance, and other plausible confounders, so the large DI coefficients may reflect underlying firm capability or success rather than a digital-transformation effect. The operationalisation of DI appears to mix broad technology adoption with transformation capability, while the paper does not provide the actual survey items or explain how technologies such as AI, cloud computing, analytics, and IoT were relevant to predominantly micro and service-sector firms. Financial, environmental, and social performance are perceptual and measured from the same respondents as DI and TMI; no audited accounts, utility or emissions data, employee measures, customer data, or external ratings validate the outcomes. The interpretation of statistically significant DI paths as “influences” and as evidence of sustainability benefits exceeds what the design can establish. The contradictory significance labels in Table 7 and the unreported model-fit statistics reduce confidence in the analysis and reporting. Finally, the high EP–FP association and HTMT value of 0.925 suggest that the outcome constructs may not be as empirically distinct as claimed. Bottom Line The paper is worth reading for its South African micro-enterprise context and its useful null result for transformation-management intensity, but its single-source cross-sectional design and reporting inconsistencies make it weak evidence for the causal claim that digital transformation improves SME sustainability.

Problem & Motivation: The work addresses the governance of AI-enabled transformation in construction and the built environment, including design, project execution, building operation, infrastructure management, and integration with smart-city systems. Construction firms, infrastructure owners, municipalities, governments, technology providers, workers, and citizens face fragmented data and information systems, weak interoperability, project delays and cost overruns, safety risks, skills shortages, cybersecurity exposure, regulatory uncertainty, and uneven distribution of benefits. The paper identifies a gap between technology-centric research on AI, BIM, IoT, robotics, and digital twins and policy research on smart cities and sustainable development: prior work often studies operational applications or isolated governance dimensions without integrating institutional coordination, industrial policy, data governance, workforce transformation, adaptive regulation, and economic, environmental, and social objectives. It also highlights limited attention to developing and emerging economies, although it does not supply new evidence about them. Key Idea: The central insight is that AI capability does not automatically produce sustainable construction outcomes; value emerges when technical capabilities interact with innovation capacity, governance quality, human capital, data institutions, and mission-oriented policy. The proposed framework organizes this interaction into five mutually reinforcing pillars and models a feedback loop in which implementation outcomes generate technical, organizational, regulatory, and societal learning that informs subsequent policy and innovation. This is a systems-level synthesis of National Innovation Systems, Triple/Quadruple/Quintuple Helix, Mission-Oriented Innovation Policy, Responsible Research and Innovation, Adaptive Governance, Data Governance, and socio-technical transitions theory, rather than a new computational mechanism. Methodology: The paper is a conceptual research article/chapter based on a narrative synthesis of literature spanning AI, smart construction, BIM, digital twins, smart cities, sustainability, and STI policy; it does not report a systematic-review protocol, formal model estimation, fieldwork, experiments, or deployment evaluation. The conceptual pipeline is: characterize the AI-enabled construction ecosystem and lifecycle applications; establish STI-policy and socio-technical foundations; define five framework pillars; map policy instruments to those pillars; assign responsibilities across international, national, regional, municipal, and organizational levels; propose a staged roadmap; and derive eight testable propositions. The framework recommends R&D support, university–industry collaboration, innovation-oriented procurement, regulatory sandboxes, data standards, workforce programs, SME finance, ethical-AI controls, and monitoring. Critical design decisions are the five-pillar architecture, the use of adaptive feedback rather than static regulation, and the mission-oriented triple-value lens covering economic, environmental, and social outcomes. These choices are conceptually motivated through cited theory, but their relative necessity, interactions, and effectiveness are not empirically or formally justified. No explicit optimization objective, statistical model, algorithm, or formal causal identification strategy is provided. Key Results: The paper reports no experiments, measurements, benchmark results, case-study outcomes, survey estimates, or comparative policy analysis. Consequently, it provides no accuracy, F1, cost reduction, energy reduction, productivity, safety, adoption, speed, or scalability numbers for the framework or for the AI applications it discusses. It presents two qualitative tables: one mapping nine policy-instrument classes to functions, and another listing illustrative indicators across innovation, digital readiness, economic, environmental, social, governance, and resilience dimensions. It also presents a conceptual architecture and eight propositions asserting that scientific and technological capability, institutional coordination, effective and adaptive governance, mission orientation, human capital, data quality/interoperability, and joint economic-environmental-social evaluation improve smart-construction outcomes. These are claims for future empirical testing, not measured findings. The paper does not compare its framework with existing AI-governance, smart-city, construction-adoption, or STI-policy frameworks, and therefore does not establish superiority or incremental explanatory power. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL-FREE SYNTHESIS are the most defensible classifications, with a secondary POLICY FRAMEWORK contribution; the paper’s genuinely distinctive element is the explicit integration of construction lifecycle technologies, STI capabilities, multi-level governance, adaptive feedback, and sustainability missions, while most underlying theories, technologies, policy instruments, and governance principles are established ideas recombined for the AI-driven smart-construction setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper cites 28 references and presents a coherent conceptual argument, but it does not state a search strategy, inclusion criteria, coding procedure, evidence-quality assessment, or systematic synthesis method, so the completeness and selection bias of the literature review cannot be assessed. No ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, formal validation, stakeholder validation, or empirical proposition tests are present. No code, dataset, model weights, implementation toolkit, operational measurement instrument, or repository URL is provided. The work does not evaluate the framework on an author-created dataset, but it also lacks standard comparative baselines and does not test whether its proposed pillars predict adoption or sustainability outcomes. Several cited sources are recent reviews or conceptual works, and the manuscript is explicitly a Research Square preprint posted August 24, 2026; it should therefore be treated as preliminary and not as peer-reviewed evidence. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL/CONCEPTUAL—the paper proposes a policy framework and roadmap without primary experiments, proofs, or a deployed system. Sound: The framework’s normative assumptions and causal propositions are stated in qualitative terms, but there is no formal derivation, proof, operational definition of constructs, or empirical test establishing that the proposed interactions hold. General: The claims are intended to span countries, cities, firms, and lifecycle stages, but applicability is not demonstrated across institutional contexts, especially developing and emerging economies, SMEs, legacy infrastructure, or conflicting regulatory regimes. Tight: Not applicable as a mathematical bound; the paper does not quantify effect sizes, identify necessary or sufficient conditions, or establish that its framework is more complete or predictive than competing governance models. Implementable: The roadmap suggests implementable instruments such as procurement criteria, sandboxes, interoperability standards, skills programs, and monitoring indicators, but the paper supplies no implementation protocol, governance templates, budget model, prioritization rule, or tested decision procedure. It stops at paper form and does not deliver a software artifact, dataset, trained model, or reusable formal proof technique. Strengths: - It identifies a consequential failure mode in technology-policy discussions: treating AI deployment as sufficient without addressing data institutions, organizational capacity, regulation, skills, procurement, and distributional effects. - It creates a usable organizing structure by linking five policy pillars to concrete instruments and to governance levels from international institutions through individual organizations. - It covers the full construction lifecycle and explicitly connects building-level systems to energy, transport, water, emergency, and other urban infrastructures. - It acknowledges important second-order risks—including AI’s own energy footprint, privacy, bias, cyber-physical attack surfaces, liability ambiguity, workforce disruption, SME barriers, and policy lag—instead of presenting AI adoption as unconditionally beneficial. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge interoperability problems, high upfront costs, incomplete and context-dependent data, model degradation across materials, climates, and organizations, organizational resistance, policy lag, overly rigid regulation, workforce transition needs, and the difficulty of integrating AI with legacy building stock. They also state that the framework’s eight propositions require quantitative indices and cross-country, cross-city, organizational, longitudinal, and systems-dynamics research. The paper confronts these limitations directly and identifies future empirical testing as necessary, although it does not quantify the scope or severity of any limitation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The literature synthesis is not reproducible: there is no database search, screening process, evidence taxonomy, or explanation of why particular theories and references were included. - The framework does not define measurable constructs for AI readiness, governance quality, STI capacity, interoperability, sustainability, public value, or institutional coordination, despite proposing indicators in broad categories. - The eight propositions are directional and largely intuitive; they do not specify mechanisms, boundary conditions, competing explanations, expected effect sizes, or how propositions could be falsified. - The paper does not compare the framework with established AI-risk-management, responsible-innovation, smart-city governance, technology-adoption, innovation-system, or construction-management frameworks, making incremental novelty difficult to establish. - The roadmap gives no prioritization method for conflicts among objectives, such as energy efficiency versus occupant comfort, automation versus employment, open data versus privacy, or regulatory flexibility versus safety. - Claims about sustainable value, improved safety, lower costs, reduced emissions, and resilience remain cited possibilities rather than evidence generated or synthesized quantitatively by this paper. - The treatment of developing economies and SMEs is acknowledged but not grounded in cases, institutional comparisons, financing constraints, or differentiated policy designs. - The multi-level governance architecture does not specify accountability when international standards, national regulation, municipal procurement, organizational controls, and vendor responsibilities conflict. Bottom Line: This is a useful policy-conceptual synthesis and agenda-setting framework for readers entering AI governance in construction, but its broad recombination of established ideas and complete absence of empirical validation make it substantially weaker than a research contribution that operationalizes and tests the proposed propositions.

A Policy-Aligned Agentic RAG Framework for Risk-Aware Decision Support in Enterprise Customer Relationship Management

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PAL-CRM-RAG, a ten-layer policy-aligned Agentic RAG prototype that combines CRM ticket understanding, risk classification, hybrid retrieval, policy validation, self-verification, human escalation, and audit logging. - Why it's important: CRM recommendations can affect refunds, privacy, contractual service commitments, legal exposure, and customer rights, so factual retrieval alone does not ensure safe or authorised decisions. - How it does it: It embeds a rule-based policy validator and risk-triggered escalation controller inside a BM25+dense retrieval, reciprocal-rank-fusion, cross-encoder-reranking, and response-verification loop. - The good: On the paper's closed synthetic evaluation, explicit policy validation reduced the encoded unsafe-response rate from 6% for the strongest self-checking RAG baseline to 0% and produced 100% policy-compliance and escalation-F1 scores. - The missing: The central safety results are not validated with real LLM generations, authentic enterprise policies, human reviewers, adversarial inputs, or external CRM data; the risk labels and policy violations are largely engineered from the same controlled setup. - Read it or not: Read it as an applied design-science blueprint for governed CRM RAG, but skip it as evidence of production-grade safety or generalisable Agentic RAG performance until the evaluation is substantially strengthened.

Problem & Motivation: Enterprise CRM systems increasingly support decisions about refunds, service-level commitments, complaints, privacy requests, account access, fraud, and escalation. Conventional RAG can retrieve relevant text and generate fluent answers but does not by itself determine whether evidence is policy-authorised, whether a case is high risk, whether a recommendation contains an unauthorised commitment, or whether a human must approve the outcome. The paper targets the gap between domain-general RAG/Agentic RAG and a CRM decision-support workflow with explicit governance, risk sensitivity, human accountability, and auditability. The intended users are CRM service agents, managers, and enterprise governance teams, although the paper does not evaluate actual users or operational workflows. Key Idea: The core insight is architectural rather than algorithmic: policy validation and risk-aware escalation should be inside the Agentic RAG control loop, not added as an external post-processing checklist. The system first classifies ticket risk, retrieves and reranks policy evidence, checks policy conditions, generates a grounded recommendation, verifies it, and either releases, revises, or escalates it while logging the decision path. This is a sensible decomposition for governed decision support, but most individual components—BM25, dense retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder reranking, rule-based validation, self-checking, escalation, and audit logging—are established techniques; the paper's main distinctiveness is their CRM-specific integration. Methodology: The artifact is a Python prototype organized into ten sequential layers. L1 parses a CRM ticket into a structured query. L2 assigns Low, Medium, or High risk and identifies escalation triggers using a weighted scoring formula over priority, issue category, inverse satisfaction, SLA delay, privacy/refund/complaint keyword indicators, and enterprise-email status. The weights are 0.20, 0.25, 0.10, 0.15, 0.10, 0.10, 0.07, and 0.03 respectively, with thresholds 0.318 and 0.443 calibrated to produce an approximately 45:40:15 class distribution. L3 retrieves the top 20 chunks independently with BM25 and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 dense embeddings. L4 fuses the lists with reciprocal rank fusion using k=60, retains 15 candidates, and reranks them with cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 before passing the top five chunks onward. L5 checks evidence and generated content against constructed policy rules. L6 chooses among generation, query rewriting, additional retrieval, revision, and escalation. L7 produces a structured evidence-citing recommendation; L8 self-verifies faithfulness and policy consistency; L9 routes high-risk or policy-failing cases to a human; and L10 records the query, evidence, risk, compliance result, verification outcome, and final action. The evaluation uses 20,000 synthetic Kaggle CRM tickets, a 30-document constructed policy corpus divided into 60 chunks, a 70/15/15 train-validation-test split, and a stratified 300-ticket evaluation sample. Baselines are a non-RAG LLM, BM25-RAG, vector-RAG, hybrid-RAG, hybrid-RAG with reranking, and self-check RAG. The main design decisions—hybrid retrieval, explicit policy validation, and risk-based escalation—are motivated plausibly, but the risk labels, policy corpus, violation patterns, and template-based generation are all author-engineered, which substantially limits causal and external validity. Key Results: Risk classification on the stated 3,000-ticket test set is reported at 95.1% accuracy and 94.4% macro-F1, with the displayed confusion matrix giving 464 of 487 high-risk cases correctly identified and 23 missed or misclassified. On the 300-ticket evaluation sample, PAL-CRM-RAG reports Recall@5=0.112, Precision@5=0.643, MRR=0.790, NDCG@5=0.656, faithfulness=0.707, context relevance=0.643, policy compliance=1.000, unsafe-response rate=0.000, escalation F1=1.000, and mean latency=1,364 ms on CPU. Retrieval and generation are essentially unchanged from the strongest retrieval baselines: Hybrid+Reranker and Self-check RAG also have Precision@5=0.643, faithfulness=0.706, and context relevance=0.643, while the proposed system has lower MRR than vector-RAG (0.790 versus 0.844) and hybrid-RAG without reranking (0.823). Compliance improves from 0.900 for Hybrid+Reranker and 0.940 for Self-check RAG to 1.000, while escalation F1 rises from 0.040 for Self-check RAG and 0.000 for B0–B4 to 1.000. The ablations attribute policy compliance primarily to the validator, escalation to the risk classifier and escalation layer, and faithfulness to self-verification: removing the validator yields compliance 0.000, removing risk classification or escalation yields escalation F1=0.000, and removing self-verification lowers faithfulness from 0.706 to 0.635. The paper's quantitative comparisons are not all internally consistent: some prose reports PAL-CRM-RAG latency as 1,364 ms while figures show approximately 1,338 ms, and the reported risk-distribution counts and approximate confusion-matrix values should be reconciled. The reported perfect compliance and escalation are expected in a closed set where the system enforces the same engineered rules used to define the evaluation. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, NEW FORMULATION, NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING, and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is the CRM-specific governance formulation and integration of risk classification, policy validation, escalation, and audit logging into an Agentic RAG workflow; the retrieval, verification, and rule-based components are standard combinations, and the empirical findings primarily demonstrate that explicitly encoded controls enforce explicitly encoded synthetic rules. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper includes component-removal ablations, multiple baselines, stratified sampling, bootstrap confidence intervals in principle, and paired-comparison methodology using McNemar-style logic and paired bootstrap intervals. However, the paper does not report the actual confidence intervals, p-values, bootstrap count, per-class precision/recall, multiple random seeds, or detailed implementation parameters sufficient to independently reproduce every result. The risk classifier is not clearly a learned model evaluated against independent human labels; its labels are generated by a transparent weighted formula and the confusion matrix is described as approximate and based on 7% simulated noise. The generator uses templates with controlled violation injection rather than a real LLM, and policy compliance is assessed by author-defined rule-based regular expressions. This creates circularity: the validator is evaluated against the same closed policy and violation vocabulary it was designed to enforce. Retrieval relevance is based on an issue-category-to-policy-group mapping rather than ticket-level expert judgments, and only 300 of the 3,000 test tickets are used for most system comparisons. No repository URL, code release, model-weight release, or permanent dataset/policy-corpus release is provided; processed splits and outputs are said to be available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The baselines are useful component controls but omit stronger contemporary agentic, constraint-based, judge-based, or production CRM systems. Deployability (4-property check): EMPIRICAL, with a Python prototype rather than a demonstrated deployed system. Practical: The listed components can run on commercially available CPU or GPU hardware, but integration with CRM access control, tenant isolation, permissions, identity, data minimization, and production LLM APIs is not implemented or tested. Efficient: The pipeline takes 1,364 ms mean latency on CPU versus 297 ms for hybrid retrieval and 45.1 ms for the non-RAG baseline; the claimed 10–50x GPU improvement and sub-100 ms latency are projections, not measurements. Effective: Evidence supports enforcement of four synthetic violation types and routing of engineered high-risk labels, but it does not establish improved customer outcomes, recommendation correctness, human decision quality, or safety under authentic language and policy ambiguity. Scalable: The experiment uses only 20,000 short tickets, 30 policy documents, and 60 chunks; there is no 10x–100x corpus, traffic, concurrency, model-size, policy-version, or long-context stress test. The work delivers a Python prototype architecture and synthetic evaluation materials in paper form, but no publicly downloadable software artifact or deployed CRM integration. Strengths: - It identifies an important distinction between factual grounding and authorised, risk-appropriate decision support, which is especially relevant for refunds, privacy, fraud, and contractual service commitments. - The architecture makes governance controls operational: policy validation, escalation reasons, evidence citation, and audit logging are represented as pipeline outputs rather than only discussed as principles. - The ablation structure clearly shows functional dependency in the prototype: policy validation controls compliance, risk classification enables routing, and self-verification affects the chosen faithfulness metric. - The paper explicitly limits its strongest claims by acknowledging synthetic data, constructed policies, template generation, regex validation, CPU-only latency, and the need for human expert evaluation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state five main limitations: the tickets are synthetic and lack authentic enterprise context; the policy corpus is constructed and small; generation uses templates with controlled violation injection rather than a live LLM; latency is measured on a CPU prototype; and policy violations are detected with regular expressions rather than semantic methods. They also state that production deployment would require real enterprise data, larger and heterogeneous policy repositories, live LLM integration, human expert evaluation, platform access controls, customer-data permissions, enterprise security testing, and privacy-preserving or federated configurations. These limitations are directly acknowledged, although the conclusion still describes the architecture as a foundation for production-oriented governance despite the absence of deployment evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The paper does not test real LLM behavior, prompt injection, indirect document attacks, sensitive-data exfiltration, policy conflicts, outdated or contradictory policies, missing customer records, adversarial paraphrases, multilingual tickets, distribution shift, or human disagreement about risk and compliance. It does not compare against a strong constrained-decoding, classifier-plus-RAG, modern agent framework, or vendor CRM assistant baseline. The risk-label evaluation is potentially circular because the target classes arise from the same weighted formula and simulated noise used by the system, and the reported high-risk counts and approximate confusion matrix require clarification. Treating keyword matches and non-personal email domains as risk signals is an unvalidated proxy for customer harm and privacy risk. The binary compliance metric hides severity, partial compliance, false escalations, and the cost of withholding a valid answer; escalation F1 also treats the engineered High class as ground truth without evaluating human workload or decision quality. Retrieval evaluation maps broad issue categories to policy groups, which may reward category matching rather than correct case-specific policy interpretation. Audit logging is asserted but not evaluated for completeness, tamper resistance, access control, retention, or privacy leakage. Finally, the claim that GPU deployment will reduce latency by 10–50x is unsupported by measurements, and the paper does not quantify token cost, memory use, throughput, concurrency, or the operational cost of escalating 16.2% of tickets. Bottom Line: The paper offers a useful governance-oriented CRM RAG architecture and a clear prototype decomposition, but its perfect safety and escalation numbers are artifacts of a synthetic, rule-matched evaluation, so practitioners should treat it as a design checklist rather than evidence that PAL-CRM-RAG outperforms stronger real-world alternatives.

Problem & Motivation: AI coding systems rely on knowledge that is dynamic, distributed, and structurally complex: source code, documentation, configurations, diagrams, version histories, dependencies, and workflow state. Parametric LLM knowledge becomes stale as languages and frameworks evolve, while enterprise repositories can contain millions of lines of code across thousands of files, exceeding practical context limits. Existing RAG surveys generally address general-purpose knowledge-intensive NLP, and individual software-engineering studies often focus on one assistant, task, or retrieval mechanism. The paper addresses the resulting synthesis gap by examining how retrieval architectures handle software-specific requirements, including factual reliability, cross-file and cross-repository reasoning, multimodal integration, latency, privacy, developer-tool integration, and knowledge evolution. Key Idea: The central insight is that retrieval architectures form an evolutionary capability–complexity trade-off: static prompting is simple and fast but context-limited; traditional RAG adds external, query-driven access; Graph RAG represents dependencies and relationships explicitly; and Agentic RAG adds planning, persistent memory, tool use, and autonomous orchestration. The paper argues that no single paradigm addresses all software-engineering requirements and that future systems should combine vector retrieval, graph traversal, and agent-based strategy selection. This is a useful organizing hypothesis, but the paper does not establish it through controlled comparison. Methodology: The authors describe a Kitchenham-inspired systematic literature review covering IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and arXiv for 2020–2025, supplemented by citation tracking and targeted Google/Google Scholar searches. Search terms covered RAG, knowledge retrieval, code generation, Graph RAG, Agentic RAG, LLMs, and AI coding assistants. Approximately 100 candidates were identified, 50 were retained for full-text review, and 30 were selected for the final synthesis based on relevance, methodological rigor, and system-design contribution. The review extracts and organizes literature into five challenge categories—information veracity and reliability; contextual understanding and integration; scale and performance; development-workflow integration; and knowledge representation—and four architecture categories. The architecture comparison uses qualitative labels for access method, setup complexity, hallucination risk, and autonomy. Critical design decisions include the four-paradigm taxonomy, the five-dimensional challenge framework, and the recommendation to combine vector, graph, and agentic mechanisms. The paper does not state a detailed search protocol, per-database result counts, independent-reviewer procedure, inter-rater agreement, formal study-quality rubric, extraction form, or method for resolving conflicting evidence, so the systematic-review methodology is only partially specified. Key Results: The review reports 100 initial sources, 50 full-text candidates, and 30 final sources, but it presents no aggregate effect sizes, benchmark scores, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or controlled architecture comparisons. Its main result is qualitative: context-window prompting is characterized as low-complexity, medium-hallucination-risk, and low-autonomy; traditional RAG as medium-complexity, medium-risk, and low-autonomy; Graph RAG as high-complexity, low-to-medium-risk, and medium-autonomy; and Agentic RAG as high-complexity, low-risk, and high-autonomy. The cited literature is said to show improvements from RAG over prompting for code completion and documentation generation, and multi-agent systems are said to support more complex workflows, but the paper does not report the underlying numerical results or establish that the cited baselines are current, comparable, or strong. The evidence scale is literature synthesis rather than a standard, stress-scale, or production evaluation. Claims about reduced hallucination risk, improved architectural reasoning, and productivity therefore remain descriptive and citation-dependent rather than measured by this paper. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely new element is the paper’s software-development-specific synthesis combining four retrieval paradigms with five interconnected challenge dimensions and a hybrid-agentic research agenda; the individual architectures, RAG mechanisms, graph representations, and multi-agent concepts are established ideas, and the paper does not introduce a new algorithm, dataset, benchmark, or experimentally demonstrated finding. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper states explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria and identifies its databases, time window, search terms, and final source count. However, it does not provide a reproducible search string for each database, complete screening records, a PRISMA-style flow, study-level inclusion table, quality scores, coding schema, reviewer count, agreement statistics, or a quantitative synthesis. There are no ablations, multiple seeds, error bars, significance tests, or primary experiments because the paper is a survey. No code, review dataset, extraction spreadsheet, or repository is mentioned. The source base mixes peer-reviewed papers, preprints, documentation, textbooks, vendor/model reports, and non-peer-reviewed web material; the review does not clearly weight these evidence types differently. Some architecture-level labels, particularly hallucination risk and autonomy, are asserted without operational definitions or cross-study measurement. The survey also appears to rely on several broad or weakly matched citations for enterprise-scale claims, making the comparative table difficult to audit. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL, specifically a literature-based empirical synthesis rather than a primary experimental or deployed systems paper. - Practical: The paper’s recommendations concern architectures that can in principle run on commercially available hardware, but it provides no implementation, hardware configuration, latency measurement, or deployment demonstration. - Efficient: It identifies the expected complexity and maintenance burden of Graph RAG and Agentic RAG relative to prompting and traditional RAG, but supplies no memory, compute, token, indexing, graph-construction, or operating-cost measurements. - Effective: The cited literature suggests benefits for code completion, documentation, dependency reasoning, and workflow automation, but this paper does not directly demonstrate that any architecture solves software-engineering tasks better under a common evaluation protocol. - Scalable: The paper identifies enterprise-scale codebases and graph-maintenance overhead as open problems, but it tests no system at 10×–100× scale and provides no evidence supporting scalability beyond cited claims. The work delivers a reusable conceptual taxonomy and research agenda, not a software artifact, library, CLI, dataset, trained model, or benchmark. It stops at paper form. Strengths: - The taxonomy is more relevant to software engineering than a generic RAG taxonomy because it foregrounds code dependencies, repository evolution, multimodal artifacts, developer workflows, and architectural reasoning. - The five challenge categories provide a coherent lens for connecting retrieval quality to practical constraints such as latency, privacy, maintainability, explainability, and integration with version control and testing systems. - The paper correctly distinguishes retrieval capability from autonomy: adding external context does not by itself provide persistent goals, planning, tool execution, or long-horizon workflow support. - The proposed hybrid direction identifies concrete coordination problems—retrieval-strategy selection, cross-engine result fusion, conflict resolution, confidence estimation, temporal updates, and resource optimization—instead of merely advocating “more agentic” systems. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that each architecture has important weaknesses: prompting is limited by context size, traditional RAG is reactive and can miss broader relationships, Graph RAG is expensive to construct and maintain, and Agentic RAG faces coordination, communication, and scalability problems. It also recognizes the unresolved requirements of temporal knowledge maintenance, multimodal integration, explainability, privacy, organizational adaptation, and human control. These are presented as open research challenges. The paper does not explicitly acknowledge limitations in its own review protocol, source quality, taxonomy subjectivity, or absence of quantitative synthesis. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The review’s “systematic” status is under-supported: it omits detailed screening methodology, study-quality assessment, reviewer agreement, and a reproducible accounting of the 70 sources removed after the initial search. - The four architectural categories are not mutually exclusive in practice, yet the paper does not define composition rules or analyze systems that combine vector, graph, reranking, code analysis, memory, and agents under existing hybrid designs. - The comparison table assigns hallucination risk and autonomy levels without operational definitions, measured values, uncertainty, or evidence that these properties are comparable across studies. - The survey does not separate task types sufficiently. Code completion, repository question answering, bug fixing, documentation generation, architectural impact analysis, testing, and deployment have different retrieval requirements and should not be treated as one capability continuum. - The literature base is small for a claimed comprehensive survey and includes heterogeneous evidence, including preprints, documentation, textbooks, a web article, and vendor/model reports. The paper does not analyze publication bias, recency bias, or conflicting findings. - The proposed hybrid-agentic architecture remains speculative: it provides no concrete protocol, objective function, routing algorithm, benchmark, cost model, or safety mechanism for validating whether hybrid orchestration improves outcomes rather than merely increasing system complexity. - Claims about productivity, reduced hallucination, enterprise-scale performance, and autonomous deployment are not supported by measurements in this paper and are sometimes presented more broadly than the cited evidence appears to warrant. Bottom Line: This is a useful but low-evidence conceptual survey for orienting newcomers and framing research questions, not a sufficiently rigorous basis for choosing an AI software-development retrieval architecture or for claiming that hybrid agentic systems outperform simpler alternatives.
